The Kālottara.
Hariḥ Om.
Thus, having uttered the mantra of Maheśa with these three [syllables], the single form of the complete Maheśvara is proclaimed. (1)
First and foremost, one should grasp the seed-syllable of Ananteśa, which is endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*, and possesses the brilliant luster of a hibiscus flower. (2)
Four-armed and three-eyed, bearing an axe and a trident;
[the mantra] consisting of the third letter of the eighth [vowel class] joined with the sixth [consonant]. (3)
That which is joined with the Bindu and Nāda is here called the subtle seed-syllable (sūkṣmabīja).
And the third [form] of the Subtle One has four arms and three eyes.
The first [syllable] of the eighth [group] and the third of the first [group],
conjoined with the Bindu and the Nāda, is the seed-syllable (bīja) of Śivottama.
One should take the eleventh [letter] of the first [vowel], which has three eyes and four arms, possesses a luster like the kunda flower, and is endowed with the bindu and nāda.
One should again take up the eleventh [letter], which resembles a dark blue cloud, has three eyes and four arms, and is endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*. (7)
The seed-syllable of Ekarudra is [as follows]:
one should meditate upon the Trimūrti, resembling saffron in hue, with three eyes and four arms.
The eighth [letter] is to be taken first; the second of the seventh [group], joined with the fourth vowel and endowed with the bindu and nāda. (9)
The seed-syllable of Śrīkaṇṭha is like the Japā flower;
it should be known as three-eyed and four-armed, bearing a trident and an axe.

That which is the third [syllable] of Indra, endowed with the *bindu* and the *nāda*, is declared to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Śikhaṇḍin, possessing a luster like that of crushed collyrium. (11ab) (10)
They have four arms and three eyes, and they carry tridents and axes;
all of them are indeed mounted upon bulls and wear crowns of matted hair.
All of them possess one face and are adorned with all ornaments;
O child, all these Saṃhitās of Śiva are seated upon lotus postures.
In which egg, within the seven worlds beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Śiva, is he eternally proclaimed as the sovereign Lord Śrīkaṇṭha? (14)
O Six-faced One, there is the eternal trident of the seven external eggs:
the Sūkṣmāṇḍa, the Śivottamāṇḍa, and the Ekanetra-rudrāṇḍaka. || 15 ||
Ananteśa is the Trimūrtyaṇḍa; Śikhaṇḍī shall be the seventh.
Taking the fifth letter of the first [group], it is conjoined with Bindu and Nāda. (16)
The seed-syllable of Umā is declared to have a luster like that of lapis lazuli;
having first taken the three components (the vowels), it is endowed with the Bindu and the Nāda. (17)
Resembling a dark blue cloud, three-eyed, and holding an axe;
it is the fifth [letter] of the five groups, conjoined with the Bindu and the Nāda. (18)
It should have three eyes and two arms, resembling the color of crushed collyrium;
it consists of the fifth letter of the sixth group, joined with the Bindu and the Nāda. (19)
Resembling a lotus leaf, with two eyes and two arms;
it is the fourth of the seventh [group] and the seventh of the first.
The form of the Bull is pervaded by the *bindu* and the *nāda*;
it resembles the stride of Viṣṇu, has three eyes, and holds a trident.
The third [letter] of the second group, adorned with a crest of dots (bindus),
resembling dark collyrium— this is the true form of Gaṇeśa.
He has the face of an elephant, the trunk of an elephant, and the ears of an elephant; he is three-eyed, pot-bellied, and youthful, seated upon a white lotus.
The god Gaṇeśa, the leader of obstacles, who has a mouse as his vehicle;
Bhṛṅgin; and the great-souled Ruṭi—these are the fourth [deities] of the sixth [chapter].
It is joined together by sinews and bones, possesses two eyes, and resembles the bulbous root of a conch shell;
it is adorned with the third and sixth [letters] of the eighth [varga]. (25)
The god has four arms and two eyes, with the luster of a pomegranate flower; he is mounted upon a peacock and holds a spear and a javelin.
He is joined with a bell and a vajra, holds a cock as his banner, displays the gesture of fearlessness and wears the sacred thread, and has the appearance of a ten-year-old child. (27)
Only a brief summary has been told; it shall be proclaimed again in detail.
O Six-faced One, listen as I declare the seed-syllable (bīja) of the Eight-formed Lord.
The fourth [letter] of the sixth group, joined with the bindu and nāda,
is white as a conch or cow’s milk, possessing three eyes and four arms. (29)
O child, one should place [the deity] adorned with a crown of matted hair and decorated with all ornaments, seated upon a white lotus, in the eastern direction.
The fifth [syllable] of the group of seven is endowed with the bindu and nāda;
it has four arms and three eyes, and its radiance is like the rising sun. (31)
One should visualize him endowed with all ornaments in the south-eastern direction;
and Īśāna, the Lord, in the fourth quarter, that very [quarter] of the vowels.
Overwhelmed by Bindu and Nāda, possessing the luster of frost and silver,
four-armed and three-eyed, he holds a trident and an axe.
First, [one should meditate on] the sixth group, adorned with a dot on its crest, four-armed and three-eyed, situated in the southern part. (34)
One should [worship] the great-souled Paśupati, who bears a trident and an axe, Rudra, located in the southwestern direction, having two eyes and four arms. (35)
The second [syllable] of the seventh [group], however, with the fifth of the first [group] mounted upon it as a crest-jewel, wearing a crown of matted locks. (36)
Taking the fifth [vowel] from the first [group], endowed with the Bindu and Nāda, [one should meditate on the deity] who has four arms, three eyes, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair. (37)
In the western direction (vāruṇī), the wise one should visualize Śūla holding an axe;
this is the fourth [consonant] of the sixth group (ṣa) joined with the fourth vowel (ū). (38)
One should visualize [the deity] mounted upon the peak of Mount Bīdu in the northwestern direction,
four-armed and three-eyed, bearing a trident and an axe.
The fifth [syllable] of the sixth group, conjoined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, should be visualized by Guha as four-armed and three-eyed in the southern direction. (p. 5) 40.
Wearing crowns of matted hair and holding tridents and axes,
they are all seated upon lotus-thrones and endowed with all powers.
One should sequentially visualize [the deities] beginning with Vāmā and ending with Sarvabhūta:
Mahādeva, Hara, Rudra, Śaṅkara, and Nīlalohita.
Īśāna, Vijaya, Bhīma, Devadeva, and Bhavodbhava—these eleven Rudras are known as the subordinates of Kapālīśa. (43)
All [the deities] are white as cow’s milk and wear serpents as sacred threads;
their respective initial syllables are indeed joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*. (44)
Four-armed and three-eyed, holding a trident and an axe, wearing a crown of matted hair, and adorned with all ornaments. || 45 ||
All of these are indeed seated upon lotuses and are all endowed with power;
they are Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, as well as Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī.
O observer of noble vows, Śruti, Smṛti, Dayā, Kṣānti, Medhā, and Prajñā are the eleven Śaktis; and indeed, the Rudras are eleven.
Vai-kartana, Vivasvat, Mārtāṇḍa, Bhāskara, Ravi, Lokaprakāśaka, Lokasākṣin, and Trivikrama. || 48 ||
Āditya, as well as Sūrya, Aṃśumālī, and Divākara—these indeed are the twelve Ādityas; one should worship them outside the pedestal (pīṭha). || 49 ||
Each of them should be known as having two arms, one face, or two faces, and as being endowed with their own initial syllable together with the *bindu* and *nāda*. (50)
Adorned with all ornaments, all are situated within the mandala;
all are mounted upon their Śaktis, holding lotuses in their hands, and are red in color. (51)
Uṣā, Prabhā, Sandhyā, Prajñā, Medhā, Mālinī, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Dhṛti, Kānti, Mati, and Dyuti. || 52 ||
These twelve powers are the twelve solar powers:
ether, touch, fire, taste, and earth. (53)
One should worship Candra, Sūrya, that Ātman, and the eight Vasus,
using their own initial syllables accompanied by the Bindu and Nāda.
All of them should be known as having two arms, one face, and two eyes;
they are adorned with all ornaments and all are seated upon lotus postures. || 55 ||
All of them resembled molten gold and were endowed with power:
Tejovāpī, Dhāriṇī, Somī, and Sūryavatī.
The illustrious ones are proclaimed to be eight: Gāganī and Vāyavī, as well as the eight Vasu-śaktis; one should arrange them in their proper order.
One should worship Gabhasti, Sparśana, Vāyu, Anila, Māruta, Prāṇa, Prāṇeśa, Jīveśa, Marut, and Aśva. (58)
Each of them is endowed with their own name-syllable, accompanied by the *bindu* and *nāda*;
they all have two arms, two eyes, and one face. (59)
All were as radiant as emeralds and adorned with every kind of ornament;
they were charming, facing him, beautiful in form, and illustrious.
Candrā, Candramukhī, Nirmalā, and Pūrṇacandrikā—all these are seed-syllables of Śakti; their initial letter shall be the first syllable of their respective names.
The long [vowel] of the powers (śakti) is said to be that which is pervaded by the Bindu, Nāda, and Śikhā.
Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, and Kinnaras [are there]. (62) p. 7)
The Vidyādharas, Yātudhānas, Gāruḍas, and Mahormikas; Jaya, Asparśarāsa, and the thirteen Asuras. (63)
Each of them should be known to have two arms, two eyes, and one face; they are formed from the first letter of their respective names, conjoined with the *bindu* and *nāda*. (64)
Having fully worshipped [the deities] in the outer enclosure, everyone shall attain accomplishment;
one should worship all the remaining groups of Mothers with their respective names preceded by [the syllable] *sva*.
Indeed, there are ten [missiles] belonging to the world-protectors (lokapālas), and likewise those of the weapons:
Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, and Vāyu. || 66 ||
Someśa, Ananta, and Brahmā constitute the group of ten;
likewise, there are the thunderbolt (vajra), the spear (śakti), the staff (daṇḍa), the sword (khaḍga), the noose (pāśa), and the goad (aṅkuśa).
One should likewise worship Khaḍga, Dābha, Triśūla, and Padma;
all of them should be known as having two arms, one face, and two eyes. (68)
And [he visualizes] the Lord as four-armed, three-eyed, and single-faced;
wearing a crown of matted hair and having a serpent for his sacred thread. || 69 ||
Each is formed with the first letter of their own name, conjoined with the *bindu* and *nāda*;
all of them are seated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), with their gaze fixed solely upon Śiva.
O Guha, the powers (śaktis) of all [the deities] indeed begin with their own respective names;
and O Guha, they exist as the very foundation for all those powers.
"The gods are presided over by their own respective powers upon the lotus, O Guha.
Thus ends the second chapter, on the Extraction of Mantras, in the Śrī Kālottara.
Ishvara said:
Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme bath that removes all sins.
Clay, wood, cow dung, flowers, sesame seeds, and auspicious myrobalan fruit. || 1 ||
Having taken kuśa grass, let the man go to the river together with his wife;
he should bathe there with great care, but not with water from a domestic reservoir.
Especially one that flows to the ocean; in its absence, a large lake; in its absence, a pond; and in its absence, a lotus-pool. || 3 ||
If that is not available, one should go to Danumukha with a concentrated mind;
when there is plenty, one should never perform a bath with only a small amount [of water].
Having washed himself, the preceptor should deposit [the waste] on the bank of the water;
during the day, the voiding of feces and urine should be performed with the sun to one's right.
Having covered his head, he should depart in silence;
he should take only a coconut fruit and earth for the purpose of purification.
A householder should apply earth ten times to the anus;
he should likewise apply three applications of earth to the penis and to the scrotum.
Having washed the left hand five times, there should indeed be ten washings for the two [other hands];
one should wash one foot with the amount of water equal to an *āmalaka* fruit.
Furthermore, having sipped water according to the rule in this manner,
one who knows the ritual procedure should sip water three times, wipe the mouth twice, sprinkle water on the feet, and then wipe them clean.
One should touch the two eyes with the thumb and the ring finger;
likewise, having touched the two nostrils, one should [touch] the two ears.
The wise one should touch both arms with the thumb and forefinger;
then the preceptor, having touched the navel with all the fingers, [should proceed]. (11)
One should touch the heart with the palm of the hand and the head with the thumb.
A Brahmin is purified by [mantras] reaching the heart, while a Kṣatriya is purified by those reaching the ears.
A Vaiśya [is purified] by merely tasting [the clay], and a Śūdra by being touched with water;
O child, the wise man should apply one-third of the clay to his heart.
O child, one should cast the eastern portion of the clay toward the east, south, north, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, and Vāma, [and likewise] in the ten directions.
With the Śivāstra-mantra alone, the wise man, composed and following the prescribed order,
should touch all his limbs with clay from the right side.
One should smear all the limbs with the heart-mantra using the ghee-mudrā; then, with the northern mantra and with clay, one should prepare the Śiva-tīrtha.
Having first performed the impurity-bath, you should then perform the mantra-bath;
by means of the application of the Nārāca weapon, one should cast [the water] into the midst of the water.
Having bathed thus in the midst of the sacred ford (tīrtha), one should wipe oneself three times with the morning sun;
then, indeed, one should touch all the limbs again with cow dung.
One should smear the head with the Īśāna mantra, the face with the Tatpuruṣa mantra,
the heart with the Aghora mantra, and the private parts with the Vāma mantra.
Having smeared the feet with the *sadyojāta* mantra, one should cleanse them;
having thus cleansed them with the *pavitra* and *vyomavyāpin* mantras, the knower of mantras [should proceed].
One should cleanse [the area] seven or five times with the Prāsāda mantra;
having visualized the jar-seal (kalaśamudrā), one should perform the consecration with the Prāsāda mantra.
Having stood at the navel in water up to the neck, facing the sun in its presence, [one should contemplate] those twenty-five and twenty-seven principles. (22)
Having gratified right there with purifying offerings consisting of the limbs of Śiva, as well as Vidyeśvara, Śiva himself, and the eleven Rudras; || 23 ||
Having reached the sacred ford, the knower of mantras should [worship] the lords of the eight forms and also the twelve Ādityas, using kusha grass and flowers.
Having smeared all his limbs with cow dung and earth, or indeed with water while reciting the Śiva-mantra, he should then purify himself by wiping with sacred blades of grass (pavitrakas).
With cow dung and earth combined with flowers and fragrance, one should, being composed, sprinkle it while reciting the root mantra. (26)
Right there, one should offer water dedicated to the Sun with the six-syllable mantra;
having reached a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), the knower of mantras should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules.
With great concentration, he should cause [the child] to sip water with the Vāmadeva hymn, saying:
"O child, may the waters purify you," using the non-terrible (aghorā) piṇḍa-mantra. || 28 ||
Having purified [the area] with the *Īśa* mantra,
O child, one should perform the *mārjana* (sprinkling) over the *piṇḍeśa* either with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā" or with the *vyoma* mantra.
Having circumambulated [the water], one should then offer a *añjali* to the Sun;
the wise person should recite the *tatpuruṣa* mantra one thousand and eight times.
The wise one should recite half of that, or indeed one hundred and eight times;
likewise, he should recite the Sāvitra mantra and then recite the Prāsāda mantra again.
The wise one should mutter the Prāsāda mantra, which grants the fulfillment of all desires and aims;
O Mahāsena, with the Prāsāda mantra, one should offer water to the Sun.
O child, one should recite the *upasthāna* with the five Brahma-mantras and the Śiva-aṅga-mantras,
as well as the mantras of the eight Vidyeśvaras and the eleven Rudra-mantras. (33)
Having repeated the mantras pertaining to the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti), as well as those of the Ādityas and the Vasus,
the wise one stands with arms raised, reciting the Vyomavyāpin mantra.
Having likewise recited this Rudra-sūkta beginning with "upāṃśu," and having performed three circumambulations, one should prostrate oneself on the ground like a staff.
Having offered the *arghya* according to the rule with the three-syllabled and six-syllabled mantras, [one should offer] red sandalwood paste, fragrance, unbroken grains, and rice. (36)
O observer of noble vows, having placed either the Karaṃvīra flower, or the Japā flower, or even both of them in a copper vessel upon a mandala measuring one cubit, || 37 ||
Having invoked that Sun-god while being absorbed in the six-syllable mantra,
and having offered water for the feet and water for sipping, one should present the *arghya* offering to him.
One should then conquer the three-syllabled reality one hundred and eight times;
having bid farewell to the Lord of Gods, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) preceded by the mantra.
One should satisfy the gods, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors with the Vāma, Aghora, and Sadyojāta [faces], and ten times with the root mantra of Śiva. || 40 ||
One should offer libations nine times to Sadāśiva and Maheśa,
as well as to the Vidyeśvaras, the guardians of the forms (Mūrtipās), and the eleven Rudras.
As well as the Ādityas and the Vasus, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Guha,
the two Aśvins, the Maruts, and the lords of the hosts of world-protectors.
As well as yakṣas, vidyādharas, kiṃpuruṣas, and likewise garuḍas;
gandharvas, cāraṇas, siddhas, nāgas, and indeed yātudhānas. || 43 ||
[He saw] the sages and the apsarases, the asuras and the piśācas,
the bhūtas, vetālas, and kuśmāṇḍas, as well as the kumārapāhas and pūtanas. (44)
Likewise, the wise man should offer libations to the planetary deities (devagrahas) by reciting their names first,
as well as to their wives and their sons.
One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and other rites by reciting [the mantra] with such devotion;
one should offer libations seven times each to Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra.
One should satisfy the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Yakṣas—these five groups;
and one should likewise satisfy all the remaining deities three times over. || 47 ||
O Guha, one should satisfy the Gandharvas three times, others once,
and the wives of the gods and the sons of the gods three times.

Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavīta), he should offer libations to the gods; wearing it suspended from the ear (karṇalambita), to the sages; and wearing it over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), being well-composed, he should satisfy the ancestors. 49.
A wise person should satisfy the deities with the *daivika* (divine) *tīrtha*,
and furthermore, he should satisfy the sages with the *ārṣa* (sage-related) *tīrtha*.
One should again satisfy the ancestors with the *tīrtha* belonging to the fathers;
the base of the little finger is said to be the *tīrtha* of the gods.
The *ṛṣitīrtha* is at the tips [of the fingers], the *paitṛka* at the base of the thumb, and the *śaiva* tīrtha is said to be in the middle of the palm. (52)
The Vaiṣṇava [tīrtha] is on its left, while the Brāhma is said to be on its right;
the Sūryatīrtha is to its east, and the Vāruṇa is to its west.
In the southeast is the Agnitīrtha, while in the southwest is the Āsura;
in the northwest is the Pāvana Tīrtha, and in the northeast is the Rudratīrtha.
(13) Twelve sacred fords (tīrtha) are proclaimed to be on the right hand of Brahmins;
therefore, with every effort, [one should accept] that which has fallen from the hand of a Brāhmaṇa. 55.
O child, the water shall be equal to the Gaṅgā and become the destroyer of all sins;
likewise, the sages Agastya, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, and Aṅgiras [shall be present].
Viśvāmitra, Bharadvāja, Atri, and Nārada; Paiṅga, Dīrghatamas, Vyāsa, Śaunaka, and Māmateya—if [these are the sages]. (57)
Parāśara and Āpastamba, Bodhāyana and Sumantu, Śāliki and Jamadagni, as well as Upamanyu and Vāmadeva; || 58 ||
One should satisfy these three times, as well as all other sages;
one should satisfy all the sages using the *ārṣa* (sage’s) *tīrtha* itself.
The fathers, the grandfathers, and those known as the great-grandfathers; likewise the maternal grandfather, the maternal great-grandfather, and the maternal great-great-grandmother.
One should satisfy the maternal grandmother and those who are like her with the paternal offering;
likewise the teacher, the mother, the father, his mother, and his father as well. (61)
A wise man should satisfy his friends, sons, and wives with offerings intended for the ancestors;
he should satisfy the gods with kusha grass, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
One should satisfy all the sages with kusa grass, the ancestors with sesame seeds,
and the gods as well as the sages with water alone.
On the bank of the water, for the ancestors, according to the eternal rule and the prescribed ritual,
one should offer the power of liberation (mukti-śakti) with sesame seeds from a jar into the hand of the deceased.
Having gratified [the ancestors] according to the rule and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rule,
he should then perform the recitation of the Vedas and other texts with the [proper] utterances.
(14) One should then mutter the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra, the *Śiva-vastra*, the *Tryambaka* mantra quickly and swiftly, as well as the eleven *Rudra* mantras and the *Puruṣasūkta*. 66.
One who is well-restrained should daily recite the *Aruṇa-śivasaṃkalpa* mantra while holding the index finger and thumb together in both the left and right hands.
Afterwards, being composed, the wise man should recite the *prāsāda* mantra until he is fully concentrated;
then, having wrung out his bathing garment and withdrawn the sacred water (*tīrtha*), he should proceed.
With the ritual service of a wheel-like arrangement using fragrant myrobalan and other substances,
one should prepare oil, a paste, fragrance, and the powder of the Akṣa tree.
Accompanied by the eight types of earth and the sounds of conchs and drums, one should perform the bath with diligence; first, however, one should perform the Brāhma bath.
In bathing, in the worship of the gods, in meditative absorption, as well as in recitation, in eating, and in the performance of duties for all beings, silence is prescribed in six ways.
Having bathed in this manner according to the prescribed rite, the destruction of all sins shall occur;
and there shall be the swift eradication of various obstacles. (72)
He should withdraw the sacred water (tīrtha) with the heart-mantra and place it within his own heart;
then, wise in mantra, he should go to the temple with flowers in his hand.
Thus ends the third chapter, on bathing, in the Kālottara.
Īśvara said:
O Ṣaṇmukha, listen now as I shall describe the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna).
The cow of Kapila is most excellent, as is the cow that is free from old age.
Having grasped the cloth with the *hṛdaya* mantra, and having dried it again over his head,
he should cause it to be taken hold of with the *sadyojāta* mantra after it has been burnt with the *śiraḥ* mantra. (2)
The wise one should place it in a gourd vessel or perhaps in a leaf-cup; or, having placed it in a new earthen jar, it should be protected by the armor-mantra (kavaca).
O child, having consecrated it once with each of all the mantras, one should place it in the left hand using the right hand alone.
The practitioner of mantra should [place it] either on a bed of ashes, or in a conch shell, or in a copper vessel;
a golden vessel is best, while one of silver would be middling.
A copper vessel is the lowest; in its absence, it may be made of clay.
A gourd vessel is inferior, and a cloth bundle (poṭṭalī) is the lowest of the low.
One should recite the Pañcabrahma mantras along with the Vyomavyāpin mantra once;
[one should worship] the head with the Aghora mantra and the face with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.

O child, one should smear [the body] with the Aghora mantra on the heart, the arms, the belly, and the navel; indeed, on the back and the chest with the Bahurūpa mantra; and on the private parts and the anus, as well as the two generative organs, with the Vāmadeva mantra.
The two arms, the two knees, the two shanks, and likewise the bones of the two sides and both the backs; || 9 ||
The knower of mantras, using the Sadyojāta mantra, should perform the bathing of all the limbs for lifelong celibate Brahmins (naiṣṭhika) on both their feet and hands.
A wise man should cause the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) to be made for kings and for Vaiśyas;
or he should perform the bath with ashes or apply the triple mark at the three junctions of the day.
With his soul purified of all sins, he rejoices together with Śiva;
[he who wears] the Tripuṇḍra at the three junctions of the day on thirty-two or sixteen limbs. || 12 ||
(16) It brings about the destruction of all sins and the eradication of all diseases;
[it should be applied] to the crown of the head, the forehead, the two ears, the two eyes, and also to the two nostrils. (13)
The mouth and neck, the two shoulders, the two elbows with the two forearms, the wrists, as well as the heart, the navel, the genitals, and the anus; 14.
The two thighs, the two knees, the two bones of the shanks, the two feet, and the two backs [of the heels]—this is declared to be the thirty-two-fold Tripuṇḍra. (15)
I shall describe the sixteenth station; listen briefly, O Six-faced One:
[it consists of] the forehead, the neck, the two shoulders, and the pair of arms and elbows. (16)
One should indeed apply the Tripuṇḍra in sixteen locations—the heart, the belly, the navel, the two sides, and the back—for the sake of attaining Śiva. || 17 ||
The thirty-two previous locations are the toes and the fingers;
on these thirty-two locations, one should apply the Tripuṇḍra, which consists of the thirty-six principles (tattvas) and their presiding deities.
In the sixteenth place, one should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) for the sixteen deities:
Śiva, Sadāśiva, Maheśa, and the five Brahmans.
O child, the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) are indeed the presiding deities of the sixteenth;
I shall likewise describe the three-fold sectarian mark (tripuṇḍra) and its deity in the eight locations.
Brahmā himself is in the place of the head, and Skanda is on the forehead;
Vināyaka is pleased in the throat, and Viṣṇu indeed is in the two arms.
The Lord is pleased in the heart, and the Earth in the navel;
the ancestors are also pleased on the back—thus eight deities are proclaimed to be present in the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
A width of six finger-breadths is prescribed for the *tripuṇḍra* of Brāhmaṇas;
that of Kṣatriyas is four finger-breadths in width. (23)
A triple mark (tripuṇḍra) three finger-breadths wide grants all desires for those of the Vaiśya caste;
however, for Śūdras and especially for women, it should be one finger-breadth wide. || 24 ||
For women, that very same [mark] produced from their respective caste is prescribed;
the *tripuṇḍra* is made with the middle finger, the ring finger, and the forefinger. (25)
Among all the spiritual preceptors, however, it is like the slightly crescent moon;
among kings, it is specifically like the mere sliver of the new moon. (26)
For Śūdras, however, the wise man should apply the mark of the Tripuṇḍra merely by touching it with three fingers upon the surface of the forehead.
O Six-faced One, that triple mark (tripuṇḍra), renowned by the name Lakṣmī,
belongs to the Samayin, the Putraka, the Sādhaka, and the Ācārya.
By means of the rite of the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka), complete protection is ordained, even upon seeing a bad dream or being touched by an evil person. || 29 ||
For men who are ill, bathing is in every way impossible;
through the ash-bath alone shall there be purity and also fitness for worship. (30)
The wise declare that the fivefold bath consists of the Āgneya, Vāruṇa, Vāyavya, Mantra, and Śiva baths.
The fire-purification bath is with ashes; the Varuṇa bath is by immersion;
the Mantra bath consists of the hymn "āpo hi ṣṭhā"; and the Vāyu bath is with the dust raised by cows.
That which is the shower of pleasant rain is declared to be Śivatīrtha;
among all of those, O dear one, the Āgneya-śaiva is the most excellent.
The gods and the sages, as well as the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras;
the hosts of Maruts, the hosts of Pitṛs, and even all the hosts of Mothers. || 34 ||

"O Six-faced One, they have proclaimed that the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) should always be performed with every effort for the sake of protection, for the sake of auspiciousness, and for the sake of purification. (35)
In former times, I gave ash to the ascetics and those wearing sectarian marks;
yet in their food there were chaff and hair, as well as foul-smelling charcoal and other impurities. (36)
All reptiles, as well as other flies,
bugs, dogs, bees, and gadflies, are purified by the ashes of cow dung.
Curd, milk, ghee, oil, honey, and molasses, as well as coconut, water, and plain drink—these constitute the side dishes. || 38 ||
Indeed, that which is defiled by hair and the like, as well as that which has been touched by an untouchable, becomes pure by removing just that much and sprinkling ashes. || 39 ||
Indeed, for all those of the four castes—whether woman, man, or neuter—the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be worn at three times, twice, or once a day. || 40 ||
Indeed, O child, it provides all protection and one goes to the world of Śiva;
neither gods, nor Rākṣasas, nor Piśācas, nor Asuras, nor those who are Dhānakas [can harm him]. 41.
O Prince, there are the grahas, bhūtas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and likewise ḍākinīs;
the brahmarākṣasas, those defiled by leftovers, the pūtanās, and those afflicted by leprosy and abdominal tumors. || 42 ||
All the intermediate [sections] consist of eighty-two diseases born of wind (vāta), sixty-four diseases of bile (pitta), and fifty-six diseases of phlegm (śleṣman). || 43 ||
O Alī, whatever fear there may be from anything whatsoever, one is purified by the ash-bath;
for it illuminates human beings and it illuminates that which is auspicious.
Because it consumes all sins, it is proclaimed as "Bhasma" (ashes);
whether during a meal in the forenoon, or even in a dream, or upon departing. (45)
With ashes, one should apply the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*); this is ordained as protection against all [evils]. Fearlessness is granted by Brahmā and Viṣṇu... [46]
"And having applied the ash with every effort, O Guha," thus ends the fourth chapter on the ash-bath in the *Kālottara*.
Prosperity!
Īśvara said: Listen here in brief regarding all flowers—
those to be avoided and those not to be avoided— and listen also to the [astrological] determination of fruits.
The karavīra flower is superior to a thousand arka flowers;
a single bilva leaf is superior to a thousand [other] leaves. (2)
Now, the white lotus (puṇḍarīka) is superior to a thousand other flowers;
the hundred-petaled lotus (śatapatra) is superior to a thousand white lotuses. || 3 ||
The thousand-petaled lotus is superior to hundreds of hundred-petaled lotuses;
the apāmārga plant is superior even to the most excellent thousand-petaled lotuses. || 4 ||
Among the various species of Apāmārga, a single Kuśa blade is superior; among a thousand Kuśa flowers, a Śamī flower is superior. (5)
Vyāghāta is superior to a thousand śamī flowers;
bakapuṣpa is superior to a thousand vyāghātas.
A single *dhurdhūraka* flower is superior to a thousand *bakapuṣpa* flowers;
a *droṇapuṣpa* is more distinguished than a thousand *dhurdhūraka* flowers.
A single *sadābhadra* flower is always superior to thousands of *droṇa* flowers; and the black *nirguṇḍikā* is even more excellent than thousands of *sadābhadra* flowers.
A *bṛhatpuṣpa* is superior to thousands of *kṛṣṇakuṇḍī* flowers;
a white *arka* flower is superior to thousands of *bṛhatpuṣpa* flowers. (9)
A large droṇa measure of white lotuses excels thousands [of other flowers];
a glorious blue lotus is superior to thousands of large droṇas.
A thousand golden flowers would be equal to a single blue lotus;
a blue lotus and a golden flower become like faded garlands after a year.
Having washed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should again commence the worship;
jasmine, jātī, and dūrvā grass should be used in equal measure.
Campaka, nāgadantī, and bilva—bilva and bilvapatra should be in equal measure; mālatī and kovidāra, as well as kara and jīra, should likewise be in equal measure. || 13 ||
The *vakula* and the *pāṭalī* shall be equal to the lotus flower;
the white *aśoka* and the *mandāra* shall be equal to the *vyāghātaka*. || 14 ||
The red lotus, the white water-lily, and the apāmārga shall be equal;
the japā, the kadamba, the punnāga, and the droṇapuṣpa shall be equal. || 15 ||
Madana and Dvīpava should be equal to Bṛhatpuṣpa;
Lakṣmī and Sahadevī should be equal to Bilvapatra. || 16 ||
Viṣṇukrānti and Nṛpa should be equal to Arka flowers;
Cibuka and Gūḍhapuṣpa should be equal to Padma flowers. || 17 ||
Tulasī and candravallī are equal to the arka flower; the blue lotus and the white water-lily are equal to the kuṭila flower. || 18 ||
Vejikā and utpala should be equal to apāmārga;
palāśa and musalī flowers should be equal to droṇapuṣpa. || 19 ||
The *ādhika*, the flax flower (*atasīpuṣpa*), and the *bakapuṣpa* are equal [in effect].
So too are the peacock’s eye (*mayūra*), the conch flower (*śaṅkhapuṣpa*), the *sūryāvarta*, and the *nāgaka*. (20)
The Dhurdhūraka flower is to be known as equal [in merit] to the Siṃhakesaripālaka; so too are Kaṃsaka and Kṛṣṇatulasī. || 21 ||
Dhurdhūraka is known as another name for both Mahābhadra and Tṛṇa.
Vajra, ruby, emerald, and pearls;
sapphire, great blue gem, sun-stone, and moonstone. || 23 ||
Indeed, all gems should be known as equal to the blue lotus;
likewise, barley, wheat, wild rice, śāli rice, and bamboo [seeds]. (24)
The wise man, having cooked these eleven seeds— sesamum, mung bean, peas, flat bean, black gram, and likewise the śyāma bean— should proceed.
Having crossed over the seven-colored [lines], one should worship the sprouts;
the sprouts, resembling flowers, are to be worshipped individually. 26.
The white mountain (śvetagiri), the karṇikā, the nandyāvarta as a worshipper, the kadalī flower, and the flowers of the śāribā; || 27 ||
The flowers of the kadamba, arjuna, and sindūra, as well as karavīra, madhūka, and the mango (cūta), are to be known [as the appropriate offerings]. || 28 ||
The eight flowers that are like vajras for Śiva, the Supreme Self, are:
ketakī, mādhavī, kunda, yūthikā, and madayantikā; || 29 ||
One should avoid the śirīṣa, the sarja, the bandhūka, and the aṣṭapuṣpa;
likewise, the kiṃśuka, the green [leaves], and the blue karṇika.
One should avoid *talapoṭa* flowers, *piśāca* flowers, *śigru*, *nyagrodha*, and *matsyākṣa*. (31)
Having offered these flowers, one should worship Mahāviṣṇu;
O Guha, one should also worship the Talapoṭaka flowers by the millions.
One should worship Umādevī with black flowers along with their stalks, māhiṣākṣī flowers, and the blossoms of the śiṃśumāra tree.
A *palāśa* flower [pleases] Brahmā, a *tulasī* flower [pleases] Keśava;
the *indravallī* and the golden flower (*kanakapuṣpa*) greatly bring delight to Indra. (34)
One should worship Śiva with all white flowers with devotion;
likewise, one should worship him with ketakī flowers and wild jasmine (araṇyamālatī).
With a concentrated mind, one should worship all kinds of jewels and flowers;
however, O child, the practitioner should avoid the *kiṃśuka* flower with great effort. (36)
One should worship all the jewels, excluding the *talapoṭaka*;
one should worship with black flowers, for he is the Piśāca of the Mountain-Ear.
One should worship all dark-colored flowers and avoid those that are limitless [in number];
one should worship all green flowers as well. (38)
They should diligently avoid *tīvra*, *jyāmaka*, and *puṣpa* flowers, as well as sandalwood, saffron, rhinoceros horn, leaves, and fruits. (39)
The bilva fruit, uśīra, and great, pleasing fragrance;
turuṣka, ghana, cela, vanaloha, and aṅganā. 40.
For these fragrances are indeed pleasing; incense should consist of ten ingredients:
abala, caṇḍī, śaṅkha, kuṅkuma, and guggulu. (41)
Incense that pleases Śiva yields tenfold fruit;
likewise do kuṣṭha, mīsasamora, and māṃsusākala. (42)
The fragrance that pleases Śiva should consist of ten parts of incense;
it should include honey, sugar, guggulu, and four parts of kunduruṣka.
Likewise, among other fragrances, there is one that is greatly pleasing and auspicious;
[these consist of] one, two, three, or four parts of khaga, candana, and vāyasa.
O child, prepare an incense equal to *turuṣka*, increased with *kṛṇeṣa*, cooled, and likewise thoroughly saturated with honey. 45.
Two *prasthas* of *śaṅkha*, *rohitaka*, or *turuṣka*, with four times as much root and eight times as much *devadāru*, constitute the incense fashioned by Rudra. (46)
Nāsikā, cūtapatra, priyaṅgu, ghanasāra, and the resin of gulgulu—this incense, known as Kalabha, is dear to Śaṅkara. (47)
Maramāṃsī is the fourth, and pūtikeśa is equal to that;
indeed, this incense with the fragrance created by Rudra contains no resin.
If rotten hair and human flesh, one, two, or three parts combined,
are fumigated with jaggery and clarified butter, the resulting scent will be that which is created by Śiva.
The three fruits, sandalwood, saffron, turuṣka, caṇḍī, ghanasāra, conch-shell, and kambala; these are to be taken for their essence, not the ash or the foot-powder.
The supreme unguent fashioned by Śambhu.
Or perhaps it is the body of Varuṇa, with its beautiful limbs, adorned with a girdle of sandalwood and lotuses?
The lover [of Śiva] offered incense of agallochum and monkey-wood, which, according to the doctrine of Śiva, wafts forth a most excellent fragrance. || 51 ||
Produced from thick clouds, with its excellent body colored by saffron, born of water and water-born lotuses, and originating from mountain tamāla trees— this supreme fragrance is kissed by the bees.
The *varaṇḍakuṭṭa* consists of eight jars, twelve petals, two rims, and one [central] element;
it is heated with the oil of the sun’s rays and campaka oil, which is dear to Śiva.

This garment, ripened by the intense cooking of sugarcane juice, perfumed with agallochum, red sandalwood, and incense, and mixed with the down of the *vāpya* bird— wear this [garment] made of *pūka* fruit fibers. Take the powder of cloves, camphor, and the three fruits (*phalatraya*), along with honey and sugar.

This supreme mouth-perfume, which bestows auspiciousness, removes sin, and is dear to Śiva, is to be used; it is composed of sandalwood, kunduru, conch-shell, yellow orpiment, camphor, and agallochum, and is the highest of divine things.
Indeed, this excellent incense is truly a home fashioned by Śiva himself.
One should always burn incense—agallochum, sandalwood, aloeswood, and saffron—with molasses and ghee; this fragrance is ever dear to Rudra.
One should fumigate with turuṣka the three fruits, kāramāṃsī, sandalwood, saffron, aguru, honey, sugar, and iron.
One should, with every effort, apply this fragrance beloved by Śiva, consisting of camphor, madana, and medhā, perfumed with mallikā and bakula flowers. (59)
For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas,
he shall dwell eternally in the city of Śiva and rejoice together with Śiva.
Flowers, fragrance, incense, and mouth-perfume have been shown;
likewise the lamp, the water of honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamanīya), and the sacrificial oblation (havis). (61)
"O child, the procedure for the distribution of colors is likewise proclaimed by Madhu.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, on flowers and perfumes, in the Kālottara.
Śrīḥ!
Īśvara said:
One should offer a lamp with the ghee of a tawny cow (kapilā), or else with old ghee;
if these are unavailable, one may now offer a lamp with goat's ghee or pure oil.
One should indeed avoid the ghee of camels, buffaloes, and horses; the ghee of a tawny cow is supreme, for it is said that a lamp made of such pure (sāttvika) ghee brings success.
Ghee from an old cow is called the middling lamp, which is said to be of the nature of *rajas*.
One should avoid using any oil from trees for the Śiva-lamp.
O child, this water for the feet, combined with ela and camphor and endowed with the three fruits, is the most excellent; it bears the lotus feet of Śiva.
Uśīra, pākala, patra, and kuṣṭha in equal parts are to be known as the "middle" water for washing, used for cleansing the lotus feet of Śiva.
O child, māṃsī is said to be the bark; the lowest grade of water for washing the feet (pādya) consists of takkola, kaṭaka, jātikośa, and likewise tuṭī.
One should cause this excellent water for sipping (ācamanīya) to be offered over Śiva; it should contain saffron, cloves, nutmeg, and camphor. (7)
O Lord, here is water for sipping, purified by a cloth;
the *arghya* is said to consist of eight ingredients, prepared in a golden vessel.
It should consist of a Palāśa leaf, a lotus, and an earthen vessel.
Water, milk, tips of Kuśa grass, unbroken rice,
barley, rice grains, sesame seeds, and white mustard seeds are said to constitute the eightfold *arghya* offering.
An *arghya* offering combined with excellent flowers and fragrances yields a hundredfold fruit;
so too do *śamī*, *vyāghāta* flowers, *droṇa*, and indeed *bilva* leaves.
Neither the flower of the blue lotus, nor the white lotus, nor even the apāmārga or the bṛhatī with its beautiful blossoms is prescribed [for this purpose]. (12)
If it is combined with *vyāghranakha* and *rudrajaṭā*, the fruit is ten thousandfold;
if combined with *elā* or *suvarṇapuṣpa*, the fruit is ten millionfold.
One should prescribe a hundred thousand white mandāra flowers as the fruit;
therefore, with every effort, [one should offer] that which is endowed with the fragrance of flowers.
O child, one should present the *arghya* offering; it shall yield the fruit of all sacrifices.
[One should avoid flowers] that are infested with insects or hair, or those covered by spiderwebs. (15)

One should discard flowers that have passed through clothing, those brought by hand, those touched by a crow, those that have fallen on their own, and those that have been offered [to another deity]. (16)
Flowers gathered on a path, those that have blossomed at night, the *utpala* and the *moca*, as well as those brought from below the navel or even those touched by the feet [are forbidden]. (17)
It has been smelled by birds such as cocks and the like,
and it has been touched by cats, mice, buffaloes, goats, and wild oxen.
That which is defiled by habitual tendencies, touched by those afflicted with sinful diseases, touched by women in their menses and the like, or even corrupted by those of the lowest castes; || 19 ||
O Guha, one should avoid flowers grown on impure ground such as cremation grounds;
flowers purchased with wealth yield middling results. (20)
One should declare the fruit to be excellent when the flower arises from one's own garden;
one should declare the fruit to be inferior when the flower arises from another's garden. || 21 ||
One should prescribe the best fruit produced from forest mountains;
however, with each successive month, one should omit one flower.
One should discard the flowers, starting from one and so on, in sequence throughout the twelve months:
the *arka*, the *bilva*, the *apāmārga*, the *droṇa*, and the blue and white lotuses. (23)
The wise man should procure, month by month, one flower each from the vyāghratī, bṛhatī, vyāghrī, śamī, campaka, and pāṭalī for the sake of nourishment and other benefits.
Whatever desired fruit one obtains, as well as the very destruction of death—
if one performs this sacrifice for a year, it shall yield the fruit of an Aśvamedha.
[One should offer] sandalwood, saffron, agallochum, and indeed khagama.
Takola, nutmeg, long pepper, and its fruit, as well as resin and pākala, [should be used] one month at a time in their respective order. || 27 ||
O child, one should worship according to the prescribed rite; it shall be twice as effective as previously stated.
Buffalo-dung resin (mahiṣāguggula) mixed with ghee is excellent for all months. (28)
The merit of incense and lamps is ten times that of what was previously mentioned;
the merit of an offering consisting of rice and lotus stalks combined is ten times that of [the previous] offering.
Thus ends the sixth chapter on specific flowers, perfumes, incense, and water-offerings in the Kālottara.
Śrī Īśvara said:
O Six-faced One, listen now as I shall explain the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). Having first performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), you should then perform the internal organ.
Having first performed the ritual placement (karanyāsa), one should subsequently carry out the purification;
one should purify the palms and the backs of the hands with the seed-syllable of the Weapon (astra).
Furthermore, the wise one should again perform the placement of the five Brahmans, from the thumb to the little finger,
having placed them in order starting with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta.
The five [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Īśāna are assigned from the little finger (kaniṣṭhikā) to the thumb (aṅguṣṭha);
this is declared to be the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* (the rite of emanation), which proceeds from the thumb to the little finger.

The placement from the little finger to the thumb is called the placement of withdrawal (saṃhāranyāsa); the placement from the middle finger to the little finger is declared to be the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa). || 5 ||
One should indeed install the limbs of Śiva according to the paths of emanation and withdrawal;
with those two, one should install the "Pervasive Sky" (Vyomavyāpin) and designate the "All-Facing" (Sarvatomukha).
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should perform the worship of the sides;
thereafter, one should install the Vidyeśvaras, followed by Sadāśiva and Maheśvara.
One should place [the deities] beginning with Ananta and ending with Ekarudra on the left hand;
then, one should again place the eight deities beginning with Trimūrti on the right hand.
In this manner, one should then assign the three mandalas and the three qualities;
having assigned the three selves (ātman) in sequence across all the fingers.
Having placed the Netra-mantra on the palm of the hand, one should again perform the placement of the limbs (aṅga-vinyāsa).
Then, one should again place the Prāsāda-mantra upon all the fingers of the hand.
O God, one should place the Hand of Śiva upon the head of the disciple;
thereafter, one should unite the self with Śiva, the supreme cause. (11)
At the tip of the crest-lock, twelve finger-breadths long, pure as clear crystal,
within the supreme Śiva-tattva, subtle, stainless, and of the nature of light— 12.
One should join [the deity] with the heart-mantra using the saṃhāra-mudrā;
she is in the triangular world of fire, in the second [triangle] which is threefold.
Having meditated upon the tip of the big toe, one should burn the body like a piece of wood;
having thus burnt one's own body, one should meditate here upon a heap of ashes.
Situated in the center of the syllable *tāra* is the moon, and upon it is the fourth letter of the *ya*-group,
seated on a white lotus, facing downward upon the seat of yoga (*yogapīṭha*).
One should know that the letter A, resembling pure crystal, is born of the Self;
the letter U is the principle of Vidyā, and the letter Ma is the principle of Śiva.
Having flooded [the body] with nectar,
the wise one should then flood all the limbs with that nectar which resides in the center at the end of the body.
Having cast off the natural state, one should contemplate "I am Śiva.
Having first performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should then [purify] the internal organ. 18.
One who constantly maintains the earth-element (pārthavī) should join it with the seed-syllable of the heart;
however, one should maintain that which grants all desires by conjoining it with the seed-syllable of the head. 19.
Being well-composed, one should maintain the fire-element by means of the seed-syllable of the *śikhā*;
this brings about the destruction of all sins as well as the subduing of enemies. (20)
One should maintain the wind conjoined with the kavaca [mantra] as a protection for all;
one should maintain the temple with the śivāstra [mantra], which destroys death. (21)
(30) O Six-faced One, the five elements— earth, water, fire, air, and space— situated within the body, are purified. 22.
The earth should be purified in five parts, from the feet up to the knees;
O Guha, the purification of sins should be fourfold, from the knees up to the navel.
The purification of fire is indeed threefold, from the navel up to the end of the throat;
the purification of air is indeed twofold, and one should retain it at the end of the throat.
One should pierce the four knots by means of the Pāśupata scripture;
one should pierce the Suṣumṇā-knot and the Ākāśa-knot with the weapon of Śiva.
Five, four, two, and one thousand;
all is void, without support, and pure consciousness alone remains. || 26 ||
One should again contemplate Śiva as the nectar situated within the process;
one should thus constantly contemplate the Lord well within the form [of the Suṣumṇā]. || 27 ||
Know that Maheśvara is indeed both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala), as well as both with and without parts; know Sadāśiva to be both with parts and without parts. || 28 ||
"Know Śiva to be partless (niṣkala), and the wise man should contemplate him as abiding in three places.
Now I shall speak of the manifest (sakala); listen, O Six-faced One."
Resembling pure crystal, with a luster white as cow’s milk, three-eyed, ten-armed, peaceful, and adorned with a crown of matted locks. || 30 ||
He has three faces and three heads, adorned with all ornaments;
he is the god wearing divine garments, with divine perfumes and fragrances for his adornment.
The god is seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), resting upon a white lotus;
he has the bull as his vehicle and holds a trident and an axe.
To the god Maheśvara, the Lord of the World, who holds a sword, an axe, and a bow, and who wields a thunderbolt and a lance, and who bears fire and serpents. (33)
Resembling a thousand suns and resembling pure crystal,
he is endowed with sixteen arms, five faces, and three eyes.
He has five faces and three eyes, adorned with five heads,
endowed with a sacred thread, and decorated with all ornaments.
The supreme lord (Parameśvara) should be known as being covered with the colors of fine silk cloths (dukūlapaṭṭa),
and the all-pervading one (Vibhu) should be known as having a crown adorned with all kinds of jewels.
On his forehead was a golden band adorned with all kinds of jewels;
the Supreme Lord was further embellished by five arrows whose tips were blunted.
Adorned with five armlets and embellished with all kinds of jewels, he was mounted upon a white lotus graced with a thousand petals. (38)
The Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Gomatī, Narmadā, Sarasvatī, Sarayū, and Gaṇḍakī likewise held chowries busily in their hands. (39)
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes and draped with celestial garlands;
his couch was strewn with whirling flowers—mallikā, utpala, and campaka.
The God of gods, perfectly pure, was seated upon the nine Śaktis, his five heads adorned with Jāti, Vakula, and Mandāra flowers. (41)
The wise know the western face to be Sadyojāta, white as a conch shell; Vāmadeva is in the north, resembling the Japā flower or vermilion.
The southern face is Aghora, resembling a dark blue cloud;
the eastern face is Tatpuruṣa, resembling the rising sun. (43)
The face of Īśāna is at the top, with a luster as white as cow’s milk;
indeed, everything from the head onwards is of that very color and is vast. (44)
It is joined above with three broad five-faced [projections], and it is variegated with five jewels upon its five heads, O Six-faced One. (45)
One should contemplate Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the Lord of Gods as the cause of all causes in the heart; and one should place Maheśvara in the region of the navel as Sadāśiva.
But Śiva is the supreme, eternal Brahman in the perpetual abode—partless, stainless, tranquil, beyond phenomenal expansion, and devoid of defining characteristics. || 47 ||
Inconceivable, without support, and devoid of destruction or origination;
it is absolute liberation, solitary, peaceful, and free from both that which is to be discarded and that which is to be grasped. || 48 ||
Free from "is" and "is not," subtler than the subtlest, supreme, devoid of conceptual construction, divine, and self-realized—such is Śiva, the Lord. 49.
But in the center of the body is established that supreme reality, which is incomparable, free from disease,
beyond the senses, and devoid of all limiting adjuncts.
That [reality] is attainable through the grace of the Guru; it is eternal, the wonder of the world-lord.
With eyes on every side and faces on every side, with arms on every side and feet on every side, He alone has become the support for all beings, as if giving birth to the worlds.
That supreme reality, to be reached through meditation, rises up from beyond the darkness.
If you meditate upon the void with the void,
O Six-faced One, having contemplated the void state within the void body, you shall attain liberation.
One should always meditate upon the god Maheśvara within the lotus of the heart with the mind,
offering him perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as incense, lamps, and the water-offering (arghya).
With curd, milk, ghee, and even offerings of honey,
the wise man should meditate upon Maheśa with a purely mental disposition. (54)
In this way, one should likewise [worship] Sadāśiva, together with the seed-syllables and sprouts of Śakti, the five Brahmans, the limbs of Śiva, and the Vidyeśvaras. (55)
Then by the lords of the Gaṇas, the guardians of the world, the eight-formed ones (the Aṣṭamūrtis), the eight Vasus, and the eleven Rudras; 56.
The twelve Ādityas, as well as the other Siddhas and the Maruts, the Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Yakṣas, and Pannagas. || 57 ||
Asuras, rākṣasas, yātudhānas, piśācas,
remnants of beings, bhūtas, vetālas, and even guhyakas— 58.
One should worship the planets, the zodiac signs, the lunar days, and likewise the constellations and apsarases as the twenty-seventh enclosure in the center of the navel.
One should worship with mental flowers alone, with mental incenses, and with mental offerings of food, water for honor, and water for the feet— all indeed with the mind.
Furthermore, one should meditate on the state of retention (kumbhaka) within the central body;
one should worship the cause of that which abides in retention with sixteen measures (mātrās).
O Six-faced One, the wise man should exhale thirty-two times at the heart and the navel;
by performing this sacrifice for six months alone, he shall attain the destruction of death.
O Guha, having abandoned both exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), and indeed having abandoned retention (kumbhaka),
one should constantly worship Śiva directly through the very nature of a serpent.
O Guha, by worshipping with a state that is both empty and non-empty, one attains victory over death; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Thus, for one who constantly meditates upon consciousness as bliss established in the middle of the body, there is the supreme destruction of death. (65)
Abandoning exhalation and inhalation, and without even the practice of retention or mental recollection,
that which is endowed with its own natural movement is "piṇḍastha," the destroyer of death.
The worship is of three kinds—sakala, niṣkala, and likewise sakalaniṣkala; this is the most excellent. One should perform sacrifice unto Varuṇa, again and again. (67)
Having worshipped the enclosures in sequence according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures, [one should worship] the twenty-seven enclosures and also the groups of the seven Mothers. (68)
One who is well-composed should indeed worship everything with the mind alone;
one should perform meditative absorption (samādhi), recitation (japa), hymns of praise (stotra), and circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa). 69.
One should perform the fire-ritual again when the sacrificial fire is well-kindled. Thus ends the seventh chapter, on the internal organ, in the Kālottara.
Śrīḥ!
Īśvara said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the sequence of the ritual for the worship of Śiva.
[One should prepare] a space thirty-six finger-breadths in length with thirty-six auspicious *darbha* grasses. || 1 ||
Having fashioned the *kūrca* according to the prescribed rule, the wise practitioner should place it facing east;
then, having assumed the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), he should commence the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*).

Then, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should place the five Brahmans in sequence upon the palms and fingers of the hands, starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger.
O Guha, one should place [the mantras] from the middle finger to the tips of the other fingers, ending with Śiva;
[namely] Sadāśiva, Maheśa, and the eight universal monarchs (cakravartin). (4)
O child, having again performed the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) according to the procedure seen in the scriptures, using the right and left hands in the sequence beginning with the thumb; 5.
Having performed the placement [of the letters] from *ka* to the end of the feet with the thumb and ring finger,
the wise practitioner should perform the placement of the Mātṛkā from *a* to *kṣa*.
On the head, the forehead, the two temples, the throat, the two cheeks, both the nose and the lips, and also on the two rows of teeth; || 7 ||
The *ka*-group [of consonants] on the right hand, the *pa*-group on the left hand;
the *ṭa*-group on the right foot, and the *ta*-group on the left foot.
One should place [the letters] with the sixteen vowels upon the tongue and in the cavity of the palate; then *pa* and *pha* on the right side, and *ba* and *ga* on the left side.
One should place the syllable *ma* at the region of the throat, from the navel up to the heart,
and in the bodily constituents such as skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
The letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *sa* are located from the navel up to the heart;
in the heart is the letter ending with *ha*, and the letter *la* is in the two testicles.

O Guha, one should assign the syllable *kṣa* to the region of the penis and the temple (*prāsāda*) also from the penis; each one [of these] should be assigned beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
With a well-concentrated mind, one should maintain that external path for the sake of the Yajurveda;
the wise practitioner should then place the syllable *huṃ* as a weapon-mantra in the ten directions.

The water-vessel, the *vardhanī*, the vessel for water for the feet (*pādya*), the *ardhapātra*, and likewise the *pautraka*, as well as the vessel for sipping water (*ācamana-pātra*) and the vessels for perfumes, flowers, and food. (15)

A lamp-stand, an incense-burner, and likewise a vessel for the sacrificial porridge (caru), along with water-jars, small pitchers, and vessels for the ingredients of the honey-mixture (madhuparka). || 16 ||
O Six-faced One, having washed everything with the heart-mantra and purified it with the weapon-mantra, one should then enclose it with the armor-mantra.
Having fumigated it with the *śikhā* mantra and offered a lamp with the *cakṣus* mantra,
one should then sprinkle water there with the *brahma* mantras, O child.

Having stirred the perfume with the *hṛdaya* mantra, the wise one should sprinkle saffron with the *śiras* mantra; he should then consecrate the ritual substances with the *śivāstra* and the *hṛdaya*.
First is the purification of oneself, second is the purification of the site, and third is the purification of the materials; the preceptor performs these with the Heart-Astra mantra.
The fourth is the purification of the *liṅga*, while the fifth is the purification of the mantra;
[this is performed] with the five Brahmans, the limbs of Śiva, and also with the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s).
Having recited once the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra along with the thirty-eight *kalā* mantras over the water, one should offer incense and a lamp.
Then, one should wash the liṅga with the mantra of the Śiva-weapon (Śivāstra) alone;
having removed the old floral offerings (nirmālya), one should present them to Caṇḍeśa.
If the worship has become stale, one should arrange it as before;
then, according to the Pāśupata scripture itself, one should wash the pedestal.
Thereafter, one should prepare the seat according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures;
the wise practitioner should indeed place the seed-syllable of Śakti and the sprout in the center.
The wise one should place the fourfold [qualities]— dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty— beginning from the southeast (āgneya) and so forth, in the intermediate directions. (26)
One should place the front part [of the body] in the east, the right limb in the south,
the rear limb in the west, and the upper limb in the north.
One should sequentially place [the syllables] beginning with one's own name as the seed-syllable in the heart;
thereafter, one should place the middle foot [of the mantra], beginning with one's own name, for Keśava.
First is the Anantāsana, and the second should be the Yogāsana;
having placed the third, the Padmāsana, one should place the fourth, the Vimala.
One should place the lower petals and the upper petals with the heart mantra;
one should then fashion the pericarp and the filaments upon the lotus.
One should place an excellent white eight-petaled lotus there;
the Śaktis should be visualized in due order within its filaments.
Beginning from the eastern petal up to the son of Śaṅkara, [the goddesses are] Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and Kalavikāriṇī. (32)
One should place Kalavikariṇī, Kalapramathinī, and likewise Sarvabhūtadamanī;
then one should place Manonmanī in the center as the Śakti whose nature is that of the instrument.
One should arrange *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* one above the other;
likewise, one should arrange the *ātman*, the *antarātman*, and the *paramātman* one above the other, using the first syllable of each respective name.
Then the knower of mantras should invoke the deity with the Sadyojāta mantra;
he should establish him with the Vāmadeva mantra and restrain him with the Aghora mantra.
One should worship with the presence of the Supreme Person, Īśāna himself. First, one should offer water for the feet to Śiva who has arrived. (37)
One should offer water for sipping (ācamana) into the mouths and present the respectful offering (arghya) upon the head [of the deity],
who resembles pure crystal, is radiant, and blazes with splendor.
Three-eyed and five-faced, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, wearing a crown of matted locks, and with eyes like lotus petals. || 39 ||
The Lord of Gods has five faces and five heads, endowed with bliss,
possessed of all auspicious marks, and adorned with every ornament.
A crown, earrings, armlets, and likewise bracelets;
a golden sacred thread, along with a waist-belt and a girdle for the abdomen. (41)
With girdles and anklets adorned with all kinds of jewels,
the god wore celestial garments and was anointed with divine garlands and fragrant unguents.
One should worship the seat and the deity fanned by the waving of chowries;
[worship] Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna. (43)
O child, one should assign Īśāna and the others to the face and the secret organ;
having assigned Sadyojāta to the feet, one should perform the assignment with their respective seed-syllables.
Immediately [one should worship] Vāmadeva with eight kalās, Trayodaśa with thirteen, Aghora with eight for malevolent rites, and Vaktra with four. (45)
One should likewise install Īśāna fivefold, along with the thirty-eight kalās,
in the east, the south, the west, and the north.
One should likewise visualize Īśāna as joined with the upward-facing head, as well as the eastern, southern, western, and northern [faces]. (47)
One should place the five-faced Puruṣa, joined with the upward-facing [face], in the heart, the throat, the two shoulders, the navel, and the belly. (48)
O child, one should indeed place the Aghora mantra eightfold upon the back,
the chest, the linga, the anus, the two thighs, the two knees, and the two shanks.
Likewise, one should place these thirteen digits (kalās) upon the buttocks, the waist, and both sides [of the body] using the Vāma mantra. (50)
O child, one should place the seed-syllable of Sadyojāta on the feet, the hands, the nose, the head, and both arms; thus one should perform the placement in these eight locations.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) in this manner according to the rule, one should thereafter commence the worship;
just as it is in the body, so it is with the deity, and likewise in the fire during the oblation (homa).
One should perform the ritual of worship in the heart, arrange the fire-oblation (homa) at the navel,
and meditate upon the Lord, the granter of boons, who faces in all directions, in the forehead.
Mahēśa, Sadāśiva, and Śiva—these are the threefold [forms];
one should contemplate them respectively upon the head, in the heart, and in the middle [of the body]. || 54 ||

One should know that the *ātmatattva* (self-principle) is in the south and the *vidyātattva* (knowledge-principle) is in the north; the *śivatattva* (Śiva-principle) is indeed in the center—one should well-arrange these three [principles] as five.
Having placed the heart-mantra on the heart, one should place the head-mantra on the head;
having placed the crest-mantra on the crest, one should place the armor-mantra between the breasts.
One should place the Astra-mantra on the regions of the hands and the Netra-mantra on the eyes;
one should display the Netra-mudrā over the five eyes.
O child, one should fashion the *kṣurikā* on the right side of the waist;
there, one should place the *śivāstra* at a distance of one cubit.
One should place [the deities] upon all the tips of the petals and in the ten directions;
on the right side of Śiva, at a distance of one cubit. (p. 40) 59.
One should install the divine Pāśupata weapon with its own seed-syllable;
one should install the Aghora weapon at the location of the feet with the third [case-ending].
Having thus performed the ritual placement according to the prescribed rule, the knower of mantras should thereafter commence the worship,
employing the five mantras together with the heart-mantra.
O child, one should cause the consecration to be performed according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures:
with water containing jewels, water with gold, water with flowers, and water with barley.
Or with one hundred and eight, or even sixty-four;
or thirty-two, or sixteen, or even nine jars.

Having filled [the vessels] with scented water, one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with the honors due to a universal monarch (cakravartin), using fragrant myrobalan fruits and other such substances. 64.
Curd, milk, honey, clarified butter, and likewise the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as coconut water or even sugarcane juice. (65)
Having bathed [the image] again with scented water and water filtered through a cloth,
[one should apply] sandalwood, saffron, or even aloe-wood and conch-shell powder.
Resin, the three myrobalans (triphalā), uśīra, and vālaka,
along with the fragrance of sudhūpa— this is desired as the eightfold fruit of the qualities.
One should worship with *droṇa* flowers or with *karavīraka* flowers, using the heart-mantra alone.
Having offered the previously mentioned lamp, one should offer another lamp with a concentrated mind;
indeed, at the initial invocation, one should cause the arghya and the worship to be presented.
At the conclusion of the worship, there should be an *arghya* offering; one should present the *arghya* three times.
At the time of invocation, however, one should first cause the "well-faced" (*sumukha*) *arghya* to be offered. (70)

At the conclusion of the worship, one should offer the "favorable face" (sumukha) and cause the "turned-away face" (parāṅmukha) to be given; at the time of dismissal, one should cause the "turned-away face" to be offered, and indeed, one should offer the water for honor (arghya) with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
And, my child, being well-composed, one should display the mudrās with the fingers joined together:
the liṅga-mudrā, the padma-mudrā, and likewise the mūla-mudrā. (72)
A hammer and a thunderbolt, Surabhi and Niṣṭhurā, as well as a bull;
a noose, a sword, a bow, an iron arrow, and a fragment. (73)
One should display the khaṭvāṅga, the skull-cup, the iron arrow, and likewise the hand-drum, together with perfumes and flowers, using the heart-mantra itself. (74)
One should prepare five-colored sacrificial oblations (caru) for the five-faced deity:
milk-rice, barley-gruel, rice-and-pulse porridge, turmeric-infused rice, and jaggery-rice.
One should offer water for rinsing the mouth (ācamana) at the five faces, beginning with Sadyojāta;
separately, one should provide a *kuḍuba* of ghee and three plantains.
Three separate pieces of jaggery and five snacks for each of the five [deities];
first, one should offer a *prastha* measure of cow's curd with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
One should offer mouth-freshener, betel-leaf combined with camphor and nutmeg,
and water, using the previously mentioned heart-mantra.
One who is endowed with devotion and firm in their vow should thus offer [the food] at the three junctions of the day:
that which is to be chewed, that which is to be eaten, that which is to be drunk, that which is to be licked, and that which is to be sucked—these five kinds.
One should likewise offer these with the heart-mantra in the three intermediate spaces:
ghee-filled lamps, yogavarti, flattened rice, and coconut.
One should present *anusakta* cakes, *śaṣkulī* cakes, and other edible foods, along with fruits such as mango, jackfruit, orange, and citron. (81)
The fruit of the *badarī*, the *kapittha*, and the *karkarī* fruit, as well as the *tarasīka* and the *hasa* fruit, [should be eaten] with milk. || 82 ||
One should offer these with the heart itself, endowed with devotion and composed in mind;
having offered those things fit for consumption—lickable, suckable, and most pure—one should keep them within the heart. (83)
Having worshipped Mahādeva, one should thereafter worship the Brahmamantras:
having worshipped Sadyojāta in the west, one should worship Vāmadeva in the north.
Having worshipped Aghora in the south, one should worship Puruṣa in the east;
one should then worship Īśāna in the pericarp with perfumes and flowers.
Having worshipped the Heart in the southeast, one should worship the Head in the northeast;
having worshipped the Crest in the southwest, one should worship the Armor in the northwest. || 86 ||
Having thoroughly worshipped the Astra-mantra in the [southern] direction, one should worship the Netra-mantra in the northeast;
then, in the center, one should worship the Śiva-tattva with perfumes and flowers.
One should worship Sadāśiva in the center and perform a slight rite pertaining to Agni;
in the middle [space], however, one should worship the god Śiva, the supreme cause.
One should worship the Lord Maheśvara as *sakala* (with form) and Śiva as *niṣkala* (formless);
know that Sadāśiva is the divine form who is both *sakala* and *niṣkala*.
Know Maheśvara to be the gross form and Sadāśiva to be the subtle form;
indeed, the Supreme Śiva is to be known as that which is higher than Śiva, and there is nothing higher than Him.
The waking state is Maheśa, the dreaming state is Sadāśiva, and the fourth state (turīya), which is free from the three states, is indeed Śiva himself. || 91 ||
Know me indeed to be Maheśvara; O Ajā, you are Manonmanī. You are my very own form, and Ambikā is my middle [aspect]. (92)
This has been declared as divine; everything shall become identical with Śiva.
There is no dharma equal to the worship of Śiva here in the three worlds. (93)
Thus, having understood this, Sadāśiva should be worshipped with diligent effort.
Thus ends the eighth chapter on the worship of Śiva in the Kālottara.
Chapters 9, 10, 11, and 12 are missing.
Īśvara said:
[He created] the Vidyeśvaras, the Gaṇeśas, and likewise the Lokapālas.
The eightfold form (Aṣṭamūrti) is to be known, and the eleven [forms] beginning with Rudra are traditionally taught. || 1 ||
Having worshipped the twelve Ādityas, one should also honor the eight Vasus,
as well as the Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, and Kinnaras.
The Vidyādharas, Yātudhānas, and the highly powerful Gāruḍas, as well as the Ṛṣis, Apsarases, and Asuras—these are considered the twelve [classes]. || 3 ||
With a well-concentrated mind, one should worship the twenty-eight enclosures:
Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, Śivokta, and Ekanetraka; || 4 ||
O Guha, one should worship these— Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīka, and Śikhaṇḍaka— at the edge of the pedestal in the first enclosure.
Bhava, Śarva, and likewise Uśāna; then Paśupati, Rudra, Bhūta, and likewise Bhīma; Mahāsena shall be the eighth.
One should constantly worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in the second enclosure:
Mahādeva, Śiva, Rudra, Śaṅkara, and Nīlalohita. (7)
Īśāna, Vijaya, Bhīma, Devadeva, Bhavodbhava,
and Kapālīśa— these are to be known as the eleven Rudras who are traditionally remembered. (8)
O child, O Guha, one should worship on the seat in the second enclosure;
O Six-faced One, one should worship the lords of the Gaṇas outside the temple.
Umā, Caṇḍeśa, Nandīśa, Mahākāla, Vṛṣa, Gaṇapati, Bhṛṅgīśa, and Subrahmaṇya shall be the Gaṇas. (10)
In the fourth enclosure, one should worship these [deities] individually with perfumes and flowers;
O child, in the fifth enclosure is the worship of the twelve Ādityas.
Vaikartana, Vivasvat, Martanda, Bhaskara, Ravi, Lokaprakāśaka, Lokasākṣin, and Trivikrama. || 12 ||
Āditya, as well as Sūrya, Aṃśumālī, and Divākara—
the wise man should worship these twelve Ādityas on the exterior of that [mandala].
One should worship the touch of the sky, fire, taste, and earth; as well as the moon, the sun, the self of peace, and the eight Vasus.
The vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, as well as the goad, the mace, the trident, the discus, and the lotus, respectively. || 15 ||
Gabhasti, Sparśana, Vāṭī, Nīla, Marut, Prāṇa, Prāṇeśa, and Jīveśa—these are remembered as the eight Maruts. (16)
And in the ninth enclosure, one should worship the eight Gandharvas:
Citrasena, Mahāsena, Sumitra, and the one known as Sumukha. (17)
Viśvāvasu, Sugādhi, Svarajña, and Pañcabhītaka—
one should indeed place these Cāraṇas as the Lord in the eleventh enclosure.
Khagacārī, Sucārī, Brahmagā, and the best knower of Brahman (Brahmavittama);
Śāśvata, Sarvagopuṣṭa, and Supuṣṭa is considered the eighth. (19)
In the twelfth enclosure, eight rows of Siddhas are indeed to be worshipped:
the knower of mantras, the knower of Brahman, the wise one, and those honored by Haṃsa, Rāma, and the Siddhas. || 20 ||
One should worship these eight: Siddhavat, Paramasiddha, and so forth;
and in the thirteenth enclosure, one should worship the eight Yakṣeśas.
The Lord of Yakṣas, Dhanada, Jambhala, Maṇibhadraka, Pūrṇabhadra, Vimala, and also Ḍivikuṇḍima; || 22 ||
And indeed, O dear one, Narendra should worship eight yakṣas:
Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and likewise Ārkoṭaka; || 23 ||
One should worship Padma, Mahāpadma, Gulaka, and Śaṅkhapālaka in the fourteenth enclosure with perfumes and flowers. (24)
In the fifteenth enclosure, one should worship Virajānanda;
[and] Virāja, Kinnarajña, Śūrasena, and Pramardaka. || 25 ||
Atiśaya, Supraja, Gīta, and Gītajña shall be the eighth;
O child, one should worship these eight Vidyādharas on the sixteenth [day]. (26)
And in the seventeenth enclosure, one should worship the Hayagrīvas:
Hayagrīva, Mahājambha, and the mighty Kālanemi. || 27 ||
Sugrīva, Mardaka, Piśitāṅga, and Devamardaka—these are the [deities] in the eighteenth enclosure; one should worship eight sages there.
Agastya, Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, Manu, Kāśyapa, Nārada, Upamanyu, and Ruru are indeed to be honored with perfumes and flowers. (29)
Ūrvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Tilottamā,
Sumukhī, Sundarī, Kaundakī, and Kāmavardhanī. (30)
In the nineteenth enclosure, one should worship the eight Apsarases;
in the twentieth enclosure, O child, one should worship the eight Asuras.
Bala, Jambala, Subala, Bhābala, Devaśatru, Indraśatru, Viṣṇuśatru, and Sukaṇṭaka. || 32 ||
Thus, in the twenty-fold enclosure, there are eight Śaktis beginning with Strī;
they are Śrīdevī, Dhāriṇī, Durgā, and Sarasvatī. (33)
One should worship Gāyatrī, Uṣas, Gaṅgā, and Śamī—these eight—as well as Prabhā, Sandhyā, Medhā, Svadhā, Svāhā, and Vaṣaṭkṛtā. || 34 ||
Śruti and Smṛti—these eight are to be worshipped; such is the arrangement of twenty-two.
In the twenty-third enclosure, one should worship the twelve zodiac signs (rāśis). || 35 ||
The wise practitioner should worship the eight planets— Soma, Aṅgāraka, Budha, Jīva, Śukra, and Śanaiścara— in the twenty-third enclosure.
O child, one should worship Rāhu and Ketu with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
in the twenty-fourth enclosure, one should worship the twelve zodiac signs.
Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and Leo;
Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, and Capricorn. (38)
O child, Kumbha and Mīna are indeed to be worshipped with auspicious perfumes and other offerings;
one should worship the Nakṣatras and the Mātṛkās in the twenty-fifth enclosure.
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, as well as Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, and Āśleṣā; || 40 ||
In the twenty-sixth enclosure, one should worship the eight [deities] beginning with Makha;
[these are] Mahā, Pūrvaphalgunī, and Uttarāphalgunī. (41)
Hasta, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, and Anurādhā;
O Guha, one should worship Jyeṣṭhā and the others within the twenty-seventh enclosure.
Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and likewise Uttarāṣāḍhā;
Śravaṇa, Śraviṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣak, and also Pūrvaproṣṭhapadā. || 43 ||
One should worship Uttarā Proṣṭhapadā and Pauṣṇa;
in the twenty-eighth enclosure, one should sacrifice to the eight lords of the Pramathas.
Jvara, Kuṇḍodara, the mighty Śaṅkukarṇa, Jihvāśikha, Śikhājihva, Pādākṣa, and Akṣapādaka; || 45 ||
Pretajit alone, as a Pramatha, [subdues] eight crores of sovereign kings—
whether by groups of one, three, five, seven, nine, or sixteen.
