In whatever manner they are, those twenty-eight great-souled ones who have become Rudras are to be worshipped as supreme; for indeed, there are eight crores of them upon this earth.
Piśācas, hosts of pretas, ucchuṣmas, and likewise rākṣasas;
devagrahas, kaumāras, ḍākinīs, and likewise pūtanas. || 48 ||

One should offer oblations upon the seat of the spirits (bhūtapīṭha) to those dwelling in heaven, the atmosphere, on earth, and in the depths of the netherworld, using their respective names preceded by "svāhā" in every case.
In the third enclosure on the outside, one should worship the Mothers to the south:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī.
One should worship Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍī, and the lords of the Gaṇas,
together with Vīrabhadra, with perfumes and flowers.
One should offer incense, lamps, and oblations, worshipping with a well-composed mind;
outside all the enclosures, one should worship the eight Kṣetrapālas. (52)
Tālajaṅgha, Lohajaṅgha, as well as Parvatajaṅghaka, Samudraghoṣa, Vāyughoṣa, Analākṣa, and Pramardana. || 53 ||
Sughoradaṃṣṭra—these eight, holding staffs in their hands, were most terrifying; they resembled dark blue clouds and carried various weapons in their hands. (54)
One should worship the Kṣetrapālas outside the enclosure wall; they have hair standing on end, blood-red eyes, and are of terrifying and fearsome form. || 55 ||
In this manner, by means of the prescribed ritual of worship, one should purify the temple;
one should smear it with cow dung there and wash both feet and hands.
Having sipped water according to the rule, one should commence the fire-rite;
in this very sequence of procedure, one should perform the oblation with a concentrated mind.
One should undertake meditative concentration (samādhi), recitation (japa), hymn-singing (stotra), and circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa);
according to one's capacity, there should be meditative concentration endowed with the eight limbs of yoga.
The wise one should recite the Prāsāda mantra either one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times, and should also perform the mental worship.

One should perform the recitation of the divine (daivika), the rishi-composed (ārṣaka), and the Thousand Names (sahasranāma) and other such hymns as much as one's capacity allows, and likewise perform circumambulation.
In the case of a liṅga, the rite of circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa) should be performed by moving both to the left and to the right;
however, in the case of a temple (prāsāda), one should avoid the path to the left.
Now, the eight-limbed prostration is concentrated in thirty-three [parts];
or else, the prostration may consist of twenty-one or sixteen [parts].
One should perform ten prostrations to the gods in each of the ten directions; eightfold prostrations to the sages, and three prostrations to human beings. (63)
With a concentrated mind, one should perform prostrations with the staff-like body toward the ten directions;
one should perform them three times in front while recollecting the six-syllable mantra.
O Piśāca, you who have well taken refuge in the abode of the gods of gods and men—bow down three times with your chest and your head! (65)
O child, prostration performed with the eyes, speech, the intellect, the throat, the nose, and indeed with both hands, is called the eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga) salutation.
With a concentrated mind, one should offer [these] at the lotus-feet of the God;
with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and with flowers and water, one should present each offering separately.
Having offered all this, one should then offer oneself;
one should offer [these] at the base of the feet with water scented with camphor and flowers. 68.
Afterwards, being composed, one should dismiss the deity with the Īśa mantra, [granting him] permission to depart.
(Here there is a gap in the text) Having placed the two hands palms-upward, one should perform the *veṇibandha* (the flute-binding gesture). || 70 ||
O God, having then extended the two index fingers, one should perform the mudrā of Tatpuruṣa;
having placed the hands with palms upward, one should form the bamboo-joint (veṇibandha) gesture.
Then, O Six-faced One, having extended two hands in the añjali gesture, one should bend the other two.
The wise know this to be the mudrā of mendicancy (bhaikṣamudrā), either on the right or on the left;
having made the right hand bent and extended it, O Six-faced One. (73)
(50) This shall be the village seal, which accomplishes all desires and aims;
and that seal, O child, as well as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) among the twice-born. 74.
For a Śūdra, however, the Antyajas are never placed in the left hand;
rather, both hands should be turned upward and joined together with the palms touching one another.
The middle and index fingers should be concealed, as well as the little and ring fingers;
then, having extended both thumbs, this is proclaimed as the Surabhi-mudrā.
Having placed the two palms face upward, with the thumbs positioned between [the fingers],
one should extend the fingers of the hands while keeping them slightly curved.
This is the grain-mudrā (dhānyamudrā), which increases all grains;
it is formed by placing both hands palm-upward, [touching] the joints of the fingers. (78)
When the tips are slightly bent, these are proclaimed as the *udaka-mudrās*.
Having placed both hands palm-upward, [the thumbs and index fingers]—both the thumbs and the two index fingers—[are joined]. (79)
Indeed, having formed their fists, these are proclaimed as the food mudrās:
the ghee mudrā, the curd mudrā, the milk mudrā, and likewise the curd [mudrā]. (80)
Extending both hands from the index finger to the little finger, they should face each other;
the right thumb and index finger should be slightly bent, as should the left thumb.
The mudrā for the rosary, however, is used at the time of recitation and for rites of desire;
it is the lotus mudrā, with both thumbs placed upon the two feet in that same manner. 82.

Having raised [the hands] upward, O child, one should perform the installation with the *maya* [mudrā]; the cessation is by means of the fist, and the presence is by means of the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*).
The Visarga and the Astra-mudrā may be performed both together or as one alone;
having placed the two hands palms upward, one should bring them together and join them evenly.
The *stambha-mudrā* is formed by placing the hands on the opposite sides and then throwing them upward;
the *japa-mudrā*, however, the mantra-practitioner should cast those [hands] upward. (85)
The two thumbs joined with the two index fingers are proclaimed as the golden mudrā;
the joining of the middle finger and the thumb is proclaimed as the silver mudrā. || 86 ||
The copper mudrās are proclaimed as those in which the thumb and ring finger are joined;
the mudrās of the diamond, ruby, emerald, and pearl are likewise proclaimed. (87)
Extending the fingers from the index to the little finger while the thumbs are bent,
one should then extend both fists and release the mantra for the inexhaustible [offering].
When the thumb is pressed between [the fingers] and the remaining [fingers] are then extended, this becomes the *paśumudrā*, as well as for offerings such as lotus flowers. (89)
Having concealed the little finger and the thumb, listen next to the lamp-mudrā:
one should press down on the little, ring, and middle fingers with the thumb.
Having placed the index finger upwards, one should display the lamp mudrā;
having turned both hands palms-upward, one should likewise extend both [thumbs and index fingers] as "adorners. 91.
The knower of mantras, having joined all the fingers together with the mantras, should perform the offering mudrā and indeed display it during the food offering (naivedya). || 92 ||
The two hands should be joined in the añjali gesture, slightly curved;
the mudrā consists of the right [hand] and the thumbs bound together as one.
This shall be the mudrā of reclining; one should display it at the time of sleep.
It is the characteristic sign for those of little strength, such as piśācas, serpents, cūnas, and the like.
O Six-faced One, the wise one [should place] the left thumb at the base of the little finger. || 95 ||
On the right, the index finger itself [is used] when one is agitated by desire regarding what should be heard;
it is taught that [this applies] in all cases concerning the wives of others. (96)
With the two middle fingers merged into the thumbs, this is the Treasure Mudrā (nidhimudrā), which accomplishes all desires. || 97 ||
For the lotus mudrā, one should press the thumb into the lotus-treasure;
indeed, one should press all the fingers together quite evenly. || 98 ||
This should remain a secret and must not be disclosed.
The Yoni-mudrā brings delight to Umā; the Padma-mudrikā brings delight to Śrī. (99)
Having turned the two hands palms-upward, one should form fists starting from the little fingers. || 100 ||
By pressing from the thumb up to the wind-finger (the index finger), it becomes the *pustaka-mudrā*.
O Six-faced One, when the thumbs are placed together with the other fingers [extended], it is the *karāla* [mudrā].
This shall be the Earth Mudrā; it accomplishes all stages (bhūmis). There should be a movement from below all the fingers of the hands. || 102 ||
Having placed the two hands palm-upward, one should extend the two middle fingers. || 103 ||
For the remaining [fingers], one should indeed clench the fist and conceal the thumbs within;
this shall be the fire-mudrā (agnimudrā), which burns even all enemies. 104.
The wise one should press the left thumb with the right thumb;
this shall be the Vāyu-mudrā, which effects all [attainments]. || 105 ||
The Gaganamudrās are proclaimed for both hands;
the thumbs and index fingers should be in the shape of a coil. (106)
Having indeed formed a fist with the remaining [fingers], one should display the ear-seal (karṇamudrā);
having extended both the middle and index fingers, one should bind the rest. || 107 ||
This shall be the Ghrāṇamudrā; it brings mastery over all the winds.
The wise one should then move the tongue and move both hands. 108.
This is the *jihvāmudrā*; by it, one obtains food along with ghee and other delicacies.
Having placed the two hands palms-upward and joined them closely together with each other... (109)
The finger [mudrās] are proclaimed as the Dharma-mudrās; having raised the fingers upward and extended them, one should bind the thumbs together. 110.
This shall be the hand-gesture (pāṇimudrā): having made both hands wrapped, turned upward, level, and joined together with one another. 111.
One should cast the two [hands] downward and display the foot-seal;
having placed both hands face upward, with the palms facing backward. (112)
Having caused the tongue to vibrate upwards and downwards, one then causes it to move about;
this is the Vāṅmudrā, which accomplishes all that pertains to speech. || 113 ||
Having formed a fist with both hands, the practitioner should join the index fingers and thumbs;
O Guha, one who desires offspring should display this mudrā of the testicles and genitals.
One should press the left and right earrings with the thumb;
this is the *gudamudrā*, by which one may discharge feces, urine, and so forth. || 115 ||
O Guha, one should always employ the thumb and the index finger;
by encircling and pointing them out, one should display the mudrā of death.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell—just as these [are the objects], so too should the two hands be employed; therein the mudrās are proclaimed.
Having pressed together the thumbs and the index fingers at the [tip of the] nose, this is the mudrā of the ego; one should display it above one's own body. (118)
Having repeatedly raised the hands toward the sky, the wise man should bind the two thumbs with clay; thus he shall become great. 119.
The thumb should be positioned for the *sattvika* [mudrā], while the middle fingers and others are for the *rājasa*;
the *tāmasī* mudrā is proclaimed by [the positioning of] the index fingers (*tarjanī*). || 120 ||
Having placed the two hands palm upwards, they should be interlaced;
with the thumbs at the base of the other fingers, this is proclaimed as the Prakṛti-mudrā.
Having placed the two hands palm upwards, one should extend the two thumbs;
by this fivefold mudrā are represented Passion (rāga), Illusion (māyā), Knowledge (vidyā), Limited Agency (kalā), and Necessity (niyati).
Having extended the fingers from the thumb to the little finger, these mudrās are performed in successive order.
Vigraheśa, [and] * * * * * la, as well as Śuddhamāyā, Śuddhavidyā, and Śuddhakalā; the little finger (kaniṣṭhā) is extended. || 124 ||
The wise one should always form a fist with the remaining fingers everywhere;
the Śivamudrā for Sadāśiva is that which was previously extended.
The Ādityabimba-mudrā should be like a hand-clenched fist;
one should display the liṅga-mudrā to all the eleven Rudras.
The Liṅga-mudrā extends to the space between the breasts, while the Śūla-mudrā belongs to the guardians of the images (mūrtipās).
The mudrā for Gaṇeśa is the gesture of salutation (namaskāra), and that for the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśās) is the trident (śūlatā).

The world-protectors (*lokapālas*) should each display their own respective *svāstika* mudrās; likewise, one should display the respective weapons of the seven groups of mothers (*mātṛgaṇas*). || 128 ||
The perfected Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, hosts of Maruts, Kinnaras, Asuras,
Rākṣasas, Garuḍas, Apsarases, and Cāraṇas as well. (129)
Salutation is prescribed for the bhūtas, piśācas, and kṣetrapālas;
likewise for the specific liṅga-mudrā, the wives of the ṛṣis, and the ṛṣis as well. (130)

The *namaskāramudrā*, the *liṅgamudrā*, and the supreme *mudrā* in every respect—thus ends the thirteenth chapter, on the characteristics of the *mudrās*, in the *Kālottara*, the compendium of thirty thousand verses. 13.
The Blessed Lord said: I shall now describe the procedure for the mandala in its proper sequence.
The earth of a Brāhmaṇa is white, while that of a Kṣatriya is indeed red. || 1 ||
For a Vaiśya, earth that has been ploughed is recommended; for a Śūdra, black soil is praised.
The land of a Brāhmaṇa should be sweet, while that of a Kṣatriya should be astringent.
That [scent] of Vaiśva is to be known as such; for a Śūdra, it is recorded as being like the smell of a water-jar (karakā).
For a Brāhmaṇa, it has the fragrance of clarified butter (ājyagandhā), while for a Kṣatriya, it has the fragrance of blood (raktagandhā).
The [womb] of a Vaiśya has the smell of urine, while that of a Śūdra smells like excrement;
likewise, it has the smell of a wound and a particular taste—one should recognize these by such characteristics. || 4 ||
One indeed attains all accomplishments and whatever desired siddhis one seeks;
one should dig the ground to the depth of a cubit and fill it back with the excavated earth.
Where the dust is abundant, that ground grants all desires;
where the dust is moderate, it is middling; and where it is even less, it becomes inferior and lowly.
Having dug a pit measuring one bow in depth and five or seven spans in width,
O Guha, one should remove the ashes, charcoal, husks, hair, and bones.
The wise preceptor should pour the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) into that copper vessel,
and he should pour the five red substances there with the root mantra.
Having indeed covered the hearth (dhiṣṇya) with darbha grass, one should properly commence [the rite];
it should be square on all sides and resemble the surface of a mirror. || 9 ||
On Kailāsa or Mandara, on Niṣadha or the Nīla mountain, on Himavat, Hemakūṭa, Vindhya, and Pāriyātraka; || 10 ||

On Mount Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śrīśaila, or Svāmiparvata, or in their respective sacred fires, the wise man should perform [the rite], or he may have it performed at a holy pilgrimage site (tīrtha).
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, one should establish a very beautiful sacrificial site;
or one may do so on either side of those two, or even at the Sarayū or the Gaṇḍakī.
It may be near the Gomatī, or in Kurukṣetra, or at the bank of the Sarasvatī, or at the bank of the Dṛṣadvatī. (13)
Either near the Godāvarī, or on the bank of the Narmadā, or on the shore of a sacred field, or in Vārāṇasī, or indeed at Badaryāśrama. (14)
Either in Ujjayinī, or in Bhairava, or likewise in Virajā, or in the Devadāru forest, or in Naimiṣa, or even at Puṣkara; || 15 ||
One should commence the sacrifice at Gokarṇa, or at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), or on its bank or nearby, or in a holy grove, or in a cow-pen. || 16 ||
Or wherever the ground is delightful, such as on the bank of a large lake, near a temple, or on the shore of a sacred river. || 17 ||
Alternatively, even in a pure house, near a temple of Śiva,
one may construct either a pavilion (*kūṭa*) or a hall (*maṇḍapa*), devoid of internal pillars. (18)
It is provided with four gates, adorned with four archways, covered above with a canopy, and decorated with bells and chowries. || 19 ||
Encircled by a garland of *darbha* grass and adorned with hanging flower garlands, it was rich with the sweet fragrance of a divine land and provided with incense and lamps. || 20 ||
It was strewn with offerings of water and flowers, filled with the recitation of benedictions,
resounding with the blasts of conchs and drums, and accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas.
Then, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should perform the laying of the thread;
one should observe the signs located in the divine, the atmospheric, and the terrestrial realms.
One should extend the thread toward the auspicious [directions] and withdraw it from the inauspicious;
one should first establish the primary thread in the east and then extend it toward the west.
One should construct the third [line] in the southwest and extend it toward the northeast;
having made it square and even, one should draw the excellent lotus.
One should have stakes driven into the ground there on all sides in the nine directions;
one should make the stakes of khadira wood, or those produced from the cūta, bilva, and kadamba trees.
The seat should be made of Madhūka wood, Devadāru, or indeed Śarva wood;
its height is sixteen finger-breadths, and half of that is said to be its width.
The tip should be made sharp, and one should perform the upward vow;
one should mark the drop for as far as the extent of the maṇḍala. || 27 ||
Having thus performed the ritual procedure, O Guha, one should draw the mandala upon the platform: first the center of the pericarp, and second the filaments.
The fourth [line] of the petals should be with the third; then,
having wound the *prativāraṇa*, one should thereafter wind the *pīcīs*.
One should subsequently fashion the doors, and from that, the beauty shall arise;
the *upaga* and the *śobhā* are not as many [as some claim], and thereafter one should draw the mandala.
White, red, black, green, and yellow—
these are declared to be the five types of dust, provided with the five jewels.
Rice and wheat flour mixed with pearl powder, as well as ruby powder along with the powders of red ochre and brick; || 32 ||
With the powder of sapphire, with the powders of husks and charcoal, with the powder of emerald, and with the powder of bilva leaves. (33)
One should recognize that which is yellow in color as being made from ruby powder mixed with turmeric powder; it is proclaimed to be of five colors.
The king should have the mandala drawn with powders of the five jewels;
the wise man should have the rest of the mandala drawn using mixed colors.
First, one should draw an excellent lotus with white color;
furthermore, the wise man should draw it with eight petals using white powder. (36)
The pericarp is on the yellow path, while the filaments are colored with red;
at their base they are white, and their tips are indeed red.
One should fashion a dust-line with the width of the little finger; within that space, Yama is said to be located, and one should again drop [the line] with Puṣṭi.
O Six-faced One, it should be drawn either white or red; the measurement is three *prativāraṇas*, and the interval between them should be two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The pathways should be drawn with four lines using jeweled powder; having delineated the four doors, one should draw a single *śobhā* outside. (40)
O Six-faced One, one should draw pathways all around with five colors; one should also depict the Prābala and other highly beautiful varieties of creepers.
The lotus should be one cubit in measure according to the prescribed rule, and likewise in its width;
the gateway, however, should be one span, and it may be either green or yellow.
One cubit, two cubits, or likewise four;
or eight, twelve, sixteen, or twenty cubits.
It may be thirty cubits, or even more than that; one should not make it larger. Having drawn the sixteenth petal, it should be yellow in color.
One should draw [the lotus] with sixty-four petals, or one hundred and eight;
furthermore, one should draw as many petals as there are cubits in the extent of the lotus.
Then, O God, one should invoke the five [deities]...
just as in the ritual worship, so too in the external location. || 46 ||
In that manner, O Mahāsena, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and incense,
beginning from a single enclosure up to a hundred enclosures.
O Six-faced One, just as it has been shown in the twenty-eight enclosures,
so too should one worship in the mandala according to the prescribed rite.
Thereafter, one should offer the *caru* as before, preceded by the recitation of mantras;
having offered half of it to Śiva, the wise one should then perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the remaining half.
One should cause those who have fasted to give half of that [to the preceptor];
first, indeed, a tooth-stick measuring twelve finger-breadths [should be given]. 50.
The wise practitioner should cause a *pippala*, a *vaṭa* tree, or even a *khadira* tree to be offered; having recited the *aghorāstra* mantra, he should cause it to be consumed. (51)
Having sipped water according to the rule, one should then mutter the mantra over the mouth;
thereafter, one should offer the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) consecrated with the Īśāna mantra.
O child, the number of arrows shall be determined; having sipped water repeatedly, one should cause them to be given.
There may be thirty-two fire-pits, or sixteen, or twelve. (53)
Or eight, or according to the number of Vedas, or as many as the digits of the moon for those who are poor;
one should have the sacrificial pit (homakuṇḍa) constructed according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, plakṣa, and nyagrodha; likewise bilva, udumbara, śasya, vaikaṅkata, and śamī. || 55 ||
The *upāmārga* has been explained; now the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) are fully described:
fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, sesame seeds, *mālī* flowers, and mustard seeds. (56)
One who has reached the further shore of the practice should offer various kinds of barley and edible foods there;
O child, one should perform ten times that number of oblations for Śiva, the Supreme Self. (57)
One should perform the fire-oblation for the Lords of Knowledge and all the Rudras with the number of elements (five);
and for the Gaṇeśas and the World-Protectors, one should perform the oblation with the number of qualities (three).
O Guha, one should indeed offer a single oblation with each respective mantra;
and there, to the south of the mandala, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) for the disciples.
Having arranged nine jars, one should place the nine gems within them;
they should be provided with cloths, lids, and *kūrca* grass-bunches, and wrapped with threads.
They should be placed upon a heap of grain, filled with sandalwood water;
one who has undertaken the practice of darbha grass should remain intent on meditation upon Śiva.
p.
61) "Having recited [the mantra] over a young boy while dreaming, one should sleep at night together with the Guru.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the Ritual of the Maṇḍala, in the *Kālottara*, the Compendium of Thirty Thousand Verses. 14.
Īśvara said:
O Ṣaṇmukha, listen as I explain the path of dreams according to their true nature.
A dream occurring in the first watch of the night bears fruit in three years. || 1 ||
By the second [practice], ripening occurs in two [years]; in the third as well, it occurs within one year;
but in the final watch, O child, success is certain within six months.
If one practices at dawn for twelve days, success will be attained on the fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight;
if one practices at the time of the dawn's first light, one shall attain perfection within seven days.
One might see a raft upon turbid water in a river or even in a lake;
having bathed in that great water and reached the further shore, one awakens.
In a dream, the wise man may obtain wealth and grain in a great body of water,
or he may see a lotus, a blue water-lily, a nandyāvarta flower, or a jasmine.
Or likewise, one who sees jasmine or *vakuḷa* garlands, or various objects, or even a cow, at the end of a dream, shall experience fear. (6)
Whether he obtains a boar, or even a deer, or a parrot, or a myna bird,
upon waking up, his household shall prosper.
But for those who experience the touch of a white serpent on the right arm,
there shall be a gain of a thousandfold, or else an excellent son is born.
Mounting bulls, elephants, palaces, mountain peaks, and trees;
being smeared with excrement; and [encountering] blood and a corpse. (p. 62)
And having sexual intercourse with a woman who is forbidden is meritorious in dreams. || 9 ||
If one sees an elephant in a dream, or having found one, wakes up,
he shall obtain great wealth and receive honor from the king.
If one should wake up having found a bull, or even a lotus flower,
or even a cock in a dream, one should predict the acquisition of land.
Whether it be a beautiful tree in bloom, bearing fruit, or even ripe;
when it is in bloom, one should act when it is in bloom, and when it has borne fruit, the result shall be fruit.
One should recognize that which is ripe as ripe; if one sees a great field of ripened śāli rice at the end of a dream, it is an auspicious sign of visible results. (13)
Within ten days, one will undoubtedly obtain rice that is very easy to acquire—
whether it be fragrant rice (gandhaśāli), great rice (mahāśāli), or even kalama-rice.
But he who, at the end of a dream, sees his own well-favored cow, his lifespan shall increase; this is the truth, O Six-faced One. (15)
If a large monkey, a cricket, or a snake is seen, one prospers with wealth, grain, and excellent sons, as well as with sons and grandsons. || 16 ||
Whoever sees this at the end of a dream, his poverty shall perish;
likewise, seeing a beautiful, well-scented cow with her calf at the end of a dream. (15)
"O Six-faced One, it is true that his lifespan would increase;
for he beholds a monkey, a jubīka, or a serpent appearing large. (16)
He who sees silver or even gold at the end of a dream increases in wealth, grain, and excellent sons, as well as in sons and grandsons. (17)
By worshipping either Devajña or Bhūdhara in one's home, one shall swiftly obtain wealth;
there is a gain of a hundredfold from the foot alone, and a thousandfold when the arms are consumed [in the ritual]. (18)
Then, by means of Puṣkara, he offered him milk-rice mixed with ghee.
O auspicious lady, one should know that he who was formerly seated in the city as the lord of the earth,
having likewise become [the ruler] of the palace and of the seals (mudrās), is that very person.
Those who are always born into that family attain kingship;
they see the solar disc or even consume it. || 21 ||
By seeing it, one obtains a kingdom; by eating it, prosperity is attained.
Whether seen or eaten at the end of a dream, [the fruit is the same] regarding the lunar disc.
By seeing it one obtains wealth; by eating it one may obtain a kingdom.
Or if, in a dream, one drinks liquor or drinks blood. (23)
The Brāhmaṇa shall become learned, and the Kṣatriya shall obtain wealth, if he floats upon the river of blood, floating indeed in the blood. (24)
A man attains great wealth or obtains a kingdom;
or else he may even see, eat, or smear himself with impure substances. (25)
In the case of seeing [the deity], one gains a small benefit; in the case of anointing, one obtains a hundredfold;
through eating [the offerings], a thousandfold is obtained, and at the end of a dream, one attains success.
By drinking milk, one removes disease; by holding it [in the mouth], death is destroyed;
by drinking curd, one attains a kingdom; and by drinking buttermilk, great fear arises. (27)
He who sees either a bone, or a shackle, or even a cotton seed at the end of a dream, shall suffer from a great disease.
A woman wearing red garments, anointed with red perfumes and unguents,
bearing red garlands, and dark in complexion, is stationed at the region of the feet. (29)
If one who is healthy contracts a disease, or if one already afflicted by disease meets with death,
he shall be led toward the southern direction mounted upon a chariot yoked with donkeys.
Within a month one meets death; this is the truth, O Six-faced One.
Having put on red garments and being adorned with red garlands and unguents, [one should proceed]. (31)
If one who is healthy contracts a disease, or if one who is diseased meets death; || 32 ||
If a crow suddenly settles on one's head in a dream, one meets death within a month; this is the truth, O Six-faced One.
An owl, a deer-hunter, a donkey, or even a hawk;
or one who eats [the flesh] from the head in a dream... || 34 ||
If one's teeth break and fall onto the palm of the hand, he meets death within a month, as if struck by a great disease.
If he sees his side-teeth falling to the ground,
or his mother, father, kinsmen, sons, or dearest friends [falling likewise], || 36 ||
If a widow covers her garment with a soiled cloth, she will suffer from a great disease or incur the loss of wealth. (37)
Whoever sees a follower of Śakti, a Kṣapaṇaka, or one who has renounced the world and observes vows at the end of a dream, his death is certain; of this there is no doubt. (38)
A Brāhmaṇa with flowers in his hand, or likewise a Śaiva Ācārya, adorned with all ornaments, red in complexion, and highly auspicious. (39)
(He who sees [this] at the end of a dream, for him death is certain, there is no doubt;
but he who sees [it] at the end of a dream shall attain great prosperity.)
All fruits are recommended, but one should avoid the palmyra fruit. || 40 ||
Jewel-like flowers are recommended; indeed, one shall obtain all that is auspicious. However, one should avoid the flowers of the *kiṃśuka* and the *karavīra*. (41)
O Six-faced One, all white flowers are recommended;
however, one should avoid the dhurdhūra there, as well as the white girikarṇikā.
Everything black, however, should be avoided; sesame seeds and snakes, on the other hand, bestow nourishment.
Green is middling, yellow is mediocre, and black is said to be the lowest.
Among men, the Brāhmaṇa is the best; one should designate the king as the middlemost.
Among all birds as well, the parrot and the swan are praised. (44)
Among all wild animals, the lion is the best;
among all domestic animals, the cow, the bull, and the goat are auspicious. (45)
Among all reptiles, the white snake is most highly praised;
so too are fragrant substances, flowers, fruits, products of the cow, auspicious garments, and ornaments.
One should predict that the wealth of whoever sees these at the end of a dream— kodrava, mung beans, black pepper, and minerals— is not auspicious.
In a dream, one may see a coconut fruit, or even a plantain fruit, or a pomegranate, a citron, or a jackfruit or a mango. (48)
But he who sees at the end of a dream Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Guha, or the guardians of the world (Lokapālas), shall obtain wealth and grain. (49)
He who sees sages, or even apsarases, or the wives of the gods at the end of a dream, shall obtain wealth, long life, and fame. (50)
If one sees these [omens] at the time of sleep, or with the wives of the gods,
his family prospers at the conclusion of that dream.
He who sees a tiger, or even a buffalo, or a seer, or a thief at the end of his sleep, shall suffer oppression from the king. (52)
He who sees in the end of a dream being struck with blows from fists or even being killed by weapons shall incur a great disease.
But in a dream, O King, if one sees being oppressed by men and so forth, there will be illness, or loss of wealth, or departure abroad. (54)
If one obtains sandals or shoes even at the end of a dream,
there will be a journey for him, or else there will be suffering.
Whether it be clothing or ornaments, weapons, wealth, or grain;
fruits, flowers, food, drink, and other such household requisites—|| 56 ||
But he who sees this at the end of a dream shall encounter suffering;
he shall be bound with a noose and even with fetters by the king's command. (57)
From the binding of hair, one incurs imprisonment;
from that same act, one immediately incurs disease and shall enter a prison cell.
If one obtains meat or even fish in a dream, it will be auspicious;
however, from eating them, one incurs suffering, or one should cause [the patient] to drink barley-grain water.
If one dreams of anointing oneself with oil or [entering] a womb, one will contract a great disease or even drown in the ocean. (60)
If one drinks turbid water or even bathes in a pool of snakes during a dream,
that person is immediately freed from disease and becomes healthy once again. (61)
Whether at a well, a pond, a pit, a cave, or even on a mountain, one should strike when it is full; however, one should avoid doing so with the left hand.
He incurs a great disease or even imprisonment;
having ascended a high mound adorned with white garlands of flowers. (63)
His family shall increase and he shall indeed constantly attain prosperity;
whether it be a rampart, a drink-hall, an assembly hall, or a garden-house, [he shall obtain it].
By prostrating with the head, one attains inexhaustible prosperity; by [prostrating] with the rain-like [body], one obtains elephants, herds of horses, or even groups of men. (65)
Or if one sees a multitude of weapons, he shall obtain rain;
a man outside [the ritual area] should cause [the dreamer] to hear of a bad dream, while one inside should cause him to perceive a good dream.
If it is auspicious, one should enter the initiation; if inauspicious, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa).
Furthermore, if in a dream one sees a black cow, a boat, or eats a young girl.
If one sees a widow, or even a woman adorned with ornaments, or a naked woman at the end of a dream, there will be a loss of wealth and grain. (68)
If one voids excrement or even voids urine in a dream, O child, from excrement there is loss of wealth, and from urine there will be loss of grain. (69)
Having made the sound "huṃ," one who dreams of rice mixed with ghee in a fine golden vessel at the end of sleep increases their lifespan, prosperity, and fame. (70)
"O King, O God, [the fruit] of Brahmā...
praised... the gain is indeed... thus, in the Kālottara, the fifteenth chapter on Dreams. || 15 ||
The illustrious Lord said:
I shall proclaim the ritual procedure for initiation; listen, O Six-faced One, according to the truth:
[to those who are] adorned with mudrās, bathed, purified, and have conquered their senses.
Having bound the eyes with a *dukūla* silk cloth, one should cause [the disciple] to enter;
or else with a cotton cloth that is white and smooth. (2)
If it is worn out, cracked, or burnt, death will occur;
if it produces no reflection, death will come; if it bears fruit, one shall incur disease.
Therefore, with every effort, one should bind it with an auspicious cloth.
One should have it fashioned with golden flowers, joined with lotus flowers,
and with a hundred-petaled flower, or even with half of that.
Alternatively, one should have it fashioned from thirty *parṇa* measures of gold;
with the *Īśāna* mantra alone, one should cast a flower into the hollowed palms.
Having performed three circumambulations with a single-minded focus, the wise man,
having meditated upon the Lord of the gods, should cast a flower while remaining composed.
Upon whichever mantra the flower falls, that mantra— characterized by the name and lineage [of the recipient]—
is mastered by him, or else it bestows its grace.
Having touched [the disciple] with water and with ashes using the Aghora-weapon mantra,
and having sprinkled them upon the head of the disciple, one should then worship him with perfumes and other offerings.
Having placed Īśāna on the head, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face;
having placed Aghora on the heart, one should place Vāma on the private parts.
One should place Sadyojāta on the feet, placing it along with its respective syllables;
having placed Hṛdaya on the heart, one should place Śiras on the head at the junction of the three. (10)
Having placed the *śikhā* on the crest-lock, the *kavaca* between the breasts, and the *astra* on the regions of the hands, one should place the *netra* upon each eye. (11)
One should place a seat made of a bunch of *palāśa* leaves upon them,
and install it on the right side of the deity.
Then, O Six-faced One, one should subsequently deposit the worship within the body of the disciple:
the path of mantra, the path of words, and the path of principles consisting of the worlds.
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) and the path of energies (kalādhvan), numbering twenty-one, constitute the state of Śiva.
One should place the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) upon the head and place the path of words (padādhvan) in the mouth.
Having placed the path of principles (tattvādhvan) in the heart, the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) in the region of the navel,
the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) at the base of the genitals, one should place the path of kalās (kalādhvan) in the feet.
The preceptor, however, should perform the path of the digits (kalādhvan) at the two feet with their respective mantras,
[proceeding] from the east, south, west, north, and upwards.
One should collect the five crores of mantras by means of the five mantras;
O child, one should install the five mantras beginning with Vāgbhava.
One should place the path of the words (padādhvan) in the mouth; the wise know this to consist of four points.
One should join it with the five steps by means of the five [faces], beginning with Sadyojāta.

Having assigned the path of the words within the *tatpuruṣa* [mantra], conjoined with their respective Brahmās, one should place the word beginning with *praṇava* in the middle and append the salutation (*namaskāra*). (19)
Having placed the path of the principles (tattvādhvan) within the heart, which indeed consists of the thirty-six principles—namely earth, water, fire, air, and space; || 20 ||
The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose are the five; and speech, the feet, the hands, the anus, and the generative organ are likewise the five. (21)
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
mind, ego, the Great Principle (mahat), primordial nature (prakṛti), and likewise the Spirit (puruṣa). || 22 ||
Passion (rāga), illusion (māyā), knowledge (vidyā), time (kāla), destiny (niyati), and form (vigraha);
then time (kāla) and pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā), and finally the pure Sadāśiva is supreme. (23)
O child, one should deposit the thirty-six principles (tattvas) in their proper sequence;
then, one should dissolve the twenty-eight worlds and the sixty-four [elements].
One should conceive of the twenty-one hells, beginning with Kālāgni and Andhakāra, as being situated above the genitals and below the heart.
Raurava, Kumbhīpāka, and Mahāraurava, as well as Kṣuradhāra, Asipatravana, Jāṅgala, and Śītala.
Uṣṇa, Saṃtāpana, and likewise Taptaloha;
Kūṭaśālmalīkūpa, Tilayantra, and Ikṣuyantraka. (27)
The Dhanurnirya, Vajraniraya, Sthala-niraya, Pāṣāṇa, Tapta-pāṃsu, and likewise Taraṇī. || 28 ||
Tala, Vitala, Nitala, Talātala,
Sutala, Mahātala, and Rasātala above them.
The world of the earth (bhūrloka), the world of the atmosphere (bhuvarloka), and likewise the world of the gods (suraloka);
and Maharloka is to be known, as well as Janaloka. || 30 ||
The world of heat (tapaloka), the world of truth (satyaloka), the world of the Gandharvas, the world of the Yakṣas, the world of the Vidyādharas, and the worlds of the Siddhas and Cāraṇas. || 31 ||
And also the world of the Apsarases, the worlds of the Kinnaras,
the world of Indra, the world of Agni, and the worlds of Yama and Nirṛti. (32)
The world of Varuṇa, the world of Vāyu, and likewise the world of Soma;
the world of Īśāna, the world of Brahmā, and beyond that, the world of Viṣṇu. || 33 ||
And the world of Ananteśa, and beyond that the Sūkṣmaloka;
then the world of Śivottama and the world of Ekanetra.
The world of Ekarudra, then beyond that the world of Trimūrti, the world of Śrīkaṇṭha, and beyond that the world of Śikhaṇḍin. || 35 ||
The world of the Vasus, the world of the Moon, and beyond that the world of Pradhāna; then Goloka, the world of the Yogins, and beyond that the Pure World (Śuddhaloka). || 36 ||
They know the world of Maheśvara, the world of Sadāśiva, and indeed the world of Śiva as the supreme among all worlds. || 37 ||
Above the world of Śiva, however, there exists no further world.
[This extends] starting from the root of the navel up to the region of the heart. (38)
O child, one should indeed place sixty-four [syllables] one above the other;
one should then place the Vāgbhava [syllable] in the middle of the body, specifically upon the pericarp.
Upon that, one should place Śiva, the supreme cause, together with the letter *sa*;
and on all the filaments (*kesara*), one should install the sixteen vowels.
Having placed *a* and *ā* in the east, *i* and *ī* indeed in the filaments of Agni;
having placed *u* and *ū* in Yama, and *ṛ* and *ṝ* in the filaments of Nirṛti. (41)
Having assigned Ḷ and Ḹ to the region of Varuṇa, E and Ai to the domain of Vāyu;
O and Au to the region of Soma, and Aṃ and Aḥ to the domain of Īśāna. || 42 ||
Having assigned the *ka*-group to the eastern petal and the *ca*-group to the fire-petal,
one should assign the *ṭa*-group to the southern petal and the *ta*-group to the domain of Nirṛti. (43)
Having assigned the *pa*-group to the western direction (Vāruṇa), the *ya*-group to the domain of Vāyu;
having assigned the *pa*-group to the petal of Vāyu, one should assign the *bha*-group to the direction of Īśa (the northeast).
O child, one should practice this Mṛtyuñjaya-cakra elsewhere than during initiation;
it consists of thirty-nine kalās, extending from the head down to the feet.
Tārā, Sutārā, Ramaṇī, Tārayantī, and Sutāraṇī;
likewise Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti. || 46 ||
Having placed the Nāda in the supreme void beyond Śānti, the knower of reality [recites]:
"Obeisance! Homā, Akṣayā, Nidrā, Mṛtyu, Māyā, Bhayā, Ajayā. (47)
Rajā, Rakṣā, Rati, Pā, Mā, Tṛṣṇā, Mati, Kriyā, Dhṛti, Kāryā, Dhātrī, Grāmaṇī, and likewise Homanī. (48)
Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Yuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Svadhā, and Sthiti—these are indeed the thirty-nine digits (kalās) of the wise God of gods. (49)
O child, one should assign thirteen digits (kalās) beginning with the penis; first the digits of Vāmadeva, and afterwards they should be placed in their respective locations.
One should thus perform the deposition of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) upon the very body of the disciple.
Thus ends the sixteenth [chapter], the Six Paths, in the Kālottara, within the ritual procedure for initiation (dīkṣā). || 16 ||
The illustrious Lord said:
I shall proclaim the initiation of yoga in brief, and not in detail.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space as well. || 1 ||
(73) These five great principles pervade everything; one should abandon [the notion of] them as being separate.
Mantras are indeed the form of mantras, and words are the form of words.
The letters consist of the form of the letters, while the path of the kalās consists of the nature of the kalās;
indeed, the entire world, both stationary and moving, consists of the five elements.
Having placed the earth element at the knees, one should place the water element up to the navel;
having placed the fire element up to the throat, one should place the air element up to the crown of the head.
Having placed the void (vyoma) at the end of the head, the knower of mantras, perceiving through the vision of yoga, should place it with its respective seed-syllable by means of the subtle impeller.
Impelled by means of the divine path of yoga, may they be empowered according to their capacity;
then, by means of the Viṣuva yoga, one should place them in the eternal state.
But through yoga at the equinox, one is liberated from bondage even before the end of the kalpa;
having known this, Mahāsena may initiate even those of low caste (śvapaca). || 7 ||
But he who, without knowing this reality, endeavors to perform initiation, his labor is in vain; he shall certainly not obtain its fruit.
Having worshipped the Lord of each principle (tattva) with perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and the water-offering (arghya), one should likewise worship the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) individually.
Then, one should perform the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception), worshipping each separately;
one should perform the *garbhādhāna* and the *puṃsavana* (rite for a male child) with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and offer oblations (*homayet*).
Having properly visualized Manonmanī, who is in her menses and possesses beautiful eyes, in the center of the yoni,
one should offer fifty oblations.

In this manner, the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) shall be accomplished; then perform the rite for the birth of a male child (puṃsavana) by offering the sixth oblation and worshipping, O Six-faced One.
(74) This indeed shall be the *puṃsavana* rite; perform the *sīmantonnayana* with a lock of hair.
Having offered oblations of ghee on the seventh lunar day, O Guha, let there be the *sīmanta* ceremony. 13.

One should perform the *jātakarman* with the *kavaca* mantra and offer oblations with the eighty [syllables]; the *nāmakarman* with the *astra* mantra, and the *niṣkrāmaṇa* with the *netra* mantra. || 14 ||

One should perform the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) with the Sadyojāta mantra, the tonsure ceremony (caula) with the Īśāna mantra, the initiation (upanayana) with the Puruṣa mantra itself, and observe the vow with the Aghora mantra. 15.
Or, O Six-faced One, one should also cause a marriage with the deity to be performed;
with the Astra-mantra alone, one hundred oblations should be offered during the rite of bringing [the child] forth.
O child, one should offer two hundred oblations in the rite of the first feeding of solid food;
three hundred in the tonsure ceremony, and four hundred in the initiation ceremony.
The wise one should cause one hundred oblations to be offered for each of the seven vows:
the Mahānāndī, the Mahāvrata, the Upaniṣad, and the Godāna.
The fifth is the Maheśavrata, and the sixth is indeed the Sadāśiva;
the seventh is the Śivavrata, which is considered the most excellent among all vows. (19)
But if it is difficult to retain, O Six-faced One, one should perform a hundred oblations for each [instance];
indeed, the Śūdra caste within the body is consumed by fire.
Having established his true Śūdra status, perform the sixteen rites; once he has truly attained the state of a Brāhmaṇa, you may then indeed administer initiation.
Furthermore, one should perform the ritual action ending with the word "namaḥ" according to the prescribed rule;
this includes worship, striking, attracting, and establishing.
Sprinkling, striking, as well as splitting and opening; piercing, joining, and the wandering of the sacrificial animal (paśu). || 23 ||
O Six-faced One, the paralyzing of the nooses as well as their re-establishment must likewise be performed with the Heart-mantra; indeed, every rite is to be done thus. (24)
A garment, a sacred thread, a deerskin, a tooth-stick, a girdle, a turban, a loincloth, and even ashes—these alone [are required]. || 25 ||
One should give the garment and the girdle with the Vāmadeva mantra;
one should cause the sacred thread to be given with the Aghora mantra.
One should cause him to take the tooth-stick with the Tatpuruṣa mantra; the loincloth with the Vāmadeva mantra, and the sacred ash with the Īśa mantra. (27)
One should personally wear a rudrākṣa with the Tatpuruṣa mantra;
a very white one is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, while one that is reddish-brown (kṣauma) is for a Kṣatriya.
Yellow cloth is for the Vaiśya, while cotton is said to be for the Śūdra;
however, O Six-faced One, the sacred thread for a Brāhmaṇa is made of cotton.
The waist-thread of a Vaiśya king should be made of hempen fibers;
the skin of a Brāhmaṇa should be that of a black antelope, while for a king it should be the skin of a tiger.
For a Vaiśya, however, it should be made of a goat-skin; [the width] should be three finger-breadths, two finger-breadths, or one finger-breadth.
Having wrapped the skin around the navel from left to right, the skin itself serves as the sacred thread (upavīta). || 31 ||
One should make the cord tight with one, three, or even five knots;
and having performed the consecration (adhivāsa) for the triad, one should fashion the second sacred thread (upavītaka).

A staff made of *pālāśa* wood is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, while that of a Kṣatriya is made of *khādira*; for a Vaiśya, it should be of *śimā* leaves; one should grant these staves according to the order of the castes.

One should fashion these three [heights]: the elevation of the forehead for a Brahmin reaching as far as the nose; for a Kṣatriya, reaching as far as the throat; and for the Vaiśya caste, reaching as far as the throat. Thus one should determine these three.
(76) This is the duty of the twice-born; he should ordain it for women as well.
For the sake of favoring all women, he should be auspicious toward them. (35)
Since all women are portions of Umā and he possesses the status of the twice-born, this rule applies;
however, O Six-faced One, one should perform the initiation (upanayana) during the consecration ceremony.
According to the prescribed method of propitiation, for all women of the twice-born castes, there shall be both the topknot and the sacred thread. 37.
Śiva has declared the authority [for practice] especially for twice-born women;
indeed, the initiation ceremony (upanayana) occurs at the time of their consecration (dīkṣā), and the marriage ceremony takes place at that same time.

Rites such as the tonsure ceremony (caula), the performance of the *pānīsa* sacrifice, and so forth, as well as the sacrificial offering (*yāga*) and the *agnihotra*, are designated by the term "Mantra-Brahman. (39)
Therefore, with every effort, one should provide the sacred thread for women as well;
indeed, by means of sacrifices such as the Agniṣoma, the sacrificer [is accompanied] by his wives.

The casting of fuel sticks with a mantra, the consumption of the sacrificial porridge (caru) with a mantra, the topknot, and the sacred thread—all these are prescribed by rule. One should perform the ritual in this manner; otherwise, the sacrificial act remains unperformed.
The entitlement to the Veda is by means of the root mantra and the sacred thread (upavītaka);
indeed, every sacrifice performed by women without the sacred thread is fruitless.
The topknot and the sacred thread are prescribed for all;
one should perform this rite and afterwards cause the sacrifice to be performed. (44)
The sacrifice of oblations (haviryajña), the cooked sacrifice (pākayajña), and the soma sacrifice (somayajña) constitute the threefold division.
The Agniṣṭoma is the first, followed by the Atyagniṣṭoma. (45)
The Ukthya sacrifice is the third, while the Ṣoḍaśin is the fourth;
the Vājapeya is the fifth, and the Atirātra is said to be the sixth. (46)
The seventh is indeed the Aptoryāma; these are the seven Soma-sacrifices.
With the five mantras beginning with "Sadyojāta," one should [worship] the ten-syllabled Vyomavyāpin.
Then, one should perform the seven sacrifices beginning with the Agniṣṭoma separately;
likewise, the Śrāddha on the Aṣṭakā and Parvan days, as well as the Śrāvaṇa and Āgrayaṇa rites.
The wise know that the Caitra and Āśvayuja months are for the *pākayajña*;
one should offer sixty oblations for each with the *bindu* as the principal [mantra]. (49)
During the lunar eclipses, the equinoxes, the solstices, and at the new and full moon sacrifices,
one should offer thirty oblations for each [deity] with the Hṛdaya mantra.
The Abhijit, the Vijit, the Rājasūya, the Sautrāmaṇī,
the Pauṇḍarīka, and likewise the Trivṛt— these protect him.
One should offer oblations with ghee and milk, two hundred times each, for the Mahāvrata and the Kāmuka rites using the Bahurūpa mantra.
O Guha, one should perform ten thousand oblations for the great sacrifice of the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha), the most excellent among all sacrifices, using the mantra of Prasāda.
Thereafter, the preceptor should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Prāsāda mantra;
having taken sixteen portions [of the offering substance], he should then perform the homa by pouring them into the fire.
Then, having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering with the five [mantras] ending in *anupāta*,
one should then offer the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and thereafter sacrifice with the *īśāna* mantra.
Thus the initiation is completed; one should dismiss the rites of birth and so forth.
Just as copper touched by mercury does not return to its state of being copper again. || 56 ||
The Śiva-principle is excellent, subtle, incomparable, and free from ailment; it is beyond ratiocination, without support, partless, peaceful, and immutable. (57)
The supreme, eternal, and ancient Brahman is free from conceptual construction, devoid of both the expressed and the expresser, and divested of anything to be rejected or accepted. || 58 ||

Pure, all-pervading, empty, self-cognizable, and both supreme and non-supreme—[the teacher] should indeed apply the words "horrific" (*ghora*) and the knitting of the eyebrows to the disciple alone. (59)
But one should join the disciple's very self [to the Self];
he is liberated, there is no doubt about this, even a killer of a fetus, O Six-faced One.
Having performed the ritual acceptance, one should cause five [vessels] to be broken from the jar into that [fire],
accompanied by the Īśāna mantra and the Prāsāda mantra.
There, one should honor the preceptor with a crown, earrings and the like, as well as armlets, ear-rings, bracelets, and waist-bands.
With heroes covered by waist-bands, with golden sacred threads, with golden rings, and with variegated yak-tail whisks; || 63 ||
With numerous male and female servants for the tasks of bedding and conveyance, with oxen, milch-cows, buffaloes, and many silken garments; || 64 ||
With elephants, swans, desired chariots, and other decorated villages;
with household utensils and other used vessels and cooking pots.
With spittle and other such things, as well as with a frying pan, a pestle, and a mortar,
one should present [the offering] to the Person (Puruṣa) with the Hṛdaya mantra.
One should draw a mandala with cow dung, having four corners and the Vedas as its sides;
and in the center, one should depict a lotus with various designs made from rice flour.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus there, complete with a pericarp and other parts;
one should place the auspicious [deity] there, and the Guru should cause [the disciple] to enter therein. (68)
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and water offerings;
the most excellent preceptor should perform the worship with the Īśāna mantra. (69)
One should worship with garments, ornaments, and gems while reciting the Vāmadeva mantra;
one should worship with armlets, earrings, and necklaces while reciting the Aghora mantra.
One should worship with crowns, earrings, and turbans, as well as with Īśāna, bracelets, finger-rings, anklets, elephants, and so forth. (71)
One who is endowed with devotion and firm in his vows should give [the offering] with the Sadyojāta mantra;
however, he should cause other household utensils to be given with the Hṛdaya mantra.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should then prostrate;
having bowed down, one should perform the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga) by falling like a staff upon the ground with the three [upper parts].
O Guru, by your grace, having obtained initiation which is very difficult to attain,
I have acquired the knowledge of Śiva for the four castes and other [teachings] from the Lord of the Gods.
Having spoken these words and taken leave of Śiva, the God of gods,
the Guru, the Teacher, then [placed] two *mala*s on his right ears, O dear one.
Saying "O son, release, release," one should consecrate [the child] with the Īśāna mantra:
"O lord of men, enjoy dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as the kingdom. (76)
Thus, when the recitation is complete, the knower of mantras should, out of devotion, personally lead the disciple—who has been purified in three ways—to the abode of the preceptor. || 77 ||
A Brāhmaṇa attains the Veda; a Kṣatriya becomes victorious;
a Vaiśya acquires wealth; and a Śūdra is liberated from sin. || 78 ||
In this very world he shall become wealthy and illustrious, and at the end, he shall attain the state of Rudra.
Thereafter, one should perform the Caṇḍayāga according to the ritual procedure prescribed in the scriptures. (79)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, on the initiation of yoga, in the Kālottara.
Śrīḥ!
Īśvara said:
I shall now describe, in due order, the sacrifice of Caṇḍeśvara.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus, complete with a pericarp and filaments.
One should draw [the mandala] with white, red, black, or yellow;
or, O child, one should draw the auspicious Three-Jewels mandala with green.
Having first caused [the image] to be painted, one should then invoke Caṇḍa;
having honored him with a pair of garments, one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should offer cooked rice prepared with *droṇa* rice;
likewise, mung beans, black gram, horse gram, pigeon pea, and flat bean. (4)
With *śāli*, *nīvāra*, wheat, barley, and bamboo-rice, as well as red *śāli*, great *śāli*, and fragrant *śāli* [rice]. (5)
One should cause [the rice] to grow using *kalama* black rice, *priyaṅgu* black rice, or even with other rice grains, provided that *kodrava* is avoided.
One should cause all types of rice to be taken, together with all kinds of fragrant substances,
as well as the root of the *śiṃśu*, the *bṛhatkanda*, and the tuber of the *sūraṇa*.
The bulb of the *śambā*, the bulb of the *vallī*, the five fruits of the plantain, the fruit of the two types of *bṛhatī*, the *kūśmāṇḍa*, and the two types of *karkarī*. (8)
The fruit of the *panasa* (jackfruit), its seed alone, *bṛndāraka*,
the fifth, *rājamāṣa*, *meghanāda*, and *punarbhava*. (9)
It should be provided with a vessel for food, accompanied by hundreds of vidhurī fruits, along with black pepper,
white mustard, asafoetida, and the two types of cumin.
Haridrā combined with milk and combined with the fruit of the tamarind yields thirty-two times the benefit; matsyamaṇḍī yields half of that.
Thirty-two prasthas of milk, two prasthas of ghee,
and sixteen prasthas of mung beans— these should all be mixed together in one place.
The wise one, accompanied by the mantra, should offer the sacrificial oblation (caru) to Caṇḍeśa;
he should perform one hundred and eight oblations with the root-mantra of Caṇḍa.
Having doubled the [measure] for Śiva, one should fashion fifty [images] of the Cakravartin; likewise, the eight-formed Rudras, the Rudras, and also the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and Kāma. (14)
The Mātṛkās, the divisions [of the Vedas], the world-protectors, the Siddhas, the Ṛṣis, the hosts of Maruts, the Vidyādharas, the Cāraṇas, the Nāgas, along with the Apsarases and Pannagas; || 15 ||
The Śivāstra, the Pāśupatāstra, and likewise the Aghorāstra;
[he also worshipped] the Lokapālas, the Kṣetrapālas, and the Dvārapālas on all sides. || 16 ||
The knower of mantras should offer one oblation after another with the entire mantra,
using the twenty-five [syllables] of the Rudras for both the Śakti and the limbs of Śiva.
Having performed the fire oblation according to the prescribed rite, one should cause the sacrificial offering (bali) to be given everywhere,
as well as to the preceptor, the patron, his kinsmen, and indeed everyone else.
O friend, O lord of the city, one should cause [the substance] to be given in the measure of an akṣa;
right there, the teacher, together with the disciple, should take his meal. (19)
One should cause them, along with their sons, wives, and servants, to eat together.
At the end of the meal, O dear one, [one should offer] the *caru*, which is the supreme remover of all diseases. (20)
It brings about the increase of wealth and grain, the proliferation of sons and grandsons, abundance of food, an abundance of cattle, longevity, and great auspiciousness. (21)
Through the sacrifice to Caṇḍeśvara, one becomes free from disease and free from calamity;
at the conclusion of the initiation, one should diligently perform that sacrifice to Caṇḍeśvara.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, on the Sacrifice to Caṇḍeśvara, in the Kālottara, the compendium of twelve thousand verses. 18.
The Lord said: I shall now describe, in due order, the procedure for the great consecration (mahābhiṣeka).
During the period of the northern solstice, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day. || 1 ||
One should perform the consecration during the asterisms of Hasta, Tiṣya, Vāruṇa, Vāyavya, Rohiṇī, that called Mṛga, and the three Uttaras.
The consecration of the king should take place when the sun is in Aquarius, Capricorn, Taurus, Cancer, Leo, or Gemini.
One should recite it on the second or the fifth lunar day, or indeed on a Nandā day; Monday, Friday, Wednesday, or Thursday are auspicious days for this.
The consecration of a king should be performed at the rising of Jupiter, or likewise at the rising of Venus, or at the rising of Mercury.
In the sixty-third year, eleven malefic planets are situated in the eleventh house;
Jupiter may be in the seventh house or in another house. (6)
If Venus or the Moon is situated in the house of a kinsman, or even in half of that house;
or if the Moon is in the third house or the eleventh house, it is most excellent for anointing. (7)
On the seventh day, preceded by the ritual of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa),
one should prepare one hundred and eight or eighteen *pālikās*.
Likewise, the shallow bowls (śarāva) are said to be two hundred each;
and there should be wild rice, barley, śāli rice, sesame, and bamboo shoots.
Mudga, māṣa, kulattha, śimba, and niṣpāva; red śāli, mahāśāli, kalama, and śāli. || 10 ||
The practitioner of mantras should sow three *droṇas* of each— fragrant rice (*gandhaśāli*) and *priyaṅgu*— or even one *droṇa* of all together, using a respectful offering (*prāsāda*).
Perform it in a temple where the deity is well-present, or at a sacred pilgrimage site,
or in a cow-pen, or on a riverbank, or at the confluence of a river and the ocean.
A temple pinnacle (kūṭa) or even a pavilion (maṇṭapa), measuring thirty-six cubits [in extent], may be circular, square, or indeed rectangular. || 13 ||
It should be made either circular or rectangular, devoid of internal pillars,
provided with four archways, and endowed with four gates.
It was covered with a canopy, adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass, joined by the elephants of the eight directions, and beautified by auspicious sprouts. || 15 ||
It is rich with fruits and garlands of sprouts, adorned with bells and chowries, endowed with the eight auspicious symbols, and strewn with fragrant flowers. || 16 ||
Abundantly filled with incense and lamps, and adorned at the entrance with water-pots (kalaśas),
there should be either one hundred and eight or sixty-four [of them].
(84) Adorned with thirty-two, sixteen, and eight fire-pits (agnikuṇḍas),
it is beautifully embellished by all the pits endowed with the characteristics previously described. || 18 ||
By Brahmins who were pure, devoted to Vedic vows, established in the Vedic sacrifices and observances,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and lacking none of the qualities of the best of the twice-born.

Then, the preceptor, having been properly installed, should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with auspicious priests who are proficient in the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas and are experts in the ritual manuals and mantras.
With thousands of jars, or with half that number, or with eighty-one; or with sixty-four, thirty-two, or sixteen apertures.
Or a man of limited means may perform it with nine jars made of gold,
silver, copper, or very beautiful earthenware.
With jars containing Akālamūla [roots], free from all defects, filled with two āḍhakas—or even one or two—of the second [type]. || 23 ||

[The vessels] should be provided with cloths, covered with lids, equipped with kūrca-grass mats, wrapped with threads, accompanied by sprouts, and made of white mango, pippala, and sandalwood wood. || 24 ||
O Six-faced One, having caused twenty-five chambers to be constructed, which are honored, fumigated, washed, and adorned with white rice grains; || 25 ||
The wise man should have a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) constructed with one thousand droṇas of śāli rice,
or else half of that, or half of that again, using one hundred droṇas of śāli rice.
Taking either fifty, twenty-five, or ten *droṇas* of rice— or even half of that— one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
One should place the aquatic substances and mantras in successive order;
one should place the ninth [mantra] in the center, and not in a corner.
Padmarāga, emerald, pearl, coral, as well as topaz,
sapphire, sun-crystal, and moonstone. (29)
One should install the eight Vidyeśvaras from Indra in the east to Īśāna in the northeast;
and in the center of that same nine-square grid belonging to Indra, one should place gold.
Tāra, tāmra, āyasa, cāra, nāgasam, vimala,
as well as sakāśa and vidula, [should be offered] with mantras beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna.
In the southeast, within the group of nine, the wise one should place a lotus in the center;
likewise, a palm tree, a jar of perfume, a vessel from Saurāṣṭra, and a vessel from Tairika.
The wise one should place the honey, the curd, and the collyrium as the eighth auspicious item, arranging them as before, starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna.
In the center of the southern group of nine, one should place the bark of the mango tree,
as well as the bark of the *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *palāśa* trees.
O child, one should place the śamī, bilva, vyāghāta, and the bark of madhūka in the same manner as before, starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna.
In the southwest, in the center of the nine [squares], the wise man should place the altar-ground (vedi) made from earth originating from a river,
a serpent's horn, a boar, or the root of kuśa grass.
The knower of mantras should take earth from a field, a granary, or an anthill and place it [in the center];
O child, he should arrange it as before with the respective mantra for each.
In the center of the ninefold [array] dedicated to Varuṇa, one should place a lotus flower,
as well as a karavīra, a śoka, a nandyāvarta, and a mallikā.
The wise one should place a white lotus, a blue water-lily, and a bimba fruit as before;
the wise one should place camphor in the center of the ninefold [array] in the northwest.
One should place sandalwood, saffron, iron, jīvaka, kālavānara, mālatraka, and kaṭuka in the eight directions starting from the northwest. (40)
In the center of the nine [plants] in the north-eastern quarter, one should install Mahālakṣmī;
likewise, Viṣṇukrānti, Sahā, O Goddess, and Indravallī. (41)
The wise practitioner should likewise place sūryāvarta, bhṛṅgarāja, śaṅkhapuṣpa, balā, and atibalā as before.
Milk, curd, ghee, honey, as well as sugarcane juice, coconut water, turmeric water, and water with kuśa grass; 43.
Water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, water with parched grain, water with groats, water with all kinds of perfumes, and likewise water with all kinds of flowers; || 44 ||
And the tip of a blade of kusha grass with water, with the water of the ocean, the mud of the Ganges and Yamuna, and likewise the mud of the Sarasvati; || 45 ||
And snow-water with the juice of the lāṅgalī fruit, and the water of ripe mango fruit with the juice of the mātuluṅga fruit. (46)
Likewise, water from an orange tree, as well as water from a mango tree, the fruit-water of a pomegranate, and similarly water from a bilva fruit. (47)
Thus, one hundred and eight divine [vessels] are prescribed for each jar;
however, the wise man should place them within the principal jar, which is the thousandth.
One should employ this in both the daily and occasional rites of bathing;
one should likewise provide perfume, flowers, incense, and lamps along with food.
Having established [the deity] with fragrance, the knower of mantras should perform everything else;
having filled the remainder with pure water, he should set it aside separately with the *prāsāda* mantra.
Having placed the desired jars, the knower of mantras should worship them with their respective mantras,
using perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and water offerings. || 51 ||
O child, one should worship each separately with auspicious fragrant flowers, joined with the Prāsāda mantra and the Hṛdaya mantra.
Having worshipped with fragrant perfumes, one should worship with [offerings] beginning with Śakra;
then, having covered [the deity] with a pair of garments, one should sacrifice either separately or together.
There, one should perform the fire oblation (homa) in the cardinal and intermediate directions with the best of the twice-born,
using fuel-sticks of Palāśa, Khadira, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Nyagrodha, and Bilva.
One should arrange the Audumbara and Śamī wood, as well as sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame, śāli rice, and barley, starting from the east.
One should offer one thousand each of *priyaṅgu* and *siddhārthaka*;
for every thousand [of other materials], one should offer one thousand of these, or half of that, which is five hundred.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for as many times as there are jars;
for each one, one should establish [the oblation] one hundred and eight times, according to the number of jars.
There, one should have the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) recited by the best of the twice-born in the eight directions,
and likewise the study of the Vedas— specifically the recitation of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas— should be performed by those in the eight directions.
O child, one should place the Ṛgveda in the eastern quarter, the Yajurveda in the south, the Sāmaveda in the west, and the Atharvaveda with its reciters in the north.
One should perform the Vasordhārā rite in the center with auspicious persons learned in the four Vedas,
having duly propitiated the deity with great offerings of perfumes, flowers, and other articles.
To the west of the sacrificial site and to the east of Mahādeva,
the knower of mantras should perform the consecration there by whatever means possible.
(88) Having established the King upon a throne made of gold, silver, copper, or even wood, the knower of mantras [should proceed]. (62)
With the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, with the auspicious noise of cymbals and trumpets,
with flutes, lutes, and drums, and with the chanting of the Vedas on all sides.
By means of an ox-horn, one obtains the highest fruit;
by means of a golden vessel equal in size to an ox-horn, one obtains the middling fruit. (64)
Whether made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay,
it should be a magnificent vessel, beautifully adorned and filled with five *droṇas*.
There are [channels] with a hundred streams, eighty streams, fifty, five, twenty, sixteen streams, nine streams, or five. || 66 ||
The preceptor should perform the consecration with either eight or four [vessels];
having placed the vessel upon a tripod, he should then perform the consecration.
Having touched two [vessels] with water from the jar in the vessel, one should recite the mantra;
the wise say that an uninterrupted consecration is the best.
Anointing with cow-horn [conch] is indeed the most excellent of the excellent;
one should designate the fruit as middling when using a conch or a golden vessel. (69)
With the Puruṣasūktas, the Rudrasūktas, and likewise the Viṣṇusūktas,
[one worships] Aruṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Pavana, and Hiraṇyaka.
The Ekādaśatva, the Raudra, and the Śatarudrīya;
the Brahmasāman, the Jyeṣṭhasāman, and the Bṛhadrathantara. || 71 ||
The Bahiṣpāvana-vikāra, the Atharvaveda, the Brahmaśiras, the Amṛtarudra, the Mahārudra, the Pippalāda, and the Mahas [Mahopaniṣad]. || 72 ||
The Brāhma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Āheśa, and likewise the Bārhaspatya;
the Kaumāra, O dear one, as well as the Tryambaka and the Jātavedasa. (73)
O Six-faced One, one should cause the recitation of the Śaunavanya section, the Brāhma chapter, and the Ghoṣa; or likewise, one should have a disciple who has been initiated perform it.
One attains vast sovereignty, an increase in longevity and health, abundance of wealth and grain, and indeed the destruction of death. (75)
A king who has lost his kingdom shall regain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin);
O dear one, a wise man should indeed employ the Prāsāda [mantra] from beginning to end.
The wise one should perform the rite at every step with the Vyomavyāpin mantra joined with the principal seed-syllable, and likewise with the Prāsāda mantra. (77)
For this supreme consecration indeed surpasses the four Vedas.
Alternatively, one should enclose it with the *prāsāda* mantra consisting of the five Brahmans.
O child, one should cause the consecration (abhiṣeka) to be performed; he shall become an external person of great fortune.
[This occurs] when Mahāmāyā is enclosed within the Prāsāda mantra by means of the Lakṣmī-bīja. || 79 ||
For this is the supreme consecration that destroys birth and death;
[it is performed] with the one ending in *prāṇa* (the letter *ha*) and likewise with the one ending in *mā* (the letter *ma*).
And indeed, O child, by means of that very fourth [state],
and by means of the fourth mantra, and indeed by means of the fourth itself.
The fourth of the fourth, the fourth of the third, and the fourth of the second, joined with Māyā and Anala. (82)
The King of Mantras is proclaimed as being joined with the Bindu and Nāda.
With these mantras, the knower of mantras should cause the king to receive consecration. 83.
For this indeed removes all diseases and truly destroys death;
one should perform it during a lunar eclipse, at the equinox, or at the solstice. (84)
At the end of the year, during a solar transit (saṃkrānti), or on one's own birth asterism; or likewise under Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Hasta, Puṣya, or the Uttaraphalgunī constellation.
In the Pauṣa, Vāruṇa, Vāyavya, and Mṛgaśīrṣa [nakṣatras], O child, one shall have a lifespan of ten thousand years; such is the certainty of the scripture. (86)
By performing an ablution on a Saturday coinciding with the Rohiṇī asterism, one lives for five thousand years;
and one should properly perform the ablution on a Monday coinciding with the Saumya (Mṛgaśiras) asterism.
He attains vast prosperity and lives for six thousand years;
furthermore, an ablution performed at Bhṛgupauṣṇa brings about the immediate destruction of death.
Through consecration under the asterisms of Bharaṇī and Aśvinī, one shall immediately obtain sovereignty;
likewise, [it is auspicious] in Taurus, Gemini, Leo, and Capricorn as well. (89)
The royal consecration should be performed when the Sun is in Aquarius or Scorpio;
however, one must avoid Pisces, Scorpio, Libra, and Aries.
One should predict middling results for the signs of Virgo and Cancer;
furthermore, at the time of the Great Consecration, there shall be a feeding of Brahmins.
The recitation of the Puṇyāha formula, the Vasordhārā rite, the feeding of Brahmins, and the bathing of Śiva with ghee are established as the rites. (92)
One should cause the gift of cows, the gift of sesame seeds, the gift of gold,
the gift of clothing, and the gift of land to be performed according to the prescribed ritual.
At the time of the great consecration, one should have twelve [images] made;
by performing it according to the rite, one shall attain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin). || 94 ||
It destroys untimely death for one hundred and one [years];
however, five types of death must be avoided, and it increases the number of sons and grandsons. (95)

O child, one who is proficient in all the scriptures should cause the consecration to be performed by those who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas; indeed, this is the great consecration of the mantra.
One who knows the ten and eighteen Tantras, is proficient in the Pañcarātra, and has reached the further shore of the fourteen Vidyā-tantras, is the most excellent of teachers (deśikottama). || 97 ||
Therefore, even a killer of a fetus or one who has committed a mixture of sins should perform the consecration;
once the consecration has been performed, he shall not be blunted in his attainment of sovereignty.
Having covered it with a linen cloth, one should wipe it with collyrium,
along with nutmeg, sandalwood, saffron, musk, and the three types of *kapila*.

Having anointed [the image] with incense, cooling agents, and the like, and having performed the viewing of the eight auspicious symbols, one should [proceed] at an auspicious moment during the day, on a favorable lunar date, and in the presence of pure water.
At the rising of Jupiter, or even at the rising of Mercury or Venus,
one should first place [the deity] during Jupiter's rise, which grants all desires.
One attains the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) and shall obtain a supreme lifespan.
At the rising of Venus, one should place the crown with the root mantra.
One attains the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) and obtains elephants, horses, and chariots;
by placing a crown during the rising of Mercury, one attains the yoga of knowledge.
Upon being gazed upon by a maiden, he shall become the lord of a mandala and the like;
he should have a crown made of all kinds of jewels fashioned from gold.
A crown made of the five jewels—diamond, emerald, ruby, pearl, and coral—consisting of three thousand [beads], shall be the most excellent in the Trisāhasra world-system. || 105 ||
With two thousand [gold pieces], the middle crown should be made; with one thousand, one should know it to be the smallest crown. This is the measurement of the crown. (106)
The height should be one *vitasti*, with the bases [of the pillars] being three *tālas*;
or it may be three and a half *tālas*, or even consisting of three sections.
Then, one should place five gems upon the crown of the head;
one should adorn it everywhere with a diamond, an emerald, and pearls. (108)
One should place the crown upon a very aged Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas;
for whatever the age of that Brahmin, such shall be the lifespan of the king.
Having recollected the Supreme Lord with devotion, one should perform the ritual placement;
