having constantly recited the six-syllabled mantra, one should contemplate the mandala as offered.
Having thus placed the crown, the preceptor should perform the consecration with the ear-rings, the breast-ornament, the armlets, and likewise the crown. (111)
The most excellent preceptor should worship the golden sacred thread, along with the waist-string and the belly-band, using the Prāsāda mantra.
Having covered it with a linen cloth, one should cause [the ritual] to be performed on that day;
likewise, the necessary materials such as cows, land, gold, and so forth.
"It must be given to the preceptor by the king with devotion. Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, the Chapter on the Consecration of Kings, in the Kālottara. 19.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
I shall now describe this subtle navel-cakra in its proper sequence.
Below the navel is the kanda, from which sprouts have emerged. || 1 ||
Seventy-two thousand [channels] are situated within the center of the navel;
they pervade everything in all directions—horizontally, upwards, and downwards.
For these thirty principal channels are situated like a wheel below;
namely, the Iḍā, the Piṅgalā, and likewise the Suṣumnā. (3)
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, the illustrious Pūṣā, Alambuṣā, Kuhū, Śaṅkhinī, and likewise Pālinī. || 4 ||
Hrādinī, Mohinī, Kampinī, Puninī, Śubhā, Vikṛti, Viṣamā, Mānyā, Haṃsinī, and Viśvamālinī. (5)
Aṅginī, Ghoṣiṇī, Tejinī, Rasavāhinī,
Vāhinī, Dharaṇī, Rasabhaimī, and Rasakriyā.
Those with cold potency and those with hot potency—[these], along with the thirty-two channels that are subject to tactile sensation, have been described. (7)
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. || 8 ||
O Six-faced One, there are ten principal channels that carry the vital breaths, and thirty-two others;
however, twenty-eight million channels always carry [the subtle elements].
Among all the winds, by means of the ten principal winds—consisting of prāṇa and apāna—the vital breaths [are engaged] for the purpose of filling [the body]. 10.
This prāṇa, residing in the chest of living beings, constantly fills it; supported by the individual soul (jīva), it manifests as inhalation, exhalation, and coughing.
Because it departs [from the body], it is therefore proclaimed as *prāṇa*.
Wind, fire, and likewise space—the third—reside within the *jīva*. (12)
The Puruṣa, joined with the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka), resides in the heart;
the Puruṣa is the individual soul (jīva) and the vital breath (prāṇa)—these three transcend the body. (13)
When conjoined with the principle of the individual soul (jīva), the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) proceeds;
when joined with passion (rajas), it experiences sense objects.
Then, joined with tamas, evil prevails;
likewise, recitation, meditation, concentration, knowledge, and the worship of the gods [cease]. || 15 ||
Various kinds of sacrifices and works of public utility, diverse acts of charity, as well as the study of Vedic doctrines and the treatises on Yoga; || 16 ||

The observances such as the restraints (yama) and the disciplines (niyama), purity, the construction of temples and dwellings, the digging of ponds, the offering of water at Prayāga, and the giving of garments and other gifts; || 17 ||
The gift of land, jewels, elephants, horses, sesame seeds, daughters, and so forth—when a person is endowed with such virtue, the knowledge of the Dharma proceeds. || 18 ||
Singing, dancing, and instrumental music; the acquisition of gold, cattle, and land; female and male slaves, horses, goats, and buffaloes as well. (19)
Sensual enjoyments such as sound and other objects, the pursuit of women, as well as diamonds, emeralds, rubies, pearls, and corals; || 20 ||
And perfumes, flowers, incense, as well as clothing, bedding, and so forth;
other household utensils such as pots, pans, mortars, and pestles. (21)
The person endowed with the quality of rajas is the gatherer of all;
thus has the nature of rajas been described to you in brief.
(95) Laziness, indulgence in sensual desires, excessive sleep, sexual intercourse, theft, slander, and even the employment of thieves; || 23 ||
Ignorance is exceedingly deceitful, as is the seizing of another's property; likewise, constant speaking of untruth, the theft of cattle and grain, and the stealing of land [are likewise]. (24)
He was constantly violent, cruel toward others, half-blind with rage, and a slayer of wild animals;
he was harsh toward all beings and a reviler of the gods and Brahmins. || 25 ||
The Puruṣa always creates [the world] joined with the qualities of tamas;
so too do Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Śakra, and all the other deities. || 26 ||
The Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras stand together by their very essence;
as do the Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Yakṣas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others. || 27 ||
Nāgas and Garuḍas, as well as Kinnaras and great sages;
Piśācas, Bhūtas, Vetālas, Śabaras, and Pulindas. || 28 ||
Men endowed with the quality of darkness (tamas) face the east;
they are sages perfected within their own lineages, truly perfected ones of firm vows.
But the life-force dependent on the Puruṣa is the size of a thumb, possessing the luster of a sapphire, and situated in the midst of the three circles.
The life-span [of the first stage] is half of half a thumb-breadth below the person;
its measure is half of that, and its established measure is half of that again. || 31 ||
Within the *jīva*, however, is the *pramāṇa* [cakra], which has the luster of a *rājāvarta* gem;
in its center is the *apāna* [vāyu], resembling the wrath of Indra (*indrakopaka*).
And in the middle of that is Vyāna, with a luster like cow's milk;
and in the middle of that is Udāna, with a luster like frost or silver. || 33 ||
In the center of that [mandala] is the Equal One (Samāna), with a luster like the autumnal moon;
and in the center of that is the Naga, with a luster like the rising sun. (34)
And in the center of that is the tortoise, with the luster of an *atasī* flower; in the center of that is the *kṛkara*, with a luster like the filaments of a lotus.
In its center is Devadatta, resembling a hibiscus flower;
in his center is Dhanañjaya, with a radiance like cow's milk.
Prāṇa is situated from the heart, the navel, and the tip of the nose down to the big toes;
apāna is established in the penis, the anus, the navel, and so forth. (37)
Vyāna, however, resides in all the limbs for the sake of universal accomplishment; it is located at the knees, the ankles, and the arms.
Kṛkara, moreover, is situated in the forehead, the throat, the elbows, and the hands. (38)
Udāna resides in the two sides, as well as in the joints of the hips, chest, testicles, thighs, knees, shanks, back, and arms. (39)
The *samāna* wind is present in all the limbs; the ears, nose, and eyes;
on the tongue and in the cavity of the palate; and in the stomach, the navel, and the feet. (40)
In both hands and in all the fingers alike,
it is equal and pervades every limb.
But the Vaiśvānara-supāka [rite] is performed by those who do not eat food, drink, and so forth. || 42 ||
It carries away feces, semen, urine, and all disturbances of wind downward; therefore, it is celebrated as the apāna.
Vyāna resides in the vyāna-āśaya; it provokes the diseases of vāta, pitta, and śleṣman, as well as the threefold combination (sānnipātaka) of these humors. || 44 ||
(97) [One is freed from] urinary disorders, leprosy, and abdominal tumors; fever, consumption, fistula-in-ano, hernia, external hemorrhoids, enlargement of the abdomen, and jaundice. (45)
And because it causes all diseases to grow, the thunderbolt (or *krama*) strikes the lower lip without being requested; in this lineage, it is a provocation. (46)
The ears, the nose, the tongue, the skin, the feet, and the hands; likewise, the organs of evacuation, procreation, and speech, as well as inhalation and exhalation. || 47 ||
The vital air named udāna pierces the vital points (marmas);
it indeed brings about pleasure, the narration of one's own destruction, decrepitude, and old age. 48.
[Whatever is] drunk, eaten, or smelled [by it destroys] blood-bile and phlegm,
as well as all movements, limbs, fevers, leprosy, and urinary disorders.
Vāyu does not cause consumption, abdominal tumors, or enlargement of the abdomen, nor even all diseases and old age; it acts for the benefit of all living beings.
The wind named Samāna leads the limbs evenly;
the one called Udgāra is said to be Nāga, while Kūrma is situated in the act of opening the eyes. (51)
Kṛkara is indeed in the sneeze, and Devadatta is in the yawn;
Dhanañjaya resides in the voice and does not leave even when one is dead. (52)
The ten life-sustaining channels (nāḍīs) are proclaimed to be thirty-two;
the individual soul (jīva) and the vital breath (prāṇa) move within the Suṣumṇā at all times.
O child, in the iḍā and piṅgalā, the udāna moves together with the prāṇa;
however, in the kumbhī of the minor tree, the apāna alone should circulate.
Vyāna indeed moves in the eyes, the throat, and also in the nostrils and mouth;
Nāga and Kūrma, however, move in the mouth, the nose, and the eyes. 55.
The tortoise, the kṛkara, and the devadatta should always circulate in the two ears;
the devadatta and the dhanañjaya should circulate in the penis. (56)
In the remaining channels, the ten [vital winds] always flow within the prāṇa;
the channels are situated like a wheel, and the wind moves among them.
This ten-spoked wheel, which forms the gateways of the eight directions,
together with the two gates above and below, is proclaimed as the wheel of the channels (nāḍīcakra).
These sixteen digits belong to the Sun; likewise, there are the digits of the Moon.
O child, two by two they form the hips, as do the Iḍā and Piṅgalā.
O child, two and a half ghaṭikās move from the left and the right;
five ghaṭikās in the south and likewise five in the north.
O child, [the procedure] for the wheel in the chapter will be explained...
(*text missing*). Now, O Six-faced One, only a brief summary has indeed been told.
In the ten-spoked lotus, men [dwell] constantly for two ghaṭikās.
On the left is the five-petaled fire, and on the right there are likewise five;
[the petals] are situated on the north and the south, as well as on the left and the right.
In the middle, however, the equinox (viṣuva) is proclaimed, emerging from both nostrils;
likewise, the transits (saṃkrānti), the equinoxes, and the divisions of day and night.
The intercalary month is indeed the debt, and the day and night are the wealth for her.
Cough arises as the debt, while exhalation is called the wealth.
Furthermore, the transit [of the sun] is the very foundation, and the station is simply the state of being established.
Iḍā, Suṣumnā, and Amā are fully integrated;
this transition within the limbs in the midst of the Suṣumnā is called *saṃkrānti*. (66)
Both the Iḍā and the Piṅgalā emerge from the base of the waist;
resting upon the knot of the navel, they are situated on the left and the right respectively.
Relying upon the *punarbhū* knot, the two *galagandha* [channels] meet;
relying upon the *mūrdhni-granthi*, they emerge from the nostrils. (68)
Having entered twelve finger-breadths from the tip of the nose, one should drink the *kautuka*;
then one should enter the supreme Self within the body of the supreme altar.
At the end of its dissolution, Kālāgnirudra resides in the Suṣumnā at the sixteenth level;
it is situated in the center of both [channels] and extends into the Brahma-randhra.
One should begin with Gāndhārī, Hastinī, and Mūlā;
when the two knots of the navel are brought together, they again join with the knot of the womb.

Having returned again to the throat-gland (galagranthi) and having drunk [the nectar] from twelve finger-breadths, there is the vision of all things; then indeed, one should enter the center once more.
Pūṣan and Yaśasvinī, along with Śūla and the others, having emerged and joined together at the knot of the Punarbhū, [attain their goal]. 73.
Having reached the throat-knot, it then joins with the knot at the crown of the head;
having gone again to both ears, it enters [the central channel]. || 74 ||
Having drunk the ether at the dvādaśānta, one should re-enter that same path;
having entered the center of the body, one hears all sounds. 75.
Alampuruṣā and Kuhū emerge from the penis and anus;
Śaṅkhinī and Mālinī, however, are both supported by the root of the *kanda*.
Below those two are Vatsālambuṣā and Kuhū;
likewise, Śaṅkhinī is both above and below, having emerged from the navel upwards. (77)
Below the wind [channel] and the penis, however, the Śaṅkhinī has emerged;
it is auspicious, possessing the qualities of Hlādinī, Mohinī, Kampinī, and Meghanī.
Emerging from the root of the navel, it comes to the right foot;
having entered the knot of the hips, it meets at the knot of the knee. (79)
Having joined at the ankle-joint, she emerges through the five toes;
she is Vikṛti, Viṣamāmātyā, Haṃsinī, and Viśvamālinī. (80)
Emerging from the root of the *kanda* in the left foot, it ascends, embraces the knot of the waist, and takes its seat at the knot of the knee. (81)
Having joined at the ankle-joint, they emerge from the five toes:
Gaginī, Ghoṣaṇī, Tejinī, and Rasavāhinī.
And Dharaṇī—these five have indeed emerged from the bulb (kanda);
having joined at the knot of the navel, they are connected to the knot of the heart. || 83 ||
Resorting to the throat-knot and resorting to the armpit-knot,
they are joined with the joints and the elbow-knots on the right hand.
Clinging again to the jewel-knot, they emerged from the five fingers;
they are the Earth, the consumer of tastes, the one whose action is cooling in potency. (85)
These five, possessing a hot potency, have emerged from the bulbous root;
they rely upon the knot of the navel and take recourse in the knot of the heart. (86)
Resting upon the throat-gland, it emerges from the left arm;
reaching the joint of the forearm and elbow, it rests upon the wrist-joint.
O child, five channels indeed emerge from the five fingers;
they provide space for tactile sensation and extend toward the left and right sides. (88)
O child, there are thirty-two channels (nāḍikās), beginning with Prāṇa, which are the days of the week (vāyuvārakas).
The great channel is firmly bound; these supreme thirty-two channels [are thus established]. (89)
Among the seventy-two thousand channels, the central channel is auspicious;
twenty-eight crores of them are proclaimed as the principal ones.
When the pipal leaf has withered, those [channels] situated horizontally, upwards,
and downwards within all the pores of the skin are proclaimed to be the *nāḍīs*.
The individual soul (jīva) moves about together with the vital breaths (prāṇas);
the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the person (puruṣa), remains established in himself, though ignorant and endowed with experience. || 92 ||

The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) always resides within the hollow of the heart-lotus of all living beings, together with the individual soul (jīva) and the vital breaths (prāṇa), loving happiness and hating suffering.
The Lord Śiva sports from Brahmā down to a blade of grass,
just as a dry leaf is carried by the wind in the sky.
In that same way, O Śivaguha, this living soul wanders, having drawn up the vital breaths and other elements from the lotus;
though peaceful, it falls and rises again and again within the body.
Indeed, the central body is directly [the Self], free from all activity;
it is the eternal, subtle Puruṣa, the supportless, supreme Śiva.

The person situated in the heart-lotus is the life-force (jīva-prāṇa) well-united [with it]. He has four hands; likewise in the southern petal, in the south-western [petal], in the western petal, and likewise in the north-western [petal]. (98)
In the north there are four ghaṭikās, and likewise in the northeast;
thus the great person moves through thirty-two ghaṭikās. (99)
O child, by means of the three instruments, one should indeed move through the nine gates;
while the two [eyes] always move through thirty-two [parts], [the other senses] move through one-eighth and one-sixteenth [of those parts]. 100.
O Mahāsena, even if one were to take a single part from a hundred parts, it would not be found by the seventy-two thousand gods, including Indra, even after a further [search]. 101.
O Guha, twenty-eight crores [of breaths] circulate through the navel;
among those channels, nine channels move as a thousandth part.
The Lord resides in the middle of the body, changeless and stainless;
he is omniscient, all-pervading, peaceful, and at all times facing every direction. (103)
He is to be known as the Supreme Brahman, Sadāśiva, who pervades the sky;
he is the Supreme Self, the Great Cause, the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña) residing within the heart. || 104 ||
The inner self, residing at the twelve-finger limit (dvādaśānta), is established within all beings;
however, O child, at the time of death, it is situated within the channel (nāḍī). 105.
Furthermore, through consciousness, everything indeed resides within the heart, the self, and the senses;
thus, this group of vital airs (vāyavaḥ) is established in the wheel of welfare (hitacakra). || 106 ||
With inhalations, exhalations, and coughs, the body trembles and is agitated by the vital winds (*vāyu*).

Birth brings about both the eternal and the non-eternal; in the forest of worldly existence, due to the absence of childhood innocence, one is tormented by calamities. At the end of life, as if playing, one sports with all the principles (*tattva*) born of birth and death.
I shall describe to you in its entirety the nīḍīcakra as it exists:
prāṇa is said to be above, while apāna is below, and it is indeed night.
When there is a conjunction of the Aindra and Vāruṇa [asterisms], it is called the Dakṣiṇāyana.
In the southern [solstice] it occurs during the pair of Āśvayuj months, and in the northern [solstice] during the Caitra months; these are the two equinoxes (viṣuva).
O Mahāsena, for thirty days the sun [traverses one sign], and for the other [two] months;
O Deva, because it moves correctly [through the signs], it is called a *saṃkrānti*.
The waning of the moon is the new moon (amāvāsyā), while its increase is the full moon (pūrṇamāsika).
Because the moon wanes starting from the new moon, it is therefore called amāvāsī.
O Guha, sixteen parts of the moon are drunk by the gods;
fifteen of them he constantly gives, yet the moon remains full.
During the fifteen days of the waxing fortnight, each single digit (kalā) increases one by one;
when the digits are full, it is designated as the full moon (paurṇamāsī) by those learned in the ritual systems.
The dark fortnight belongs to Soma, while the bright fortnight indeed belongs to the Sun;
the Moon and the Sun are the enjoyers of the full moon, and [the other] belongs to the New Moon.
The wise know the conjunction of the moon and the sun to be the new moon day;
having withdrawn everything, O Guha, the wise man [dissolves] the vital breaths into the heart.

The wise man should lead the vital breath (prāṇa) from the palace (the heart) through the seed-syllable, to the throat, the palate, the aperture (between the eyebrows), and finally to the crown of the head. 116.
Having cast off the bolt and the skull, the individual soul ascends;
having reached the state of Sadāśiva, it shall not undergo birth again. || 117 ||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter on the Wheel of Channels in the Kālottara. || 20 ||
Śrīḥ!
Īśvara said:
I shall now proclaim the wheel of the digits (kalācakra), the supreme and auspicious knowledge of time.
The protection of one's own position is characterized by four parts. || 1 ||
Those who know [the truth] say that time is a *truṭi*; from the knowledge of that, one remains transcendent.
Two *truṭis* are declared to be a *kṣaṇa*, and the third would be momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
Listen now to [the measure of] four *truṭis*, which is a *nimeṣa*, and half a *nimeṣa*:
a *truṭi* should be known as thirty-two *kalās*, and eight *kalās* constitute a *karaṇa*. (3)
This procedure has been enjoined for you regarding that which is produced by the eight instruments;
likewise, it applies to the past, the future, and the present as well.
Gain and loss, pleasure and pain—[and so forth]—this ten-spoked wheel is said to revolve among all living beings:
that of Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, and likewise Varuṇa. (6)
Then there is the one belonging to Vāyu, the one belonging to Soma, and the one belonging to Īśāna; these constitute the eight.
The ninth is said to be above, and the tenth is below.
When the month of Puṣya has arrived, it is called Mārgaśīrṣaka;
at its transition (saṃkrānti), one should examine the breath, O Six-faced One.
The *sāman* [breath] consists of five *ghaṭikās*, and the *dakṣiṇa* likewise consists of five;
sixty breaths (*ucchvāsa*) constitute one *prāṇa*, and six *prāṇas* constitute one *ghaṭikā*. (9)
He performs the recitation count for a day and night of sixty ghaṭikās;
if it occurs during five ghaṭikās on the left [side], he is freed from all misfortunes.
If one practices for seven *ghaṭikās* on the left side while accompanied by a slight warmth,
the wise man, through perfect knowledge, indeed attains a lifespan of eighty years.
If there are eight ghaṭikās on the left side, accompanied by a rough sensation and mild warmth, the lifespan is seventy years; thus it was declared by Śiva. (12)
If it moves for nine ghaṭikās in the left [nostril], slightly accompanied by warmth,
repeatedly, O child, he lives for sixty years.
If it moves repeatedly for ten ghaṭikās within the iḍā, that person shall live for thirty-five [years]; such is the certainty of the scripture. (14)
Indeed, he who remains supported by the heart, the navel, and the stomach shall live for thirty years, even if his body lasts for only fourteen ghaṭikās. || 15 ||
If it flows through the left [nostril] for fourteen half-ghatikās, O Six-faced One, one lives for twenty-seven years. (16)
When the *iḍā* flows for fourteen ghaṭikās less one quarter,
the lifespan of that man is indeed twenty-six years.
Half a day, a full day, and likewise a day and night;
[he saw] the sixteen Vasus, who possess the qualities of three and a half pairs, as they were being carried away by the Sun.
From the fifth [tithi], for twenty-five days, one ascends the form of movement; increased by five, from that [point] it is ten multiplied by three, minus three, until [the end].
When the month of Pauṣa has concluded, by the moon with three eyes (Śiva), there are six times three pairs of lords of the *kalās*.

Furthermore, I shall explain another [aspect] of the Kālacakra in brief:
during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), when it is on the left, its light is not seen.
O Six-faced One, having practiced for three years, he indeed lives;
and when the sun is in its northern course, the upward light is seen.
Death will be attained within two years; there is no doubt about this.
Furthermore, if the light below is seen only on the left side and not even for half [a year], [the same result follows]. (22)
He shall live for one year, as declared by those who know the times;
when that light of Brahma is seen on both the left and the right [sides].
For six months his life was indeed foretold by the Lord;
a light was seen in the south, southward, not at midnight.
If [the light] is seen outside through the right or the left [nostril], one meets death within three months by means of the wind; of this there is no doubt. || 25 ||
O Six-faced One, everyone meets death within a month;
however, when the life-force is no longer seen at the ankles or in the feet of a man, [death occurs sooner].
One should not entertain any doubt regarding that [sin] which is equal to ten million ghargharas for one who does not perform the recitation (japa) below the elbow.
The experts in the knowledge of time have declared that his death will occur within ten days,
when he can no longer perceive even a single drop of water in the ocean of his navel.
If a crow perches upon the head, or if a dog likewise perches there, [these are the five... || 29 ||
This Jīva moves through Ilā thirty-three times, and it lives for thirty-five ghaṭikās; of this there is no doubt.
If a man strikes with a staff made from the entrails of a dung-eating worm and wrapped in red cloth,
death will occur within seven days.
If one sees in a dream, or even while awake, a woman wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands and unguents, embracing him; || 32 ||
His death shall occur within ten days; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
A woman in her menses, one mounted upon a camel, a widow, and one with a shaven head—(33).
If one sees oneself being embraced either in a dream or while awake, one shall live for eight days; such is the certainty of the scripture. (34)
Whether it be a Śākya or a Śapaṇaka, for him who experiences an embrace [with such a person] either in a dream or even while awake, death will come; of this there is no doubt. (35)
Furthermore, if one mounts a donkey in a dream and leads it along the southern path, having become clad in red garments and adorned with red garlands and unguents; || 36 ||
One meets death through fever; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
One may see an upward-pointing lamp, or it flickers and then becomes still. (37)
"O Six-faced One, it is true that one meets death within a month;
however, a wise man does not perceive the light below within the middle of the body. (38)
The wise have declared that death occurs after twenty-seven days if a light with the luster of an *atasī* flower appears in the petal of the southern direction and so forth. (39)
For thirty-three days, one is constantly afflicted by the disease of death-like darkness;
in the southwestern petal of the lotus, there is a light with the brilliance of a rājāvarta gem.
If at midnight a light resembling the luster of crystal is seen in the western quarter, death will occur within a month; of this there is no doubt.
Death is declared by those learned in the scriptures to occur after forty days;
in the petal of the northwest direction, there is a light resembling the color of turmeric juice.
O Guha, when [the breath] is not seen at night, death will occur after five days;
but if it is at midday on the new moon day, [death occurs] in a large vessel of water.
If a hollow is seen in the solar disc for the duration of one *ghaṭikā*, his death will certainly and constantly occur; this is certain within three fortnights. (44)
On the new moon day, one who sees a phantom in ghee does not perceive forms with his eyes;
for him there is death, without a doubt—no deliberation is required in this matter. (45)
If the flow of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā should shift from one ghaṭikā to another, death will occur within eighteen days; such is the constant teaching of the scriptures. (46)
If one sees a shadowless person in the sky at midday during intense heat from ten directions, death will occur within three months. || 47 ||
A large, white-colored person is seen in the sky;
he meets death within six months, for Śiva does not behold him.
If one does not see a person at all during the eighth watch of the forenoon,
but instead sees a headless trunk (kabandha), his death shall occur within three months.
A large black woman with her left hand raised is seen in the sky;
whether in the waking state or in a dream, his life remains for only three months. (50)
With a sword in hand, dark-complexioned, and holding a noose, most terrible,
she was seen in human form in the sky above his head.
"The wise say that one attains an island [of rebirth]:
a great woman with a severed nose, black in color, and bearing a noose and a sword. (52)
O child, a woman wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands and ointments,
is seen in the sky and is indeed bound by a noose.
If he strikes with a sword, death will occur within five days;
or if a black dog enters at the tip of the *suṣumnā* or even into the house.
"O Six-faced One, it is true that one meets death after three days;
that one meets death after a fortnight is the certainty of the scripture."
With a chariot yoked to a pair of horses and draped in red cloth. || 56 ||
If one wearing red garlands and garments is seen during the sun's southern course,
whether in waking life or in a dream, death will occur within six months.
If a great meteor falls at midday, or if the moon and sun [are eclipsed],
or if there is an earthquake against one's will, death shall occur within ten days.
If one hears a rattling sound like a thick, heavy rain-cloud or the roar of a thunderbolt within the middle of the body,
he will live for two days.
When one perceives a crow, a tawny animal, or even the sound of a rat or a cat in the middle of the body, [there is a specific result]. || 60 ||
One certainly suffers from madhumeha for ten days;
[if one perceives] the Teacher as a sound or the Teacher within the heart in the middle of the body. (61)
If one repeatedly seizes two black cows by their horns and runs about, there will be ten deaths from that place on earth. 62.
There, in the stomach, there is constant pain; from convulsions there, death occurs.
At the end of the bow, in the eternal place, it extends twelve finger-breadths to the end of the head.
If it is seen at the location of the *bindu*, one lives for three days;
now listen, O Six-faced One, to the meditation concerning death. (64)
The wise one, having encapsulated the temple within the lunar orb, places the co-wife in the center of the pericarp.
One who is always composed in meditation should contemplate the power that inspires confidence in the Self;
O child, within a year, this supreme [practice] brings about the destruction of death. (66)
One who meditates [thus] indeed for twelve years lives for a thousand years;
one should meditate on the temple as resembling Indra’s peak and like the orb of the moon.
The wise one, having encapsulated the self with the fourth [vowel],
with the bindu and nāda crowning the crest, it becomes the seventh ghaṭikā.
He lives for twenty-one thousand five hundred years;
in the middle part of his body, there is a palace as white as a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon.
Enclosing it within the syllable *indu* (the moon), one should meditate on the six thousand [breaths] for thirty-two years, ten *ghaṭikās* each day; he shall live [for that duration]. || 70 ||
In the middle of the body, one should visualize a palace resembling the whiteness of cow’s milk;
and in the center of that, one should enclose oneself within the orb of the moon.
O child, for twelve ghaṭikās and twenty-three years,
he shall live for seven thousand years, O Six-faced One.
The wise one, having enclosed the central body— which resembles molten gold— within a lunar orb both above and below, [should contemplate it] from the palace.
If the heart-mass is made of gold, it becomes a *ghaṭikā* for fifteen [years];
he lives for twenty-four thousand years.
The wise one [should visualize] a palace resembling a conch shell within the hollow of the heart-lotus;
in its center, he should encapsulate the Self with the fourth [syllable].
For twenty-five years, there shall be sixteen ghaṭikās;
he shall live for nine thousand [years]—this is the truth, O Six-faced One. (76)
One should constantly contemplate the palace, resembling snow, the kunda flower, and the moon;
indeed, it is endowed with the fourth [vowel], namely the Bindu, together with the Nāda. (77)
One should flood the temple there with nectar joined with the moon;
one should meditate for seventeen *ghaṭikās* or twenty-six years.
Indeed, by the power of the potency of the mantra, one lives there for ten thousand years;
there, within the mandala of the heart-lotus, the person should enfold the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
The wise and intelligent one should visualize the palace in the center with the fourth [vowel]; joined with the *bindu*, he shall [attain success] for twenty-seven years. (80)
One should meditate with a one-pointed mind for eighteen *ghaṭikās*;
he shall live for twenty-two thousand [years], of this there is no doubt. || 81 ||
O child, one should contemplate the temple situated between the two bows, located in the midst of the moon, fire, and sun, within the heart and in the center of the left side.
One should always contemplate [the deity], who resembles a hibiscus flower, enclosed within the twelve-syllable mantra of Prajāpati joined with the *bindu*. 83.
The wise one should utter the *prāsāda* mantra with sixteen *mātrās*,
and he should always place it within a duration of nineteen *ghaṭikās*;
such a person, O Six-faced One, lives for fifteen thousand years.
One should contemplate an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp at the tip of the Suṣumnā;
there, one should contemplate the Prāsāda mantra adorned with the sixteen vowels. (86)
O child, one should always meditate upon [the letter] resembling a bee, enclosed within the moon (the vowel *i*),
and indeed, O child, conjoined with the fourth [vowel] accompanied by the bindu.
Having filled [the vessels] with nectar itself, one who is composed should flood them;
in all the fire-pits (homakūpa), one should contemplate the form of Kṛṣṇa. || 88 ||
One should contemplate black nectar extending from the crown of the head down to the soles of the feet;
for this is the means of arresting graying hair for nineteen years. (89)
A self-controlled man who practices this daily for twenty ghaṭikās shall live for twenty thousand years, remaining steadfast in the vow of celibacy.
At the end of the Suṣumnā, four finger-breadths [above], there is a most beautiful white lotus with a hundred petals; the wise one should enclose it within the lunar orb. 91.
One should visualize a palace in the center and flood it with nectar;
one should contemplate it as white, extending as far as Kālāgniśiva.
One should practice this Mṛtyuñjaya Yoga for thirty years;
liberated from old age and death, he lives for thirty thousand years.
One should visualize oneself in the center of a thousand-petaled lotus, white as a conch shell or cow’s milk, situated atop a temple. 94.
Then, one should flood the body with the nectar of the lunar orb, [the mantra] being endowed with the bindu and nāda of the fourth letter of the seventh group.
O child, one should meditate for thirty-five years and thirty-two ghaṭikās;
by performing ten thousand recitations of the fourth [mantra], which consists of the square of sixteen syllables, one shall live [for that duration].
Above that, four finger-breadths high, is a circle adorned with ten thousand petals;
in its center is a palace enclosed within the moon.
One should meditate on the Suṣumnā piercing the crown of the head and flowing with nectar; one should contemplate oneself being bathed by it and completely filled. 98.
If one meditates for thirty-two years, it shall amount to thirty-two ghaṭikās; one shall live for fifty thousand [years]—there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (99)
The wise one should contemplate a palace that is an extremely white and stainless lotus with a hundred thousand petals, and [he should contemplate] himself as situated in its center.
Having encased it within the moon, the wise practitioner should meditate on the yoga-seat as facing downwards, dripping nectar; having filled it, he should cause it to overflow.
One should meditate for thirty-five years, yet it is accomplished in just as many ghaṭikās;
[the deity] is gentle, white as cow’s milk, and extends from the soles of the feet to the middle of the body. 102.
The yogi should contemplate the filling [of the breath] for one hundred thousand times; he lives [long].
Abandoning exhalation (recaka), he should always practice inhalation (pūraka). 103.
It is somewhat like nirvāṇa, yet it ends in illusion;
it is the destruction of death by means of the self through the nose, reaching the very end within the interior of the belly.
The wise one should first contemplate a subtle crystal support; in its center, however, he should contemplate himself enclosed within the moon. 105.
One should meditate there upon the supreme equal flavor (samarasa), which destroys death;
place yourself in the midst of space, and place space in the midst of yourself.
Having rendered oneself bodiless, one should not think of anything;
such a yoga is the direct conquest of death, and he lives through the great dissolution.
The yogi should contemplate the space resembling a red bubble, which has the bindu as its deity; by that, death is destroyed.
The practitioner of yoga who contemplates the state of equal flavor (samarasa) effects the destruction of death. || 109 ||
(114) The wise one should constantly meditate upon the Self in its center as having the shape of a *kadamba* flower bud and resembling a red bubble. || 110 ||
This is indeed the supreme Mṛtyuñjaya; one shall attain the state of being like the sky.
Resembling clear crystal, like a drop, incomparable and beyond comparison;
through the yoga of the state of equal flavor (samarasībhāva), it is the supreme destroyer of death. 112.
The wise man should constantly contemplate within the middle of the body that which resembles the whiteness of cow’s milk, in the form of a drop, perfectly pure and of uniform essence.
By this yoga of Mṛtyuñjaya, one attains freedom from old age and decay;
or, one may drink a mouthful in the morning that has been steeped in the nectar-water of Soma. (114)
Having meditated upon the nectar of the palace, one conquers death without a doubt;
by grinding with the sound [of the breath], the Moon becomes Śiva in the center of the Moon. 115.
One should practice meditating on the Self within the middle of Śiva, in the center of the palate;
having abandoned exhalation and inhalation, one should practice retention (kumbhaka). || 116 ||
Remember, O Indra, the supreme destroyer of death:
having placed the syllable *A* on the crown of the head and the syllable *Ā* on the forehead. (117)
Having assigned *i* and *ī* to the two eyes, one should assign *u* and *ū* to the two ears;
having assigned *ṛ* and *ṝ* to the two nostrils, one should assign *ḷ* and *ḹ* to the two cheeks. (118)
Having assigned *e* and *ai* to the two eyes, one should assign *o* and *au* to the two lips;
having assigned *aṃ* and *aḥ* to the two rows of teeth, the wise man should assign *taṃ*.
One should place the *ka*-group on the right hand and the *ca*-group on the left;
the *ṭa*-group on the right side and the *pa*-group on the left foot. (120)
He drank [the letter *pa*] on the right side, while it shone indeed on the left side;
having placed the letter *ha* in the heart and the letter *ma* in the region of the navel. (121)
One should place the syllable *ya* in the regions of the skin, the syllable *ra* in the region of the blood,
the syllable *la* in the region of the flesh, and the syllable *va* in the region of the fat.
The letter Śa is in the region of the bones, the letter Ṣa in the region of the marrow;
the letter Sa is said to be the semen, and the letter Ha in the region of the genitals.
Having placed the letter *la* on the two testicles and the letter *va* in the middle of the feet, one should place all these [syllables] in sequence, joined with the *bindu*. 124.

Having thus performed the ritual of abandonment according to the rules, the wise practitioner should subsequently commence meditation, having correctly applied the Mātṛkā-mantra to all ritual actions in accordance with reality.
Worship, recitation, meditation, absorption, and likewise the fire-oblation—thus ends the twenty-first chapter, the Chapter on Kālacakra, in the *Kālottara*, the *Ayutakṣayasaṃhitā*. 21.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
I shall now proclaim the yoga of touch (sparśayoga), which is the means for achieving the yoga of being (bhāvayoga)—
the all-pervading, most excellent, pure, and supreme sustainer of youth.

It destroys wrinkles, grey hair, and impurities, and always increases gentleness and vigor. At whatever age one undergoes shaving, bathing, or sowing the seed [of ritual action], at that very age one becomes wise; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
But in the Kali age, one should indeed undertake [the practice] as prescribed in the scriptures. || 3 ||
In the Dvāpara age it is said to be one-sixth [of its efficacy], while in the Tretā age it is one-thirtieth;
however, in the Kṛta age one attains perfection according to what is taught in the scriptures—of this there is no doubt. (4)
But in an auspicious place, O child, having carefully leveled the ground— whether at Naimiṣa, or Puṣkara, or the bliss-bestowing Kurukṣetra— (5)
Whether at Gaṅgādvāra, or at Prayāga, or at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, or at Aṣṭabhāsa, or at Prabhāsa, or even in the Devadāru forest; || 6 ||
Whether on Kailāsa or Mandara, or on the summit of Mount Meru, on Himavat or Hemakūṭa, on Niṣadha or the Nīla mountain; || 7 ||
On Mount Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, or at the peak of the Vindhya mountains; on Śrīśaila or Svāmiśaila; or by the Godāvarī or the Sarasvatī.
One should have it performed at Gokarṇa, or Śaṅkukarṇa, or indeed at Kanyātīrtha;
or on the bank of the Sindhu lake, or even on the shore of the Sarasvatī.
The earth of a Brahmin is white; however, the earth of a king is red.
The earth of a Vaiśya is yellow, while that of a fourth [caste] is black;
the earth of a Brāhmaṇa has the fragrance of ghee, whereas that of a Kṣatriya has the fragrance of blood.
If it has the smell of urine, it belongs to a Vaiśya; if it smells like excrement, it belongs to a Śūdra.
Having ascertained the color, smell, and taste, one should begin the construction of the yoga-chamber.
The place of initiation, the place of Śiva, and likewise the place of ritual bathing—all these are places for yoga; this is the rule that has been proclaimed. (13)
Whether it be a palace, a pavilion, a peaked roofed structure, or even a house—be it three-storied, two-storied, or even single-storied. || 14 ||
One should have an auspicious dwelling constructed using clay or hair according to one's unseen destiny (adṛṣṭa);
it should be provided with doors and bolts, and equipped with long ramparts. (15)
It was crowded with flowering trees and endowed with jackfruit, mango, and other varieties; it was filled with coconut palms, *kamuka* trees, *puṃnāga*, and *vakula* trees.

The cows should dwell for seven days in a place provided with śamī, bilva, palāśa, and other trees, as well as kuśa grass, kāśa grass, and the like; the master [of the rite] should remain for ten or nine days.
In front, there is a shrine and other structures adorned with Lakṣmī, free from thieves and the like;
to the north is a village by the water, and to the west is a lotus-pavilion.
To the south, however, is the Bahisthāna region, while to the east is Satyasthāna;
it is devoid of Barbaras, Pulindas, and Kirātas.
On a seat spread with kusha grass, rags, or deerskin, facing either east or north,
with his feet placed upward on his thighs and his left hand resting upon the right,
with his tongue motionless against the palate and his mouth closed, he should remain firm in resolve. (21)
Seated with his gaze fixed on the tip of his nose, touching tooth against tooth,
the lord of yogis prostrated before Śiva, the peaceful one who bears the moon upon his crest.
One should gradually undertake the yoga that brings about existence;
[one perceives] at the tip of the nose a lunar disc spread with a network of moonlight.
Then, joined with the fourth vowel (N), situated in the middle of the moon,
it emerges through the five forms along with the *iḍā* channel and the armor (*varman*).
Having filled [the vessel], one should subsequently exhale through Piṅgalā with the fire-armor mantra;
that which is the second [syllable] joined with a bindu, situated in the triangle conjoined with fire. (25)
O Guha, having visualized as before the [deity] in front, surrounded by a garland of fever-flames,
one should fill the breath through the right channel as before. (26)

In the same manner, one should subsequently expel [the air] slowly and gradually through the *iḍā* [nāḍī]; one should practice this three or four times during each *savana* (daily ritual period) for a month, or indeed for a fortnight or a month.
One attains the purification of the channels, characterized by distinct signs,
through a slightly specialized means and by means of the mental *praṇava*.
The exhalations and so forth should be performed in sequence as before, or otherwise;
through this practice at the three junctions of the day for three months, purification is declared. (29)
Lightness of the body, radiance, and the absence of digestive fire in the stomach— this manifestation of knowledge is severed [from worldly ties] and indicates that purity.
The pure [vital breaths] reside within the written [channels]; the path of the channels belongs to one who has conquered the senses.
Kalā, Karma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—O child, [attain] victory over these through the letters. 32.
In the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it moves within the range from the tip of the big toe to the nose;
it resembles the color blue and is joined with the letter *ra* and a nasal drop (*bindu*). (33)

Through the application of the centers beginning with the heart, one should always practice exhalation (recaka) as far as the tips of the big toes, followed by inhalation (pūraka), and then retention (kumbhaka).
First, the wise one should practice inhalation for thirty-two measures;
then, O Śiva, he should practice retention (kumbhaka) for sixty-four days while united with Śiva.
One should perform the *kumbhaka* twice as long and exhale very slowly during the *recaka*.
O child, in the fourth year, the Guru should practice this thirty-two times.
In the fifth year, the practitioner shall possess sixty-four qualities.

O Six-faced One, the means for conquering all vital breaths has indeed been taught by Keśava through the path of victory over the Maruts and by means of the removal of conceptual construction (vikalpa). 38.
Holding [the breath] at these locations—the big toe, the navel, and the tip of the nose—this practice of going and returning is another [method], following the sequence as before. (39)

Through the increase of inhalation (pūraka) and the rest, and by resorting to the peak of exhalation (recaka), this [practice] has been described as "two years" in sequence; thus it was detailed by Keśava.
Furthermore, Kṛṣṇa [purifies] the little toe, the heel, the knee, the ankle, both joints, and the back. (41)
Even for a corpse, such practice is thus proclaimed. || 43 ||

Whether the practice is one whose self has departed, or it is afflicted by disease due to its placement, such is the exhaling breath (*recaka*); the setting forth is through the support of the *haṃsa* in the inhaling breath (*pūraka*). (44)
"I am the Lord, the means of victory, conjoined with Śiva;
I abide in the heart, the navel, and all the seats of accomplishment (siddhis), as well as in the hips, elbows, and knees. (45)
In the thirty-two junction points (sandhi), it is proclaimed to be white in color;
it is endowed with the seed-syllable of the Moon and the Prāsāda mantra joined with the Bindu. 46.
The restraint of the stations of concentration has been described as "Victory" (vijaya);
through the uninterrupted practice of yoga, exhalation (recaka) occurs in the sequence of the two preceding [stages]. 47.
(120) It extends for two hand-measures and attains victory very swiftly;
[it is located] in the heart, throat, palate, between the eyebrows, and also in the ears and the eyes. (48)
The fever located in the head, the waist, and the back is caused by wind and blood; when combined with phlegm (prasāda), it is a quotidian fever, but from wind alone, it is a tertian fever.
On both sides, O child, on both hands as well, on both palms, and on both armpits; || 50 ||
Now listen to the description of the form and color of Udāna:
Udāna is the color of a bumblebee; the letter Ya is situated above it, followed by two others. (51)
It is situated in the calves, thighs, wrists, and the hollow of the throat; it resides in the heart, the navel, the belly, the back, and in all the limbs and all the joints.
The syllable *ikāra*, red in color and joined with Śiva,
should be used for inhalation (*pūraka*), exhalation (*recaka*), or retention (*kumbhaka*) as before.
Through the practice of going and coming, mastery over the vyāna and udāna breaths is attained;
the fourth [consonant] beginning with *ya* and the fifth ending in *bha*. (54)
Combined with the seed-syllables of Prāṇa and the others, there is no doubt that through the Prāsāda mantra one attains victory over the Nātha and the rest by means of the divine Prāsāda. 55.
Perform inhalation, retention, and exhalation;
one should perform them in reverse order for the wise Keśava. (56)
Dhanañjaya, through the practice and application of this knowledge, should desire mastery over all the vital winds (vāyu) by means of the heart, throat, navel, eyes, and the entire body. 57.
Having joined the function of the prāṇa with the apāna and drawn it up into the heart,
one should bring the udāna to that very place, conjoined with the vyāna.
p.
121) Having brought together there the elephant, the tortoise, as well as the lizard and Devadatta, Dhananjaya, the knower of the principles of drawing, drew them evenly. 59.
The ears, palate, and mouth... || 60 ||
Having fixed [the gaze] on the tip of the nose, between the eyebrows, on the surface of the forehead, and on the crown of the head,
one should indeed perform [the practice] above that and further lead it to the power of all (sarvaśakti).
[One should contemplate] the Bindu and Nāda;
from that, one should lead [the soul] to the eternal state of Śiva, the imperishable liberation.
Thus, by means of the path of simultaneous mastery over all the winds,
this is the path of mastery regarding the wind in this supreme *Vijaya-tantra*.
Now, the method of the sevenfold path, known as the yoga of touch (*sparśayoga*), shall be explained.
Inhalation (pūraka), exhalation (recaka), and even the superior retention (kumbhaka) below; || 64 ||
Withdrawal (pratyāhāra) and restraint (nirodha) are recognized as its own internal divisions.
Here, one should fill the vital air through the nostrils and the apertures of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*). (65)
One who is composed and has conquered the self should perform the filling of the corner with the wind-palace, as delimited by space, time, and other factors. (66)
When the breath is like a full pitcher, from the thumb up to the region of the head, that should be known as Kumbhaka; it is the seventh in the sequence of Sparśayoga.

On the crown of the head, between the forehead and the eyebrows, in the two cavities of the palate, in the ears, the heart, the belly, the navel, the throat, and the penis—there, O Sage, [is] me. || 68 ||
One should exhale in succession from the abdomen, the buttocks, and the toes of both feet;
O child, this [practice] is threefold, sixfold, or even ninefold compared to the kumbhaka.
One should gradually exhale for twelve or sixteen years;
likewise, inhalation is from *apāna*, and *kumbhaka* consists in remaining hidden within.
Endowed with the number of Kāla at the regions of the navel, heart, and throat, the Vānaprastha is proclaimed as the form of Ardhanārīśvara without the jar (akumbha). || 71 ||
Outside of the recitation, the water-pot is the wind-pot, which is considered to be the breath;
having drawn [the breath] upward from the downward-breath (apāna), its retention occurs in the heart and other locations.
That [state] is to be known as "higher" (uttara), while the opposite is "lower" (adhara);
it reaches the previously mentioned locations starting from the big toe and ending at the head. || 73 ||
The body is pervaded by another garment, yet it has gone to dissolution in Nirvana.
That indeed should be known as cessation (nirodha), for it is truly the destruction of death;
such is the summary of the means for mastering all the vital winds (vāyu). || 75 ||
Alternatively, having filled all the winds within the body with the *kūṭa* of the *prāsāda*, one should perform the *kumbhaka*.
O dear one, when it has gone out, one should exhale for the sake of lightness and reach a definitive conclusion;
first there is the covering, and then a slight touch within the chamber.
One should again perform inhalation (pūraka) and retention (kumbhaka) immediately thereafter;
this [practice] regarding the touch of the aged one at the time of Nirvāṇa was indeed described by Keśava. || 78 ||
Joined at the navel, heart, ears, and hair, it was released from the mouth of the monkey... [the rest of the verse is obscured]. || 79 ||
The external pillars of the *recika* are considered to be beyond that;
or else, having drawn them upward, they are to be held in the region of the navel.
The *tavarga* [consonant group] is in the practice of Varuṇa; the *pavarga* is in the practice of Vāyu;
the *yavarga* is in the practice of Uttara; and the *ravarga* is in the practice of Īśāna. (81)

O child, one should indeed contemplate the palace [of the body] in the case of malevolent rites (nābhicāra), but the syllable *ṣa* is not uttered; having filled it with the breath-retention (kumbhaka) in due order, one should meditate upon it.
O child, one should lead Nāda, Bindu, Śakti, Maheśa, and Sadāśiva toward Śiva,
who possesses a majesty free from all affliction.
"O child, this is the wheel-base; through its touch, supreme victory is attained.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, on the meditation on the wheel of the ten winds within the *Sparśayoga* section of the *Kālottara*. 22.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
Having reflected upon everything with the mind during the night and having restrained it, one should fix the consciousness within the middle of the body upon Śiva, the supreme cause. (1)
Then one attains identity with that; there is no doubt that one becomes Śiva himself, even as one exhales through the aperture of the skull.
I shall explain the inference, the seed-syllable, and the deity; one should meditate upon the temple in the navel, endowed with the *nāda* and the *bindu*. (3)
Having restrained all the vital airs, one should place them in the center of the navel;
one should fill [the breath] through the *iḍā* or through the *suṣumnā* during inhalation (*pūraka*). || 4 ||
Having meditated with a focused mind upon the center of the heart-lotus, which possesses the luster of a lapis lazuli gem, one should contemplate the supreme opening of the door.
Having joined [the breath] with the cavity of the palate, one should lead it slowly through the *suṣumnā*;
one should lead Śiva into the *suṣumnā* at the heart, throat, palate, and the middle of the eyebrows. (6)
Filled with the touch of the mind, Nila is indeed completely full;
by means of the palace, Śakti has opened the door of the crest.
When the posture has been mastered and the yoga of breath control (prāṇāyāma) has likewise been conquered,
one should diligently practice the means for entering another's body.
Residing within the lotus of the heart, situated in the midst of the three mandalas,
and endowed with the three qualities (guṇas), I am that individual soul (jīva) who maintains his own essential nature.
On the left side of the eight-petalled lotus, it is marked by the syllables *ve* and *nu*;
the letter *ma* is in the middle of the body, while the *nāda* and *bindu* are in the *virodhaka*.
The person, endowed with the vision of dharma and adharma, is joined with the city of eight constituents (puryaṣṭaka);
he possesses a body of consciousness that is entirely pure and endowed with a brilliant luster.
But if this descendant of Rajas and Tamas sits upon this lotus-throne,
he shall pierce the Brahma-knot and then depart from the city of Vāyu.
The yogi should enter the pericarp of the heart-lotus through the piṅgalā;
remaining there, he should settle all [the deities] in their respective places.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
likewise, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, and devadatta are proclaimed. || 14 ||
And Dhanañjaya as the tenth should establish them each in their own respective places:
the ear, the skin, the eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth. (15)
One should place the five organs of perception each in their own respective location;
likewise, speech, feet, hands, the anus, and the genitals as the fifth [are the organs of action]. (16)
One should establish the five organs of action each in their own respective place;
likewise, the fourfold group consisting of the mind, intellect, ego, and the Great Principle (mahat), along with the Infinite (ananta). (17)
O child, the wise one should offer [the self] higher and higher within the heart;
through this union with the body, the self-controlled one rejoices as before.
"One may enter many final bodies with the desire for a single [final] instruction.
Such, O Six-faced One, is the rule for entering a dead body. (19)
I shall now describe, in brief, the entry of the living soul into the body:
having emerged through the previously mentioned door, preceded by the seed-syllable of Śakti.
Having entered through the gate of the wind and taken recourse in the navel-cakra,
one should emerge by means of the Mahāmāya [mantra] from the previously mentioned *payabīja*.
Then, being fully concentrated, one should go from there to the navel-cakra,
which is situated in the center of the support of the mandala, namely the pericarp of the heart-lotus.
There, having restrained the movement of that [external] breath by means of one's own vital airs,
one should continue to restrain it until it is entirely devoid of activity.
While that [breath] falls to the ground, one should remain very firm for that duration;
[so too should one restrain] all the sense organs and the fourfold group beginning with the vital breath (prāṇa).
The wise man should cease the activity of desire while remaining in his own respective state;
thus, with his senses gradually withdrawn, he becomes liberated at the end of the body.
"One should remain in all activities as if in another body were superior to one's own former body;
when one's own body has decayed, the wise man should always enter another body.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Primacy of the Rites for the Dead and the Rites for the Living," in the *Kālottara*, within the section on the rules for the Yoga of Touch (*sparśayoga*). 23.
Īśvara said:
Now, indeed, knowledge and dispassion arise truly from purification alone;
I shall now proclaim the Great Yoga, which is the means for accomplishing all desires and goals.
Through the grace of Śiva alone, who is as vast as an ocean of knowledge,
one enters this state of Śiva called the Temple (Prāsāda) within the center of the lotus.
There, one should meditate upon one's own maṇḍala, consisting of the wells in its natural form;
therein, one should contemplate the lunar maṇḍala as being slightly diminished.
Above that is the form of the Puruṣa, consisting of light and incomparable;
first, a circle of fire, triangular in shape, [generated] from the seed-mantra.
Above that is the lunar disc, which is joined with the fourth [vowel];
it is devoid of the three fire-discs and is the supreme solar mandala.
From the solar disc, the practitioner of mantra [visualizes] the unsurpassed lunar disc;
above that, he visualizes the Puruṣa endowed with the twenty-five [principles].
Resembling the rājāvarta gem, with the luster of an atasī flower,
possessing a divine radiance like that of a ruby, and slightly resembling the hue of a bumblebee.
The principle known as Īśvara has a height of one thumb and is fashioned like a hundred rising suns; by it this world is impelled.
In the midst of that, however, is a slender crest-lock (śikhā) with the radiance of a flashing lightning bolt;
they call that the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti), while beyond that is Supreme Śiva.
Having thus reflected in due order with his mind, O Śiva, he should remain absorbed in that [state], practicing the recitation while restraining all fluctuations of the mind.

When the mind has attained identity with that [object] through the state of being absorbed in its nature, one becomes the direct creator of all creation and dissolution, having realized everything. (11)
Having reached that state there, you indeed emerged through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) by way of the rays,
the day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern course, and the year.
The manifestation of the abode of the gods, whose stride is marked by the pure moon—these are the twelve Ādityas, the eleven Rudras, and Īśvara. (13)
Navaśakti, Navālakṣmī, Sāvitrī, and Dharaṇī;
and the great power of the Lord, Manonmanī, who is both supreme and inferior.
The twelvefold form is presided over by the twelve great powers;
by that [practice], one who is freed from all impurities shall go to Śiva.
Eternal, pure, perfectly contented, blissful, windless, and fixed;
omniscient, of true resolve, and the cause of all causes. || 16 ||
Having attained the supreme form of Śiva, which destroys all afflictions, the means to liberation has been described by those who have conquered the activities of all the gods. || 17 ||
But by means of this very practice performed upon the previous reality, the teacher indeed attains nirvāṇa; death remains established within the body.

One whose mind is thus focused on the aforementioned [practice], even without mastery over the vital air (vāyu), attains liberation just as a person who has departed from the body by his own will. || 19 ||
I shall proclaim the divine method, endowed with the essence of the seed-syllable;
it resides within the mantra of the third group of consonants and is extracted by means of fire and wind.
Having placed the Lord of Bījas at the navel, endowed with the tenth vowel and the sixth [vowel] and adorned with the Bindu on its crest, and likewise having placed the next [Bīja] at the heart; 21.

That letter which is well-conjoined with the third [vowel] and joined with the preceding letter— one should subsequently place that letter, the Lord of Letters, upon the head, both forward and backward. (22)
One should install the heart-mantra and the others in their proper sequence, joined with their respective preceding syllables;
these should be conjoined with the *prāsāda* mantra and accompanied by the purificatory limb-mantras (*pavitra-aṅga*).
O dear one, one should perform the placement [of mantras] in the middle body and take refuge in the state of equanimity;
the mind then attains the state of the Great Earth and subsequently reaches Nirvāṇa.
Nirvāṇa is indeed the destruction of death; this is truly one and the same.
One should meditate upon this Yoga of the Conqueror of Death within the center of the body. (25)
First, one should go from the heart to the navel, and from there to the central point;
thereafter, one should meditate upon the supreme western gate of Śiva.
Having worshipped the God according to the prescribed rule, one should meditate upon Him constantly and without sloth—
the omniscient creator of all, whose eyes, heads, and mouths are on every side.
Having performed the ritual of self-projection (sakalīkaraṇa), one should meditate upon Śiva, the stainless one,
who is of the nature of light, supreme and divine, and joined by the lords of the eight directions.
One should meditate for a watch (yāma), free from inhalation and other [breath-control techniques] due to its state of being a continuous thread;
for this is indeed the supreme Mṛtyuñjaya [mantra], through the practice of yoga for six months. (29)
One attains eightfold supernatural powers within three months; of this there is no doubt.
Or else, [one attains] the state of Brahmā.
Having internalized the reality within himself, he should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
in an instant, he attains that state which is designated as Nirvāṇa.
For thus, by one who has traversed that path, the supreme object of meditation [is attained].
Having thus brought the vital breath (prāṇa) under control, one should practice dhāraṇā and the other [yogic stages].
Dhāraṇā is the restraint of mental fluctuations regarding the principle of Śiva and so forth; that [restraint] is practiced upon moving objects.
That meditation, which is a continuous flow of its activity and consists merely of a partial manifestation, is empty of its own nature; that is called *samādhi*, which is yoga. (34)
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the third [stage], cessation, occurs in one who remains seated as previously described, having slowly exhaled the breath. (35)
One should indeed fill [the body] starting from the big toe up to the *iḍā* channel;
having restrained the mind for a long time at the big toe, it remains fixed right there.
One should wear it on the heel, then the ankle, then sequentially on the two shanks and knees, then on the thigh, the penis, and the navel; thus one should hold it upon the ear.

Situated in the cavity of the palate, between the eyebrows, at the end of the Suṣumṇā, and in the twelfth [center], he remains for half a ghaṭikā; in due order, he ascends further until he is established in Śiva for a yāma.
O child, this *mṛtyuñjaya* [mantra] leads one directly to nirvāṇa;
if one practices it for one year, one will attain a lifespan of ten thousand years. (39)
One should lead [the breath] from there up to the city of Brahmā by the path already described;
having brought it to the tip of the big toe, it is then established within the middle of the body.
Then one should expel the wind through the path situated in the *prāṇa*;
by means of the application of the previously mentioned locations, the *dhāraṇā* shall last for one *ghaṭikā*.
"Having restrained the breath for one watch (yāma), one shall conquer death from above and below.
Thus has been described divine concentration (dhāraṇā), which is indeed the destruction of death. 42.
By practicing for one watch (yāma), the yogi of consciousness attains supreme Śiva.
Hereafter, I shall explain dhāraṇā, which bestows liberation. || 43 ||
Within six months, there is no doubt that one attains the sovereign power (*aiśvarya*) of the qualities such as *aṇiman* and the rest;
the entire world, moving and unmoving, is pervaded by him—above, below, and across. (44)
One should mentally project the three worlds in sequential order,
or even the seven worlds, into the midst of the *piṇḍa*.
O child, having gradually brought forth the palace within the triple mandala, joined with the seed-syllables and endowed with the mind, the islands, the oceans, and the mountains.
Having condensed Jambudvīpa by means of yoga and attained that [state],
one should bring that [consciousness] and cast it into the Supreme Self within the mass of consciousness.
At all times indeed, O child, at the summit of the entire world,
within the midst of the three mandalas, there is the touch of the mind.
And within six months, one perceives there the entire collection of the seven worlds;
one attains omniscience and reaches the all-pervading Śiva. || 49 ||
For him, there shall be victory over death; it will certainly come to pass within a year.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva himself [will grant this]. (50)
For those who maintain the fivefold *amā* [vow], that very thing shall come to pass;
Brahmā, four-faced, is to be meditated upon as residing in the center of the heart-lotus. (51)
Consisting of the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), red in color, [he is generated] from his own seed-syllable by means of the syllable Om;
he has four faces and four arms, and is the supreme cause of creation. 52.
He was endowed with knowledge that is never opposed [to its object], as well as with dispassion,
sovereignty, and righteousness, holding in his hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Holding a water-pot in his left hand and a rosary of beads in his right, he is mounted upon a swan; thus [he is] Rādhā, the one who pierces the knots of ignorance regarding the Self and knowledge.
The knowledge of the stars, the attainment of liberation, as well as all sovereign power,
and the various perfections resulting from specific yoga— all these arise from yoga. (55)
Consisting of self-conceit, dark-complexioned, four-faced, and eight-armed,
he holds a trident and is meditated upon in the heart with the Bindu and the Pṛṣṭha-nāda.
Holding the Kālāgni bow and an arrow in all his hands,
as well as a sword and an axe, he moved with the speed of the fire of time and serpents.

One should meditate in the heart upon the three-eyed god who bears the crescent moon and wears an animal skin, who is endowed with qualities such as sovereignty, and who possesses the eightfold qualities of meditation. (58)
O child, by mere meditation, one who is always permeated by a state of being true attains mastery over Prakṛti as well as victory over death. (59)
The yogin shall attain the accomplishment of whatever he desires regarding all things, and by virtue of this practice for one year, he shall reach the world of Śiva, even if he has committed sins.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Meditation on Kālāgnirudra and Brahmā," within the section on the Path of Dhāraṇā in the Sparśayoga of the Kālottara.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said: Listen, I shall now explain the yoga of the eight-limbed touch: yama and niyama, as well as āsana and prāṇāyāma. (1)
Withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and absorption—these are declared to be the eight limbs; the wise know this as the yoga of touch (sparśayoga). || 2 ||
The fourfold set beginning with *yama* and ending with *prāṇāyāma* is the external limb; that beginning with *pratyāhāra* and ending with *samādhi* is declared to be the internal limb. (3)
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, forgiveness, fortitude, compassion, and knowledge—these, categorized according to their nature, constitute the internal limbs [of yoga]. (4)
And those restraints (yamas) which have been declared in this auspicious Vijaya Tantra are:
purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and worship of the Lord. (5)
Listening to the established doctrine, as well as recitation, oblation, and the observance of vows—these ten are proclaimed in the glorious [tradition] and are honored in all scriptures. (6)
One should practice this until the yoga of the touch of accomplishment and victory is attained; twenty postures (āsanas) are taught in this auspicious Vijaya Tantra.
The Padmaka, the Svastika, the Gomukha, and likewise the Vikaṭa; the Sūci, the Ekapāda, the Kukkuṭa, and the Vīra as well. (8)
The lotus-seat (padmāsana), the single-back (ekapṛṣṭha), the tortoise (kūrma), and the stainless (vimala);
then the staff (daṇḍa), the triple-staff (tridaṇḍa), the cow-ear (gokarṇa), and beyond that, the lion-throne (siṃhāsana).
The vṛtta, utkuṭika, gajāsya, and gajakarṇaka—these twenty postures have been declared; one should practice them along with the single vāñcita posture. (10)
A stable and comfortable seat is prescribed and honored in all tantras;
it should be firmly established on three legs, just as the vessels of crows and other birds are.
Having resorted to a blissful state of concentration that remains stable for a long time, one should therefore practice every posture with all possible effort. (12)
O Guha, by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one indeed obtains the fruit of heaven and liberation,
as well as the fruit of all the Vedas and the fruit of all sacrifices.
O child, by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one indeed obtains the fruit of all gifts, the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas), and the fruit of the worship of Śiva. (14)
Upon a soft seat, he should place kusha grass and then a deerskin as a covering; seated comfortably upon that, facing either east or north. (15)
In brief, having avoided both overeating and fasting, one should remain in a house that is free from wind, devoid of fear, and cleared of worms, insects, and the like. || 16 ||
Keeping the neck and head erect, touching tooth to tooth, sitting with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose and not looking toward the quarters; || 17 ||
Having purified the channels in the temple accompanied by me,
one should fill [the right] with the right [nostril] and exhale through the left alone.
The wise one, being composed, should fill the Varuṇa-maṇḍala with the letter *la* joined with the second vowel (*i*), using the left [hand] as before. || 19 ||
Starting from the big toe up to the vital breath,
one should indeed exhale everything through the iḍā on the left and the piṅgalā on the right.

In this way, after five, six, or seven [days], or for six months, or even a year, one attains the purification of the channels (nāḍīśuddhi), freed from the three types of knots and the three humors (doṣas). || 21 ||
O Six-faced One, the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) should follow with the Prāsāda mantra;
first, the wise one should fill the belly with sixteen mātrās.
The retention of breath (kumbhaka) should be complete for sixty-four measures, like a full jar;
O Guha, one should exhale the air from the head with thirty-two measures.
Thus let there be the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), consisting of exhalation, inhalation, and retention;
performed daily sixteen times, and indeed always sixteen-fold.
O Guha, by means of *prāṇāyāma*, one indeed attains the supreme goal;
thereafter comes the conquest of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and so forth, as well as the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the phoneme (*varṇa*), and that which is the essence. (25)

The syllable *ya* is the seed-syllable of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), possessing the luster of a dark blue cloud; the syllable *ra* is the downward breath (*apāna*), likewise possessing the radiance of a throbbing heart. (26)

The letter *la* is said to be the apāna breath, belonging to the Śākha [deity] and resembling the bandhūka flower; the letter *pa* is said to be the udāna breath, belonging to Varuṇa and resembling a conch shell. || 27 ||
The letter *Bha* is said to be the *samāna* [vāyu]; it is auspicious and resembles crystal.
It is situated in the heart, the navel, the nose, the ears, and the big toe. (28)
The seat of the prāṇa is said to be the Brahma-granthi and the chest; that of the apāna is the penis, the anus, the thighs, the knees, and the shins. (29)
In the abdomen and the shanks, as well as in the region of the hips and the base of the navel;
Vyāna, Śrotra, and Cakṣus are in the two meditations from the region of the throat. (30)
The udāna breath resides in the sides, the back of the neck, the standing posture, and also in the ankles; it abides in all accomplishments within the feet, the hands, and the fingers.
The *samāna* [vāyu], however, is present throughout the entire body from the big toe up to the crown;
it is established within the seventy-two thousand pathways of the channels (*nāḍī*).
Residing within the twenty-eight million pores of the skin, the Samāna and Prāṇa breaths are indeed one with the individual soul (jīva). || 33 ||
Having gradually drawn everything inward into the hollow of the heart-lotus and filled it as before, the kumbhaka (retention) should be performed as previously described.
Having performed the exhalation (recaka) as before, one should place [the breath] at the ear, the cavity of the palate,
between the two eyebrows, and in the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) for one possessed of power.
The ray, the moonlight, the sound, and the drop—the state of Maheśvara;
then Sadāśiva and Śiva—these [are the stages] for those two, and by the Lord, the teacher [establishes them]. (36)
Then, having conquered death, he undoubtedly attains nirvāṇa;
thereafter, he leads [the soul] along the path of creation, and Śiva indeed [resides] in the Yāmaka.
In Sadāśiva there are six ghaṭikās; in Śakti, five ghaṭikās;
in Bindu, four ghaṭikās; and in Nāda, there should be three.
In the moonlight, however, it remains for two ghaṭikās;
with one less [digit], it is established in the rays for half a ghaṭikā, and half of that again within the range of the Śakti.
Between the eyebrows, in the cavity of the palate, and in the stable cave of the nose,
the teacher should effect the union with the half of Śiva in the heart by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
For three years he should thus practice with *prasāda*;
O Six-faced One, he should practice *prasāda* and *prāṇāyāma* in the external limb.
One attains victory over death, and from that, mastery over the vital air (vāyu) shall arise;
I shall now explain the expansion [of breath], which is the ladder for concentration (dhāraṇā).
The knower of mantras, having drawn everything upward by means of the mind joined with the vital air (māruta),
should indeed restrain it for three ghaṭikās at the big toe for a long time.
With all [the fingers], it is doubled by the thumb; by the *prāsāda* [mudrā], it is likewise from the staff. Then the ankle on the left side, and the left [ankle] on the right side.
Having restrained each six-ghaṭikā period through the practice of *kumbhaka* alone,
one should indeed block [the breath] between the two shanks at the base of the excrement and urine.
One should restrain all [the breath] there by drawing it inward;
it should be held for eight ghaṭikās, established in the supreme kumbhaka.
Furthermore, O dear one, having drawn the touch toward the two thighs, the preceptor should cause it to be restrained;
the number of doors should be blocked by means of the *prāsāda* mantra. (47)

O Guha, by drawing [the breath] to the root of the anus and the root of the penis and touching them, one should constantly and properly restrain [the mind] through the union of the mind and the vital air (māruta). 48.
O Guha, at that very moment the base of the penis vanishes into the base of the anus;
then indeed the Kuṇḍalinī is in the middle of the navel, within the center of the Kuṇḍalinī.
Having restrained the number of breaths for the duration of a ghaṭikā and having drawn in the touch [of the breath],
the knower of mantras should then restrain it with the seed-syllable of Prāsāda.
In the practice of pratyāhāra, however, the supreme and most excellent place is the station of Kuṇḍalinī;
it destroys diseases of the anus, the calves, and the ankles, as well as diseases of the wind (vāta). || 51 ||
O Guha, one should destroy the eighty diseases born of wind— such as external extension, internal contraction, and convulsions— by means of pratyāhāra.
Furthermore, the practitioner, remaining for one ghaṭikā in the eleventh [position], should propitiate everything within the heart.
The practitioner of yoga, having blocked the well of the throat and drawn everything upward, effects the destruction of wrinkles and gray hair, as well as the destruction of death itself. (54)
Having filled the iḍā, one should restrain [the breath] for twelve ghaṭikās or even half of that. || 55 ||
Hunger and thirst are destroyed, as well as thirst and fever;
one should block the wind together with the vital breath (marut) within the cavity of the palate. 56.
Or else, the thirteenth [should be] a water-clock (ghaṭikā), or even a warrior-force (yodhaśakti);
and the third [type] is a temple (prāsāda) which is the principal among all gateways.
O child, one should indeed suppress all mental fluctuations by means of the [breath] accompanied by the emission (visarga);
for this removes all diseases arising from bile, phlegm, and wind. (58)
For this is indeed the supreme Mṛtyuñjaya; the wise man, having always drawn all that [breath] into the cavity of the palate, places it between the two bows.
Having drawn in the palace formed by the swan, the practitioner of touch becomes happy;
O child, he should restrain it for fourteen ghaṭikās or for that duration.
