O Guha, if one constantly restrains the power of inhalation and exhalation,
one attains omniscience and masters the Vedas and the Shastras.
And there, with the eye of yoga, one beholds the seven worlds;
thereafter, one should restrain [the breath] at the tip of the Suṣumnā, and then, having drawn it back, touch the point of contact.
In the palace [of the body], the knower of mantras, having repeatedly drawn [the breath] by means of the lunar orb joined with the mind-wind, should restrain it for three watches.
One should cause [the mantra] to overflow through the pores of the skin with a [visualization] resembling a black bee;
in this way, it effects the paralysis of rivals as well as the destruction of death.
One should restrain all tactile sensation right there with the mind;
having restrained it, one should gradually flood [the body] with the nectars of Śiva and the Moon.
Thereafter, having drawn [the breath] back by means of the winds during the light of the fire of passion,
the self-controlled one should then restrain all [the senses] with the moon of Śiva.
Having restrained everything— namely sixteen, seventeen, and then eighteen ghaṭīs— the wise one should flood it with the state of immortality.
One obtains a lifespan of a thousand ghaṭikās; there is no doubt about this.
This secret has been declared: the withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), which is very difficult to attain. (68)
(138) O child, by mastery over the upward-moving wind (udāna), there is entry into another's body;
whether [the other] is dead or alive, through that [mastery], one enters them entirely. || 69 ||
The temple, adorned with swans and moon-motifs, measures nineteen ghaṭikās;
from the soles of the feet upwards, it is marked by the three sounds beginning with 'ka'.
By bathing [the self] with the nectar itself, a man shall attain a lifespan of ten thousand years;
by obstructing the movement at the seat of *nāda*, for twenty-one *ghaṭikās*.
O child, one should indeed draw in the entire breath and restrain it there,
together with the Moon and Mahānāda-Śiva.
One who performs the flooding [of the breath] from the letter *kha* to the end of the feet (*pādānta*) for twenty thousand times lives;
furthermore, O child, he always possesses longevity through all the vital airs (*vāyu*). || 73 ||
O Guha, one should restrain [the breath] there with focused meditation for thirty ghaṭikās;
then, O dear one, Śiva, the giver of the Haṃsa, shall replenish it by means of his wheel.
He may live for a hundred billion years and flood his entire body;
thus, through the prior practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), there shall be mastery over the vital winds (vāyu) with ease.
O Guha, one should indeed ascend and descend from station to station by means of the iḍā and piṅgalā; that is the sequential practice of pūraka.
Furthermore, the wise one should plant the three difficult-to-attain [seeds] along with their qualities.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter on Pratyāhāra in the Kālottara. 25.
Prosperity!
Īśvara said:
I shall now describe the concentration on the vital air (*vāyu-dhāraṇā*), which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
He obtains good fortune, wealth, longevity, strength, and prosperity. || 1 ||
In a solitary, secluded place, free from wind and sun,
and without abandoning the four external limbs according to the prescribed rule.
One should practice withdrawal (pratyāhāra) and the concentration on touch (sparśa-dhāraṇā) on the sword;
for one must first indeed perform the concentration on the five faces beginning with earth.
Afterwards, one should maintain the Great Wheel (Mahācakra);
then, O child, one should again maintain the Earth [mantra] three times or twice a day.
The earth is mastered by the yogi, and he attains the status of a sovereign ruler (sārvabhauma).
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these [are the elements]. || 5 ||
One should meditate upon the orb of the earth endowed with five qualities;
one thereby attains victory over death and the fullness of all sovereign powers.
Thus one should meditate according to the rule upon [the deity] seated upon a half-moon and a lotus—
white as cow’s milk, gentle, and possessing a luster like a conch or a jasmine flower.
One should meditate upon the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) conjoined with the sixth vowel [u] and the nasal drop (bindu);
one should meditate on the nectar as facing downwards, and thus, O Guha, one should meditate.
Having flooded oneself with that [breath] and remaining in the kumbhaka state,
O child, one should properly maintain meditation for twice as long as the previous [inhalation].
One attains victory over death, being freed from all diseases—whether they be stationary, mobile, or artificial—and the destruction of one's enemies. 10.
One attains ageless immortality through meditation on the mandala of Varuṇa, which possesses four qualities: sound, touch, form, and taste. || 11 ||
One should visualize the auspicious mandala of Varuṇa, endowed with four qualities;
one should meditate on the triangular mandala of Agni, adorned with svastikas. (12)
O Six-faced One, the fire-god is red in color, surrounded by thousands of garlands of flames; it is the sixth [vowel] joined with the tenth [consonant] and endowed with the nasal drop (bindu). 13.
One should meditate on the god as a sublime fire, conjoined with the three qualities;
one should contemplate the form of the fire as sound, touch, and form. 14.
One should perform the kumbhaka as before, and indeed the kumbhaka as before;
one should perform the recaka as before and conquer the vital breath with the mind. 15.
O child, eighty diseases born of wind and seventy-seven born of phlegm perish at that very moment, just as an elephant perishes before a lion. 16.
O dear child, it is circular, black in color, marked with the sign of a dot (bindu),
has the sun as its presiding deity, and is endowed with double [the usual] measure.
One should meditate upon [the syllable] joined with sound and touch, endowed with the second [vowel], mounted on the crest of the bindu, within the hollow of the throat. 18.
O Guha, one should meditate upon all the vital airs simultaneously right there;
one should fill them within the iḍā, the piṅgalā, and the suṣumnā.
Having performed the retention (kumbhaka) as before, the exhalation (recaka) should be done slowly;
by meditating in this way, my son, mastery over all the vital winds (vāyu) will be attained. (20)
One attains mastery over the mind and becomes all-pervading;
those who [meditate on] the space born from the heart-lotus as having a dark-blue luster [attain this].
Resembling pure crystal, endowed with the single quality of sound,
he is the Supreme Lord, the presiding deity, and the cause of all causes.
One should meditate upon the fourth group of eight, adorned with a crest of dots, as the pure sky, the support of Śiva, in the center of the head. (23)
One should restrain the entire vital air right there through focused meditation;
as before, one should perform inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka).
One attains omniscience and gains mastery over all the winds;
one should then meditate upon the Great Wheel (Mahācakra), which is practiced by all the gods.
O child, this great lotus, endowed with thirty-six petals and possessed of a pericarp and filaments, is the most beautiful lotus of Śiva.
One should construct a palace upon the pericarp for the Lord of all Lords of Knowledge,
and one should designate one hundred and eight individual deities for the filaments.
There were the eight Vidyeśvaras, the twelve Ādityas, the eight Vasus, and likewise the eight Gaṇeśvaras. (28)
And likewise the ten world-protectors, as well as the [divine] weapons, the hosts of Rudras and Mothers, and the Yakṣas and Vidyādharas; || 29 ||
Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Siddhas, Kiṃpuruṣas, and Garuḍas, as well as the hosts of Maruts, the hosts of Pitṛs, Kinnaras, and Apsarases. || 30 ||
Sages, Rākṣasas, gods, Yātudhānas, and Pannagas;
Nāgas of various kinds, as well as the lunar mansions, planets, and zodiac signs. || 31 ||

The wives of the gods and the wives of the sages, as well as the divine youths, the daughters of the gods and the daughters of the sages, the spirits, and indeed the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālakas). || 32 ||
Having arranged these thirty-six [syllables] upon the petals in their proper sequence,
one should place them with the great outer [circle] and, having tripled them, encircle [the mandala].
Indeed, everything joined with the bindu is adorned with the bindu as its crest;
all consonants, moreover, are to be understood [in this manner]. (34)
It may be obtained merely by hearing it, yet it is truly obtained through the grace of the Guru.
Herein is seen the entire Vidya and Maheśa;
the Sakala, Niṣkala, Supta, Suṣupta, and Sadāśiva. || 36 ||
In the palace, however, one should know Bindudeva;
indeed, one should know Bindu as Śiva, who is proclaimed as the fourth.
That very [reality] is all-pervading, partless, stainless, and auspicious;
it is devoid of the denoted and the denoter, and empty of anything to be rejected or accepted.
Brahman is eternal, omnipresent, self-realizable, and the auspicious state;
it is the cause of all the gods, devoid of both the imperishable and the perishable. (39)
Thus should one contemplate within the support (ādhāra) for the yogin established in samādhi;
Brahman, which is ever beneficial and easily perceived, is like the constant bliss of a maiden.
The one who lacks yoga does not know [the Self] at all, just as a person blind from birth does not know a jar;
for the jar [is contained within] space by necessity, and likewise the individual soul is like the sky. 41.
Without the ear he hears; another [sense] that is not the eye, he sees.
Without the breath he lives; and without the skin, he experiences touch. (42)
One would perceive taste without a tongue; they prattle with fire;
one grasps without hands; one walks without feet. (43)
O Guha, even without the movement of breath, one should indeed perform the emission at all times;
and even without the penis, there is bliss—indeed, everything is thus eternally.
(143) Mind does not exist within the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, when it is accompanied by conceptualization;
for, my child, apart from egoism, the one who possesses egoism is himself [non-existent]. 45.
The Great One possesses greatness and an imperishable form;
without primordial nature (prakṛti), Mahādeva brings forth the entire universe. || 46 ||
If there were no Puruṣa joined with the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka), then who would move about, enjoy, and experience all this? 47.
He drinks and he grasps, he sees and he touches;
he goes, he dances, he sings, and he even leaps.
O child, this world, extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, consists of three hundred and eighty thousand [worlds],
which is always completely filled by that which is woven lengthwise and crosswise.
"You shall meditate thus: 'The void by means of a void entity.
Having contemplated the state of the void within the body, you will attain liberation, O Six-faced One. (50)
O Guha, it is empty above, empty below, and empty in the middle; it is free from affliction, empty as space, empty of power, and indeed empty of non-existence.

One should meditate upon Maheśa and Sadāśiva as empty of the Mother (mātṛ) and empty of the Bindu; likewise, one should meditate upon Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra as the universal void (sarvaśūnya). || 52 ||
It is empty of the thirty-six principles and empty of the relationship between support and supported; indeed, "you" and "I" are likewise empty, for in reality, everything does not exist. (53)
The supreme Lord Śiva is to be grasped through meditative absorptions that are self-evident;
this seedless absorption (nirbīja-samādhi), O Six-faced One, is indeed perceived.
The Supreme Brahman resides within the central body, situated both externally and internally;
it is eternally present like fragrance in flowers or oil in sesame seeds.
Like ghee from curd, like fire residing within wood,
that light which faces every direction is obtained through the grace of the teacher’s mouth. (56)
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter on the procedure for *dhāraṇā* in the *Kālottara*.
|| Śrīḥ ||
Īśvara said:
I shall proclaim the yoga of contemplation (*bhāvayoga*), a yoga that is very difficult to attain—
a meditation devoid of mental fixation (*dhāraṇā*) and free from recitation (*japa*) and fire-offerings (*homa*).
O Six-faced One, for him there is no lunar day, no zodiac sign, no asterism, no restrictive rule, and no fasting; neither time, nor place, nor postures matter to him.

One should avoid *dhāraṇā* and *pratyāhāra*, as well as [the mantras] beginning with *kulakṣā*; one should likewise abandon *recaka*, *pūraka*, and *kumbhaka*. There is no *varṇa*, no ninefold seed-syllable (*navabīja*), and neither the *sakala* nor the *niṣkala* [mantra].
The pain in the heart extends from the navel up to the ears, but not beyond the middle of the ears;
there are indeed the *iḍā*, the *piṅgalā*, the *suṣumnā*, and the *prāṇa*.
It constantly moves within the well of the twenty-eight crores of forms.
O Pārtha, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is [pervaded] by that yoga-sun... || 7 ||
At the base of the support, at the root of the knot, the supreme Śiva, who pervades the void,
exists as this supreme reality in the form of light, established as the underlying thread.
Having caused the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) there to enter into the Śiva-field-knower, one should cast [it] forth;
having made the mind bodiless, one should not think of anything at all. (9)
Resembling a flash of lightning, with the lips positioned within,
it is joined by the sixteen mantras beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa'.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) separately for each, accompanied by all the drops (bindu),
one must certainly first place [the syllables] on the eastern petal and then place the remaining ones in their proper sequence.
O child, the five Brahmās and the limbs of Śiva are situated in the center within the pericarp; and the second [element] is the triangular mandala of fire.
[Surrounded by] garlands of flames...
in its center is a solar disc resembling a hibiscus flower. (13)
Joined with the peaceful *bindu* and endowed with the quality of *rajas*, it is slightly less than the form of fire—the supreme solar orb. (14)
The second [syllable] is joined with it, adorned with a crest-bindu;
it is the unsurpassed lunar orb, its lower part diminished by the solar orb. (15)
O child, one should place [the deity] resembling the full moon upon a white lotus;
with the quality of sattva, one should place it in the heart.
One should place sattva, rajas, and tamas within each and every mandala;
however, in the center of the three mandalas, one should place the twenty-fifth principle, Puruṣa.
The person (puruṣa), joined with the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka), is the size of a thumb;
it resembles a thumb in measure and has the luster of a lapis lazuli gem (rājāvarta-maṇi). || 18 ||
In its center, one should meditate upon Maheśāna, who is proclaimed as the twenty-sixth principle;
resembling molten gold, one should practice the seed-syllable of the heart three times.
One should meditate upon Sadāśiva in the center of that [lotus], endowed with the heart of grace (prasādahṛdaya), possessing a radiance like lightning and the sun, and having a subtle form. (20)
In its center, one should constantly meditate upon the supreme deity, the flawless Sadāśiva, the Lord who is indeed the twenty-seventh deity.
In its center, O child, is Śiva, the twenty-eighth,
most excellent, omniscient, omnipresent, peaceful, accessible to yogis, and both supreme and non-supreme.
Free from conceptual construction, peaceful, non-dual, and stainless—by mere meditation, my child, one shall indeed attain the state of liberation free from affliction. (23)
To his left, one should constantly meditate upon the eternal Viṣṇu,
who has four arms, two eyes, and holds a conch, a discus, and a mace.
One should constantly meditate, with self-restraint, upon the form of Viṣṇu as Vāgbhava, endowed with all auspicious marks, dark-complexioned, and wearing a crown.
One attains the form of Viṣṇu, which possesses the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇiman*.
On his right side, however, is the four-faced, four-armed [Brahmā]. (26)
Resembling the filaments of a lotus, auspicious, wearing a black antelope skin,
and holding a water-pot and a rosary, he is the cause of creation.
Brahmā, the cause of the world, joined with the quality of rajas;
Viṣṇu, endowed with the quality of sattva, the healthy Nārāyaṇa.
O child, one should meditate upon Rudra as Brahmā, who is indeed endowed with the quality of darkness (tamas) and is the agent of dissolution, because of the cessation of all mental activities.
One shall eternally become a creator; one shall accomplish the eight great powers beginning with *maṇi*, as well as [the mastery over] Indra, Agni, Yama, Varuṇa, Soma, and Gandharva.
One should indeed meditate upon [the deity] within the center of the lotus, and thereby obtain various fruits;
this includes inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and the cessation of all mental fluctuations (sarvavṛttinirodhana). || 31 ||
The wise one should increase the exhalation (recaka) until it is worn away by the touch of nirvāṇa;
he becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin), possesses the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti), and is indeed the eleventh Rudra.
One should meditate with an undistracted mind upon the Ādityas, the Vasus, and all the lords of the Gaṇas; thus one shall attain their respective stations.
I shall explain the path of meditative concentration; listen to it, O Six-faced One!
One should meditate on the emptiness of form, reducing it by half a measure.
Having abandoned the ordinary state of being, one should thus meditate upon Śiva alone;
or rather, it is the state of becoming of one flavor [with Him] that is called samādhi. (35)
One should place Śiva within oneself and likewise place oneself within Śiva;
having become Sadāśiva, one should not think of anything at all.
Subtle, all-pervading, blissful, immovable, and eternal—the supreme reality that extends even to the animal realm is indeed I myself. || 37 ||
Abandoning both exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), one should practice retention (kumbhaka);
for in the middle, O child, resides Śiva himself, free from all ailment.
The state of being perceived is the object of touch; however, the Supreme Being is always free from waking and dreaming, and one should avoid even the state of deep sleep. (39)
The supreme, divine form of light, possessing the brilliance of the fire of universal dissolution;
the supreme, subtle space of Śiva, all-knowing and facing in every direction. || 40 ||
It is secret, pure, ungraspable, blissful, immovable, and eternal;
it dwells in the cave of the heart, is without beginning, and is free from all dualities.
The one, all-pervading, immeasurable, and inconceivable cause;
the subtle, auspicious, unreasoned, and untainted cause. (42)
Place the self in the middle, and place the void within the self;
having made yourself bodiless, one should not think of anything at all.
This supreme secret, which destroys death, has been declared;
it is situated in the center of the lotus, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns. 44.
O auspicious Six-faced One, visualize the Vidyā in the shape of a Kadamba bud; O Six-faced One, always place the Self in its center.
One should make space within the self and contemplate nothing at all;
this is the Yoga of the Conqueror of Death, which rests upon the state of equal flavor (samarasībhāva).
In the hollow of the throat is the supreme abode that utterly destroys hunger and thirst;
in the cavity of the palate is supreme knowledge, possessing the radiance of lightning and fire. (47)
O child, one should constantly remember the Lord Vyomaśakti within the Kadamba-golaka, who is the supreme destroyer of death and whose qualities are beyond numbering. 48.
Indeed, within the middle of the bow, situated in the center of the three mandalas,
one should project the seven worlds right there, within the center of Śiva.
Place yourself within that, and do not place it within yourself;
then the yoga of the seven worlds, rising upward, will be seen by the eye.
Through the yoga of contemplating the state of equal flavor (samarasī-bhāva), the wise one attains omniscience;
indeed, at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), he should blend the elements with the number of the earth (bhū).
One should place the power of the void (vyomaśakti) there, and within that, the Kadamba-globe;
in the center of that, however, is the form of Śiva, flashing with the brilliance of lightning.
O child, having visualized oneself as being like a shimmering day [of light], pure and with the luster of emerald,
one should place oneself within that body composed of the six sheaths. (53)
One attains the state of supreme Brahman through the yoga of becoming one with the equal flavor (samarasībhāva);
thus, by meditating for three years, one reaches the number of [the] earth.
It effects the destruction of wrinkles and grey hair, as well as the very deception of death.
Four finger-breadths above that, however, is the sphere known as Raśmi.
The wise man should contemplate the nectar, which resembles a subtle crystal and is situated within the power of the void, as the infinite, imperishable, and auspicious Śiva. 56.
Place yourself within that [Self], and place that [Self] within yourself;
having made the mind bodiless, one should not think of anything at all. (57)

Through the yoga of attaining the state of equal flavor (samarasībhāva), there is the supreme deception of death within the sphere of the Kadamba tree, which is the field of the digits numbering as the moonlight. 58.
One should place the power of space (vyomaśakti) there, and within that power one should place Śiva.
Within Śiva, establish the self; make the self endowed with Śiva. (59)
Through the yoga of attaining the state of equal flavor (samarasībhāva), that which resembles ten million moons becomes the supreme destroyer of death by means of six months of practice. 60.
One should place the power of the Lord (prabhu-śakti) within the sphere (gola), and then project the power of space (vyoma-śakti) into it;
in the center of that is the Supreme Brahman, Śiva, the supreme leader.
Place yourself within that, and place that within yourself;
having made the mind bodiless, one should not think of anything at all.
Through the yoga of becoming one in flavor (samarasībhāva), one undoubtedly lives with Lakṣmī;
Nāda is the principle of Maheśvara, and the Golaka is the supreme state.
One should place the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) there, and in the middle of that, one should cast Śiva.
Place yourself in the middle of that, and place Him in the middle of yourself. (64)
By means of the yoga of meditative absorption (bhāva), one should immerse oneself in the supreme nectar until it becomes of a single flavor;
he shall live for ten million times a hundred thousand years, as declared by Śiva.
The consciousness reached at the tip of the Suṣumnā extends four finger-breadths for each [stage];
the seventh is the supreme reality, Śiva, the supreme leader. (66)
It is eternal, situated on the left, empty, free from conceptual construction, and stainless;
it rests upon the left, is inconceivable, all-knowing, and faces in every direction.
Accessible to yogis, without support, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
it is the power of lordship, the power of knowledge, and the stainless power of wisdom.
The power of the void (vyomaśakti) is proclaimed as the supreme knowledge and as the principle of conduct (nīti);
in their midst is Śiva, the subtle one, the cause of all causes. (69)
In the midst of that, always place yourself within that Self;
having made the mind bodiless, one should not think of anything at all.
Through the yoga of meditating on the state of equal flavor (*samarasī*), there is the destruction of all death;
he lives for a thousand great dissolutions (*mahāpralaya*), of this there is no doubt. (71)
One should thus contemplate [the fire] in the support (ādhāra), resembling pure ruby;
it is proclaimed to be one span below the navel, in the middle region. (72)
Between the two planks, however, one should place the bull and the fire upon the head;
above the two thighs, moreover, are Tuṭī, Bhaṭṭī, Bhavā, and the others.
The middle body is declared to be four finger-breadths in measure;
one should place the four Śaktis there and deposit Śiva in the center.
Having made the mind bodiless, one should not think of anything at all;
through the yoga of becoming of one flavor (samarasībhāva), one should practice constantly while remaining happy. (75)
For him, death shall not exist; he lives for a million kalpas.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the *Kālottara*, the compendium of twelve thousand verses. 27.
Śrīḥ!
Īśvara said:
O Ṣaṇmukha, listen as I shall explain the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) according to their true nature:
the path of mantras (mantrādhvā), the path of words (padādhvā), the path of principles (tattvādhvā), and that which consists of the worlds (bhuvanātmaka). || 1 ||
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) and the path of kalās (kalādhvan), which together constitute twenty-one states of Śiva,
as well as the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) separately— listen now to these, O Six-faced One.
Seven thousand crores, as well as one hundred thousand crores,
and sixty-four million [verses] have gone outside from Vāmadeva.
O child, forty-four million three hundred thousand [mantras] indeed emerged from Aghora.
Eighty-four thousand million [mantras] have emerged from that Puruṣa; now hear the classification of those mantras. || 5 ||
For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas,
the Jātaka was born from the mouth of Īśāna.
When investigated with effort, no fixed limit is found;
however, the mantra of Ananteśa is proclaimed to be ten thousand (ayuta).
For Sūkṣma, ten thousand mantras; for Śivottama, thirty thousand; for Ekanetra, forty thousand; and for Ekarudra, fifty thousand.
One should know Amūrta to be sixty thousand; Śrīkaṇṭha shall be seventy thousand;
and Śikhaṇḍin eighty thousand; while Cakravartin consists of nine [thousand] mantras. (9)
The mantras of Maheśvara are proclaimed to be one hundred lakhs;
the mantras of the Eight-formed One (Aṣṭamūrti) are separately one lakh and sixty-eight thousand.
The eleven Rudra mantras should each be recited three hundred thousand times;
the twelve Ādityas, however, one hundred and twenty thousand times, and the Vasus, eight hundred thousand times.
The eight [deities] beginning with Gaṇeśvara each receive half a hundred thousand;
and for the ten world-protectors (lokapālas), there are exactly thirty thousand.
Half of that [measure] belongs to the *astras*, half of that to the Gandharvas and others,
and half of that is proclaimed for the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Yakṣas, and so forth.
The Gāruḍas, Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, and hosts of Apsarases, as well as the Ṛṣis, Pitṛs, and Bhūtas—half [of the assembly] is proclaimed to consist of these. (14)
The Nāgas and Pannagas likewise proclaim it;
so too do the Asuras, Rākṣasas, Yātudhānas, and Piśācas. (15)
Kūṣmāṇḍas, Bhūtas, and Vetālas are proclaimed to constitute half of that;
thus, O Six-faced One, the entire network of mantras has been briefly described.
All mantras, tantras, and Vedic scriptures in their entirety; all that arises from palaces; and the entire realm of speech, both moving and unmoving—[all these are contained therein]. 17.
The five limbs of Brahmā-Śiva, as well as Vyomavyāpin, the mantra of awakening in the heart, and the deities of the thousand-syllable [mantra]. (18)
And Ayutākṣaradeva, as well as Niyutākṣara;
the Chief Sound (Nādamukhya), Prasāda, Kṣurika, and the Pāśupata weapon.
The mantra of the eight Cakravartins, the mantra of the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti),
the mantra of the eleven Rudras, and the mantras of the twelve Ādityas. || 20 ||
The mantra of the eight verses for Gaṇeśa, as well as the mantras for the Gandharvas and others,
and the mantras for the groups of the Seven Mothers, have been extracted from their respective mantras.
The treasury of mantras has been briefly described in the extractions of mantras;
this web of mantras, issuing from the mouth of Īśāna, is very difficult to obtain.
O Guha, these previously mentioned words, which have arisen pervading the sky, constitute this unsurpassed king of mantras consisting of eighty-one words. (23)
The mantra known as Vyomavyāpin consists of three hundred and sixty syllables;
it is a deity of a thousand syllables that has emerged from Vāmadeva. (24)
The thirty-six thousand-word king of mantras has been proclaimed; it is the mantra that brings all under control, honored among the nine granthas. (25)
The deity Ayutākṣara emerges from Tatpuruṣa;
three hundred thousand [recitations] are prescribed, and it consists of three thousand words.
In the Yāmala, the Mātṛtantra, the Bhūtatanttra, and the Gāruḍa, as well as in the Saptabhairavatantra and the sixty-four Gulatantras; (27)
That unsurpassed king of mantras has been honored in the Mahātantra;
now I shall declare the mantras of Īśāna, which are suitable for ritual action. (28)

(Oṃ) Oṃ! To the one who pervades the sky, whose form is the sky; to Śiva, who pervades all; to the infinite; to the protectorless; to the non-dependent; to the firm; to the eternal; to the one who rests upon the seat of yoga; to the ever-yogic; to the one whose necklace is meditation; Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva! To the source of all;
to the one whose head is Īśāna; to the one whose face is Tatpuruṣa.

To the one whose heart is non-terrible (aghora); to the secret Vāmadeva; to the form of Sadyojāta. Oṃ, salutations again and again! To the most secret of secrets! To the lineage! To the undying! To the presiding authority over all yoga! To the one whose form is light! To the supreme among supreme lords! O conscious of the unconscious! O sky, O sky! O pervasive one, O pervasive one! O formless one, O formless one! O first one, O first one! O splendor, O splendor! O light, O light! O formless! O without fire! O without smoke! O without ash! O beginningless! O manifold, O manifold! Dhū, dhū, dhū, dhū! Oṃ, one should cause [the disciple] to perform the *bhūmaṇi* rite.
That Tatpuruṣa is the supreme great mantra that removes all sins;
the deity of a thousand syllables was born as that great Tatpuruṣa.
One should offer the food oblation (naivedya) and the incense and lamp, and thereby effect the presence [of the deity].
This Rudra-Gāyatrī mantra is the destroyer of great sins.
One attains the fulfillment of one's desires through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and other such rites.
"We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva; may Rudra impel us. Indeed, [one should contemplate] Tatpuruṣa alone. (31)
O child, by reciting it one thousand times, or half of that, or even one hundred and eight times at the three junctions of the day, the destruction of all sins shall occur.
From the deity Ayutākṣara, the Aghora mantra emerged:
"To those who are not terrible, to those who are terrible, and to those more terrible than the most terrible;
O Śarva, from all sides, to all you whose forms are the universe, let there be salutation to you. (33)
O Mahādeva, one should perform the bathing with the Aghora mantra and conclude it with the Karṇikā, Kaṭaka, Keyūra, and Udarabandhana mantras. (34)
The wise man, having cut the sacred thread and applied divine fragrant unguents, should offer [it] with the Aghora mantra for all ritual actions. (35)
One is liberated from food mixed with poison, various poisons themselves, and rites such as malevolent magic (*ābhicāra*) simply by means of recitation (*japa*). || 36 ||
But for those who have touched things belonging to others, water contained in another's vessel liberates them immediately upon reciting the Aghora mantra one hundred and eight times.
Emerging from the goddess Vāgdevī, who possesses ten million syllables,
is the mantra for the installation of Śiva, which is preeminent among the seven mantras.
One should install Śiva, Sadāśiva, Rudra, and the eight forms of Vidyeśvara, as well as all the eleven Rudras, by means of the Vāmadeva [mantra]. (39)
The girdle, the waist-thread, and the garment adorned with all kinds of jewels;
indeed, all the rites of power (śaktikarma), such as subjugation, attraction, and so forth. || 40 ||
O Six-faced One, one should indeed perform all that with the Vāmadeva mantra:

"Salutation to Vāmadeva, salutation to Jyeṣṭha, salutation to Rudra; salutation to Kāla; salutation to Kalavikaraṇa, salutation to Balavikaraṇa, salutation to Balapramathana; salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana, salutation to Manonmana. || 41 ||
O Guha, perform the Vāmadeva-mantra, which brings peace and prosperity;
O child, it is superior to all mantras and should be recited upon entering a house.
From the deity of the syllable *arghya*, Sadyojāta emerged;
he performed all the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*), as well as every auspicious act. (43)
Upon entering a new dwelling, a palace, or a city gate,
one should indeed perform recitation at the proper time while adorned with all ornaments.
During meals, at the time of bathing, during the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana),
and in all rites for the ancestors (pitṛkārya), a person should mutter the Sadyojāta mantra. (45)
Vāmadeva has thirteen kalās immediately with eight;
Aghora has eight kalās, O child, while Puruṣa has four kalās.
The five kalās belong to Īśāna; it consists of thirty-eight kalās.
Indeed, O child, all mantras are thus, while Puruṣa has four kalās.
In the temple, there is the origin of all things.
At the time of initiation, the knower of mantras should purify all mantras;
at the time of consecration, being well-composed, he should employ all mantras.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, on the Path of Mantras, in the Kālottara.
Śrīḥ!
Īśvara said:
I shall proclaim the path of the stages (padādhvan), by knowing which one may attain liberation. A thousand lakhs of crores [of steps] are proclaimed to be the station of Śiva (śivapada). || 1 ||
Furthermore, when it has emerged from those very steps, there are one hundred and eight;
when it has emerged from those steps, it is said to consist of thirty-six words.
One should purify the fivefold Īśāna that has emerged from those steps, both at the head and within the body; thus one shall go to the stainless Śiva.
O child, the state of Sadāśiva is proclaimed to consist of one hundred lakhs;
that which has emerged from those states is proclaimed as ninety-six [lakhs]. (4)
Therefore, O child, that [compound] of Tatpuruṣa is proclaimed to have four feet;
having purified oneself among those four-footed [categories], one should proceed to the state of Śiva, which is free from disease.
O child, the station of Aghora consists of exactly five hundred thousand;
it has emerged from those stations and is proclaimed as eighty-one.
Emerging from those steps, there shall be the eight steps of Aghora;
having purified that step in due order, one should go to the stainless Śiva.
From the station of Maheśvara, twenty-five hundred thousand [syllables] indeed arose;
from those stations, moreover, the ten-station mantra emerged.
O child, one should purify the station of Vāmadeva in due order;
having purified the thirteenth station, one shall go to the stainless Śiva.
Indeed, those who have arisen from the twelve lakṣas are the eight Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras);
that which has emerged from their stations is called the thirty-two stations.
O Guha, having indeed emerged from those eight steps, one should proceed to the next step after purifying the Sadyojāta step for eight [breaths]. || 11 ||
Indeed, the eightfold form [of the deity] emerged from the tips of the feet;
from those very steps, the six limbs beginning with the heart issued forth.
Having purified the heart, the head, the crest, the armor, the eye, and the weapon— these which are to be known— one shall go to Śiva.
Those born from the eleven Rudras know three hundred thousand [mantras] in that state;
they know the three principal seed-syllables (bīja) as having emerged from those states.
The seed-syllables of the three worlds are declared to be *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *suvaḥ*.
Having thoroughly purified these three seed-syllables, one should go to the stainless Śiva. (15)
The station produced from the twelve Ādityas consists of one hundred and ten syllables;
from those stations, the Pāśupata weapon has emerged here. (16)
Having purified the Pāśupata [mantra] in due order, one should go to the stainless Śiva;
the eight Vasus have arisen, and a hundred thousand (lakṣa) of words is proclaimed.
Having thoroughly purified the seed-syllable of the *kṣurikā* that has emerged from those positions, one should go to the stainless Śiva. 18.
That which arises from the *Gaṇeśāṣṭaka* consists of more than a hundred thousand words;
from among those words emerged the mantra consisting of the word *hṛllekhā*. (19)
First, Māyā is declared as the supreme means for bringing all under control;
it consists of sixty-four thousand [mantras] born from the group of the Seven Mothers.
Having purified the *hṛllekhā* mantra—the great deluding mantra which is the supreme and non-supreme Mahāmāyā—one shall go to the stainless state of Śiva. (21)
The station of Brahmā, consisting of thirty thousand [years], is proclaimed as being of the nature of creation;
from those stations arose the Aghora weapon, which is very difficult to attain.
The form of sustenance is the form of Viṣṇu, the form of creation is the Grandfather (Brahmā),
and the form of destruction is Rudra, who is designated as the Fire of Time (Kālāgni).
The quality of rajas is the form of Brahmā, while the quality of sattva belongs to Viṣṇu;
Rudra is said to be the quality of tamas; thus he is proclaimed to possess all three qualities.
But Śiva, the supreme cause, transcends the three qualities (guṇas);
so too do all the Vedas, the scriptures, and the fourteen branches of knowledge.
The sixty-four arts, the six systems of philosophy, and the treatises on yoga; the received Siddhānta-tantras, and the Nirguṇa [reality] through the Praṇava. || 26 ||
That Praṇava, born from Śiva, consists of speech and comprises all that is moving and unmoving;
one should purify both the Prāsāda mantra and the Praṇava according to the prescribed rule. (27)
Having purified the *praṇava*, one should thereafter purify the *prāsāda*;
by purifying these two seed-syllables, one shall go to the healthy state of Śiva. (28)
The waking state is the *praṇava*, the dreaming state is the *prāsāda*, and deep sleep is the fourth (*turīya*). The waking state is Brahmā, while deep sleep is said to be Viṣṇu. (29)
One should know the fourth state as the station of Brahman, and likewise the four states themselves;
[these are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
It is recited as fivefold and having five deities:
the heart is the station of Brahmā, and Viṣṇu is proclaimed to be in the throat. (31)
Rudra resides in the middle of the palate, while Sadāśiva is in the forehead; one should know Śiva to be at the tip of the nose; therefore, he is higher than the highest.
"There is nothing higher than the Supreme"—this is the certainty of the scripture.
[It consists of] that which has three measures, two measures, and likewise one measure. (33)
Subtler than that is the half-mora, and subtler still is its half;
these indeed are the three worlds, the three gods, and the three fires.

The three qualities (guṇas), the three aims of life (trivarga), the three junctions of the day (trisandhya), the three circles (trimaṇḍala), the three daily libations (savanatraya), power (śakti), and indeed the triad of the self (ātmatritaya). || 35 ||
The world of mortals (bhūrloka), the atmospheric world (bhuvarloka), and heaven (svargaloka) constitute the three worlds. || 36 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa are proclaimed as the three gods;
they constitute the triad of fires: the Āhavanīya, the Gārhapatya, and the Dakṣiṇāgni. || 37 ||
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are proclaimed as the three qualities (guṇas). Dharma and artha, as well as artha and kāma, are proclaimed as the three aims of life (trivargas). || 38 ||
Morning, midday, and evening are proclaimed as the three junctions (saṃdhyā).
The first is the circle of fire; the second is the circle of the sun. (39)
The third is the lunar disc; these are called the three discs. The morning libation, the midday libation, and the third [evening] libation constitute the three libations. || 40 ||
The triad consists of the power of lordship (prabhu-śakti), the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), and the power of Śiva (śiva-śakti);
and the triad consists of the self (ātman), the inner self (antarātman), and the supreme self (paramātman). || 41 ||
The great ego and the mind—these they know as the three internal organs.
This triad taken together has emerged as the temple.
O child, one should purify [the self] in due order; thus one shall go to the unmanifest Śiva.
Gandharvas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, and likewise Apsarases—[all these abide there]. (43)
The Kinnaras, Garuḍas, all the Nāgas, Sarpas, and Pannagas;
the Asuras, Rākṣasas, Yātudhānas, and Piśācas. || 44 ||
O child, one should purify them all sequentially from a single word;
one should properly purify these [mantras] consisting of the injunctions for the limbs of Śiva.
The sages (Ṛṣis) and the women (Pramadās) are to be joined with the sixteen established steps;
indeed, they are proclaimed in sequence as being diminished by one each, ending with the Piśācas.
O Guha, the path of words (padādhvan) is proclaimed to extend from Śiva down to the Piśācas;
at the time of initiation, one should restrain it within the body of the disciple.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, on the Five Paths, in the Kālottara.
The Lord said: I shall explain the path of reality (tattvādhvan), by which the arising of liberation occurs;
having understood it correctly, the wise man attains the state of Śiva. || 1 ||
Earth, water, fire, air, and space indeed;
and the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and the nose as the fifth.
Speech, feet, hands, the anus, and the generative organ as the fifth;
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth. || 3 ||
Mind, intellect, ego, primordial nature, and likewise the person; passion, ignorance, Lakṣmī, illusion, destiny, and Vṛddhi, the lord of the planets. || 4 ||
The Kalās, the Śuddhikalās, as well as Śuddhavidyā, Maheśa, and Sadāśiva—these indeed constitute the thirty-six principles (tattvas). || 5 ||
Earth is to be known as having five qualities, and water likewise has four qualities;
fire is understood to have three qualities, and wind is said to have two qualities.
And space has one quality; these qualities have been proclaimed as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth.
Earth is to be known as that which supports; O Guha, water is that which forms into a mass;
fire is indeed to be known as that which digests; and wind is said to be that which expands.
Space is proclaimed to have the function of providing room;
O child, the ear indeed hears, and the skin is the sense of touch.
For the eye perceives only what is visible, and likewise the tongue knows taste;
the nose should recognize smell—these are proclaimed as the objects of the senses.
The application of speech and body is proclaimed as the organ of speech; by means of the two feet one moves, and the anus is indeed for excretion. (11)
One attains bliss through the generative organ, which is indeed the organ of action;
one should know that sound is resonance, and it is born from space.
The wind consists of the subtle element of touch, fire of the subtle element of form, and water of the subtle element of cold; these are the life-sustainers of the entire world. (13)
O Six-faced One, from the subtle element of smell, earth was produced;
for that which is solid is earth, and that which is liquid is indeed water. (14)
That which is hot is called fire; that which moves is called air;
that which is hollow is space, proclaimed as the support of the gods. || 15 ||
From the *harat* (the seizer) comes ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and from ego arises the mind (*manas*).
The Great Principle (*mahān*) is produced from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and from the Person (*puruṣa*) primordial nature arises. (16)
The wise know the system of twenty-five principles (tattvas) as the Sāṃkhya philosophy;
Viṣṇu [is the principle] beyond the twenty-sixth... || 17 ||
In the Hiraṇyagarbha-yoga, however, twenty-seven principles are taught;
attachment (rāga), illusion (māyā), and knowledge (vidyā) are called the three coverings (kañcuka). || 18 ||
Kāla, Niyati, and Vigraheśa, who possess various sheaths such as the various vidyās, are born from the power of sovereignty (prabhu-śakti); they arise from the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti).
Kāla, Śuddhavidyā, and Śuddhakālā, who possess the triad of coverings (kañcukas), have arisen from the power of Śiva; they are the deluders of all the worlds. (20)
From Maheśa, the triad of powers was born, originating from Śiva and Sadāśiva;
yet at the dissolution of Śiva, O Six-faced One, nothing is born at all. (21)
(163) Know that from the thirty-five principles, starting from the Śiva-principle, they have emerged; their abiding is in that very place, and their dissolution occurs in that very place. 22.
Creation indeed occurs through the form of Brahmā, and power indeed belongs to Viṣṇu;
but I alone am the dissolution, endowed with the three qualities.
Creation proceeds from the quality of rajas, while maintenance occurs through sattva alone;
dissolution is likewise due to tamas—thus everything has been proclaimed by me.
O Mahāsena, at the time of initiation, one should establish the principles (tattvas);
one should join them to the body of the disciple, from the crown of the head down to the feet.
O child, one should purify [the body] gradually from the feet up to the top of the head;
at the time of the installation of the liṅga, one should join it according to the prescribed rite.
The wise one should install [the deity] in the vessel of the great consecration according to the prescribed rite; by installing it in a place of misfortune, incomparable good fortune shall arise.
A maiden obtains a virtuous husband and shall obtain sons and grandsons;
O Six-faced One, one should place the six meditations (ṣaḍadhyāna) into the pitcher and perform the ritual bath.
"Even a barren woman obtains a son, and her good fortune shall become incomparable.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, on the Path of Principles (tattvādhva), in the *Kālottara*, the compendium of twelve thousand verses. 30.
Śrīḥ!
Īśvara said:
In this Kula, which begins with Kālāgnirudra and ends with Sadāśiva, and which is preeminent among the Rudras who are knowers of the field (kṣetrajña).
And on the path, as far as one's power extends,
one effects either existence or non-existence; however, these are inferior to that which is beyond.
Having paid homage to that light, the ornament of the world, which alone is worthy of being seen by me as the foundation for my dwelling within the house of saṃsāra;
I shall speak of the path that leads to its attainment, which is like a cloak. || 2 ||
Kālāgni, Nalā, and Palā; Dharaṇī, the world beyond, and the Śāṅkara [world];
the Rudras, the five, the eight, and the established primary Yāmas;
the effect, the instrument, the qualities, the self, the person (puruṣa), attachment, knowledge, and limited agency (kalā).
And whatever other [deeds] the ascetic Śiva, awakened from his illusion, performed while counting the passing moments. || 3 ||
This verse from the Sūtra is as follows; its explanation is now given.

There exists, within this [universe], the unsurpassed abode of the serpent-king whose movements constitute the sphere of infinite enjoyment, belonging to the Blessed Lord Kālāgnirudra—the cause of the dissolution of all worlds; who is adorned by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of Rudras situated in its upper portion; whose circular expanse, measuring one hundred thousand times ten thousand *yojanas*, has an interior shaped like a vast egg; whose upper part consists of the supreme and inferior divisions made of silver and gold, extending for sixty-four crores of *yojanas* in continuous succession; and who, as the cause of the origin and end of the entire world, has the regions of the sky enveloped by the mass of flames of the upward-blazing fire. This [abode] measures three crores of *yojanas* of the Supreme Self, and its dimensions are defined on all sides.

There are thirty-two well-known places of torment for those specific sentient beings who are oppressed by men who resemble pillars made of sapphire stones, possessing great dark bodies, with foreheads furrowed by frowns born from the rebukes of exceedingly harsh words; whose drinking-places are proclaimed by fangs shaped like crescent moons; whose hair-tufts are as crooked as the mass of flames from the fire at the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*); who wear long garlands of skulls hanging from their broad chests; whose feet are adorned with tinkling bells; whose thighs are like those of lions, elephants, and boars; whose left arms are raised and brandish sharp, greedy clubs ringing with bells; and who wander without fixed dwellings, intent on the business of snatching away the life-breaths of all the worlds. Below the earth are these locations: Cakraviṇāma, Dvayavaitaraṇī, Kūṭaśālmalī, Yamalagiri, Niśvāsa, Pūtimāṃsadrava, Naputa, Tapta, Jatupaṅka, Jaiṣāsti, Titi, Bhāga, Kṛkaccheda, Moda, Asṛkpūyahṛd, Tīkṣṇāyasakhaṇḍa, Śakuni, Aṅgārarāśi, Avalāmbarīṣa, Kumbhīpāka, Asitāladruma, Gahana, Kṣuradhārāparvata, Panasūcīmukha, Kālasūtra, Mahāpadma, Saṃjīvana, Uṣṇa, Śīta, Tamasa, and Mahāraurava. Here, in the dense darkness, there is a wave extending for ten million *yojanas*. This [Mahāraurava] has seven subsidiary hells. Beyond this, there are fifteen hells—beginning with Kṛminicaya and ending with Ambarīṣa—each separated by an interval of three hundred thousand *yojanas*. In the midst of these, each consists of three hells numbering three *yojanas*. Even though surrounded by ten million *yojanas*, Kumbhīpāka is itself surrounded by seven hells; and beyond that, starting from Kartre and Sadyonara, there are fourteen successive hells, beginning with Asitāladrumagahana and ending with Mahāraurava. In the midst of these, each is surrounded by three hells; and beyond that, Raurava, extending for ten million *yojanas*, is surrounded by seven hells.

Thus, at the edge of this Pradhāna are forty crores of *asajjana-bhāsa* beings; above them are one hundred crores of *bhānarakas*; and above those is the *kūśmāṇḍa* realm. Beyond that, at a distance of seventy-four lakhs and thirty thousand *yojanas*, is the exceedingly vast river named Vaitaraṇī. Above it lie the seven subterranean realms (*pātālas*) known as Mahātala, Rasātala, Talātala, Nitala, Sutala, Vitala, and Atala. Each of these is separated from the next by an interval of thirteen thousand *yojanas*, arranged like a series of ascending staircases. Their ground surfaces, respectively, consist of black, white, red, yellow, variegated, and gold-like stones. These seven realms serve as the dwelling places for Kṛṣṇa, Pāṇḍura, Rakta, Pīta, Śabala, Śilāmaya, Kanaka-nibha, Bhūmibhāga, Ititanaya, Danusuta, Gajarāja, Garuḍa, Rākṣasa, and others. Surrounding these on all sides is a land measuring thirty crores of *yojanas*.

Furthermore, extending from Mount Kaṇṭhaka up to the Lokāloka mountain range, there is a mass of darkness surrounding [the world] on all sides, measuring twenty thousand *yojanas* less than two hundred and fifty million *yojanas*. That is the ocean-king named Garbhoda. Within it, at a distance of ten thousand *yojanas* in both width and height, stands the mountain named Lokāloka. Because the solar rays illuminate its inner half while failing to illuminate the outer half, it is thus designated. Upon its supporting summit dwell four guardians of the world (*lokapālas*): Sudhāman in the east, ... [and so forth].

To the south is Śaṅkhavat, to the west Ketumān, and to the north Hiraṇmaya; having thus approached, one reaches the delightful [regions] surrounded by mountains of living beings, shining with their own masses of creepers, shrubs, and enclosures. These portions, extending for a distance of ten yojanas, consist of gold and belong to the dwellers of heaven.

Beyond the sixty-four *yojana*s in extent of the inhabited land (*vihārabhūmi*) filled with bodies joined together, there is the great ocean named Svadūta, whose name corresponds to its reality. On this side of it, measuring the same number of *yojana*s, is the great continent named Puṣkara.
In the center of which are situated, in the eastern, southern, western, and northern regions, the royal capitals of Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera, namely Vasvokasārā.

The mountain named Mānasottara, whose peak-region is adorned with names such as Savyanibhāvatī, which is circular in form and dimension, is the king of mountains of this continent. Its king is named Sarvanara. His two sons, whose names were marked by the beginning and end of the word Rādhātajiśca, existed as two distinct regions (varṣa-bheda). Therein, the protector of the earth [resided] outside of Mānasottara; within it was the great Dvita-Dhātaki forest. Asatru...

The lifespan of those who dwell there is limited to a number of ten thousand years. Śākadvīpa is likewise delimited by that same number [of regions] from this side. There, the king named Daṇḍadhara had seven sons as his subjects; they were Jalakumāra, Sukumāra, Malina, Kumuda, Unnata, and Mahādruma. From them, the seven regions are designated by their respective names.

The kings situated in various directions and regions—the boundaries of whose territories extended from east to west and were immersed in both oceans—were born in that [lineage] as mountain-like rulers named Ambikeya and Kesarin, like clouds with rising mountain-waters.

Beyond that, extending for a distance of one hundred and sixty thousand yojanas, lies the Ocean of Curdled Milk (Dadhi-samudra). Beyond that, in a region of equal extent, there was once a king named Krauñca. He too had seven sons—Kuśala, Manonuga, Uṣṇa, Prāvaraka, Ārdhaka, Aruṇa, and Dundubhi. The lands situated there were named after them; such were their respective territories upon the earth.

The lords of ten forests are the presiding deities over these regions. Therein also are seven mountain ranges known as Krauñca, Vāmaka, Ārdhaka, Deva, Pauṇḍraka, Muni, and Dundubhi. Their extent is equal to that of the mountains previously mentioned. Beyond that, and separated by a distance of eight hundred thousand yojanas, lies the Ocean of Clarified Butter (Ghṛtoda).

Beyond that, the region delimited by that same number [of divisions] is Śākadvīpa. There, he gave to his sons— Udbhija, Veṇu, Maṇḍala, Rathaka, Kāla, Lamba, and Dhṛtimat, known as the Prabhākaras— seven regions bearing their names, corresponding to the mountain ranges named Vidruma, Śiva, Hema, Nimiñja, Kuśeśaya, Hari, and Giri-meru.

The king of that [continent] is named Jyotiṣmat. To the west of that, extending for four hundred thousand yojanas and surrounded by the ocean, is the continent named Cchinnaśālmalī, which is equal in extent [to the former]. It is ruled by King Puṣpavat, and it is supported by seven mountain ranges that sustain the earth; these consist of seven regions (*varṣas*). To the west of that, surrounded by the Ikṣurasoda ocean, which is two hundred thousand yojanas wide, is the continent named Plakṣa, whose dimensions are equal to those [of the preceding continent].

While Dvāpa was protecting him, [the king] Bhūbhuj, by whose name the lunar day is designated, begot seven sons from his own body— sons who were like the breast of Śiva, the source of the bliss arising from the welfare of his own person— and they were marked with their own names.

Indeed, like the roar of a cow-elephant, a moon, or a drum, the king of the Bhūbhujakula clan, having dispatched seven [offerings], [established] that which is delimited by a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas from here as the Kṣāroda ocean. And him— [the one] proud of the strength of his own wings— he [protected] with his own self from the Thousand-Eyed One (Indra), whose thousand eyes were fixed on the movement of the affairs of all the worlds, and whose staff-like arms were adorned with the thunderbolt engaged in the task of clipping the wings of the multitude of mountains.

Unable to protect themselves from fear, twelve great nāgas entered [the forest]. Among them—namely Bhadra, Indra, and Dhūmra—three adorned the western quarter; while those named Candra, Kaṅka, and Krodhana took refuge in the northern direction; and those named Soma, Kana, and Nārada went toward the western quarter.

The regions known as Cakra, Maināka, and Balāhaka reached the domain of Vaivasvata. There, between the two mountains named Cakra and Maināka, within the range of mountains boiled by the Śivākalpa, there is a king of fires named Baḍabāmukha, whose power of asceticism is manifested by a multitude of spirits drinking the waters of the ocean as if they were clarified butter. This entire island, its borders encircled by the ocean which is the singular form of fire’s majesty, is surrounded [by it].
Surrounded by a multitude of vassals, he was the supreme lord of all the islands within an extent of a hundred thousand *yojanas* on every side;
and there is this island-kingdom named Jambūdvīpa, and [the continent] named Kuru.

To them, that king named Soma—who indeed [was] the son born from the navel of Him who is praised by the breaking of the rains—obtained another son named Manyu. He made that bull his own object of worship; when he had relinquished his prime of life, he entrusted him, who was capable of enjoying all objects of sense as marked by youth, to his son named Bharata, and became silent on the bank of the Narmadā, holding a lute like the Āṣāḍhī festival.

Having become the self of all beings and having cast this entire burden upon it, this Bhāratavarṣa is now being neglected until its final pacification. Within this very division of the continent, there are sub-divisions known as Candradvīpa, Kaśeru, Tāmraparṇī, Gabhastimant, Āgaka-dvīpa, Saumya, Gāndharva, Varuṇa, and Kaumārī; these are separated by oceans of water measuring a thousand yojanas in extent.

Moving across a basin fifteen *yojanas* in extent, they travel back and forth around the ocean of that same number [of *yojanas*]. Thus, this land of Bhārata-varṣa should be understood as being delimited by a thousand *yojanas*, containing the great ocean and the Bindu-saras lake within its interior. Within this very Bhārata-varṣa, on Kumāra-dvīpa, there are certain [deities] who bestow the enjoyment of celestial pleasures, while others manifest the distinction between the higher and the lower.

The four Vedas— Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan— which are most fit for warding off [evil], which possess origins as dark as a dense mass of clouds, which are the source of many kinds of living beings, which are the paths for the wandering of the breaths (prāṇas), and which display the entire course of worldly affairs therein; which have the syllable Om (praṇava) as their primary entrance and exit, and which serve as the standard for distinguishing between heaven and liberation— these Vedas circulate upon the earth, and even the noble Śūdras and other castes dwell right here.
171) Setting aside specific varieties, the divisions [of time] that pervade all time are as follows by way of illustration: one-fourth of a sweet-eyed blink is a *kaṭi*;
two *kaṭis* are a *laya*; two *lavas* are fifteen blinks, which is a *kāṣṭhā*; thirty *kāṣṭhās* are a *kalā*; thirty *kalās*...

Thirty *muhūrtas* constitute a day and night (*ahorātra*). Fifteen days and nights constitute a fortnight (*pakṣa*). Two fortnights constitute a month (*māsa*). Two months constitute a season (*ṛtu*). The seasons are as follows: *Tejas*, Śravaṇa, and Proṣṭhapada are the rainy season (*varṣā*); Āśvayuja and Kārtika are autumn (*śarad*); Mārgaśīrṣa and Pauṣa are the cold season (*hemanta*); Māgha and Phālguna are the dewy season (*śiśira*); Caitra and Vaiśākha are spring (*vasanta*); and Jyeṣṭha and Āṣāḍha are summer (*grīṣma*). These are the six seasons.

The period from the winter solstice (*śiśira*) onwards is the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), while the period from the rainy season (*varṣā*) onwards is the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyaṇa*). Two such half-years constitute a year (*saṃvatsara*). By that measure, four hundred thousand years make up the Kṛta Yuga. Including the six hundred-year transitional periods (*sandhyā*) at the beginning and end of the Kṛta Yuga, and by calculating the total duration of all four ages combined, there are twelve thousand divine years. This alone constitutes a cycle of four ages (*caturyuga*). These...
Four yugas constitute one *manvantara*, and there are fourteen such *manus*; this constitutes one *kalpa*. Two *kalpas* form a day and night of Brahmā.

Seventeen *kalpas* plus twenty [make up his month], and at the end of a year, his lifespan consists of a hundred years of Brahmā. Thus, a thousand years of Brahmā’s life is a single *mātrā* (measure) of Viṣṇu; for Śrīkaṇṭhanātha it is a year; and for Maheśvara and Sadāśiva, it is successively a hundred million (*koṭi*) years. This is the time described by me.

They exist for ten million times a thousand *yugas*. Thus, of the Supreme Lord—who is differentiated by manifold divisions, who is without beginning or end, infinite, Śiva, accessible to yogis, both transcendent and immanent, immortal, and devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted—the Supreme Lord alone is the sole basis for the conventional usage of time.
Even here in Bhāratavarṣa, there are seven mountain ranges.
p.
172) "Malaya, Sahya, Mahendra, Meru, Himavat, Vindhya, and Kailāsa—these are you. Great Meru is one hundred thousand *yojanas* in height;
below that, it is fifty thousand *yojanas* in width, sixteen thousand *yojanas* in breadth, and six thousand *yojanas* in length, and it is composed of Jāmbūnada gold.
The stairways, walls, and floors [of this mountain] are made of diamonds, rubies, emeralds, and pearls; and here are the Gaṅgā, Kauśikī, Gomatī,
Gaṇḍakī, Yamunā, Sindhu, Sarasvatī, Sarayū, Candrabhāgā, Lohitā, Vipāśā, Narmadā, Śatadru, Vedasmṛti, Suprayoga, Mahānadī, Godāvarī,
Bhairavī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Pañcanadī, Śoṇa, Kṛṣṇavarṇā, Kāverī, Tāmraparṇī, and other great rivers, all marked by the splendor of this mountain.
And these are the rivers and the regions of Pāyadvāya, Pāṇḍya, Cola, Dramila, Karṇāṭaka, Āndhra, Kosala, Pāñcāla, Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Sīmā;
as well as the Madhyaprabhṛti and other districts. To the east are the givers of life and so forth; to the west, those consisting mostly of Kirātas with Yavana faces;

and in the middle, those where the four castes (*caturvarṇa*) are predominant. They generally move about therein. In that very place, the power of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-śakti*) is manifested fourfold and so on.

And regarding the specific divisions of the army seized from Pātāla: there are four Rudras belonging to the Lord Śiva who, having reached the self-manifested abodes (svayambhū-sthāna), bestow grace; they are known by the names Śrī Dākṣī, Diṇḍimuṇḍin, Bhārabhūti, and Lakulīśa.
In every age, they are adorned with eighteen limbs, beginning with the Chandas, which consist of six parts, and through the knowledge of the supreme reality (anāga-paratattva).

The limbs of Dharma are rendered false when their purpose is not protected. [These include] Āsanneva, Vastrāpada, Rudrukoṭi, Avimukta, Mahālaya, Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, Sthāṇu, Caladviraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, Maṇḍaleśvara, Kālāñjara, Dāruvana,
Aśaṅkukarṇa, Sthaleśvara, Sthūleśvara, Kurukṣetra, Nakhanākhala, Vimalāṭṭahāsa, Bhīmeśvara, Hariścandra, and Śrīparvata.

(173) Mahākāla, Āmrātikeśvara, Jalpeśvara, Madhyamakedāra, Mahābhairava, Amareśvara, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, and Puṣkara— these sacred abodes, rendered exceptionally delightful by the presence of the forms of the Blessed One, have thus been described in brief within Bhāratavarṣa alone.

In the world of earth (*bhūrloka*), there are seven oceans, seven continents, and seven principal mountain ranges, including the ocean of sweet water; beyond this lies the world of heaven (*svarloka*), where the sun travels across the mountain of the horizon (*ālokaparvata*). Above the world of earth is the world of the atmosphere (*bhuvarloka*), extending for thirty million *yojanas*, where the constellations, the nine planets, and the hosts of sages dwell.
In the world of the gods (*suraloka*) reside Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, and Īśāna; the eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, the eight Vasus, and the two Aśvins.

Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, hosts of Maruts, Kinnaras, Kiṃpuruṣas, Vidyādharas, and others dwell there. Above the intermediate space between the heavenly worlds, which extends for twenty-eight crores of yojanas, reside the Maharloka and the six Brahmās—the four-faced Prajāpati, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Tryaṣṭa, Aṣṭa, and [the sixth]. There also dwell Sanaka, Sanandana, and [Sanātana], the mind-born sons of the Grandfather (Brahmā).

Sanātana, Sanatkumāra, and others, as well as the fourteen Manus, dwell there. Above that is Janaloka. Viṣṇu, Mahāviṣṇu, Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nārasiṃha, Vāmana, the three Rāmas, Kṛṣṇa, Kalki, Viṣvaksena, Garuḍa, and others reside there.

The Janaloka is twenty-six crores of yojanas in length and breadth. Above it reside Maheśvara, Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin; as well as Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Paśupati, Rudra, Ugra, Bhīma, and Mahādeva.
Mahādeva, Śiva, Rudra, Śaṅkara, Nīlalohita,
Īśāna, Vijaya, Bhīma, Devadeva, Bhavodbhava,
and Kapālīśa are to be known as the eleven who are remembered as the Rudras.

By this [measure], there dwell in the world of austerity (Tapoloka) hundreds of Rudras, as well as thousands of Rudras, tens of thousands, millions, ten millions, and hundreds of millions, and even many tens of millions of Rudras. The world of austerity is forty million [yojanas] in width and length. Above that is the world of truth (Satyaloka).
Sadāśiva is the manifest cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of all the worlds. Thousands of lakhs of many millions [of beings] who resemble Sadāśiva dwell there.

Satyaloka is delimited by an extent of twenty-two crores of yojanas. There dwell the lords of yogins, knowers of Brahman, whose sole essence is bliss, who are satisfied, beginningless and endless, contented, exceedingly subtle, and without support.

Free from conceptual proliferation and devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted, yogins dwell within the hollows of the fissures in the solar disc. Above that [disc] is the shell of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍakapāla*), where the five tawny cows—Nandā, Subhadrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and Sumanā—who are dear to Śiva, reside. The hundred Rudras, who support the cosmic egg, are stationed in every direction: Kapālīśa, Āyu, Vajradeha, Pramardana, Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, and Pinākī.
The ten Rudras, who bear the names of the lords of the thirty-three gods, are stationed in the eastern direction;
having traversed this [direction], they are endowed with sovereign power as its fruit.
Agni, Rudra, Hutāśin, Piṅgala,
Pāvaka, Hara, Jvalana, Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmāntaka, and Kṣapāntaka—
these ten Rudras in the south-eastern direction are the sustainers of the cosmic egg.

175) Having occupied the fruit of the Āgneya [quarter], endowed with sovereign power (*prabhu-śakti*), the Rudras who support the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) reside in the southern direction. These Rudras—Mṛtyu, Vidhātṛ, Kārtarudra, Dharmādharmapati, Saṃyoktṛ, and Vidhottāra—are established in the southern quarter.
Having overcome the realm of Yama, they are endowed with sovereign power;
they are the slayers and destroyers belonging to Nairṛta, possessing cruel glances and terrifying forms,
with hair standing erect, deformed eyes, and smoke-colored or red fangs.
The ten Rudras who support the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) in the southwestern direction (nair-ṛtyā),
having overcome the power of Nirṛti and being endowed with sovereign energy (prabhu-śakti),
are Bala, Atibala, Prāśahasta, Mahābala, Ceta, Jayabhadra, Dīrghabāhu, Jalāntaka, Baḍabāmukha, and Bhīṣaṇa; these are the ten Rudras who support the cosmic egg in the western direction (vāruṇyā).
Having overcome the power of Varuṇa, they were endowed with sovereign might and patience.
[He is] swift, light, possessing the speed of wind, subtle, sharp, the ender of decay,
the ender of the five, five-crested, skull-bearing, and having the clouds as his vehicle.
In the northwestern direction (Vāyavyā) are the ten Rudras, the sustainers of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa).

Having mastered the power of Vāyu and endowed with sovereign energy (prabhu-śakti), they are matted-haired, bearing axes, wearing various jewels, lords of treasures, handsome, fortunate, gentle-bodied, radiant, and able to assume any form at will (*kāmarūpin*). These ten Rudras are situated in the northern direction (Kauberī), supporting the cosmic egg.
Having overcome the power of Soma, they are endowed with sovereign power;
they are lords of knowledge, enjoyers of wisdom, and have reached the further shore of the Vedas in every respect.
Mātṛpitṛviśālā, Bhūtavahā, Balipriyā, Savitā, and Vī... [and] another who causes pleasure and pain; in the northeastern direction are the ten Rudras, the sustainers of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Having overcome the power of Īśāna, they are endowed with sovereign energy (*prabhu-śakti*):
Ananta, Pālaka, Dhīra, Pratāpa, Vegin, and Vṛṣadhara.
Below are the ten Rudras who support the cosmic egg;
having assumed infinite strength, they are endowed with sovereign power:
Śambhu, Vibhu, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Tryakṣa, and Tridaśavandita.
Saṃvāha, Vivāha, and the three-eyed Trilocana, who desired to reach the sky.

Above are the ten Rudras who support the Egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa). Having overcome the power of the Four-faced One (Brahmā), they are endowed with sovereign power (*prabhu-śakti*). Such is the arrangement of these ten Rudras. Furthermore, each of these Rudras has a retinue of one hundred Rudras; each of those has a retinue of one hundred thousand Rudras. Surrounding this [Egg] on all sides, it is encircled a hundredfold by the covering of water; the covering of fire is encircled a hundredfold by the covering of water; the covering of air is encircled a hundredfold by the covering of fire; the covering of ether is encircled a hundredfold by the covering of air; the covering of Śakti is encircled a hundredfold by the covering of ether; the covering of Nāda is encircled a hundredfold by the covering of Śakti; the covering of Maheśvara is encircled a hundredfold by the covering of Nāda; the covering of Sadāśiva is encircled a hundredfold by the covering of Maheśvara.

(177) This entire enclosure of Śiva— whether higher or lower, and comprising the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth— is, O Mahāsena, entirely composed of Śiva. All the world, both stationary and moving, resides within the central body.
"Becoming absorbed with the mind fixed on that, and having the consciousness attained to that state,
one speaks of the established forms of yoga through the grace of the Guru's mouth.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the *Kālottara*.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
I shall proclaim the supreme path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan), which removes all sins; one attains all perfections and the highest immediate realization. 1.
Desiring to create within the supreme subtle state, the *bindu* was produced by me;
from the *bindu*, the *nāda* arose, and from the *nāda*, the *śakti* was born.
From Śakti, that which consists of speech was born; from that which consists of speech, the sixteen digits (kalās) arose.
From the digits, the consonant was born; from Vāgbhava, the fire of Vāgbhava came into being.
From the letter *a* everything is born; indeed, the entire Vāgbhava-mantra is thus.
It is both with parts and without parts, empty yet enriched by its digits, and fashioned as a lotus.
The eighth is known as Kṣavaṇa, situated in the impurity of decay (kṣayamala), located at the throat and lips; O child, these eight divisions of Śiva indeed arise within the letter Ha.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī are established in the trident;
Kālī and Kalavikaraṇī are likewise to be known [there]. (6)
Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathanī,
Sarvabhūtadamanī, and Manonmanī are likewise stationed on the neck.
Umāśrī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Jyeṣṭhā, Vasundharā,
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī. (8)
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, Uṣā, and Prabhā—
these and ten million others like Uṣā stand upon his neck.
The peaceful fourth part (turiyāṃśa) is established within the letter A;
within the letter Ā is the deity Viṣṇu, endowed with ten million powers.
The letter *i*, adorned with a *bindu* on its head, is the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha himself, pervaded by the power of the *bindu*, and it is the protection of all. 11.
O Six-faced One, the supreme form of Vāsudeva, which is the very nature of Ananteśa,
has a bindu upon its head and brings all under control.
The subtle form, however, is the syllable *ī*, which is directly the very form of Viṣṇu;
when mounted upon a nasal dot (*bindu*) at its head, it is the supreme means for bringing kings under one's control.
The syllable *u* is Śivottama, and after that is Saṃkarṣaṇa;
the syllable *ū* is Puruṣa, the Vaiśya, adorned with a dot (*bindu*) upon its head.
The letter *ū* with a single eye (the anusvāra) becomes the pure [seed-mantra] of Pradyumna;
when mounted upon a crest of a bindu, this supreme [mantra] brings men under control. (15)
White in color, as well as red, green, and blue, and resembling a pigeon; thus it is proclaimed to be of six colors. (16)

O Six-faced One, that which has been proclaimed regarding the principle of the syllable *A*—namely, within the syllable *A* itself—is the protection of all, the subjugation of all, and indeed the destruction of poison. (17)
One should practice *ṛṣāra* as Ekarudra; there is no doubt that this is Aniruddha.
When the head of the *bindu* is overcome, it destroys eighty types of wind disorders.
The syllable *ṛ*, which has the form of the Trinity (Trimūrti) and is the very nature of the power of the Lord,
destroys fever, leprosy, poison, phlegm, and all forms of epilepsy. (19)
The syllables *ḷ* and *ḹ* have the form of a horse and are supreme for removing all diseases;
when marked with a dot on the head (*bindu*), they destroy eighty types of wind disorders.
Mounted upon the crest of the Bindu, it possesses the luster of molten gold.
The letter E is said to be wind, having a luster like crushed collyrium;
O Guha, it bestows all protection when joined with the Bindu.
For expulsion (*uccāṭana*), it is without the nasal dot (*bindu*); for killing (*māraṇa*), it is with the syllable *phaṭ*.
The syllable *oṃ*, which has the form of a crest (*śikhaṇḍi*), is joined with the nasal dot and always accompanied by its limbs (*aṅga*). (23)
They say that Śiva alone is possessed of the *bindu*, whose form is light, incomparable, resembling pure crystal, divine in appearance, and free from ailment. (24)
Through recitation, one attains both enjoyment and liberation, having conquered death; of this there is no doubt.
The wise man should meditate upon [the deity] facing downwards in the center of a white lotus. (25)
O Six-faced One, by means of the syllable *praṇava*, one attains freedom from old age and death;
the syllable *oṃ* is red in color, representing Maheśa, the supreme and great. (26)
One attains the paralysis of the enemy army; one should mutter the *mūla* mantra three times.
The letter *A* is the supreme reality (*tattva*), which is both the form of worldly existence and the Great One (*mahat*). (27)
That which resembles great silver is declared to be the pillar of poison;
however, the form of the letter A is shapeless and like pure crystal. (28)
For this supreme form of Śarva is the ultimate destroyer of poison;
it renders even those bitten by a venomous snake free from poison, provided they possess a virtuous mind. || 29 ||
One should recite it mentally ten thousand times; even when out of sight, it removes poison.
Thus, the sixteen vowels are indeed the great digit of the moon in person. (30)
It is nectar even for nectar, and indeed born from nectar;
it is floating, cool in potency, a destroyer of heat, and a vanquisher of death. || 31 ||
The moonlight from the frosty region [of the Himalayas] downward is reviving, refreshing, thirst-quenching, and disease-destroying; beyond that, it is the supreme reviver of the dead.
She is known as the leader of the constellations and the digit of the moon;
she is celebrated as the sixteenfold form of the universe, ending with the emission (visarga).
Know the syllable *A* to be the Grandfather (Brahmā), resembling the filaments of a lotus;
it is the complete destroyer of poison and the promoter of all creation. (34)
One should know the syllable *kha* to be Garuḍa, with a luster like refined gold;
it destroys all poisons, whether stationary, mobile, or artificial. (35)
Gaṇapati is indeed the letter *ga*, the manifest Vighnanāyaka, who has the ears of an elephant, the face of an elephant, the trunk of an elephant, and three eyes. (36)
Resembling crushed collyrium, with a large belly and four arms, he is always fond of eating all things while seated upon a white lotus. (37)
The letter *gha* is Tripurāntaka, resembling the flax flower (*atasīpuṣpa*), four-armed and three-eyed, and bearing a trident and an axe. || 38 ||
The seed-syllable that destroys all enemies is said to slay all demons;
it is the letter *gha*, whose presiding deity is the Earth, which has two arms and resembles a bee. (39)
One should know [the syllable] as having two eyes and two arms; from its recitation, the accomplishment of the earth [is attained].
One should know the letter *ca* in the form of a shaven-headed one (*muṇḍin*), with a luster like a dark cloud of doom. (40)
Eight-armed and three-eyed, bearing a snake, a bell, and a hand-drum (ḍamaruka),
wearing a garland of heads, fierce, and the crusher of all asuras. (41)
He is the letter *cha*, the auspicious time (*bhadrakāla*), possessing the luster of the *rājāvarta* gem;
he is endowed with sixteen arms, has three eyes, and is embodied upon the earth. || 42 ||
Seated in the midst of a red lotus, possessing terrible fangs and inspiring fear,
[he holds] a skull, a trident, a bow, a discus, a thunderbolt, and an axe.
He holds a sword, a bell, and a sound; he bears an arrow and a javelin, an elephant-goad, a slingshot, and an auspicious iron club.
One should know that the letter *ja* is Śuka, Jṛmbhala, and Yanadeva, located in the left, in the left [of the others], and in the right among the eight arms; of this there is no doubt. (45)
One should know him as having two eyes and two arms, of dark complexion and auspicious countenance,
endowed with all ornaments and adorned with every kind of jewel.
O Guha, one should always satisfy [the ancestors] with water one hundred and eight times;
