indeed, having touched the water, one should always offer libations using handfuls of water.
They behold the great treasure that satisfies for three years; indeed, they behold the syllable *jhakāra*, the supreme imperishable, which is the manifest form of the Lord of Nectar.
One-footed, one-armed, with hands raised, three-eyed, mounted upon the crest of the Bindu, and endowed with the power of Nāda. || 49 ||
In some places it was white, in some red, in some yellow, and golden;
in some places it resembled the hibiscus flower, and in some it had the luster of Indra’s bow (a rainbow).
He may have eight arms and three eyes, or sometimes he may have only one arm;
sometimes he has but one foot, and sometimes he has but one eye.
O child, in the Ardhanārīśvara [form], Jhakāreśa is present without a doubt;
by merely reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, the Puruṣa comes to abide [there]. (52)
With two hundred thousand [recitations] one conquers the pillar of the army; with three hundred thousand, one conquers the earth, as well as the world, the king, and likewise individual men.
Subjugation of women, subjugation of lions, and subjugation of elephants are achieved; likewise, there is the neutralization of poison, even that of one bitten by Vāsuki himself.
The syllable *au* joined with the letter *ra* destroys the enemy army;
the syllable *ḷ* has the form of a *koddalī* flower, the color of a bumblebee, and three eyes.
O child, he has two arms, is naked in form, dwells in the forest, and is auspicious; though appearing uncivilized, he is a benefactor who is pleased by the dance of the naked.
By mere remembrance, a woman gives birth to a son easily through Koṭavī.
[One should meditate on] the letter Ṭa as Viśvarūpa, having two arms and three eyes. (57)
The syllable *ṭha* resembles the *bandhūka* flower; it destroys disease through mere remembrance. It is like the moon itself, possessing the pure luster of jasmine and the moon. (58)
He has two arms and three eyes, adorned with everything,
endowed with all ornaments, and likewise possesses a single curl of hair.
Indeed, it is the manifest form of nectar, seated upon a white lotus;
O Mahāsena, by mere meditation upon it, both stationary and mobile poisons are neutralized.
It perishes at that very moment merely by being uttered once;
with the long [form], there is the paralysis of poison, while with the short [form], there is the destruction of poison. (61)
By means of the *pluta* [vowel], stationary and mobile poison becomes paralyzed.
One should meditate upon the syllable *ḍa*, which has the form of Yama, possessing two eyes, two arms, and supreme [splendor]. (62)
One who recites [the mantra of] the Supreme One, who resembles a dark blue cloud and holds a staff and a noose,
for exactly one hundred lakhs [of times], shall attain victory over death. (63)
The syllable *ḍha* is indeed the form of Time (Kāla), possessing five eyes and three faces;
it has many hands, a terrifying appearance, and is mounted upon a supreme buffalo.
O child, by mere remembrance, it indeed manifests throughout the three periods of time;
the letter *E* is the form of death, exceedingly black and possessing beautiful eyes. (65)
He has seven arms and seven faces, holding a noose and a sword;
he wears red garlands and garments, possesses terrible fangs, and is terrifying.
O child, by mere remembrance, one shall indeed attain the destruction of death;
O Six-faced One, one should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times, joined with the nasal drop (bindu).
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the *Kālottara*, concerning the procedure for the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*).
Śrī.
Īśvara said:
The letter *ta* represents Umā’s Lord, the supreme one who has the bull as his vehicle;
he is three-eyed, possesses the three aims of life (*trivarga*), and wields the threefold weapons. (1)
Resembling pure crystal and adorned with a crown of matted locks,
O child, one beholds this great treasure merely by remembering it.
The syllable *Tha* has the form of a crest, with a luster like black collyrium;
it is four-armed and three-eyed, and holds a trident and an axe. || 3 ||
Through recitation and mere remembrance, the destruction of all sins occurs;
the syllable *Da* is the form of Durgā, dark-complexioned and three-eyed.
Having eight arms, mounted upon a buffalo, and having the supreme lion as his vehicle—
one attains perfection through recitation, and victory shall be achieved in battle. (5)
The syllable *Dha* is of the nature of wealth; it has two eyes and is tawny-dark in color.
It is surrounded by Jambha and other [demons], and encircled by the weapons of the conch and the lotus.
By reciting [this mantra] for twelve years, one beholds two treasures.
The letter *Na* is indeed the form of Sāvitrī, possessing three colors and four arms;
in the morning it is white in color, and at midday it is said to be dark blue.
In the evening, she indeed has the form of a jewel and accomplishes all desires and goals;
the syllable *pa* has the form of Parjanya, and he is white, four-armed.
The three-eyed one, mounted upon a cloud, bestows rain; this is the characteristic of the recitation (*japa*).
An oblation (*homa*) performed with ghee and milk brings about an abundance of food.
The syllable *pha* is the Pāśupata weapon, joined with the form of the six syllables;
preceded by the syllable *huṃ*, it is the supreme Mahāpāśupata.
One who recites it ten thousand times—[visualizing Him] as having a thousand eyes, a thousand arms, and endowed with a thousand heads—O Mahāsena, shall become victorious in battle. (12)
The syllable *baka* is the form of Yama, possessing a massive body, four arms, or eighteen arms, blazing, holding a staff in his hand, and having two eyes. (13)

One should perform the encapsulation with the *jīvantī* mantra joined at the beginning and end with the syllable *sa*; by reciting it exactly three hundred thousand times, death is utterly destroyed. 14.
The letter *bha* should be in accordance with Bāṇa; Kapālarudra is on the right, while Rudra with skull in hand and Vāsudeva are on the left.
(185) Know Pitāmaha to be on the right; between those two is Kapālin, twelve-armed, with three eyes, white, red, and dark blue. 18.
The vehicle is proclaimed to be Garuḍa, the bull, or the swan; by the mere recollection [of this], one shall accomplish dharma, artha, and kāma. || 17 ||
O Six-faced One, the syllable *Dha* is Rudra himself, the direct destroyer of poison;
it has the color of the fire of universal destruction and possesses a thousand heads.
He had a thousand arms and eyes, as well as a thousand mouths;
he possessed a thousand bellies and arms, and was likewise armed with a thousand weapons.
Sadāśiva is the upward line, and Saṃhāra is on the right;
Amṛteśa is the left line, while the supreme Śiva is in the form of the Bindu.
O Six-faced One, Mahāviṣṇu, in the form of sound, is the Aghora weapon because of its deluding power;
by means of the Visarga, one should destroy all enemies.
The letter *ya* is the wind, blue in color, and indeed the wind of universal dissolution;
it has ten arms, three eyes, and a luster like a dark cloud at the end of time.
O child, the line on the right is indeed Caṇḍarudra, the three-eyed one;
the line on the left is Pralayānila, the supreme deluder of the three worlds.
Rites such as eradication (uccāṭana) and others are accomplished by ten thousand recitations;
indeed, O child, by a hundred thousand recitations in a fortnight, one attains the speed of thought.
The letter *ra* is Krodharudra and indeed the fire of universal dissolution;
the line on the right is the fire of dissolution, while the fire of dissolution occurs on the left.
Above, however, is the form of withdrawal (saṃhāra), which has a hundred arms and three eyes;
one should withdraw [the universe] from Brahmā down to a blade of grass by means of that [mantra] joined with the Bindu.
The letter *va* is indeed the form of Indra, thousand-eyed and many-armed;
it is directly the form of the Earth, two-eyed and four-armed. (27)
Likewise, [he should be depicted] mounted upon the elephant Airāvata with a thunderbolt in his hand;
furthermore, on the right side is Rudrarekhā, and on the left is Janārdana.
The vertical line is the central body, containing various wonderful meanings;
one should know the *bindu* to be Sadāśiva, the bestower of the fruits of all desires. (29)
The letter *va* is the form of the moon, situated upon a white lotus;
it is the manifest form of nectar and the form of the wind, O Six-faced One. (30)
One should know him as having two eyes and four arms, resembling a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon;
Varuṇa is of the nature of nectar on the left, while his form is on the right.
O General, by mere remembrance, it shall be the destroyer of death;
by ten thousand recitations, it destroys all poisons, whether stationary or mobile. (32)
Having employed the destruction of death, that *sāman* may arise;
indeed, it is the very form of Lakṣmī, while Śaṅkara possesses the radiance of filaments.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī are located in the left, right, and middle [positions],
as are Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā.
In the center, above, and below, all these lines are firmly established;
the wise one should mutter [the mantra] joined with Māyā, Agni, and Bindu three hundred thousand times.
At that very moment, O Six-faced One, even a slayer of a Brahmin attains perfection;
[one should meditate on] the syllable *ṣa* as the twelve suns, red in color and three-eyed.
Manifestly twelve-armed and four-colored, they possess universal forms:
indeed, Kartana, Vivasvat, Mārtāṇḍa, Bhāskara, and Ravi. (37)
The illuminator of the world, the witness of the world, Trivikrama;
likewise Āditya, Sūrya, Aṃśupālī, and Divākara. (38)
These twelve Ādityas are indeed established in the syllable *va*;
the syllable *sa*, which is white in color, is the very form of Sarasvatī herself. (39)
Śruti-smṛti, Mahākāyā, Umā, Śraddhā, Vasundharā, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Vāgīśī, together with Medhā; (40)
Wisdom, compassion, patience, and faith are established in the letter *sa*;
it is the very form of immortality and the form of the living soul—of this there is no doubt. (41)
By reciting it exactly three hundred thousand times, there is the supreme destruction of death;
one shall live for ten thousand years, O Six-faced One, without a doubt, provided it is joined with the Bindu.
By reciting it ten thousand times, the wise man shall attain mastery over speech;
by reciting it one hundred thousand times, O child, he indeed acquires the four Vedas.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikaraṇī, Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathanī, Sarvabhūtadamanī, and Manonmanī. (44)
Likewise, all the lords of knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) and Umā and the others along with their powers [arise];
in the letter *ha*, the entire three worlds, including the moving and the unmoving, are produced. (45)
The unmanifest, necessity, time, and that which arises from time—this is the fourfold [set];
as well as substance, quality, action, generality, and particularity. (46)
And all that aggregate has emerged within the letter *ha*;
indeed, without the division of Rudra, the world does not abide at the tip of the nose.
No living being drinks without [the world], nor does the world eat without [the living being];
no living being is born without [the world], nor does the world obtain [existence] without [the living being]. || 48 ||
(188) No living being runs without [it], nor does the world leap without [it];
no living being sees without [it], nor does the world hear without [it]. 49.
A living being does not perceive without [taste], nor does it perceive flavor without [taste];
a living being does not smell without [smell], nor does the Great One perform excretion without [the power of smell]. 50.
Without the phallus there is no bliss, and without it the world is not perceived;
all knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the entire world are woven and interwoven in every way. 51.
Indeed, she sports alone, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass;
she resembles pure crystal, possesses ten arms, and has three eyes.
O child, with great self-restraint, one should recite the mantra of the god Maheśvara, the Supreme Lord whose vehicle is the bull, together with the *bindu*, one hundred thousand times.
O Guha, one indeed attains victory over death by reciting it ten lakh times;
the letter *la* is to be known as the earth, the goddess Bhūmi—of this there is no doubt. (54)
O Six-faced One, by reciting [the mantra] ten thousand times, one of yellow complexion, two eyes, four arms, and a single color shall indeed obtain land. 55.
The syllable Kṣa is the form of Viṣṇu, dark-complexioned and four-armed;
it emits the entire universe, and thus the syllable Kṣa is celebrated.
Therefore, Vāsudeva is joined with the letter *ra* above;
it is conjoined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, and endowed with the thirteenth [vowel]. || 57 ||
Joined with Saṃhārarudra and adorned with the sixth vowel, this is declared to be the Nārasiṃha [mantra], the supreme destroyer of enemies. (58)
O child, this supreme Amareśa, whose vehicle is Garuḍa,
indeed brings victory over the three worlds through three hundred thousand [recitations], O child.
(189) O Six-faced One, out of affection for you, I have explained to you the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan).
One should place the phonemes, together with the bindu and nāda, within the body of the disciple. 60.
Indeed, all three lines are produced from the three powers;
one should certainly place them upon the body with an undistracted mind, and one will attain liberation without a doubt.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, the Chapter on the Path of the Phonemes (varṇādhva), in the Kālottara.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
I shall now describe Kaladhvāna in brief; listen.
First is the upward-facing [face], then the eastern, southern, western, and northern.
The mantras of Tārā and Sutārā deliver one across [the ocean of existence]; they are the excellent saviors.
One should also place the collection of parts belonging to Īśāna upon the five heads. (2)
One should assign these five— the east, the south, the west, the north, and likewise the upward-facing— to the five faces.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and likewise Śāntyatītā— these are the five kalās, beginning with Oṃ and ending with Namaḥ.
The knower of mantras should place the portion of Aghora on the heart, the neck, the shoulders, and likewise on the navel, the belly, the back, and the chest.
Tamas, delusion, non-decay, the ultimate, death, illusion, fear, and old age;
[these are located] in the region of the anus, in the genitals, above, and likewise between the knees.
O child, one should place the Vāmadeva-kalā in thirteen locations: in the two calves, the two buttocks, the waist, and both sides.
Rajā, Rajā, Rati, Pālyā, Kāmyā, Tṛṣṇā, Mati, Kriyā, Dhṛti, Kāryā, Dhātrī, Brāhmaṇī, and likewise Mohinī. (8)
O child, one should indeed place the Sadyojāta-kalā in eight locations: in the two hands, the two feet, the nose, the head, and both arms.
O Guha, one should indeed place Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dhṛti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Svadhā, and Sthiti in the eight locations by means of the *sadya* [mantra] in their proper sequence.
These thirty-nine digits have indeed been extracted from among millions of digits;
at the time of initiation, the wise teacher should place them within the body of the disciple.
O child, by performing the fire-oblation according to the rules and indeed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the six paths,
one certainly attains liberation as well as success in this world.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, the Kalādhvapaṭala, in the venerable Kālottara.
Śrī.
Īśvara said:
I shall now proclaim, in due order, the ritual procedure for the Rudrākṣa,
beginning from the one-faced variety up to the sixteen-faced.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras—
the four castes [attain] success through the Rudrākṣa according to their respective classes.
A Brāhmaṇa should wear white, while a Kṣatriya should wear red;
a Vaiśya should wear yellow, and a Śūdra should wear black. || 3 ||
Copper-colored, glossy, firm, thick, and with well-developed tips are auspicious;
however, those bitten by insects, cut, split, or pierced by thorns are inauspicious.
(191) Pradhāna is indeed Rudrākṣa itself, which has its opening facing forward;
one should avoid that which has its opening reversed and likewise that which faces downward. || 5 ||
O child, a man should wear a rudrākṣa free from the six defects—
whether it be one, two, three, or even four [of them].
Five, six, seven, or eight, or the ninth, or even the tenth;
or the twelfth, or the sixteenth, or twenty, or twenty-five. (7)
Or thirty, or thirty-three, or likewise thirty-eight; or indeed forty, my dear, fifty, and even sixty. (8)
One may wear seventy, eighty, ninety, or one hundred and eight;
or two hundred, five hundred, or even a thousand [beads]. || 9 ||
A person who wears a rudrākṣa on the hand, the head,
and the neck is honored in the world of Rudra for thousands of crores of kalpas.
This fruit is proclaimed to be obtained by means of three rudrākṣas alone;
it should be known that the fruit of a thousandfold [merit] arises from wearing a thousand rudrākṣas.
In brief, each single [bead] should be known to yield the fruit of giving one cow;
that Rudra becomes [one's own] through the gift of rudrākṣas—what wonder is there in this? (12)
Rudra transfers that [power] onto the earth along with the garland into his hand;
having initiated him according to the prescribed rite, he should subsequently wear it while reciting the mantra. || 13 ||
It should be worn on the head with Īśāna, and on the neck with Tatpuruṣa;
it should be worn on the throat with Aghora, and one should wear it on the heart with Aghora.
One should hold [the rosary] in the hand with the Aghora mantra and the primary seed-syllables;
and with the mantra "Vyomavyāpin," one should hold fifty beads of the garland.
The wise man should wear five, three, or seven rosaries with the *pañcabrahma* mantra;
likewise, he should wear seven rudrākṣa beads with the *prāsāda* mantra alone. (16)
O child, indeed, the hand-garland, the head-garland, and the neck-garland—all of these Rudrākṣas [should be worn] in the temple, and certainly not with a mantra. 17.
The recitation of all Śiva-mantras with rudrākṣa beads becomes [efficacious];
it should be known that with leaf-lamps the merit is a hundredfold, while with lotus seeds it is a thousandfold.
One shall obtain ten thousandfold fruit by means of jewels, pearls, and coral;
likewise with red sandalwood, palāśa wood, white sandalwood, and dāru wood. || 19 ||
With a *vyāghāta* seed and a *kuśa*-grass knot, there would be thirty thousand fruits; with forty copper beads and fifty silver beads, [the same result is obtained]. (20)
A hundred thousand with golden beads is said to be equal to ten million rudrākṣas;
however, O child, if one recites while using a finger, one shall incur poverty and disease.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform recitation (japa) using rudrākṣas;
in brief, one should perform the recitation while circumambulating Mount Meru.
One should indeed fashion a rosary consisting of thirty-seven beads, or fifty-four,
or even one hundred and eight.
The thumb and the ring finger bring success in this world and the next;
for all acts of subjugation, one should indeed recite with the thumb and the middle finger. (24)
One should indeed recite [the mantra] with the thumb and index finger for rites such as summoning;
with the union of the little finger and the thumb, one performs the rites of causing hatred, eradication, and killing. (25)
A wise person should always recite [the mantra] using the thumb and the ring finger;
thus one shall obtain dharma, wealth, desire, and liberation, as well as riches and sons. || 26 ||
Wealth, grain, gold, and the means such as cows and buffaloes;
female and male slaves, oxen, land, clothing, and a wife. (27)
The thumb and the ring finger alone bestow the fruit of all desires;
O child, one should avoid all recitation performed without a rosary.
Therefore, with every effort, one should begin the recitation (*japa*) with rudrākṣas.
A single-faced rudrākṣa is the supreme Brahman, Śiva himself. (29)
O child, a two-faced rudrākṣa is Ardhanārīśvara;
O six-faced one, the three-faced has Agni as its deity and belongs to Maheśa.
O Six-faced One, know that the four-faced rudrākṣa has the four-faced one as its presiding deity; it is Sadāśiva himself, the Grandfather (Brahmā). 31.
The five-faced blue rudrākṣa is undoubtedly Rudra;
however, O child, some wise ones say it is Nārāyaṇa.
O Six-faced One, you indeed are the six-faced rudrākṣa;
and the seven-faced rudrākṣa is the thousand-rayed sun.
One shall obtain great joy from the group of the Seven Mothers, and one shall attain the great joy of the eight universal monarchs (cakravartins). || 34 ||
O Six-faced One, the nine-faced rudrākṣa has the form of Umā;
the eight-faced rudrākṣa is Umeśa—of this there is no doubt. (35)
With the nine powers beginning with Vāmā—Dharaṇī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Aṣṭā, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and likewise Śacī. || 36 ||
O child, one should wear the nine-faced [rudrākṣa], and one shall obtain the affection of all;
however, the ten-faced rudrākṣa is undoubtedly the form of Yama.
One attains the delight of the ten directions; there is no doubt in this matter.
O child, the eleven-faced Rudrākṣa has Indra as its presiding deity. (38)
The propitiation of the eleven Rudras increases the pleasure of Sadāśiva;
the twelve-faced rudrākṣa is the very form of Mahāviṣṇu. (39)
The propitiation of the twelve Ādityas always increases good fortune;
a man attains union with Viṣṇu and obtains this desire.
Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha;
then the forms beginning with Matsya and Kūrma, and the twelve beginning with Keśava. (41)
May all, being filled with joy, bestow prosperity, longevity, and strength; O Six-faced One, [I salute] the one with thirteen mouths, the eye, and the one who takes any form at will.
A man attains constant satisfaction from the hundred Rudras and obtains his desired object;
he beholds the fourteenth face and the eye of Rudra, which is very difficult to attain. (43)
The form [of the deity] consists of the two Aśvins and likewise the eight Vasus;
O child, it removes all diseases, and one shall always attain good health.
The rudrākṣa with fifteen faces is indeed very difficult to obtain;
it is truly the manifest form of the Moon and the form of Varuṇa, without a doubt. (45)
Kubera, the giver of wealth, the Yakṣa Jambhala, Maṇibhadra, the Gandharvas, Apsarases, Nāgas, Cāraṇas, Siddhas, and Kinnaras. || 46 ||
All shall be eternally endowed with joy through the retention of the Rudralocana;
indeed, this is the deception of Time and the destruction of untimely death.
Poisons, planetary spirits, piśācas, and all classes of bhūtas and vetālas are eternally destroyed by the wearing of rudrākṣas; it is the destroyer of all calamities. (48)
The sixteen-faced rudrākṣa contains Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha (Brahmā), as well as the thirty-three deities; they attain delight through its wearing. (49)
Wealth, longevity, fame, valor, and incomparable power shall be attained;
as well as diamonds, emeralds, lapis lazuli, and coral. (50)
The fifth is to be known as pearl; these are proclaimed as the five jewels.
Together with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, one should wear them, for they destroy poison.
One should immediately wear the Rudranetra [amulet] with the five jewels;
it [protects against] fevers, planetary seizures, piśācas, urinary disorders, leprosy, and diseases of the female organs.
Indeed, by wearing it, Kumāragraha and Apasmāra are surely destroyed;
for the twice-born, a Rudrākṣa bead should be covered with the sacred thread (upavīta).
One should fasten [the gems] upon the crown, the earrings, the ear-ornaments, and the necklaces; likewise upon the armlets, the bracelets, and the waist-band.
A man should always wear the rudrākṣa when his heroism has been severed;
it destroys untimely death and increases longevity and fame. (55)
One should wear it at the time of sacrifice and during the study of the Vedas;
however, for Brahmins, one should wear it at all times, conjoined with mantras.
During the time of battle, when kings behold their elephants and storehouses, they should always wear a rudrākṣa; thus they shall ever attain victory. || 57 ||
At the time of agriculture, at the time of trade, and upon seeing cattle, a Vaiśya indeed should wear the rudrākṣa, for it is highly recommended for him. || 58 ||
Having performed the ritual bath, one should wear it for Śūdras and those who have been initiated;
and during the time of agriculture, one should wear it while performing service for the three [higher] castes.
Rudralocana destroys poisons, fevers, and planetary seizures;
one should perform the fire-oblation with the principal seed-mantra using Takṣaka and artisans for the sake of [neutralizing] touch. (60)
Having washed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should purify it with the Pañcabrahma mantras;
one should then cleanse it with the Vyomavyāpin mantras and with the Prāsāda mantra.
Furthermore, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed again according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures;
thereafter, one should wear a rudrākṣa bead with three faces or four faces.
One should wear [the image] with five faces, or six, or seven, eight, or nine, endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics; or one may wear even a single [face]. || 63 ||
He is glorified in the world of Śiva for thousands of millions of aeons;
indeed, whatever movement he makes with the rosary is all truly japa.
Whether it be trade, agriculture, or even service to the king, O Six-faced One, as long as one moves the rosary, that shall be considered japa. (65)
By reciting the mantras beginning with the seed-syllable (bīja), the merit becomes ten million-fold;
and by reciting the five Brahmans with the [rudrākṣa] beads, the merit becomes a hundred thousand times ten million-fold.
Rites for subjugation and attraction, as well as those for pacification and nourishment, are accomplished immediately when the recitation is performed with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads. (67)
One should wear Rudrākṣa for women who have received initiation while still bound to worldly existence;
however, O child, one should avoid the Rudrākṣa during periods of impurity following death or birth.
One should also dismiss [the guest] after touching a woman in her menses or a Caṇḍāla;
one should always avoid sexual intercourse [with such a person], and having bathed, one should indeed wear [the sacred thread]. 69.
One should diligently avoid fish, meat, garlic, kataka, and śigru, as well as śleṣmātaka and vaka.
While wearing a rudrākṣa with great care, one must not consume [forbidden food] during an eclipse,
at the equinox, at the solstice, or even at the transition of the sun into a new zodiac sign. (71)
On the new moon and full moon days, on the days of the Puṣya asterism, at the time of worship and fire-offerings, and likewise on one's own birthday; || 72 ||
"One should wear the rudrākṣa constantly; thus all sins shall be destroyed.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, the "Ritual for Wearing Rudrākṣas," in the *Kālottara-tantra*, the compendium of thirty thousand verses. 35.
Prosperity!
Īśvara said: O Ṣaṇmukha, listen now as I describe the vow of the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī),
which removes all sins and bestows supreme accomplishment upon all.
It bestows long life and health, as well as wealth, grain, and happiness; it destroys the influence of planets and spirits, and eradicates fever, leprosy, and other ailments. || 2 ||
Twelve names, twelve months, twelve mantras, twelve perfumes;
twelve flowers, twelve incenses, twelve lamps, and twelve water-offerings. || 3 ||
There should be twelve items of food, twelve items of eatables, and twelve pieces of wood suitable for the ritual;
there should be twelve oblations and twelve Brahmins, who are endowed with initiation and possessed of the auspicious marks. || 4 ||
Twelve cows, twelve images, twelve vessels fit for eating, twelve staffs, twelve whisks, twelve pairs, and twelve fine [articles]. (5)
A twelve-threaded [sacred thread], a twelvefold vehicle, twelve seals as finger-rings;
a pair of sandals of twelve pieces of wood, milk-rice, and food with ghee. || 6 ||
(198) Thus, the auspicious vow of Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī consists of seven and twelve [days]. O Ṣaṇmukha, listen now to the explanation of this sūtra according to its true meaning.
Śaṅkara, likewise Śambhu, and Maheśvara as the third;
Mahādeva, Sthāṇu, Śiva, Paśupati, and Ugra.
Śarva, Tryambaka, Hara, and likewise Rudra—these are the twelve names corresponding to the twelve months by name. (9)
The Dvādaśavrata is said to be observed with diligence on the eighth day of the dark fortnight during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa,
Puṣya, Māgha, Phālguna, and Caitra.
Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, the month of Bhādra, Āśvina, Kārttika, and likewise [Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, Māgha, Phālguna]; these are declared to be the twelve months. (11)
The seed-syllable beginning with various letters, joined with Māyā and Anala, topped with a Bindu, and united with Prāsāda. || 12 ||
The seed-syllables are twelve, and the dust-particles are eight;
the mantras are said to be twelve, as proclaimed by Śiva in the past. (13)
I shall describe twelve fragrances; one should diligently prepare them for Śiva: sandalwood, saffron, jasmine, and *takkola*. (14)
Pūtikeśa, and Kuṣṭha—these are proclaimed as the twelve perfumes. || 15 ||
The lotus, the bilva leaf, the blue water-lily, the vakula, the pāṭalī, the karavīra, the nandikāvarta, the śoka, and the vyāhata [flower]. || 16 ||
Śvetārka, karṇikāra, and dhurdhūra shall be the twelfth;
along with kunda, kuṣṭha, sarjarasa, lopya, candana, and vānara.
(199) Khaḍga, Śuddhigandharasa, Kāśmīra, Candravālaka, and Kṛṇi—these they call the twelve [types of incense], O Six-faced One; they are suitable for burning. 18.
Combined with maṇḍīgula, on each eighth day of the month,
one should offer triphalā, the three types of jāti, rhinoceros horn, iron, and sandalwood.
Alternatively, one may use uśīra or kuñjara; the wick for the lamp should be twelve [finger-breadths long].
One should employ either the ghee of a tawny cow or the ghee of a goat.
Gandhaśāli, mahāśāli, and likewise raktaśāli; kalama-rice, śāli, nīvāra, wheat, and barley—these belong to Viṣṇu.
Rice, millet, and mung beans are proclaimed as the twelfth;
likewise, kusha grass, rice grains, flowers, fragrance, milk, and mustard seeds. || 22 ||
One should indeed join each of these with *gandhaśāli* rice;
starting from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should offer twelve such oblations (*arghya*).
Cow’s ghee, cow’s urine, cow’s milk, and sesame seeds;
likewise, kuśa-water, a cow’s horn, and water from a cow’s horn. || 24 ||
One should consume bilva leaves, cow dung, rice-water,
and cow's curd as the twelfth item, eating them in this very sequence.
Śāli, nīvāra, wheat, barley, vaṇava, and śyāmaka;
likewise ratnaśāli, mahāśāli, and kalama-śāli. || 26 ||
There should be sixty *priyaṅgu* grains and twelve *rājana* seeds; three *kuḍava*s of food and one *āḍhaka* of the second [ingredient]. (27)
Combined with plantain pieces and mixed with ghee from a tawny cow,
one *kuḍuba* of ghee is prescribed, and half of that amount is said to be sugar.
One should know that three plantain fruits and a *prastha* of curd are to be offered;
month after month, the preceptor should present them while reciting the respective mantra. (29)
O Six-faced One, at the conclusion of the worship, one should consume [the offerings] with their respective mantras:
bilva-water, śāmī, bilva, sandalwood, and kadamba.
The Vaṭa, Nāga, Śākavarī, Vakula, Khadira, Aja, Kapittha, and Mahīdantaka are the tooth-sticks for the twelve months here. (31)
Śiva performs the Sadāśiva-homa, Maheśvara performs the Rudra-homa, and the Vidyeśvaras perform the Aṣṭa-homa; thus the twelvefold Homa is proclaimed.
Palāśa, aśvattha, plakṣa, and nyagrodha;
bilva, udumbara, śamī, and those made of vaikaṅkata wood. || 33 ||
Apāmārga, Vakula, and Pāśa—these twelve [plants] should be offered;
one by one, separately, month after month. || 34 ||
When the eighth day is completed, the preceptor should perform the Śiva-homa with twelve of the best of the twice-born; for them, however, it shall be twofold.

One should place a single *praṇītā* water-pot in the northeast, between the fire and the northeast; at the conclusion of the *homa*, one should perform a ritual bath on the twelfth, eighth, and [other auspicious] lunar days.
At the conclusion of the bath, one should perform the consumption [of offerings] with ghee and other substances;
[one should worship] the Prāsāda mantra, which is endowed with the principal seed-syllable, using the Vāma mantra. (37)
The wise man should offer oblations separately with the purifiers for twelve months:
sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame, śāli rice, and all [other] grains.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations for each [deity] by those who have mastered the Vedas;
one should manifest [the rite] with the primary seed-syllables using the mantra named after the temple.
When the vow is completed, on the eighth day, the wise man should perform one thousand oblations for each [deity] individually; first, he should worship the officiating priests separately. (40)
A pair of garments, a sacred thread, a vessel for food, as well as a golden ring, an umbrella, and sandals. (41)
A pair of sandals, a Vaiṣṇava breastplate, a staff, a turban, a shield, and a sacrificial fee according to one's ability. || 42 ||
One should properly honor the teacher with crowns, garments, and earrings;
with armlets, sacred threads, bracelets, and waist-bands.
One should worship with objects such as cows, land, gold, and male and female servants;
and with milk-rice mixed with ghee and completely drenched in ghee. (44)
For Śiva, [one should offer] a black-brown cow, a red one, white ones, and tawny ones;
as well as a turmeric-colored one, a fire-colored one, and a very beautiful yellow-colored one. (45)
A cow with the luster of gold from the Ma-yuga, one that is greenish-yellow and beautiful, one resembling a vessel of refined gold, and one that is tawny—these twelve [gifts] are for Śiva. (46)
O Six-faced One, at the conclusion of the vow, a great bath with ghee should be performed;
a great worship must be conducted, and one should likewise offer oblations into the fire for Brahmā.
In that great [temple], the wise man should cause a festival to be performed for seven days or even three days, beginning with the Sārvavantiya rite.
Having placed the Lord of Gods upon the chariot, he should then perform a circumambulation [of the city],
which is filled with various districts and adorned with various parasols.
Whether it be a village, a city, a town, or a hamlet, it should be provided with various banners and adorned with various crests. (50)
One should perform the circumambulation slowly and cause the opening to be provided everywhere.
One should have Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, together with his son Soma, carried in a chariot. || 51 ||
Or one may indeed fashion a blue image mounted upon an elephant;
and there should be a vessel of one *droṇa* capacity filled with boiled rice mixed with parched grain flour.
Or half of that amount, the preceptor should cause the offering to be given according to the directions;
he should cast it at a crossroads, a triple-path, a double-path, and a single-path.
Having thus performed the festival for seven days,
one should perform the ritual bathing with one hundred and eight or eighty-one jars.
O Guha, one should cause the ceremonial bath to be performed with sixty-four jars, or even with thirty-three, or with twenty-five, or with sixteen.
And in this manner, one should especially perform the ritual bath of the five rivers;
having prepared the powder... || 56 ||
The materials for the great consecration (mahābhiṣeka) are indeed those previously mentioned: made of gold, silver, or copper, or of highly beautiful earthenware. || 57 ||
Or, O Guha, one should have the bathing performed with those substances or with white jars;
afterwards, one should perform the concluding bath (avabhṛtha), especially a bath in a river.
Having first performed the powder-bath (cūrṇasnāna), one should then perform the river-bath;
listen now to the meritorious fruit of him who observes this vow with devotion on the eighth day of the dark fortnight. || 59 ||
The killer of a cow, the ungrateful person, the slayer of a Brahmin, the violator of the Guru’s bed, the murderer of one who has sought refuge, and the betrayer of trust in a mixed company; || 60 ||
Even for a killer of a father, a killer of a mother, a killer of a son, or likewise a killer of a brother,
there shall be the destruction of all sins through the vow of Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī alone.
A hundred Rājasūya sacrifices and a hundred Aśvamedhas would be equal to one Arbuda, an Aptoryāma,
an Agni-kharva, or a Vājapeya sacrifice. (62)
The Atirātra yields the fruit of a Kharva, as does the Ṣoḍaśin and the Vṛnda;
the Ukthya yields the fruit of a Prayuta, and the Agniṣṭoma likewise yields the fruit of a Niyuta. || 63 ||
Ten million Agniṣṭoma sacrifices, a hundred million Sautrāmaṇī sacrifices,
and a hundred thousand Śrī-yāgas shall yield the fruit of ten million Śyena sacrifices.
By observing each eighth day of the month (Kālāṣṭamī) month after month, one obtains the fruit of all these sacrifices; indeed, the fruit of the Agnicit sacrifice is attained a hundredfold.
A person obtains the fruit of the installation of a thousand liṅgas by performing [this rite] on the eighth day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇāṣṭamī), which is the most meritorious of all ritual acts.
All obtain heaven through leaves, flowers, and fruits;
he himself attains union [with the Divine], and there is no returning for him again to this world of destruction.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter [of the Śrī Kālottara], concerning the fruit of the vow of the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
Prosperity!
Īśvara said:
This supreme secret must not be given to an atheist, nor even to a beloved who is not so;
it should be given to a devotee of Śiva, as was declared by Śiva in the past.
Water that is resorted to by sages who know the truth of the scriptures, who are devoted to austerity, and whose senses are conquered, as well as by the gods— that on earth is called a *tīrtha*.
The places of descent of Rudra, the self-manifested ones (svayambhū), and the sacred fields (kṣetrapāṇi)—for all embodied beings who die in those sacred fields of Śiva, [there is liberation]. || 3 ||
And on the earthly realm, O Mahāsena, the station of the Self-Existent (Svayaṃbhū) yields great fruit; it is a place for worship, recitation, meditation, and indeed for attaining samādhi. (4)
One obtains inexhaustible fruit and, upon death, attains union [with the Divine].
I shall now describe the sixty-eight great sacred sites; listen.
Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Avimukta, Bahābala, Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, and the exceedingly radiant Suvarṇākṣa; || 6 ||
And Sthaṇvīśvara, renowned and celebrated throughout the three worlds—
this should be known as the eightfold station (sthānāṣṭaka), the field of Rudra (rudrakṣetra) of great prosperity.
From Vastrāpada to Sthāṇu, these places grant union with Rudra;
as well as Kala, Dviraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, and Maṇḍaleśvara.
Kālāñjana, Śaṅkukarṇa, and the one known as Sthūleśvara,
as well as Aṭṭahāsa— these are to be understood as the proclaimed group of eight purifiers.
With every effort they go to the supreme state of Śiva;
likewise, Kurukṣetra is indeed Nākhalo and Nakhalas.
Vimaleśvara, Prabhāsa, Māhendra, and Bhīma— this is the group of eight known as the Guhyāṣṭaka, which liberates one from all sins.
Having gone to Śrīparvata, Hariścandra, and likewise Mahākālavana, a glorious man attains the abode of Śiva.
Amṛtādikeśvara, Kedāra, Bhairava, Vāraṇāsī, and Vaidyanātha is proclaimed as the eighth. (13)
O Six-faced One, having crossed over all his ancestors by means of these secrets— the secret of the self-existent state— one attains the great abode of Śiva.
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Naimiśa, and likewise Puṣkara;
Āṣāḍhī, Daṇḍimuṇḍī, Bhārabhūti, and Lakulīśvara. (15)
In this world, one's own inner self is the true field that brings about union with Śiva;
[so too are] Kailāsa, Mandara, Meru, and the Nīla mountain.
Himavān, the Hiṣaya, Vindhya, and Malaya shall be the eighth;
these eight mountains indeed constitute the self-existent abode of Śiva.
Indeed, by means of the body through fasting at Vīrajñayā, one attains Śiva himself;
while at Virajā, Varuṇā, and Gollā, one conquers Koṭivarṣa.
Jālandhra, Kāśmīra, and likewise Devadāruvana—
this is the pure group of eight sacred fields (kṣetra) that brings about union with Śiva.
Māyāpurī, Merudhī, Bhūteśvara, Vaṭeśvara, Māheśvarī, Māhiricchata, and Puṇḍravardhana.
Devikoṣṭha is to be known as a highly prosperous field of accomplishment;
there, for embodied beings, the group of five [elements] becomes auspicious, bringing about union with Śiva.
Ilā, Uttarameru, Bhadrāśva, and Ketumāla—these four incomparable great fields are very difficult to attain. (22)
The sixty-eight great fields are established as the abodes of the Self-born (Svayambhū).
Whatever [practice] there is—be it the meditation on darkness, recitation, giving, or the worship of the gods—[is performed there]. (23)
A human being attains liberation and there is no destruction;
likewise, [the merit of building] a temple, a water-shed, an assembly hall, and a monastery. (24)
One shall obtain inexhaustible fruit from [the gift of] ponds, wells, and tanks;
likewise, the gift of a cow, the gift of an elephant, the gift of a daughter, and gold. (25)
O Six-faced One, the gift of a village, the gift of a house, the gift of land,
the gift of a maidservant, the gift of a chariot, and likewise the gift of knowledge; || 26 ||
The gift of a horse, the gift of food, and likewise the gift of water; the gift of a shelter and the gift of sacred knowledge—these are the sixteen. (27)
To a Brāhmaṇa who is poor, who has performed Soma sacrifices and penance, who is a devotee of Śiva, who is peaceful, and who always avoids the food of Śūdras; (28)
In the field of Svayambhū, gifts should be given during the equinoxes, eclipses, and other such occasions;
the fruit for the donor becomes infinite, as is wonderful according to the sequence.
To one devoted to Śiva, who is peaceful, who has many sons,
who is solely a learned Vedic scholar, who is poor, and who is an ascetic maintaining the sacred fires.
Having prepared a beautiful house along with household furnishings,
and having filled it with abundant wealth and grain, he offered the vessels used for eating to Śiva.
There were pestles and mortars, as well as female and male servants;
there were cooking pots, water vessels, ladles, and drinking cups.
The vessel for cooking, the bowl, the bed, the wooden seat, the pillow, the woolen blanket, and the outer rug; || 33 ||
Incense, lamps, vessels, winnowing baskets, and even leather bags; spittoons, betel-rolls, and indeed containers for holding [substances]. || 34 ||
A water-jar made of copper, vessels for pouring water, a *karaka* vessel, a *kamaṇḍalu*, a trident, and various water-pots. || 35 ||
O Guha, on the day of your birth, having prepared all these ornaments according to your means— namely, earrings and necklaces— [you should offer them].

Whether one gives [gifts] for the sake of propitiating auspicious planets and so forth, or during eclipses and other such occasions— I am not able to describe the fruit of that, even with hundreds of verses. (37)
This much can be said, O observer of noble vows:
he too obtains the entire fruit of the sacrifice; there is no doubt in this matter. (38)
O child, one obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and even a hundred foundations; there is no doubt that this is indeed an auspicious planet. (39)
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, concerning the sixty-eight locations, in the Kālottara.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the rules for expiation; listen.
Whether it be broken, cracked, or even passed down through generations, || 1 ||
Having removed that which is deformed, burnt by fire, fallen, or uprooted,
one should install another and arrange it as before.
Having likewise performed the expiation (prāyaścitta) as well as the Lakṣahoma sacrifice,
[he should perform it] thirty-two times, half of that, eight times, and four times.
The wise practitioner should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) accompanied by the Indu-kuṇḍa,
and he should carry out the ritual of great worship (mahāpūjā) with thousands of water-pots (kalaśas).
Thereafter, the artisan should fashion a small liṅga;
the new work should be performed according to the previously stated sequence.
When a temple has been constructed by a minister or a servant using worn-out materials,
the consecration of the Lord should be performed with oblations offered while reciting the appropriate mantras.
The *niṣkala* and *niṣkalārdha* [mantras] are to be established again as before. However,
when the pedestal is completely worn out, one should offer oblations of ghee with the *śakti-mantra*.
A hundred thousand oblations (lakṣāhuti) constitute the Śakti; for Sadyojāta, however, it is one thousand;
for Ananteśa, one thousand is prescribed, and for each [of the others], it is said to be tripled.
There shall be five hundred oblations for the gods beginning with the World-Protectors (Lokapālas),
and ten oblations for each of the eighteen classes [of spirits].
The artisan shall install the deity upon the *liṅga* according to the procedure taught in the *tantra*;
furthermore, the rite of consecration (*saṃskārakarma*) is to be performed by the artisan as previously prescribed.
Now hear this very manifest sign regarding those who have been consecrated;
and hear the rule for expiation concerning the place of the *baliliṅga*.
With a thousand oblations of ghee, reciting the mantra "Astrarāja" (King of Weapons). || 12 ||
The installation in the partless *liṅga* is performed with twenty-five *kumbhaka*s,
according to the procedure taught in the Tantra.
Whether in a village, a city, a hamlet, or even a town—in the designated area for those [rites]—if the wind [should blow] due to negligence; || 14 ||
That which is first is the fallen sequence; that is called meditation (dhyāna).
The offering of each respective mantra is excellent; it is called a thousand-fold oblation (sahasrāhuti).
One should offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire: one thousand for Ananteśa, one thousand for each of the Vidyeshas, and half of that number for the Astras.
Thereafter, the wise one, having performed the Vāstuhoma in due order as previously described, should do so even when [the site] has fallen into disrepair, restoring it to its proper state. || 17 ||
Having performed the bathing with a thousand jars at the base of the *liṅga* in the temple, and likewise in the eight directions, it is then called the "Eight Thousand" (*sahasrāṣṭama*). (18)
After the oblation has been performed, the wise one should conduct a festival;
having offered oblations in the eight directions, the eight-limbed mantra is recited.
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual of the Great Worship (mahāpūjāvidhi) and the festival in the sequence as before;
if [the deity] falls down beside the tutelary deity of the village, it should be worshipped there.
And seeing [the deity] nearby, which causes fear through royal agitation,
one should likewise perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) with the Bahurūpa mantra.
Afterwards, one should make the remainder equal and worship with the fallen [image];
having worshipped the original image again, the procedure is as previously stated.

If, however, it is deficient in a secondary limb (pratyaṅga), one should offer oblations of ghee with the mantras of the [primary] limbs in sequence, a thousand times; then, the remainder of that [rite] should be performed in the same order as before.
Thus, when performed according to the proper sequence, otherwise there arises a fault:
fear of royal upheaval and the kingdom, along with its ruler, becomes utterly distressed. (24)
Therefore, with every effort, the Guru should perform the rite of atonement;
now hear the rule for atonement when the fire-ritual has been omitted.

If, however, through negligence, [the site] is strewn with fire, one should perform [penance] for one day and so forth according to the years [elapsed]. For a single day's offense involving fire-seeds, one should recite the Aghora-weapon mantra a hundred times.
One should perform the bathing of Maheśvara with twenty-five jars;
thereafter, one should regularly commence the rekindling of the fire.
If, however, the fire-rite (agnikārya) has been omitted, there shall be an oblation of the Śiva-mantra;
having offered a thousand oblations of clarified butter, one should thereafter commence the daily rite.

One should perform this rite again in such a manner; it is recommended until the end of the period. However, if the fire has been extinguished within ten days, one may perform it for one day or more, up to a year.
On a single day, one should recite the Aghora-weapon mantra, which is the seed-syllable of fire, one hundred times;
then one should perform the bath for Maheśvara using twenty-five jars.
Furthermore, one should always begin the rekindling of the fire afterwards;
for if the fire-rite is omitted, it becomes an oblation to Śiva-mantras.
Having offered a thousand oblations of ghee, one should thereafter commence the daily rite;
one should perform this procedure again, which is recommended for a period of five days.
If the fire has been extinguished within ten days, it should be restored as before but doubled;
however, if it has been absent for half a month, one must perform the fire-ritual every day.
Having offered a thousand oblations of clarified butter, one should perform a bath with eight hundred jars of water,
as well as the re-consecration of the fire and the daily ritual procedure.
If the seat is devoid of fire, one should perform three thousand oblations of ghee;
thereafter, one should perform twenty oblations according to the sequence prescribed in the Tantra as before.
Thereafter, one should perform the investigation and the worship as previously described;
however, if the fire is absent, this should be done for six months with double the aforementioned effort.
Having commenced the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma), perform it according to the procedure prescribed in the Tantra;
likewise, for one year, one should offer ten lakhs of oblations into the fire.
For all [of these], one should proceed by doubling [the penance] for each subsequent [omission];
however, when the daily worship is omitted, one should perform the previously mentioned [penance] in due order.
If the worship should be devoid of mantras, one should perform the previously mentioned sequence in order;
however, listen now to the rule for expiation regarding that which is devoid of the daily festival. (39)
Every day, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance and offer eight hundred oblations of ghee;
furthermore, the wise man should perform a ritual bath with twenty-five water-jars.
Afterwards, having commenced the festival, one should assign the remaining auspicious days that bring about prosperity,
designating each day as a day that brings prosperity.
If the festive ablution (*utsavasnapana*) is omitted, one should perform a thousand oblations of clarified butter (*ghṛtāhuti*);
otherwise, the worship becomes deficient for that day, destroying a single junction (*sandhi*).
Having performed a thousand oblations of clarified butter, one should thereafter worship well. (43)
Likewise, there is an excellent expiation that brings about the increase of merit;
however, when an oblation of clarified butter is omitted, one must perform a thousand oblations of ghee.
Thereafter, the wise practitioner should begin the offering and perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
Even if lacking perfumes, clarified butter, and incense, one should nevertheless provide water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghyaka).
Having offered a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the Bahurūpa mantra and a hundred oblations with the Astra mantra, the substance is said to be complete.
During a festival or at the time of a procession, and even upon contact with artisans,
one should perform a thousand oblations with the Aghora weapon mantra.
If it is cracked, perforated, or worn out, it should be restored through the act of renovation;
one should offer three thousand oblations of clarified butter while reciting the heart-mantra.
In this way, one should duly perform the penance according to the sequence;
listen to the rule for the penance correctly performed by means of this procedure. (49)
(212) Upon touching a woman in her menses or a flower, one should avoid all ritual vessels;
likewise, one should perform a hundred-thousand-fold fire-oblation (lakṣahoma) with the Aghora weapon mantra.
If there is contact with those who deal in the dead (Pretakas) or with those who cause harm, one should likewise perform a hundred thousand oblations;
thereafter, by means of the Prāṇa-rite, purification is highly commended.
When defiled by wicked men, the practitioner of the mantra should perform one hundred thousand oblations of ghee;
in the event of contact with a Caṇḍāla, he should perform it while avoiding all ritual vessels.
For attendants and other such men, it shall be extremely difficult in succession;
having performed the sprinkling with water, one should thereafter perform the worship of the deity in due order. (53)
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter on expiation in the Kālottara. 38.
Prosperity!
Īśvara said:
O Ṣaṇmukha, listen now to the procedure for the weighing on the scale;
it should be performed during the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day. || 1 ||
On the occasion of an eclipse, at the equinox, and likewise at the northern solstice,
as well as on your birthday in the month of Puṣya, perform here this Tulābhāra rite.
In the month of Māgha on one's own birth asterism, or in Phālguna on one's own birth [asterism];
or in Caitra on one's own birth asterism, or in Vaiśākha on one's own birth [asterism]. (3)
One should perform [the rite] on one's birthday in the month of Jyeṣṭha, or under the asterism Rohiṇī,
or under Hasta, Śravaṇa, or the three Uttaras.
One should perform it under the asterism of Revatī, or Mṛgaśīrṣa, or Vāyu, or Varuṇa,
or Uttaraproṣṭhapada, or it may take place under Bhādrapadā.
One should perform the yoga on a Thursday with the Puṣya asterism, or on a Wednesday with Anurādhā;
or one may perform it on a Saturday with Rohiṇī, or on a Monday with the asterism Mṛgaśiras. (6)
One should perform it under the hand of Āditya, or it may be under Śukra or Pauṣṇa;
or one should perform it under Bhauma or Aśvinī, or it may be under a favorable conjunction of the day (vārayoga). || 7 ||
One may perform it during the Vipula yoga or indeed during the Mahāyoga;
however, the wise know that at a solar eclipse, the Tulābhāra [weight] is most excellent.
But in the absence of such a planetary conjunction, it would be thus on one's own birthday;
furthermore, it may also occur on a Siddhi yoga day or on an equinox.
Furthermore, O Mahāsena, it may also occur during the northern course of the sun or during a conjunction of the planets; however, one should avoid performing it at night or during a lunar eclipse.
In the bright fortnight, during the forenoon, in the signs of Aquarius, Taurus, Gemini, or Cancer, the weighing on the scales is commended. (11)
Whether at Naimiṣa or Puṣkara, or at Kurukṣetra or Salopa,
or at Śāligrāma, Vaidyanātha, or Gaṅgādvāra— || 12 ||
And at Prayāga, or at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, or at Gokarṇa or Bhadrakarṇa, or likewise on Mount Mahendra or Śrīparvata; (13)
On the banks of the Sarayū and Sarasvatī, on the shores of the Sindhu and Gomatī,
at Śrīkoṭa on the Lord of Mountains (the Himalayas), at Kailāsa, and at the Himavat and Vindhya ranges.
It may be on the Sahya mountain, or on the Malaya mountain, or at Kanyātīrtha;
or at Rāmeśvara, at Setubandha, at Maṣṭra, and at Puruṣottama.
On the bank of a river flowing to the ocean, at the confluence of a river and the sea, in a sacred temple, or on the shore of a great lake. || 16 ||
Or, wherever one finds delight on the ground, there one should prepare a pit;
[using] sandalwood, *khadira*, *madhūka*, and *devadāru* wood. (17)
The *āsana*, the *bilva* tree, the *kadamba*, *arjuna*, and *sālaka*; and twenty-five more, namely the *nimba*, the *iśo*, and the *śoka*. (18)
They praise the *tinduka* wood for the beautiful pillar of the balance;
the pillar of the balance is prescribed to be eight cubits in measure. || 19 ||
A height of forty-six finger-breadths is prescribed for the pillar of the neck;
the wise man should cause it to be buried one and a half cubits deep in the ground.
The base alone should be constructed with a height of one cubit;
the peak above those two should be six cubits high and exceedingly beautiful.
The wise one should construct the pillar, equal in height from south to north, with a width of one prādeśa and a thickness of one vitasti.
The space above the three tiers is proclaimed to be the length of the balance-beam;
its circumference is thirty-six finger-breadths, well-proportioned, smooth, and excellent. (23)
One should bind it with iron at both the front and the middle;
for the letter *ba*, three [strokes] should be made, which one should extend firmly and correctly.
One should project this [vowel] of the letter *ba* into the middle of the northern middle;
likewise, the earring (*kuṇḍala*) of those two is correctly situated in the north itself.
O Six-faced One, that earring of Baka, which was firm and measured one finger-breadth in width, was fastened at its tip by four fingers; [he gave it] to Kṛṣṇa.
Having correctly formed the *kuṇḍala* (the circular loop), the wise man, having properly bound the two *ba*-characters three times along with the *śa*, is indeed capable [of success]. || 27 ||
One should have the base and the support made of copper alone;
it should be five *prādeśas* in width, very firm, and circular. (28)
And four [fingers] joined together—the ring finger and the middle finger—each support is said to consist of exactly three hundred fruits. || 29 ||
The wise one should know that it should be three finger-breadths deep at the bottom and fashioned like a shallow bowl;
in this way, there shall be confidence in the balance, which is indeed auspicious for weighing heavy loads.
O Six-faced One, the knower of mantras should first cause the king— who is equipped with all weapons and adorned with all ornaments— to lie down, accompanied by the *prāsāda* mantra.
And on the western base, one should place gold there—
namely Jāmbūnada, Śātakumbha, and Rathakāñcana.
One should place within its own [image] the finest Jāmbūnada gold, the middling Śātakumbha gold, and gold consisting of Kāñcana. || 33 ||
When these two are properly balanced on a scale, one side may weigh ten niṣkas and the other one niṣka, yet the gold would be superior [in value]. || 34 ||
One hundred and more gold pieces shall constitute the best *tulābhāra*;
the middling is fifty more, and the lowest is ten *niṣkas*.
One should begin the fire-oblation with the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas;
however, the Bahvṛcas should perform the oblation specifically in the east and the southeast.
In the south and the southwest, one who knows the Yajurveda should begin the fire-oblation;
in the west and the northwest, one who chants the Sāmaveda should begin the fire-oblation. || 37 ||
The preceptor should perform the Atharva-veda oblation in the north and the northeast;
he should offer into the fire in the center and to the east of Dhanada.
One should first offer oblations from the Vedas and other scriptures; thereafter, one should offer the Puruṣasūkta, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Rudrasūkta, and the Brahmajajñāna hymn. (39)
And Aruṇa, Mahāvallī, Tvarita, and likewise Rudra;
Triyambaka, Haṃsaśuci, Tripada, and Jātavedasa—(40).
One should perform the oblations with the Daśahotṛ, the Saptahotṛ, and the Caturhotṛ;
likewise, one should chant the Brahmasāman, the Jyeṣṭhasāman, and the Bṛhat and Rathantara.
One should offer oblations to Vikarṇa, Mahāvrata, and Puruṣāṅga;
one should perform the Bahiḥpavamāna libation and offer oblations to the Viṣṇusāman.
The Rudrasāman, the Agnihoma, Indra, and indeed the Saumya;
Nārāyaṇa, the Brahmaśilā, and likewise the Atharvaśiras.
One should offer oblations to Caṇḍarudra, Nīlarudra, Brāhma, and indeed Candra;
likewise to Pippalāda, Bārhaspatya, Āṅgīrasa, Saura, and Vaiṣṇava. (44)
O child, for one of dull intellect, as well as for the sake of the supreme Brahman within,
one should offer the Vyāhṛtis a hundred times for all the officiating priests.

In that same manner, O Six-faced One, one should offer the Sāvitrī mantra with cow’s ghee eight thousand times for each, and likewise offer sacrificial fuel sticks separately eight thousand times for each.
Palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, plakṣa, and nyagrodha, as well as bilva, udumbara, śamī, and apāmārga are thus declared. (47)
One should maintain [the practice] for one thousand and eight repetitions each,
or for three thousand, or for five ghaṭikās, or for three ghaṭikās, or even for two ghaṭikās.
The king should maintain the recitation of the Prāsāda mantra for as long as the fire sacrifice (homa) continues, until the installation is completed.
At the beginning and at the end, there should be a declaration of an auspicious day accompanied by the study of the Vedas,
with abundant sounds of the Veda and shouts of victory from the Atharva-veda. (50)
With the sounds of conchs and trumpets, kettledrums, flutes, and clay drums;
with the voices of lutes and kinnaras, and the splendors of song, dance, and the like. || 51 ||
At the time of weighing the loads, one who is well-composed should cause all of these to be prepared:
sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, sesame seeds, rice, and mustard seeds.
One should offer a thousand each of wild rice, barley, and bamboo;
or one may give a thousand or half of that as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability. || 53 ||
All the substances, weighing a full load and including garments and ornaments,
[should be given] to Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, who are impoverished, and who are seekers of the sacred knowledge.
One should cause the great master Miśrabhūma to be given to the twice-born;
being peaceful, one should cause it to be given to the self-controlled according to their learning and practice.
There, O King, the monarch should indeed honor the officiating priests with other materials—
cows, land, gold, garments, and golden sacred threads.
One should worship the officiating priests individually with crowns, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, waist-bands, and many types of finger-rings.
One should cause ten times that amount to be given to the preceptor (deśika) preceded by the recitation of mantras;
one should also cause the materials used therein to be presented to the preceptor.
On that day, one should cause all kinds of food and grain to be prepared;
thus, according to the path prescribed in the scriptures, one should perform the Tulābhāra rite.
O Six-faced One, hear truly the entirety of his meritorious fruit: as many as are the hairs on his body, so much gold is the fruit [he receives]. (60)
For that many thousands of yugas, O dear one, he is glorified in the world of Śiva; for that long he shall dwell in the city of Rudra, and for that long in the city of Viṣṇu.
For that long, O dear one, shall he dwell in the city of Brahmā, for that long in the city of the Moon;
for that long shall the wise man dwell in heaven, surrounded by celestial women.
He attains this world and becomes a knower of the four Vedas;
he becomes one who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and is devoted to the essential principles of Yoga.
In a prosperous and noble family, he shall become a great lord of wealth;
through knowledge he attains dispassion, and through dispassion he attains yoga.
"Liberation shall come through the knowledge of yoga," so says the Veda;
indeed, O child, by means of the Tulābhāra [rite], one shall become happy in this world. (65)
Freed from all diseases and endowed with all sovereign powers, having conquered a hundred untimely deaths, he shall attain a long life. || 66 ||

The killer of a cow, the ungrateful person, the slayer of a fetus, the betrayer of a friend, the murderer of one who has sought refuge, the betrayer of a companion, and likewise the slayer of a mother; || 67 ||
One should destroy all that by means of a load of cotton; there is no doubt about this.
One should perform a bath with ghee for Śiva and likewise conduct a great worship.
On that day, one should perform the dressing of Keśava's hair, a grand worship with cow-products, and the worship of all the deities.
Having understood this correctly, one who is composed should display the balance and the load.
He is honored in the heavenly world for hundreds of thousands of years,
serving as an attendant at the Tulābhāra sacrifice, free from deceit and envy.
He is honored in the heavenly world for a hundred thousand years.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, the "Chapter on the Weight of the Balance," in the *Kālottara*. 39.
Śrīḥ!
Īśvara said:
O Ṣaṇmukha, listen briefly to the procedure for Hiraṇyagarbha;
by means of the Hiraṇyagarbha rite, those born from divine wombs [are purified]. || 1 ||
The forest that is the womb of Umā is the divine enclosure;
the seed-syllable of the vowel [A] with the mantra is declared to be the field of Umā (Umākṣetra). || 2 ||
Through Hiraṇyagarbha, the wise man shall attain immortality;
at the previously mentioned place and time, one should cause [the deity] to enter Hiraṇyagarbha. || 3 ||
Know that the gold from the Jāmbūnada river is the best, that from the Jātakaṃbha is middling, and ordinary gold is the lowest; a dīnāra is like [the value of] śātakumbha gold.
The golden [image] should have three hollows and be equal to Jāmbūnada gold;
indeed, O Six-faced One, the best [measure] consists of forty-six thousand [units].
One should begin the construction of the womb (the inner sanctum) with twenty-five thousand [bricks] for the middling size;
twelve thousand is declared to be the measure for the inferior Hiraṇyagarbha.
One should have the lower vessel made full with eighteen thousand [units],
and one should have the upper vessel made with twenty-eight thousand.
They say that [a vessel] with ten thousand [units] is the best; now the middling is being described. One should have a lower receptacle made for the middling womb with ten thousand [units].
With fifteen [units] for the wise one and a thousand for the vessel turned upwards, they call this the "middle embryo," as declared by Śiva. (9)
One who has reached the further shore should have the lower bowl made with five thousand [units],
and having properly fashioned the upper bowl with seven thousand, O Six-faced One. (10)
One should have the lower vessel made in the form of Umā; it should be two-armed, full, moon-faced, with two eyes and beautiful glances. (11)
One should fashion her with full breasts, a deep navel, a slender waist, and beautiful arms; with broad hips, a shell-like neck, and lovely eyebrows.
Her thighs should be like the trunk of a plantain tree, and her shanks like the shafts of arrows;
she is endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament. (13)
Thus, one should place the form of the vessel at the bottom; however, in the upper vessel, one should place Keśava, who has four arms, two eyes, and holds a conch, a discus, and a mace.
The supreme god, endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with every ornament, wearing a fresh garland, and bearing the Śārṅga bow as his weapon.
The god has lotus-eyes, a lotus-face, and lotus-hands and feet;
he wears yellow garments and is adorned with necklaces and armlets.
With a well-concentrated mind, one should have Nārāyaṇa fashioned in the upper vessel, and Mahālakṣmī, radiant as the filaments of a lotus, in the lower vessel. (17)
Endowed with all the primary marks, adorned with every ornament, possessing the luster of beautiful gold, and having hands like lotus sprouts. (18)
She wears dark blue garments, is serene, two-eyed, and two-armed; she is auspicious, with full, elevated breasts, radiant white in complexion, and adorned with two earrings.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, girdles, and anklets that beautified her feet;
with hair-ends that were neither thin nor greasy, and a face slightly smiling. || 20 ||
O Six-faced One, one should fashion the form of Śrī in this manner upon the lower vessel;
alternatively, one should have the form of a lion or Hiraṇyagarbha made. (21)
Then, one should fashion the form of the rain-god as having the shape of a cow or even the shape of an elephant; he should enter into Hiraṇyagarbha.
Alternatively, one should have the universal form of heaven and earth fashioned as the very form of Brahmā and the form of Sāvitrī. || 23 ||
One should perform [the rite] on one's birth star, or again during a Siddha yoga, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, or at the solstices or equinoxes. || 24 ||
One should enter the Hiraṇyagarbha [liṅga] and fill it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
one should fashion the Hiraṇyagarbha to be merely the height of a seated person. || 25 ||
The height should be greater than its own width by one finger-breadth (aṅgula), or six finger-breadths;
alternatively, one may make it the width of a span (prādeśa) or even greater than a palm (tāla).
O Six-faced One, one who is expert in the science of the womb (garbha-śāstra) should make the lower vessel according to its prescribed measure,
and the upper vessel should be made larger than this by the same amount.
In all cases, the two vessels should indeed be more than a span [in size];
one should comfortably place the feet and hands so that they do not touch the fire.
Having properly filled it with five elephants provided with fragrant flowers and endowed with the correct proportions, using the mantra "brahmajajñāna," || 29 ||
Having entered with the Viṣṇu-mantra, the Vedic priests should perform the *garbhādhāna* rite;
indeed, one should offer the *garbhādhāna* oblation for the sake of producing ten sons in her.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra "prājāpatyena"; according to Prajāpati's opinion, this is done with the mantras "prajāvat" and "jīvaputra. || 31 ||

(222) One should offer the remainder as an oblation with clarified butter into the right nostril of the vital breath using a single leaf-cup of the *ajitā* herb; one should, however, prepare the fuel from *pālāśa* wood. || 32 ||

In this manner, the rite for ensuring the birth of a male child (puṃsuvana) should be performed; one should offer oblations with the Vyāhṛtis during the parting of the hair (sīmanta), using twenty-one blades of kuśa grass, śamī wood, and fruits of the udumbara tree.
The wise man should join [the rites] with the Sāvitrī, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Praṇava at the beginning.
Dhātā is the second; "rākāmahaṃ" is the second [verse] of Prajāpati.
One should recite the Sīmanta-rite to the deity; now hear the Jātakarman that follows.
"To Dhṛti, I give honey with ghee"—thus [he says], and it is ghee and honey. || 35 ||
Saying "May it be for her," he should touch the second part of the vessel;
with those mantras, O child, he should perform the oblation, offering one hundred and eight times.
With ghee, sacrificial oblation, fuel-sticks, milk, and sesame seeds,
one should offer either one thousand and eight times for each, or half of that, or eight hundred.
The birth-rite (jātakarma) should be performed in this manner; now hear about the naming-rite (nāmakarma).
One should cause the naming to be done on the tenth or the twelfth day.
On an auspicious day, or at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with excellent qualities, one should employ the sounds *hava*, *tāsva*, *maśarma*, and *ghoṣānya* at the end. (39)
The practitioner of mantras should likewise offer oblations with the Puruṣasūkta, the Rudrasūkta, and the Viṣṇusūkta as before; these should be enclosed by the name of the deity. 40.
In the third year, my dear, the ceremony of tonsure (caulakarma) is prescribed; [with the mantra] "O herb, protect him," and so forth. || 41 ||
With the mantra "O Svadhiti, do not harm my life," one should apply the edge of the razor with fresh butter;
the application of the mantra should be performed, and the cutting should be done with these very mantras.
O child, one should indeed cause a master of the Vedas to perform [the rite] with the three mantras;
however, one should not cause the cutting of hair from cooked [food]. (43)
The best of the twice-born should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with all these mantras together;
he should cause it to be offered by sixteen, twelve, or nine Brahmins.
One should offer the Viśeṣa, the Pavamāna, and the Hiraṇya-śantivarga separately, either one thousand and eight times each, or one hundred and eight times each.
A wise man should cause the initiation (upanayana) to be performed in the fifth year from conception, O Guha,
or in the eighth year from conception, according to the rite seen in the Vedas.
He should offer a garment, a girdle, a staff, a sacrificial thread, and likewise a deerskin to the five ancestors there with the blazing fire and the appropriate mantras.

One should perform the oblation with the three verses beginning with "agna āyūṃṣi," with the verse "prajāpate," with the verse "tryaryamā," and with the Puruṣa-sūktas, Viṣṇu-sūktas, and Rudra-sūktas. (48)
The recitation of the Sāvitrī, the placing of fuel on the fire, and the offering of water—whatever [is performed], all that constitutes the Brahmayajña. (49)
With the mantra "O Lord of Vows, of vows," one should offer this hymn to the Worthy One;
having known it through the three [Vedas], one should perform the oblation according to the prescribed rite. || 50 ||
One should offer oblations with the *sāvitrī*, "imaṃ me varuṇa," "tattvā yāmi," those beginning with "jaya," and the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* verses;
for each of these, there is one *ghaṭikā* and sixteen ritual actions (*kriyā*).
One should offer oblations of *kūśmāṇḍa* cakes, or even after the *jaya* and other offerings have been made;
for it is thus that the feeding of Brahmins at that time is performed by the twice-born.
At that time, one should offer the Vasordhārā oblation into the Hiraṇyagarbha fire;
and there, O Six-faced One, one should cause the declaration of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) to be recited at both the beginning and the end. (53)
One should perform everything during the forenoon on an auspicious and highly meritorious day;
having taken the face [of the image] into one's own mouth, one should then emerge through that very mouth.
Taking the *kṣurikā*, one should go forth; then, with the mouth [of that mantra], one should emerge.
With the *brahman* [mantra] in the *brahmagarbha*, one should emerge with the words "svasty astu. (55)
When wealth is available, O Guha, the Hiraṇyagarbha rite should be performed by the best of the twice-born; however, it must not be performed by Vaiśyas or Śūdras even when they possess wealth.
In the works of Āpastamba, Prācīnayogya, Chāndoga, Atharva, Pippalāda, and others— among these eighteen authorities on Dharma, as well as in the Sūtras of Aitarēya— (57)
In these Itihāsas and Purāṇas, there is no such rule;
however, in the great scripture Kālottara, Hiraṇyagarbha is revealed.
One should enter facing the east while seated, indeed looking toward the east, accompanied by auspicious cries of "Auspicious Day! and "Victory!", and the pleasant sounds of conchs and trumpets. (59)
One should perform the recitation, and food with ghee should be auspicious;
mixed with honey, it should be offered along with water to Hiraṇyagarbha.
Alternatively, one should cause it to be given to a poor person for the purpose of drinking soma;
there, one should honor the officiating priests with cows, land, gold, and other such gifts.
With manifold sacrificial fees, with necklaces, armlets, and earrings,
[he is equal] to a thousand horse-sacrifices and ten thousand Vājapeya sacrifices.
O dear one, he surely obtains the fruit of [giving] a hundred thousand tawny cows;
indeed, according to Hiraṇyagarbha, it shall be the remover of all diseases.
"O Six-faced One, it is the truth that all [obstacles] along with their secondary afflictions perish.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, the Hiraṇyagarbha-paṭala, in the Kālottara. (p. 225) || 40 ||
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
O Ṣaṇmukha, now listen to the procedure for the offering of sesame seeds;
among all gifts whatsoever, the gift of sesame seeds is most highly praised. (1)
At the aforementioned place and time, the wise preceptor, learned in the Vedas and Shastras, should cause an excellent mountain of sesame seeds to be constructed.
On a level and delightful spot on the earth, in front of the temple of Śiva,
the preceptor himself, with arms raised, [performs] correctly for the patron.
One should prepare sesame seeds by means of effort involving the application of a rod,
ensuring they are free from rice-grains and stones, and devoid of worms, insects, and the like.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) with the sounds of musical instruments and flutes,
and having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should scatter a garland of flowers upon the womb-chamber.
The preceptor should fill [the vessel] with sesame seeds according to the standard measure of the staff,
together with the images and the mantra beginning with "sayojāta."
Having wrapped the mountain of sesame seeds on all sides with bright cloths,
one should surround it with flower garlands as well as various kinds of fruits.
Then, having adorned it, one should make it beautifully embellished with the nine gems;
one should fashion a mountain of sesame seeds encircled by the eight metals.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
these five forms are to be worshipped with the five auspicious Brahmans.
O Guha, having worshipped the Lotus-born (Brahmā) in the western quarter with the Sadyojāta mantra,
one should worship Viṣṇu from the northern side with the Vāmadeva mantra.
The Lord Rudra is to be worshipped from the south with the Aghora mantra;
then one should worship Īśvara in the eastern quarter with the Vaktra mantra.
The knower of mantras should always worship the god Sadāśiva in the northeastern direction;
he should have separate images made, either of gold or of silver.
Having worshipped him according to the rule with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and so forth, the pure disciple should honor the preceptor with many sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās). 13.
Together with the preceptor and the guardians of the images (mūrtipās), beginning with the five Brahmās and Śiva’s limbs,
one should then perform the rites for Soma and the others, in sequence starting with Sadyojāta and the rest.
O Guha, having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas) according to the prescribed rite in their respective directions, [this] has been proclaimed individually in each of the eighty-one tantras.
