The sesame-mountain is proclaimed as partless (niṣkala) and supremely victorious;
therefore, one should worship that God in the form of the sesame-mountain. 16.
The sacrificer, having prostrated before this Lord who was a mountain of sesame seeds,
[offered it] to a devoted follower of Śiva who was disciplined and had mastered the Vedas.
One should give a mountain of sesame seeds to a learned man who is proficient in all the scriptures;
O child, he who gives a mountain of sesame seeds according to this rite— || 18 ||
One enjoys the fruit of a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices, a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices, and the gift of a hundred thousand cows. || 19 ||
Even a cow-killer, an ungrateful person, a slayer of a Brahmin, or a murderer of one's father—
such a person is liberated from other sins as well, and at the end of the body, shall go to Śiva.
Thereafter, one should honor the teacher with earrings, ornaments, and so forth,
as well as with cows, land, gold, garments, household utensils, and other such items. (21)
Alternatively, having bathed the Supreme Lord with one hundred and eight jars and having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite; || 22 ||
The wise preceptor should recite the Hunetprāsāda mantra one hundred and eight times;
[the deity is] Mahādeva, Hara, Rudra, Śaṅkara, and Nīlalohita. (23)
Īśāna, Vijaya, Bhīma, Devadeva, Bhavodbhava, and Kapālīśa—these ten should be known as beginning with Varuṇa. 24.
One should worship [the image] of one who possesses all afflictions on all sides in due order;
having worshipped it with a black antelope skin, one should offer sixteen āḍhakas of sesame seeds.
Endowed with the three types of gold, wrapped in a pair of garments, beautified by flower garlands, and adorned with fruits and flowers. || 26 ||
Having meditated upon the eleven Rudras in their proper order,
one should cause them to be given away to a twice-born who is a devotee of Śiva, self-controlled, and learned in the Vedas.
Whoever performs this with devotion, endowed with this ritual procedure,
shall experience long life, prosperity, victory, and fame, and then go to Śiva.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, the Chapter on the Mountain of Sesame Seeds, in the Kālottara. 41.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme gift of earth;
the earth, which fulfills all desires, is the best among all gifts. (1)
All jewels, grains, and all substances and essences; as well as gods, asuras, humans, yakṣas, kinnaras, and so forth. (2)
Cows, elephants, chariots, female slaves, male slaves, gold, and wealth—one obtains the fruit of all these everywhere through the gift of the entire earth. || 3 ||
The oceans, mountains, and islands—whether level or uneven, beautiful or otherwise—I am unable to give all of these; therefore, that means [to achieve this] is extremely difficult to find.
Having fashioned everything out of gold, one should bestow it upon the twice-born;
one obtains the fruit of giving the entire world of moving and non-moving beings—of this there is no doubt. || 5 ||
At the aforementioned place and time, the wise man should cause the earth to be prepared;
the gift of the earth should be performed by the best of men.
With gold from Jambūdvīpa one should make the best [image], while that which is equal to it [in quality] is middling;
with ordinary gold one should make the middle [grade], and with common gold the lowest.
One who knows the Vedas and the Shastras should know that the middling [type of gift] is through fire-offerings (homa) and should cause it to be performed;
among the six types of renunciation of material goods, gold, Jambunada gold, and so forth are included.
Gold from the Śatakuṃbha river, gold from the Jāmbūnada river, hiraṇya, and that which is made of gold— one should cause the depletion of these by means of any one of them constantly.
One should cause the earth to be made four-cornered, with Mount Meru situated in its center;
O Six-faced One, Mahāmeru consists of three thousand [yojanas], while the smallest [Meru] is indeed six [yojanas].
The medium [size] should be with ten thousand [bricks], and the superior should be twenty;
then, one should construct Mahāmeru in the center of Jambūdvīpa.
The Nīla, Niṣadha, Pāriyātra, Himavat, Vindhya, Mahendra, Ṛkṣa, Sahya, Aya, Śrīśaila, and Svāmiparvata; || 12 ||
The one who has mastered the ritual should cause Govardhana, Supārśva, Vipula, Hariśailaka, and Mahāmeru to be fashioned there in the four directions. (13)
The Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Gomatī, Sarayū, and Sarasvatī, as well as the Sindhu and Śoṇā—the four rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā that flow toward the west—[are there]. (14)
The Dvṛṣadvatī, Vihivajrā, Haṃsī, and Plāvanī flow toward the west. || 15 ||
The Godāvarī, Kāverī, Tāmraparṇī, Supārśvā, and Catuśśailā flow toward the east from the southeastern side of Mahāmeru. (16)

One should cause Sahya to be made in the north-west; one should cause Divya and Sudivya, the Kula mountains, to be made from south to north. One should cause [them] to be made to the east of Mahāmeru. To the west, one should cause the mountain Dharadharājākaraṇa to be made. To the north, Viśāla and Samukha; Subhadra is the earth. One should maintain the fourfold support of the Dhārādharas. One should cause Bhāratavarṣa and Kiṃpuruṣa to be made to the south of Mahāmeru.

One should cause Bhadrāśva to be fashioned to the east; one should place Ketumāla, made of gold, in the north; and likewise Kuru to the north. Having thus arranged Jambūdvīpa with its center toward the north, and having placed another [mountain] to the east of Mahāmeru, one should have each fashioned from a hundred pieces of gold. One should have Śrīkailāsa fashioned from silver using five thousand [pieces]. [Likewise, one should fashion] Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmali, Gomedaka, and Puṣkara.
One should cause [the continents] to be made with seven oceans having the taste of alkaline water, milk, curd, clarified butter, sugarcane juice, wine, and [fresh] water.
The continents are surrounded by the oceans, and those oceans are likewise surrounded by the continents;
thus, they increase twofold, each one further and further out. (17)
230) One should cause islands to be made rising slightly above the ocean. In the center of Puṣkaradvīpa, one should cause Mount Mānasottara to be made with three thousand [yojanas].
In the remaining islands, [the mountains are] Kaṅka, Sukha, Karamataṅga, and Śiṃśumāra; in Bhārata, Viṣṇuparvata. In each of the islands, [one should place] thirty [yojanas].

One should have it fashioned out of gold. One should have the great mountain Trikūṭa fashioned out of salt in the great ocean of salt water with a thousand [units]. One should have the seven oceans made with islands as the intervals between them. One should have the salt ocean, measuring one *ratni*, fashioned with a hundred units of gold, doubling in size at each successive stage.
To the northeast of Mahāmeru, one should have Śvetadvīpa fashioned, extending for three thousand *yojanas*. [It should be] all around the ocean of sweet water.

One should have the Lokāloka mountain fashioned in a circular shape. One should have all the oceans fashioned from twenty thousand measures of gold, and all the mountains fashioned from gold. One should have the Vindhya and Himavat mountains, which extend from the eastern to the western ocean, fashioned from one thousand measures. One should cause the seven oceans and the seven principal mountain ranges (kulaśaila) to be inscribed in their respective locations with their own names. And upon the peaks of the Lokāloka mountain, one should [depict] the rivers and the eight world-protectors (lokapāla).

One should have [the deities] fashioned: Indra in the east, Agni in the southeast, Yama in the south, Nirṛti in the southwest, Varuṇa in the west, Vāyu in the northwest, Soma in the north, and Īśāna in the northeast. One should cause them to be depicted on Śrī Kailāsa, in the region below Mahāmeru.

And one should offer to each of them separately with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and the like, as well as with water for honor (arghya) and food offerings (naivedya). [One should also worship] with lotuses, blue lilies, and campaka flowers.

One should worship separately with flowers of *karavīra*, *jāti*, *karṇikāra*, *tulasī*, *bilva*, and *śamī*. Having bathed, with senses subdued, fasting, and performing recitation (*japa*), one should circumambulate three times, bowing to all the gods, and cause [the image] to ascend the peak of Great Meru (*mahāmeru*).
On the western side, slightly below, all the deities should be placed facing west; there, one intent on the recitation of the *praṇava* should perform the sacrifice (*homa*).

Those who know the Vedas—thirty-two, sixteen, or eight—should perform the *homa*. One should cause the stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*) to flow into the sacrificial pit located in the eastern direction of Mahāmeru, using the eight previously mentioned mantras and [wood from] the *palāśa*, *khadira*, *pippala*, *nyagrodha*, *plakṣa*, *bilva*, *śamī*, *udumbara*, and *apāmārga* trees.

The materials for the *homa* are sacrificial fuel (*samit*), clarified butter (*ājya*), cooked rice (*caru*), sesame, mustard seeds, *śāli* rice, barley, bamboo, and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

Having performed the study of the Vedas according to the prescribed rule for three days, five days, or seven days starting from one's own birth day, one should bestow [the merit] upon the twice-born (*dvija*).
By doing so, a person obtains the fruit of ten thousand horse sacrifices (*aśvamedha*).
And likewise, the gift of a thousand bay horses and the gift of a maiden. || 18 ||
O child, by the gift of the earth, the king indeed obtains that fruit;
he is liberated from all sins and freed from all diseases. (19)
"Endowed with all sovereign powers, the king shall live for a hundred years.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter on the gift of the earth in the Kālottara. 42.
Śrīḥ.
The Lord said: I shall now declare the origin of the Liṅga, as well as the characteristics of the Liṅga,
the characteristics of the temple, and likewise the characteristics of the image.
It indeed possesses the characteristics of a retinue and the characteristics of a foundation;
at all times, it is the foundation, as well as the form, the color, and the seed-syllable.
The location, the fruit, and the installation of all [deities] according to the rule,
whether in a village, a city, a town, or even a market settlement. (3)
I shall now explain in brief the installation of these [deities] as well as the characteristics of the womb (garbha); listen to all of this at once.
When this world was submerged in a single ocean with its waters rising high, and lay here overwhelmed on all sides by darkness, with the hosts of stars, the moon, and the sun vanished;
In a region of the forest where the ground was shattered, || 5 ||
In that regard, it is said that the Primordial God is both the lotus-born Brahmā and the one whose weapons are the discus, conch, and mace;
those two alone are the two excellent and ancient ones.
He wandered within the midst of the ocean, the reservoir of waters.
Once,
having first observed Govinda approaching,
the one born from the interior of a lotus performed all preliminary rites and spoke.
A broad frown upon his forehead. || 7 ||
"Who are you? Tell me, who are you, and what is the purpose for which you have come here with such great haste?
Being addressed in this manner, you, O Madhusūdana—
He spoke thus with a smile to the one born from a lotus.
The ancient Lord, the praiseworthy majesty, the sole creator and the primary cause of the universe.
Do you not know me, the Supreme God Nārāyaṇa, who holds the discus, mace, and other weapons in my hands? 9.
Having heard those exceedingly audacious words of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, his inner self agitated in an instant,
then spoke to Hari while smiling.
A speech full of finality and joined with anger. || 10 ||
Are you intoxicated that you do not know me?
For I am indeed the creator, the sustainer, and likewise the supporter of all that is moving and unmoving.
Thus, while that terrible and truly fearsome dispute between Hari and Pitāmaha was proceeding,
[there appeared] one in the form of a Liṅga, with the brilliance of a thousand suns at the time of universal dissolution.
Thereupon, some name or other arose before the two of them. || 12 ||
Beholding that mass of flames from the fire of universal destruction, which was as crooked as the crest of a peacock's tail, the two of them said:
"Who indeed is this? What is the cause for this emergence? How has this come to pass? Alas, what a tragedy! The middle of this great [city] appears utterly desolate."
The purpose of our anger is indeed liberation; who has suddenly come upon us? 13.
Having prostrated again, Brahmā spoke to Madhusūdana:
"One should observe that which moves slowly both upwards and downwards. (14)
Viṣṇu went downward as far as he could examine, and Pitāmaha went upward;
thus, more than eight thousand years passed, yet no end was found.
Then, exhausted and weary in heart, they both met there again in an instant. || 15 ||
Thus, with these bodies— wind, water, moon, sun, fire, earth, sacrificer, sky, and earth—
one should know this entire Lord.
The world, having been withdrawn by you from the enemies, shines forth. || 16 ||
"You are Agni, you are Īśa, you are Varuṇa, you are Vibhāvasu; you are Śakra, you are the god Dhaneśa, you are Yama—what are you?
O Lord of the Thirty-three, command me: what is the task here?"
O Lord, be gracious to us two, who are afflicted by the suffering of worldly existence.
Homage, homage to the All-Knowing One, to Śiva, who is both gross and subtle; homage, homage to You; homage, homage to the Cause of causes, the Self of all, the Maker of all auspiciousness. || 18 ||
I bow to Sadāśiva—the auspicious one, the maker of auspiciousness, the peaceful, whose very self is auspicious, the supreme auspiciousness, and the guide upon the path to auspiciousness. || 19 ||
I bow down to Śaṅkara, the eternal, beautiful, and pure god, the Lord of the universe, who purifies the throat of Śaṃsa. || 20 ||
I bow to the Fish who is the pillar, established in the place of abiding, whose nature is stability and steadfastness, and who stands firm, established in the yoga of abiding.
I bow to the supreme Lord, who is the highest and lowest of all, eternal, the remover of all sins, and the ultimate dispeller of distress. || 22 ||
I bow down to Īśāna, the boon-granting god, Īśāna, the leader of mantras, Īśāna of all beings, the sovereign Īśāna. || 23 ||
Having thus praised Mahādeva, Nārāyaṇa and the Four-faced One,
both of great power, fell into deep distress and prostrated themselves again and again. (24)
In the midst of the linga is the supreme linga, the manifest Supreme Lord—
the three-eyed, four-armed deity who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Having beheld Mahādeva, whose limbs are the Goddess of the Gods and who is imperishable, and having beheld the Lord Maheśvara through the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas; || 26 ||
Indeed, you alone are the creator of all this, both moving and unmoving;
O Janārdana, you alone exist for the maintenance of everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
What is declared to be the *liṅga*, or how is the *liṅga* spoken of?
By what [means] is this entire great being, Maheśvara, [perceived] in the world? (28)
Īśvara said:
"Lakṣmī-sthūlaliṅga," and so forth—these are synonyms for the term *vṛddhi* applied to this limb. Therefore, this Brahman is indeed the *liṅga* of sound.
Through knowledge, he is manifold; this is the supreme knowledge. || 29 ||
Brahmā dwells eternally at the base, and Viṣṇu resides in the central region surrounded by all the gods and the hosts of Gaṇeśa; I am established upon the summit.
Here, Siddhi, Kīrti, and Lakṣmī (the one whose abode is the lotus) are perpetually dissolved.
The moon and the sun together with the hosts of planets, as well as wind, fire, and the directions. || 30 ||
The Lord of Wealth (Kubera) shines from the north, partaking in the dance; Indra from the east, having surpassed the gods; the King of Dharma (Yama) from the south;
and when [the sun] has set, the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa), with noose in hand, is eternally present in the west.
Because it has indeed entered into dissolution (*laya*), for that reason it is called a "mark" (*liṅga*). || 31 ||
The Viśvedevas, the world-protectors, the lords of sages,
the Siddhas, the Sādhyas, the Guhyakas, the lords of the Pannagas, the gods, the Daityas, the Rākṣasas, the Yātudhānas, all the deities, the Dānavas, and the Mothers; 32.

The Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, the sciences of dharma, artha, and vidyā, the six musical notes and so forth, the mandalas of the vowels, the continents and oceans, and the lords of the serpents—all these are his playful manifestations; therefore, he is indeed the Linga.
Because it was the dwelling place of the Tāla-piśācas and bhūtas during the time of the remnants (ucchiṣṭa), it is called a liṅga;
indeed, this first liṅga was created as the third [in sequence] for the sake of bestowing grace in the past. || 34 ||
For the entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, this supreme and most sacred [liṅga] exists within my fortune and is composed of that;
for this supreme and most sacred liṅga should always be worshipped here with one's whole being. 35.
Whoever worships the Liṅga with single-minded devotion, by him the seven worlds are worshipped.
Those who remain on this [day] engaged in keeping vigil, self-restrained, practicing celibacy,
and devoted to fasting, [worship it] with Bilva leaves, lotuses, and other offerings.
Those men who at times worship [me] as if with a linga using various garlands and incense scents, they become my foremost [attendants], bearing tridents in their hands and adorned with pearls. (37)
Those who constantly worship this my linga— the body of the Lord of the Thirty-three— with offerings of perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, ritual ablutions, oblations, hymns, mantras, and gifts,
shall be freed from the suffering of the womb, the pain of ignorance, birth, exhaustion, death, old age, disease, and grief.
Those lords of the quarters who have come within my domain, holding tridents and swords in their hands and possessing three eyes, become my attendants. || 38 ||
At the end of the kalpa, all the deities dissolve into that liṅga;
Brahmā dissolves on the right side, and Janārdana on the left.
The moon and sun are the two eyes; the wind is dissolved in the nose;
the quarters are dissolved in the two ears; and the deities of the Gāyatrī are dissolved in the heart. (40)
Sarasvatī is indeed dissolved in speech; the sky is dissolved in the head;
Bhadrakālī is in the forehead; and the three worlds are dissolved in the earth. || 41 ||
The continents, oceans, and mountains are dissolved into her thighs;
the entire world, both stationary and moving, dissolves into her belly.
This has been told to you in brief out of affection, O Six-faced One, in the *Kālottara*, the compendium of twelve thousand verses, in the forty-third chapter, titled "The Origin of the Liṅga. 43.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
In a village, a city, a town, or even a hamlet, one should install the Liṅga in the eastern direction; it shall bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 1 ||
One should install a liṅga in the south-eastern direction; it brings about pacification and nourishment, increases sons and grandsons, and is beneficial for those who drink soma.
There shall be happiness for forest-dwellers, householders, and sages;
one should install a liṅga in the southern direction that indeed destroys death.
It removes all diseases and destroys consumption and leprosy;
by installing the Liṅga in the southwest (Nairṛtya), one shall obtain the destruction of enemies. || 4 ||
For victory in battle or for the immobilization of an army, one should install a liṅga in the western (vāruṇī) direction; it will bring about peace and prosperity.
One should install the liṅga in the northwestern direction; it bestows nourishment, happiness, and the growth of crops, and there shall be well-being for the Brāhmaṇas. (6)
One should install the Liṅga in the north-eastern direction; it bestows health, wealth, nourishment, peace, and happiness, and victory shall come to kings.
One should install the Liṅga in the northeast, which brings happiness to elephants, horses, chariots, mortals, and servants, and bestows the fruit of all desires.

One should install the Liṅga in the center for the sake of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation, as well as for the increase of sons and grandsons; it brings about benefits both in this world and the next.
There shall be abundance of food for cows and buffaloes, and victory for kings;
it shall bring welfare to the four castes and increase longevity, prosperity, and fame. (10)
One shall always obtain abundance of food, plenty of cattle, and perpetual well-being;
as well as [the regions] of Mahendra, Varuṇa, Āgneya, and Anila. (11)
The ground is declared to be of four kinds for the rite of installing a linga:
that of Mahendra for Kṣatriyas, and that of Vāraṇa for Brāhmaṇas.
The fire [mantra] is for those of the Vaiśya caste, the wind [mantra] for those of the Śūdra caste;
water is complete for all, while the milk-tree [mantra] is for the north and the west.
In the south there is the production of rice and grassy land; in the east, the ground becomes intensely red and its taste is astringent.
If the ground smells of blood, one should designate it as a Māhendra site;
if it is strewn with water-born flowers and surrounded by a water-fortress, [it is likewise]. || 15 ||
O child, it is filled with Kuśa and Kāśa grass and endowed with lotuses and water-lilies;
it has the appearance of a white color, resembling a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon.
It was crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned with ruddy geese,
filled with aquatic birds, and endowed with vast bodies of water. (17)
The scent of clarified butter and a sweet taste should be recognized;
they say "earth" belongs to Varuṇa, and its characteristic mark is known as belonging to Varuṇa.
That linga is named Pauṣṭika; it bestows the fruits of all desires.
It is strewn with pigeons and *samaraṅga* birds, and fashioned from the wood of the *palāśa* and *khadira* trees.
Where there are bees among madhuka flowers and a vulture with five partridges, one should indicate that the water is contained within a very small area and the ground is of fiery (āgneya) nature.
It shall always have the fragrance of the kumuda lotus, and its six flavors shall be perfectly balanced;
this is called the fiery (āgneya) liṅga, which bestows happiness upon Vaiśyas. || 21 ||
It was known for its *vihīta*, *kapilu*, and *vṛkṣa* trees, as well as *śleṣmātaka* trees;
there were *heraṇḍa* plants on the pale peaks, along with jackals, deer, and birds. || 22 ||
Whether in a forest abounding in tigers, snakes, and boars, or among poisonous trees, or even on a vine-covered thicket, in mud, in saline soil, or in narrow straits; || 23 ||
And many other trees were covered by clouds and the like;
the ground was level, free of pebbles, devoid of grass, and destitute of water.
Where the ground has the smell of impurity, is black in color, and bitter to the taste, that ground is composed of air; its characteristic sign is the performance of malevolent magic (abhicāraka).
It causes death, hatred, disease, and the destruction of prosperity;
therefore, one should not employ the Vāyavya [mantra] with any effort whatsoever.
They were white as a lotus stalk, a pearl, the moon, frost, cow’s milk, or snow;
as bright as a conch shell, with the luster of a night-lotus, and resembling the brilliance of a lordly elephant’s tusks. (27)
(240) These [practices] which have been described by me in this manner are indeed to be applied to those of the Śūdra caste.
The month of Jyeṣṭha and likewise the month of Caitra, and the fourth, the month of the constellation Citrā, should be applied [in this manner]. || 28 ||
Likewise, O dear one, there is the mark of a Śūdra; indeed, the union of these three belongs to the [other] three castes.
However, these three are never suitable for a Śūdra.
The Vaiśya characteristic is said to belong to both; one should indeed apply both to the Vaiśya. But the Kṣatriya characteristic is suitable for Brāhmaṇas as well, O Six-faced One. (30)
O Six-faced One, a deceptive mark is indeed not appropriate for a king;
one should act in accordance with the natural order (anuloma) and never cause it to be contrary (pratiloma).
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the Kālottara.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said: Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, and Meruparvata; Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śrīśaila, and Svāmiparvata. || 1 ||
In Niṣadha, Pāriyātra, Nīla, and indeed on the Himavat mountain;
in Bhuktimat-Pāriyātra and also on Mount Govardhana. || 2 ||
Furthermore, O child, in the vicinity of these very places— in the forest, in the grove, or on a sacred mountain— one should designate the supreme Liṅga.
In that place, O Guha, the linga is of medium quality, while in other places it is indeed inferior.
Having fashioned a linga from diamond (vajra), Rudra always worships it in the center. (4)
Having thereby attained the state of Rudra, endowed with incomparable qualities,
Viṣṇu constantly worships the linga made of sapphire.
Among them, however, he eternally worships a single, wonderful, and eternal Viṣṇu as the auspicious Linga made of stone, which is Brahman itself.
Through that, one attains the state of Brahmā as well as the status of being the creator of the universe;
even Śakra, the king of the gods, should worship with a ruby.
By that, one attains the status of Śakra and becomes the sovereign of the three worlds;
he always worships the fire-made liṅga which has been offered food.
By that [act], he indeed attains the state of fire among the gods as a bearer of poison;
and Yama, the King of Dharma, also possesses an auspicious linga made of sapphire.
By that worship, O child, one shall indeed attain the status of Dharmarāja;
one should worship the Kṛṣṇa Samaya Liṅga, the lord of the Rākṣasas.
By that constant worship, he shall attain the status of a lord of the Rākṣasas;
Varuṇa always worships a liṅga fashioned from crystal.
One attains lordship over the waters and the very difficult-to-attain state of immortality;
Īśāna always worships the Liṅga composed of the seven musical notes.
By worshipping him, O child, one becomes the sovereign of all the Rudras;
Pārvatī always worships with a linga made of coral.
By constantly worshipping it, one shall attain the state of Rudra’s power;
indeed, Lakṣmī always worships with a linga made of silver.
By worshipping it, one shall attain Lakṣmī and the state of great glory;
Durgā worships a beautiful Liṅga made of great sapphire (mahānīla). (15)
One should worship Durgā at all times; by that, one attains the state of Durgā.
And Śacīkā should worship the Maya-liṅga with perfumes and flowers.
By worshipping it constantly, one shall attain the status of Indra’s wife;
the Vasus worship the linga made of bell-metal according to the prescribed rite.
By worshipping the copper linga with devotion at all times, the Sun attains the status of a Vasu, arising from incomparable qualities. 18.
By worshipping the earthly linga according to the prescribed rites, he attained supreme lordship over all the luminaries, along with the two Aśvins.
Because of that, both those Aśvin gods attained divine bodies;
Dhanada always worships their beautiful linga made of gold.
By that means, the god Dhanada attained the status of the Giver of Wealth;
the high-souled Viśvedevas should always worship a silver liṅga.
Indeed, by means of that [clay], one attains universality; one should worship the earthen liṅga with fragrances, flowers, and so forth. The Maruts indeed worship it at all times.
By worshipping it, they shall attain the status of the host of Maruts;
the hosts of Pitṛs worship the water-liṅga according to the prescribed rite.
By that [act], they shall indeed attain the great sovereignty over the Pitṛs;
for the Asuras worship a linga made of tin and lead.
Through that sacrifice, he constantly attained great power as an Asura;
moreover, the emblem of Agni (Agniliṅga) was always worshipped by all the sages as well. || 25 ||
By worshipping it constantly, they shall attain the great status of sages;
for the Piśācas indeed worship this Liṅga of the Nāgas perpetually. (26)
Indeed, even for all the Piśācas, the state of being everywhere and moving with the speed of thought has been attained;
and among all beings, the Agni-liṅga is always worshipped. || 27 ||
By that, they indeed attain the state of reality and reach proximity to Śiva;
[their] intellect, wisdom, and purity, as well as their hearing, memory, dawn, and radiance.
Having constantly worshipped him according to the prescribed rite by means of his subtle mark (*daraliṅga*), [one attains] passion, joy, fortitude, and even wisdom. || 29 ||
Indeed, those various states, endowed with incomparable qualities, have been attained by the Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Yakṣas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others. || 30 ||
For by means of sacrifice, O Six-faced One, this state is indeed attained eternally.
The wives of gods and the wives of sages should always worship the Puṣpaliṅga;
by worshipping it constantly according to the prescribed rite, they shall attain the status of being his wives.
Sarasvatī is the goddess who flows with the nectar of the divine;
by that [flow], people attached to her shall eternally attain the state of being Sarasvatī herself. || 33 ||
One attains the state of a god even by worshipping the emblems of the gods;
in this way, so do the gods along with the gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas. (34)
Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Kārkoṭa, and Śaṅkhapālaka always worship the Lord Īśāna, the leader of the gods, in the form of the Liṅga. || 35 ||
Ananta, Gulika, Padma, and likewise Mahāpadma worship a liṅga made of coral according to the prescribed rite.
By worshipping him constantly, they shall attain the status of a Nāga king.
Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, and the Himavat mountain— (37)
Vindhya, Sahya, Malaya, Mahendra, Gandhamādana, Śrīparvata, Maināka, and Svāmiparvata; || 38 ||
Niṣadha, Pāriyātra, and Nīla mountain likewise, having always worshipped with devotion this linga composed of great mountains; || 39 ||
By worshipping it, they shall attain the lordship of the mountains:
Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmalī, Gomedha, and Puṣkara. || 40 ||
These indeed were the kings of the islands who worshipped Daraliṅga; by that constant worship, they attained the very status of being kings of the islands.
The gods, asuras, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas, along with the siddhas, vidyādharas, yakṣas, and garuḍas, all worship him. 42.
"For there can be no merit greater than the worship of the Liṅga;
having understood this, Sadāśiva should be worshipped with diligent effort. (43)
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the Liṅgakalpa of the Kālottara.
Prosperity!
Kārttikeya said:
"Abandoning prolixity, tell me correctly and concisely the definition of the *liṅga*,
which is subtler than the subtlest, in brief."
Īśvara said:

Now, therefore, we shall describe the characteristics of the *liṅga* in due order. Indeed, my child, there are three kinds of Śiva-liṅgas: the partless (*niṣkala*), the with-parts (*sakala*), and the both-with-and-partless (*sakalaniṣkala*).

(p. 245) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the nature of reality as it is (*tathatā-svabhāva*)."

The *sakala* (with parts) is that which is endowed with major and minor limbs (*aṅga-pratyaṅga*), while the *niṣkala* (without parts) is devoid of such divisions; the *sakala-niṣkala* is the *mukhaliṅga*. In the *niṣkala*, the form of smoke is worshipped as the Supreme Lord; in the *sakala-niṣkala*, it is light; and in the *sakala*, it is worldly experience. The first characteristic is the consciousness of the image (*arcā-citta*). The term *liṅga* is synonymous with body, meter, conforming [to rules], gross, and manifest. Among these, we shall describe the characteristics of the *niṣkala-liṅga*. The materials for the *liṅga* are stone, wood, clay, metal, gems, and so forth. Regarding these, stones are of three kinds: female, male, and neuter. A sound like a bell is male; one like cymbals is female; and a sound like a drum is neuter. A *liṅga* is made from a male stone, a pedestal (*pīṭha*) from a female stone, and a base-stone (*pāda-śilā*) from a neuter one. On an auspicious day, determined by favorable signs such as parts, omens, and portents, the preceptor himself—having fasted, offered oblations, muttered the *svapna-māṇavaka* mantra, and performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*)—should select a stone that is not damaged by wind or sun, extending from east to west or southward, and say: "Oṃ, salutation to Śambhu, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul, the Left-handed One (*Vāma*), the Universal Form, the Lord of Dreams! Oṃ hili hili, to the wielder of the *halā* weapon, svāhā! He should then offer oblations one hundred and eight times with *palāśa* wood, *śamī* wood, and clarified butter. Having touched it according to the single-fire (*ekāgni*) ritual and having seen an auspicious dream regarding the task, he should have the *liṅga* accepted. If there is an inauspicious sign, one should offer oblations separately one hundred and eight times with the *prāyaścitta-bīja-mantra* repeated thrice or five times; thus the fault is pacified. Then, the workmen, the preceptor, and the patron, facing east or north, should perform the taking up of the stone. For a *liṅga* to be installed at the eastern door, the face should naturally be toward the east; this should be applied accordingly for the western door, marking the long sides of the stone. If it is reversed, there will be confusion in the kingdom.

Alternatively, the *liṅga* may be the form [of the temple], such that the *liṅga* is proportionate to the temple (*prāsāda*). Regarding the length of the *liṅga*: for a sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) of the smallest size, it is half the length of the sanctum; for one divided into five parts, it is three parts—this is the medium size. For a sanctum divided into three parts, it is two parts—this is the largest size. [The dimensions range] from one cubit up to sixty-four cubits.

One should not construct [liṅgas] with whatever signs or features [are improper] from this point forward. The diameter (viṣkambha) shall be one-fourth of its height (āyāma). When the height is divided into nine parts, the sixth part is for the *vrata* (the base), the seventh part is for the middle, and the eighth part is for the *nābhi* (navel) together with its root; the square portion at the base of the *nābhi* is the *brahmabhāga*, the half-eighth (fourth) part is the *viṣṇubhāga*, and the upper part is the *śivabhāga*, which is sixteen-sided (*ṣoḍaśāśra*). Of the sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) divided into three parts, one part is the measurement for the pedestal (*pīṭhikā*), or rather, the height of that [pedestal] is stated to be the same. For the square [base], having discarded half of the width of the eighth part, that is the circumference (*nāha*) of the upper part; or else, having divided half the circumference into eight parts, five parts constitute the diameter. If it is excessive, there is disease and much unrest in the kingdom; if deficient, there is loss of wealth and grain. Therein, the base portion is the *pīṭhabhāga*, the worship portion (*pūjābhāga*). The base portion is the *ātmatattva*, the middle portion is the *vidyātattva*, and the upper portion is the *śivatattva*. Furthermore, [the upper part] is circular and without corners. Therein, if the base is deficient, there is disease; if the middle is deficient, loss of cattle; if the worship portion is deficient, instability in ritual action. A circle equal to the worship portion fulfills all desires. One should act thus; it is the means for accomplishing all desires and purposes, and it brings about all peace. In the case of the *vardhamāna* type, one may have it made with an increase of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). The worship portion fulfills all desires and bestows abundance of wealth. Regarding the position on the head of the liṅga, there are five varieties: the shape of a hen’s egg, the shape of a discus, the shape of a bubble, and the shape of a triple-person (*tripuruṣa*). The hen’s egg shape is praised; it bestows long life and health. The umbrella shape bestows long life, health, and sovereignty.

One that bestows health and sovereignty; one shaped like a bubble, which brings success in worship; one shaped like a woman or a man, which bestows wealth and grain. Among these, one that has the shape of the full moon bestows all desires. Those [liṅgas] that are joined with veins, cavities, whorls, knots, circles, or internal cores, as well as those that are split, rough, cracked, or fissured; those devoid of sound, or excessively thick, too light, or hollow; those with pain, a needle-like shape, a thick head, gravel-like texture, heat, or a smoky color; and those lacking roots, sides, or other parts—these are not to be accepted. Among them: a liṅga joined with veins, cavities, circles, or internal cores brings danger to the self of the patron (*yajamāna*), the preceptor (*ācārya*), and the king, as well as to all living beings. A knot causes the destruction of wealth and grain for kings; an internal core brings happiness to all beings, especially to the patron, the preceptor, and the king. If it is deficient [in size], there is distress for all beings. If it is rough, there is mental agitation for those with broken signs. If it is cracked, it brings misfortune to the patron, the preceptor, and the king. If it has a binding [defect], there is danger to the life of those who are bound, and if there is a hole in the mouth, there is loss of honor. Furthermore, there is much unrest in the kingdom and so forth. If it is thick, there is disease; if it is soft, there is success in all undertakings for those of the three wombs (*triyoni*). An internal core causes agitation for humans when there is no sound. If it is thin, there is loss of wealth. If it is excessive, the maker suffers delusion. If it has a thick shape or a thick head, there is danger to the life of the patron and the preceptor. If it is in pieces, there is drought; if it has wheels, there is unrest in the kingdom and so forth. That which is warm and honey-colored is to be accepted. If it is thin, there is loss of wealth. If it lacks a root, there is disease. If it lacks sides, there is loss of cattle. On this subject, there are these verses:
If the right side of the fetus has a color resembling madder, it will be a lizard;
in a circular [mark], a monitor lizard; in a black one, one should know it to be a serpent;
in a tawny one, one should know it to be a mouse; and in a pale-yellow one, a chameleon.
On a stone of yellow color, there is a pigeon; on a house-lizard, a snake;
on one of sword-like color, and on one of ash-like color, there is sand.
One should recognize a scorpion on a variegated [surface], a firefly on one that is honey-colored;
a white frog on a lotus stalk, and indeed a black antelope on a black [surface];
and on the skin of a white lotus, one should point out a tiger.
If the lines are excessively drawn upward and there is a lack of symmetry, one should recognize that there is an enemy therein; this is the measurement for six finger-breadths.
One should predict the presence of a vulture, a dog, a mongoose, eight blue jays, a crow, and a hawk within the womb according to their respective colors in the corresponding signs.

Alternatively, the linga devoid of that [prescribed] procedure is of two kinds: pure (*śuddha*) and mixed (*saṃkīrṇa*). That which possesses whorls in the openings of its veins, is endowed with internal knots, and is perfect in color is pure. That which is the opposite of this is mixed; it is characterized by a profusion of veins and various colors. We shall describe hereafter the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the veins and other features. On the left side of the portion intended for worship (*pūjābhāga*), the veins and other marks, whether auspicious or inauspicious, will manifest their results within six months. On the right side, they manifest within three months; on the back, within six months; and on the front, immediately. A clockwise rotation is excellent, while a counter-clockwise rotation is censured. Auspicious signs—such as a banner, umbrella, chowrie, water-pot, bull, *nandyāvarta*, trident, lotus, lion, elephant, horse, chariot, moon, sun, sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), mountain, rosary, wheel, necklace, ocean, garment, goad, fish, the *svastika*, tree, favor, thunderbolt (*vajra*), maiden, pure eyes, the *śrīvatsa*, and merit—are auspicious when located at the front, the back, the sides, or the center, bringing benefit to the patron (*yajamāna*), the preceptor (*ācārya*), the king, and the kingdom. Four lines of white, red, yellow, and black are prescribed; these are the ones that bestow defects.

A line resembling a rainbow brings grief; a line beautiful in every respect brings prosperity. A single break in the field indicates the loss of sons. Two breaks indicate the loss of kinsmen; three breaks indicate the loss of fame and honor. In the letter Śa, there is the attainment of knowledge; in the letter Ka, the destruction of royalty. There are also crows, owls, jackals, and boars.

"May the gardabha, śyena, vṛścika, karkaṭa, kaṅka, gṛdhra, kīṭa, sarpa, and mārjāra drink my royal kingdom! Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, the Section on Veins and Cavities, in the Liṅgakalpa of the Kālottara.
Prosperity!

Īśvara said: "Those with a deep-set navel, those with a lotus-petal-like whorl, those with a whorl here [in the center] that is golden-colored, those with white dust-like [spots], those with a glossy [complexion], those with a color like ripe *kākāṇḍa* fruit,

those with a crow-colored [mark], those with a pigeon-colored [mark], those with two [marks] like a domestic cow and a goat, those with a madder-colored circular whorl, and those with three red marks— [these are auspicious]."

In the color of a water-jar (*kumbha*), there is a threefold frog; in white, a yellow chameleon; in the color of a lizard or iguana, a worn-out stone; in the color of a sword, water-dust; in the dark-blue of a bee, a piece of wood; in the color of honey, a flash of honey; in the color of a variegated deer, a scorpion;
in the color of a parrot's wing, a yellowish-brown tortoise; in the long [color], a yellow-black snake; in the long red, a red snake; and in the color of all fish, a white stone.

In water of the color of a sword-blade, there is a swarm of bees; in that which is dark as a blue lotus, it contains fish and small fry; in that which exceeds [the normal color], it is like a bandhūka flower; in that which is like an indrakoṣa, there is a thief; and in that which has whirlpools and knots— (p.

Or, in a [stone] of variegated color, there is a variegated scorpion; in a whirlpool-patterned [stone], Vajragarbha; in a diamond (*vajra*), Vajragarbha; in gold, Suvarṇagarbha; in silver, Rajatagarbha; in one that is reddish-dark, Raktapāṃsu. For all sacrifices, the cause of success is as follows: white dust belongs to the Preceptor (*ācārya*); for those who know the *gaulīkāra*, crystal; for Brāhmaṇas, death; and for cows, a hundred *yojanas*. When performed, it grants a hundred *yojanas* to the sacrificer, the Preceptor, and the lord of kings, and one *yojana* to others.

There will be distress for those possessing ash-liṅgas; there will be an end to disturbances caused by mice within fourteen yojanas; there will be fear of thieves from the house-lizard (*gṛhagaulika*) within eighteen yojanas;
there will be fear of disease from the red and yellow tortoise (*kacchapa*); for those dwelling in temples and for soldiers, [there will be danger] within ten yojanas;

there will be various types of swelling from the lizard (*kṛkalāsa*) within twenty yojanas; there will be famine and suffering for the wives of the sacrificers, teachers, and kings due to the yellow snake (*pītasarpa*) within sixteen yojanas.

There is danger from snakes for the Śūdras; there is danger from serpents when a black cobra appears, and the destruction of Śūdras and Mlecchas occurs. On a cracked stone, [the calamity extends] twenty-five yojanas; on a variegated and glossy stone, there is drought. On a stone covered with water and dust, there is [distress to] animals;
on one with fireflies and frogs, there is danger to the lives of bipeds and quadrupeds; and when there is the purpose of a plague of locusts, the sacrificer and the preceptor face misfortune.

For kings and all living beings, there is the loss of sons and suffering for twelve people. Regarding the Khadyotagarbha: when the sacrificer, the preceptor, and the kings are associated with a fetus resembling a vein-tormenting knot (*sirāvarta-granthi*), and it is placed in a vessel of gold and wealth, they become free from harm.
There will be an abundance of wealth and grain for the sacrificer, the preceptor, the kings, and all living beings; there will be good rain and happiness for all creatures.

251) Now, regarding the Brahma-sūtra-vivara-pūjā-bhāga: having set aside [the portion], the upper part of the section should be fashioned with gold; that [portion] has the tip of a lotus bud and the tip facing the northwest (vāyavya). All the lines [belonging to] the portion for the worship of the officiating priests (ṛtvij) consist of the root-portion, the stalk, and the kumuda-stalk, measuring one māṣa.

The embrace occurs when the sides are slightly depressed and the back is clearly elevated. On the *uttamaliṅga*, the three lines consisting of Pārvatī, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī are explained as the Brahma-sūtra; this should be inferred for other types of lingas as well. Alternatively, having divided the length of the linga into nine parts and [measuring] from the base, one should draw the Brahma-sūtra through the middle five parts. These are: the tip of the lotus bud, the root of the lotus pericarp, and the tip of the pericarp. In that regard:

The worship of the central line (madhyamarekhā) reaches the base of the portion; it is as long as a lotus stalk, depressed by the measure of a barley grain or a bean, with its back elevated like the hollow of a wicked horse, and it is to be fashioned with all remaining details completed. On both sides of an excellent liṅga, they are depressed by half a thumb and one finger in width. In other liṅgas, this should be understood as following the same proportion. Now, for a [liṅga] of one cubit, the central line is one barley grain [in depth]; for two cubits, it is two barley grains; for three cubits—

The increase is such that they become three times the measure, up until they reach nine measures. Alternatively, having divided the width of the liṅga into one part, one should draw the central line with a measurement of one finger-breadth in the middle; its quarter-measure is the depth of the sides. Or else, one should draw the central line of the worship-section from the top of the head down to the base. On the right, in the half of the single *sarvaśakti*, [it extends] from the back portion to both sides of the right... [and so on].

In sequence, these—Raudrī, Vāmā, and Jyeṣṭhā—are said to be gradually bent inward. On the side of the supreme Śiva-liṅga, at a depth of two and a half finger-breadths, they extend for one finger-breadth in width along the inner side, gradually curving inward.

Therefore, by this method, one should bow to the others. On the ground, one should fashion a poison-free portion as the pedestal (*pīṭha*), a partless linga (*niṣkalaliṅga*) as the base, and a half-pedestal linga (*ardhapīṭhaliṅga*). Depending on the state of the devotee, in the case of a mobile linga (*caraliṅga*)... [it is] not black, not within the range of the senses, like a dog, not a crow, not a rat... liberated from [the cycle of] Māyā and so forth, liberated in Śiva, consisting of all beings, the Kauluṇḍa made firm and stable... [one should act] with such [qualities] toward the teacher of desire (*kāmācārya*).

Accompanied by four, eight, or twelve preceptors, and together with the disciples, [the officiant] should be adorned with garments, a pair of cloths, and blazing ornaments such as bracelets, waist-bands, earrings, and finger-rings; having offered five oblations to Maheśvara, he should be regarded as one whose devotion to the Vedas is manifest. Having circumambulated from the front and entered at an auspicious moment, [he should perform the rite] with a golden probe, [offering] the portion for worship.

Having divided the *vadhā* (the base) and set aside one-sixth from the bottom, one should form a lotus bud (*kamalamukulam*) in the seventh part. It should be one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) in a one-cubit structure, two fingers in a two-cubit structure, and so on according to the order of increase; alternatively, having divided the portion for worship (*pūjābhāga*) into sixteen parts, one should form the bud in the twelfth part. The *Ṛgveda* is the central line, Rudra himself is *Raudrī*; the *Yajurveda* is the left line, Viṣṇu is *Vāmā* Śakti; the *Sāmaveda* is the right face, [and] Brahmā.

The power of Jyeṣṭhā is the Praṇava, a bud, half a barleycorn, or a bud-like form; having emerged from the sides at the base of the bud, they become joined at the back. According to the opinion of Nārāyaṇa, the root of the Madhurekhā is wound at the base and extends downward. According to the opinion of Caturmukha, it is four finger-breadths in height. The three middle fingers belong to Agastya, Vasiṣṭha, and others, measuring two finger-breadths. [It is associated with] Umā, Śrī, Sarasvatī, Dharaṇī, and Gāyatrī.

The measurement for the group of Mothers beginning with Durgā is two finger-breadths greater [than the previous]; one should divide the first sūtra-line sixteenfold and fashion it into twenty-four or sixteen sections from top to bottom.
Mix [the wood] with white mineral substances (*sitadhātu*) and, having placed the *brahmasūtra* amidst the rice grains— either in five layers or a single layer—

and having installed the *liṅga*, the artisan, facing west, should mark the measurements for the front, the sides, and the top using an axe, provided with a measuring cord (*yavanikā*). At that very spot, he should provide the artisans with the sight of a tawny cow (*kapilā*), as well as a golden needle from that tawny cow, another measuring cord, and so forth.

Furthermore, one should wash [the image] with eight kinds of soft water, with decoctions of eight trees, with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), with the five purifiers, and with those called "seeds" as prescribed for the temple. One should wash it with all-fragrant waters using the *Hiraṇyavarṇa*, *Pavamāna*, and *Śuddha* hymns. Again, one should wash it with saffron, sandalwood, and camphor water, accompanied by the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Viṣṇusūkta*, and the *Brahmajñāna*.

Furthermore, having anointed [the image] with all kinds of perfumes, worshipped it with lotuses, blue water-lilies, and *bilva* fruits, and covered it with linen cloths, one should circumambulate the city or the temple three times from left to right with the most excellent seeds, and then cause it to enter the sacrificial pavilion while reciting the *Svastisūkta*. Alternatively, having mounted it upon a chariot, an elephant, or a palanquin, one should cause it to be circumambulated. Surrounded by the four castes and many people, one should offer a portion of silver.

Having caused it to resound with the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and musical instruments, and accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and shouts of "Victory!", one should cause the Śiva-liṅga to perform a circumambulation.
One should then perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) in a decorated pavilion during an auspicious moment.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter on the characteristics of the Liṅga in the Kālottara.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
I shall now describe, in brief, the consecration of the Liṅga; listen at this moment.
During the period of the sun’s northern course (uttarāyaṇa), in the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), on an auspicious day. || 1 ||
Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Puṣya, Punarvasu,
and the three Uttaras are said to be [auspicious] for the consecration and the preliminary ritual of installation. (2)
The preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) is said to take place under the asterisms of Vāruṇa, Vāyavya, Pauṣṇa, or Aindrāgneya, and during the Vāra-yoga or Siddhi-yoga.
Soma (Monday), Śukra (Friday), Budha (Wednesday), and Jīva (Thursday) [are auspicious] when joined with the second, fifth, seventh, tenth, twelfth, or thirteenth lunar days. || 4 ||
On the seventh day from the Nandā, or on the day of consecration (adhivāsana),
one should prepare a pavilion not too far in front of the palace.
It should be ten, twelve, sixteen, or twenty cubits in size,
provided with four doors and adorned with four archways.
There should be a canopy above, with canopies moving about and garlands of darbha grass hanging down;
in the center of that, one should construct a firm floor, and those two [the canopy and the floor] alone [should be made of wood].
One should scatter thirty-six *droṇas* of *śāli* rice there,
and with half that amount of *taṇḍula* rice, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
One should prepare a bed there using five [blankets] or even three;
having spread a woolen blanket (kambala) there, one should likewise place a covering (paristaraṇa) on top of it.

There, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the primary seed-syllables; for all rites are accomplished by means of the heart-mantra joined with the three primary seed-syllables.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day by those versed in the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas,
he should be joined with the Vāmadeva mantra and the Prāsāda mantra.
O child, having recited once the mantra "śanno devīrabhiṣṭaye" conjoined with the principal seed-syllable, one should cause Śiva to lie down upon the bed.
One should worship with perfumes and flowers and cover [the deity] with a pair of garments.
One should place there water-pots made of gold, silver, or copper. (13)
O child, the principal pitcher should be made of gold or silver,
or else a vessel made of copper filled with nine āḍhakas [of water].
Into that vessel, which is filled with clarified butter, one should place a hundred-petaled lotus;
or the wise man may place half of it, but not by means of a spell when [the mind] is tranquil.
The wise mantra-practitioner, recollecting the all-pervading Vyomavyāpin,
should place Śiva upon a single seat and clothe him with two garments while reciting the mantra for the garments.
One should place eight water-pots (kalaśas) extending from Indra to Īśāna;
one should pour the five-jewel water into the eastern pot, which is at the end [of that row].
The wise practitioner should place the subtle five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the southern jar;
Śivottama in the western jar, and Ekanetra in the northern jar.
Having placed milk as prescribed by Śiva into the pitcher, and ghee upon the ghee,
one should then place the Ekarudra decoction in the northeast.
In the southeast, one should place the Trimūrti pitcher containing water with eight types of earth;
in the southwest, one should place the Śrīkaṇṭha pitcher containing barley and flowers.
One should place the vessel of Śrīkaṇṭha in the northwest, filled with all kinds of fragrant water;
having worshipped it on all sides with a pair of separate garments.
The procedure for the *kūrca* and the thread should be performed separately; one should quickly wrap [the area].
Having placed the jars according to the rule, one should thereafter commence the fire sacrifice (*homa*).

The *stuhoma* should be performed in the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), and the *prāsādahoma* on the fourteenth lunar day; furthermore, for special occasions, all sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) should be made square.
256) I shall describe the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) according to the ritual procedure in the Adhivāsa pavilion:
the eastern one should be square, while that in the southeast is triangular. || 24 ||
In the south, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should have the appearance of a half-moon; in the southwest, it should be triangular;
in the west, the pit should be circular; and in the northwest, it should be five-cornered. || 25 ||
In the north (saumyā) he should place one with the luster of a lotus, and in the northeast (aiśānī) a seven-cornered one;
the expert in the science of architecture (vāstuvidyāviśārada) should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice within the square.
By Brāhmaṇas, such as Putraka and others previously mentioned, who possess the required characteristics, [adorned] with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, sacred threads, and finger-rings. || 27 ||
Covered with a pair of new garments, wearing turbans and upper cloths,
one should begin the fire-oblation from the eastern direction toward the southeast according to the prescribed attire.
Then one should perform the oblation with the Yajurveda in the south and the southwest;
and in the west and the northwest, the singer of Sāmans should commence the oblation.
In the north (Saumyā) and in the northeast (Aiśānī), he should begin the *atharva*-oblation;
the preceptor, stationed at the head [of the altar], should begin the oblation with double the quantity.
One should perform the Homa for Śaṅkara in a quadrangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
[The sacrificial wood should be] from the Palāśa, Khadira, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, and Nyagrodha trees.
The Bilva, Udumbara, Śamyā, Apāmārga, Nṛpakṣaka, Jātī, Vakula, Rājārka, Kadamba, and the Mango tree as well; || 32 ||
The fuel-sticks (samidh) may be made of śirīṣa, panasa, or vaikaṅkata wood; the faggot (idhma) should be two spans long, and the fuel-stick itself should be the length of a palm tree.
O Vatsa, I have previously described the *sruva*, the *darvī*, and the *sruk* ladles;
specifically, one should obtain fire churned from wood, or even from the house of a learned *śrotriya*. (34)
One should bring the Jātavedas [fire] into either a copper vessel or an earthenware bowl;
there, one who has mastered the ritual procedures should perform the rites beginning with the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*). (35)

The vessel for clarified butter, the *praṇītā* water, the *prokṣaṇī* water, sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, the *sruva* ladle, the *darvī* spoon, the *sruc* large ladle, rice for the offering, and a mortar. || 36 ||
Fragrance, flowers, fruit, water, charcoal, a fan, as well as a royal broom, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, rice, and bamboo. (37)
O child, wild rice and wheat should be placed to the north of the fire;
indeed, one should prepare all these items in the form of the moon.
The entire ritual procedure has been described, as well as the performance of the fire-rite;
having consecrated the fire according to the rules, one should cause it to be offered to the officiating priests.
Thereafter, all the officiating priests (ṛtvijas) should indeed cause it to be offered into the fire;
first, they should perform the oblation (homa) with the Puruṣa-mantra and with the verse "imā rudrāya".

In the southeast, one should offer oblations with the *hṛdayamantra* and also with the *tryambaka* mantra; in the south, however, one should offer the *aghoramantra*, and all around, one should offer oblations with the *rudramantra*.
With the *śikhā* mantra, [he worships] in the southwest with "Obeisance to you, O Rudra, for your wrath";
in the west, with the *sadyojāta* mantra, with "O Agni, come hither, O Guha. (42)
In the northwest, one should perform the oblation with the Kavaca mantra; in the east, with the Puruṣasūkta; and in the north, with the Vāmadevya and the verse "śanno devīrabhiṣṭaye. (43)
One should perform the oblation in the northeast with the Śiromantra and with Caṇḍarudra;
one should cause the Vāstuhoma to be performed with the Navacatvāri mantra.
A twice-born man who knows the ritual of the site (vāstu) should perform the oblation with the mantra "Vāstoṣpate" alone;
he should perform the temple-oblation (prāsādahoma) with the primary seed-mantra (bīja) consisting of eight syllables.
The Rudra-sūkta, the Puruṣa-sūkta, and likewise the Viṣṇu-sūkta;
the Haṃsa-śuci, the Śannavarga, the Anna-sūkta, and the Jātavedas [sūkta]. (46)
Pavamāna and Hiraṇya, likewise the Caturhotṛ, the Saptahotṛ, the Daśahotṛ, and Rudraikādaśa as well; || 47 ||
Indeed, the Agra-hotṛ, the Śatarudrīya, the Brahmasāman, the Samajyeṣṭha, the Sāman, the Vikarṇa, and the Rudrasāman [are the hymns]. (48)
The Mahāvrata, the Puruṣagati, and the Bahiṣpavamāna;
likewise the Nīlarudra, the Mahārudra, and the Atharvaśiras. || 49 ||
The offerings for Māhendra, Bārhaspatya, Vaiṣṇava, and Saura should be made with clarified butter according to the rules of homa by twice-born priests belonging to their respective Vedic branches.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations separately with all the materials such as fuel-sticks and clarified butter;
one should offer one hundred oblations each with the Sāvitrī and the Vyāhṛtis.
With the five purifiers (pavitra), the principal seed-syllables of the limbs of Śiva,
the all-pervading Vyomavyāpin, the eight forms (mūrtis), and together with the eight Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras).
From Gaṇeśa [he received] the world-protectors and the weapons; also the groups of Mothers, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Nāgas, and even Kiṃpuruṣas. || 53 ||
[He saw] yakṣas, the hosts of Maruts, as well as Garuḍas and Rākṣasas,
Vidyādharas and Yātudhānas, numbering five hundred and fifty.
Twenty and fifteen, ten and twelve, eight and seven, six and five, four and three indeed. (55)
Two for the Rākṣasas and one for the Piśācas;
having offered in this manner according to the rule, one should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then, with the *prāsāda* mantra, one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* offering;
having offered clarified butter, one should touch [the disciple's] head, and having offered parched grain (*lāja*), one should touch the sense organs. (57)
Having offered the *caru* oblation, one should touch the mouth; having offered fuel-sticks (*samidh*), one should touch the navel;
having offered sesame seeds, one should touch the eyes; and having offered rice, one should touch the belly. (58)
O Six-faced One, having offered wild rice with the *Praṇava* and the *Prāsāda* mantra eight times,
O Six-faced One, one should take up barley with the thighs and offer it once with the *Sakṛcchra* mantra.
The wise one, joined with the Prāsāda mantra and conjoined with the seed-syllable at its head, should touch [the disciple] with the Prasṛta mudrā.
O child, at midnight one should offer an oblation of five-colored caru;
there, one should bind a protective thread (pratisara) made primarily of lotus fiber.
There, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings;
and at that time, O Guha, one should feed eleven Brahmins with milk-rice (pāyasa).
At night, one should perform a great festival with the auspicious sounds of conchs and trumpets;
indeed, one should cause the offering of the *diśābali* to be given.
The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed at night, and the installation (sthāpana) should take place in the morning. || 64 ||
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter on the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) in the *Kālottara*. 48.
Prosperity!
Īśvara said:
I shall proclaim the supreme ritual for consecration (pratiṣṭhā), which brings about all perfections.
Having laid out the lines for the inner sanctum (garbhageha) in the eight directions according to the rule, [one should proceed]. (1)
Having first laid out the Brahma-thread, the knower of mantras, by means of the principal seed-syllable,
should properly fashion the door to the east of the womb-chamber.
Having carefully divided the door into twenty-one parts,
one should place a single part in the center and make the "flower-source" (kusumākara) consist of three parts.
One should fashion it either in the shape of a lotus petal, or in the shape of a water-lily petal; it may be like a white water-lily petal, or it may be like the flower of a female swan.
One should bind the desired twenty-eight pīṭhas;
one should likewise construct the base (upāna), the plinth (jagatī), and the three girdles (mekhalā).
The height of the Viṣṇu-portion and the width of the worship-portion [should be equal];
furthermore, the width of all the pedestals (pīṭhas) should be increased by two units.
The portion for worship is one-fourth; the navel is one-third, which is the lowest [measurement].
The pedestal (pīṭha) is equal to the door, and its own self is twice that of the pedestal.

The pedestal’s enjoyment consists of three and one; the pedestal has a hand-span of ghee-water, being square on the hips and circular [elsewhere]. Having placed two parts upon the ground with the front portion diminished, the pedestal is level with the hanging liṅga; the womb is three [parts], and the fourth is the ornament, the two dharmas, or the circumference of the width.
One should fashion the womb according to the prescribed rule and bind Mahāmāyā;
it should be performed by means of two segments, while Umā would be formed by a single one.
One should have a liṅga made of stone and its pedestal (pīṭha) made of metal;
one should make a wooden [liṅga] with wood, and a clay [liṅga] with clay.
With whatever substance the *liṅga* is made, with that same substance the pedestal (*pīṭhaka*) should be made;
[namely] diamond, emerald, ruby, pearl, and coral. (11)
(261) One should make the pedestal of crystal, ruby, sun-crystal, or moon-crystal; or else, O Kuru, it may be made of iron or brass. 12.
O Six-faced One, there is neither movement nor pressure, nor binding; however, O Six-faced One, if there is movement in the eastern [channel], it is a sign that danger will befall the Kṣatriyas. (13)
If the Liṅga moves toward the southeast, whether through negligence or by transgression, there will be danger for the Brāhmaṇas; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (14)
If the liṅga moves toward the south, immediate death will occur;
if the liṅga moves toward the southwest, there will be danger to four-footed animals. (15)
It is said that for quadrupeds and bipeds, death occurs immediately [if the seat is handled improperly].
Therefore, being composed and wise, one should worship the seat slowly.
The knower of mantras should avoid the locations of Indra and the others for the Soma-vessel;
instead, he should install the Linga in the northeast, which is to be worshipped as long as the moon and stars endure.

Whether it be a barley-corn or even half a barley-corn, if one relies on something [even] slightly toward the northeast, there will be abundance of food, an increase in cattle, and the proliferation of sons and grandsons. (18)
Therefore, with every effort, one should take some shelter in the northeast;
afterwards, one should perform the ritual bathing according to the procedure seen in the scriptures.
Having covered the liṅga with a cloth, one should perform the binding of the pedestal (pīṭhabandha).
The liṅga is Maheśāna himself in person, and the pedestal shall be Umā herself in person. (20)
The pedestal is Mahāviṣṇu himself; the liṅga is Sadāśiva himself.
The earth itself is the pedestal, while the supreme ether is indeed the liṅga.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the binding of the pedestal;
the eightfold binding should be executed within the cavity of the pedestal-liṅga.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, the Pīṭhabandha-paṭala, in the Kālottara-tantra. 49.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said: I shall describe the procedure for the ritual bathing (snāna), which destroys all sins,
brings about all peace, and annihilates all misfortunes.

At the conclusion of a consecration, during the purification of the site, when an ancient temple is renovated, during an eclipse, at the equinoxes, at the solstices, and during the Vyatīpāta yoga; (2)

At the royal consecration, during auspicious ceremonies, at a wedding, in the performance of mantra-sādhanā, at the conclusion of initiation, during extraordinary events, and upon seeing a terrible or evil dream; (3)
And at the end of a festival, in battle, during affliction by disease among the people, during an earthquake, in times of famine, and also upon the breaking of an image. || 4 ||
In the event of a sudden schism in the assembly, or due to a great plague or flood,
one should perform the consecration of the ground for the establishment of a seat (pīṭha) and the work of plastering with lime.

And for one suffering from consumption (rājayakṣmā), O Guha, one should cause a bath to be performed after physical exercise using vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, which are well-constructed.
O Guha, one should cause the ceremonial bath to be performed with a hundred thousand, or ten thousand, or a billion, or a hundred million, or ten million, or even a million offerings.
Then one should perform the ceremonial bath with five hundred, or even half of that, or eighty-eight,
or eighty-one, or sixty-four [pots].
The northern [line] should have one square, while the southern should consist of two;
between those two, the expert in the tantras should cause a large thread to be drawn.
p.
263) However, the wise one should provide water for those previously mentioned;
he should place it there, having dissolved it to the measure of half a barleycorn. 10.
One should cause the width at the base of the liṅga to be made upon the foot-stone;
one should increase it by one aṅgula, so that the width becomes eight aṅgulas.
Having properly placed [the vessel] beneath the portion for Brahmā according to the ritual injunctions,
one should recite "brahmajajñānam" and likewise "sadasaspatim."
Once these two have been established, one should firmly and properly prepare the foundation below;
the placement of jewels (ratnanyāsa) should be performed upon the Brahma-pāda stone.
O Six-faced One, [the substances are] jewels, metal, minerals, earth, water, and fragrance; as well as seeds, medicinal herbs, and flowers—these are the nine categories.
Vajra, ruby, emerald, pearl, coral, topaz, and sunstone and moonstone—these [are the gems]. || 15 ||
O Mahāsena, [one may offer] sapphire, gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead, along with mantras dedicated to Brahmā, Ādya, and Īśāna. || 16 ||
O Guha, one should place āra, vidula, and kāṃsya as before;
likewise, tālaka, gandhaka, śīla, dara, gairika, and mākṣika.
O Guha, one should place saurāṣṭra, añjana, and lead as before;
its body [is formed] from the root of a boar's tusk and kuśa grass.
O child, one should cast auspicious earth from a lake, a granary, an anthill, a field, or from the center of a sacrificial altar, preceded by mantras as before.
The root of the *paṅkaja*, the root of the *utpala*, the *kumuda*, the *kahlāra*, the *koṭī*, and the *nīlotpala* as well; || 20 ||
O child, one should scatter a hundred *nandyāvartas* or even nine roots of *vyāghāta* as before, using the mantras beginning with Brahmā and ending with Īśāna. (21)
One should prepare sandalwood, saffron, rhinoceros horn, iron, the three fruits, and musk with the leaf as the ninth, as previously described. || 22 ||
One should prepare rice, wild rice, wheat, barley, bamboo-seed, and priyaṅgu, along with sesame, mung beans, and black gram, as previously described. (23)
Lakṣmī, sahadevī, viṣṇukrāntā, and likewise nṛpa, śāribā, indravallī, sūryāvarta, and the balās; || 24 ||
One should arrange the white *girikarṇī* as before, as well as *mallikā*, *jāti* flowers, *vakula*, and *pāṭala* flowers. || 25 ||
O child, one should likewise arrange the lotus, the blue water-lily, the campaka, the nandivartaka, and the ninth, the vakula, as before.
A wise man, having fashioned the earth out of gold weighing ten *niṣkas*, should cast it [into the water];
and having fashioned a tortoise out of twelve *niṣkas* of gold, he should likewise cast it in.
O child, one should indeed have the form of a young calf made for thirty niṣkas,
as well as a bull, a lion, an elephant, the Śrīvatsa mark, and a kettle-drum.
One should arrange the mirror, the full water-pot, and the lamp as the eighth auspicious object;
likewise, one should prepare the archway with the ritual vessels as before.
One should deposit each [seed] with five gold coins (niṣkas) as the primary seed;
having recited the five purifiers (pavitrakas), one should consecrate the temple with those primary seeds.
Having recited the nine verses beginning with "skanda indra," one should cast [the offerings];
there, one should milk five separate tawny cows for these two sets of verses. || 31 ||
Having cooked milk-rice (*pāyasa*) according to the prescribed rite, one should smear it with the *tryambaka* mantra on an auspicious hour,
during the day, under a favorable asterism, and on a suitable lunar day, O Guha. (32)
Having bathed and sipped water according to the rules, the composed preceptor should install Maheśāna, the God of gods, by means of the Vāma mantra. (33)
Having recited the Sadyojāta mantra, one should say, "Arise, O Brāhmaṇa priest!
and, having raised up the God of gods, one should carry him out upon a cart.
O child, whether upon a chariot or indeed upon an elephant,
one should circumambulate a village, a city, or even a port.
The sacrificer should follow behind with his sons, brothers, and wife;
the preceptor, however, should go in front, composed and holding the *arghya* offering for him.

[He addressed] all the various people of the city, including the brahmins and others in due order, amidst the sounding of conchs and trumpets and the auspicious proclamations of "Auspicious Day! and "Victory! (37).
The Brahmins should recite the Śakuna-sūkta on all sides with auspicious sounds;
having arrived at the temple, he should enter the inner sanctum (garbha-mandira).
Having brought him to the doorway, one should offer him the *arghya*;
then, having discarded the remains of the offerings (*nirmālya*) according to all the tantras, Guha should enter. (39)
Having rested there for half a ghaṭikā, neither too quickly nor too slowly,
[he should proceed] to the divine hundred palaces, encapsulated by the principal seed-syllable.

The wise one, devoted to meditation on Śiva, having meditated upon the manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala), should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) over the Brahma-stone with the root mantra.
Therein one should deposit the five Brahmans; one should deposit the clusters of kalās in sequence. One should consecrate the deity with Sadyojāta and establish him with Vāmadeva.
The presence [of the deity] should be restrained by Aghora, but by Puruṣa;
the flowers, the crown, and the earrings [should be offered] by Īśāna. (43)
Having established Sadyojāta in the west, and likewise Vāmadeva in the north;
having established Aghora in the south, one should place Puruṣa in the east.
One should indeed install Īśāna in the middle of the head according to the path of emanation—
the three-eyed, two-armed deity who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel.
The god is endowed with five faces and possessed of five heads;
he is the god wearing divine garments and anointed with divine perfumes.
Resembling pure crystal, seated upon a white lotus, the witness of all, adorned with every ornament. || 47 ||
One should indeed install the god Sadāśiva, the God of gods, who is endowed with thirty-nine kalās, within the liṅga by means of the primary seed-syllable (bīja).
Having meditated upon the supreme reality, the God of gods, Śiva, who is partless, stainless, peaceful, free from conceptual proliferation, and without defining characteristics; || 49 ||
He is unknowable, devoid of destruction and origination, free from the expressed and the expresser—the wondrous Lord of the Assembly (Sadasaspati). 50.
Free from that which is to be rejected or accepted, devoid of salt and alkaline, the supreme Brahman accessible to yogis—therefore, rise above this. (51)
Having thus meditated upon the Lord who is Nirvāṇa, devoid of qualities, blissful, immovable, and eternal, O Mahāsena, one should be endowed with grace.
O Guha, one should place the Prāsāda mantra upon the head of the Liṅga;
one should place the Prāsāda mantra in the heart of Sadāśiva.
Having encapsulated [the mantra] with the *praṇava* and recited it five times, one should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*).
Having recited the *hṛllekhā* mantra three times over the portion belonging to Viṣṇu, one should then perform the ritual placement.
One should place the Vyāhṛtis in the Praṇava and the Brahma-portion;
then, having assigned the Vidyā-tattva, one should assign the Ātma-tattva in the middle.
O Guha, one should then place the Śiva-tattva above, along with the three seed-syllables;
furthermore, one should place the purifiers upon the body according to the rule by means of the kalā-mantras.
Having placed Īśāna on the head, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face;
having placed Aghora on the heart, one should assign Vāmadeva to the private parts.
O Six-faced One, one should place Sadyojāta on the foot with its respective syllable, likewise in the east, the south, the west, and the north. (58)
One should visualize Īśāna joined above at the crown of the head;
likewise in the east, the south, the west, and the north. (59)
One should place Tatpuruṣa, endowed with an upward-facing face, upon the five faces;
likewise, one should place Īśāna on the heart, the neck, the two shoulders, and the navel.
O Mahāsena, one should place all the Aghora-mantras on the chest and the back;
likewise on the anus, the genitals, the thighs, the knees, and the shanks as well.
Having likewise assigned the thirteen Vāmadeva-kalās in sequence to the two buttocks, the throat, and both sides; 62.
One should place the eight kalās of Sadyojāta in sequence upon the feet, the hands, the nose, the head, and both external [shoulders]. (63)
One should place the syllables beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, starting from *tārā* (the seed-syllable), in their proper sequence.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner according to the rules, one should perform the ceremonial bath with the water-pitchers.
The wise one, having combined it with the *puruṣasūkta* and the *prāsāda* [mantra],
should again bathe it with scented water and the principal seed-syllables (*bīja*). (65)
O Guha, one should worship with divine perfumes, flowers, incenses, water-offerings, and food-oblations, indeed using the primary seed-syllable of the heart-mantra.
With divine garments and ornaments such as necklaces and armlets, as well as crowns, earrings, and golden sacred threads. || 67 ||
With the waist-thread, the belly-band, and the primary seed-syllables of the letter *nā*,
one should thus prostrate according to the complete ritual procedure and ask for forgiveness.
"Having blocked the door, the wise one [should act] where there are seven digits.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter on consecration in the *Kālottara*. 50.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
Then, on that day, one should have the pedestal (pīṭha) constructed;
