having divided the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) into three parts, the excellent pedestal occupies two parts. || 1 ||
The inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall consist of five parts, and half of one part shall be the lowest [measurement];
it may be square, circular, lotus-shaped, or even in the form of a [geometric] division.
One should cause it to be made facing the fire, or as a triangle, or even as a pentagon;
or one may cause it to be made as a heptagon, or an octagon, or even a nonagon.
One should make it ten-cornered, or twelve-cornered, or even sixteen-cornered;
or one may make it eighteen-cornered, or even twenty-cornered.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should have the luster of a blue lotus flower, or the shape of a dhurdhūraka; or the pedestal may be of variegated form, or even in the shape of a tortoise. (5)
One should have it made with thirty-three,
or twenty-five, or sixteen, or nine [units] of atasī.
O Mahāsena, the ceremonial bath must certainly be performed by universal monarchs with jars filled by the learned,
just as it was performed by Mahāviṣṇu in the past, O child.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) performed the ceremonial bath with arbudas of water-jars;
Āditya performed it with nikharvas, and Guha indeed with all [the remaining] Śakras.
In this manner, O dear one, a sovereign ruler (sārvabhauma) should have [the image] made with two million [units];
a regional lord (maṇḍalika), however, with five hundred, and one who possesses no hair [on his body] with five hundred as well.
O child, the ceremonial bath should be performed with common kings and various types of Brahmins, using a thousand pitchers arranged in rows.
A bath with jars completely filled with three āḍhakas is the most excellent;
with jars completely filled with two āḍhakas, it shall be middling.
The bathing should be performed with the smallest [vessels] filled with a single measure of water;
the extent of the pavilion should be equal to the extent of the kalaśas.
There, the most excellent of men should cause twenty squares to be made across;
he should fill those twenty squares with materials according to the prescribed rule.
O Six-faced One, having performed the horizontal rite with the ten procedures,
O child, perform it with ten thousand jars and ten thousand [measures].
In this manner, O dear one, one should have ten nyarbudas performed;
one should fill [the vessels] with a hundred thousand nyarbudas of ghee. || 15 ||
A *kharva* [of offerings] consists of ablutions performed with twelve thousand jars;
through ablutions with a *niyuta* of jars, it becomes ten thousand times that. (16)
With ten thousand ablutions using ghee, one completes a thousand-fold rite;
having completed a hundred with thousands, the wise man should perform the ceremonial bath.
For five hundred [palas], there should be fifty; for a hundred, the tenth part [should be used].
Half of the ghee should indeed be milk, and half of the milk should be curd.
One should add cow dung and cow urine, along with a quarter-part of curd;
the water of the coconut should be equal in measure to the milk. || 19 ||
Half a part of curd and half of that amount of sugarcane juice is said to be honey;
O child, there are twenty-five parts of snow-water and twenty [parts of the other ingredients].
Fifteen, ten, five, three, two,
or even one thousand measures of snow-water, O Six-faced One, one should indeed prepare.
The waters of the Gaṅgā [are divided into] thirty-six, thirty, twenty-five, twenty, fifteen, ten, six, five, two, and one. || 22 ||
One [part] should be mixed with a thousand [parts] along with the remaining ingredients combined with water;
this is the "Great Bathing" (mahāsnapana), and for the rest, one should employ dances.
Now, for the sake of brevity, I shall describe the thousand-pitcher rite:
O Guha, having first scattered twenty rows extending from south to north, (one should proceed).
O Guha, it should be laid out with ten streets from south to north;
furthermore, there shall be fifty squares each from west to east.
Having first thus prepared the scattered paths and enclosed them, one should place two *prasthas* of *śāli* rice at the base of each individual jar. || 26 ||
O child, one should place half of that amount of rice at every step;
[one should also prepare] jars that have been washed, purified, fumigated, and smeared with fragrance.

(271) They [should be] provided with cloth, joined with *kūrca*-grass, accompanied by threads, and furnished with the ritual implements; they should be bound together with mango sprouts and honored with fragrant scents. || 28 ||
O Guha, the preceptor, or sixteen, or twelve, or eight, or even four preceptors, should perform the ceremonial bath.
Wearing new garments, pure, and adorned with all ornaments. || 30 ||
With golden sacrificial threads, necklaces, armlets, and earrings;
adorned with golden flowers, and wearing turbans and upper garments. (31)
With their limbs smeared with fragrant sandalwood and adorned with garlands of white flowers, [they entered] the [shrine] provided with four archways and endowed with four gates. || 32 ||
It was equipped with nine banners, beautified by a canopy above,
and adorned on all sides with strings of pearls and offerings of flowers.
Adorned with the eight auspicious symbols such as the bell, chowrie, and mirror,
it should be raised to the height of a Brahmin's command, with the eight principal mountain ranges situated in the eight directions.
One should construct Mount Mahāmeru in the center, ten cubits in height and consisting of four parts; one should likewise fashion Mount Kailāsa out of white clay, making it equal in size to Meru.
To the south of Maru, one should construct [the city] together with Śrīkailāsa,
Himavat, Vindhya, Sucakra, Mahendra, or Pāriyātraka.
Niṣadha and Nīlaśikhara shall be the ninth, Śrīśaila;
Niṣadha is in the eastern direction, and Himavat is in the south-eastern quarter.
One should place Vindhya to the south; it should be at Śrīśaila in the southwest.
Having established Suvarṇa in the west, Pāriyātraka is in the northwest. (38)
Having established Mount Nīla in the north, O Six-faced One,
one should arrange the peak of Mahendra in the northeast, my child. (39)
Having covered the sacrificial pavilion on all sides with garlands of *darbha* grass,
O dear one, the wise practitioner should place the *śivakumbha* to the east of Mount Meru.
One should cast the five jewels (pañcaratna) therein and pour water from the Gaṅgā;
or else, one may use water as cool as snow, or even pure water.
Having covered it with a pair of garments, the wise one should place the three-fold consciousness;
O Six-faced One, in the tenth row, he should fill fifty [cells] with ghee.
And in the pitchers of his western row, O Ḍaḍānana,
he should fill them with milk while reciting the fifty-syllable Vidyā.
Having filled it with ghee by means of the Īśāna mantra and joined it with the Prāsāda mantra,
there should be fifty [applications] of cow dung in its western row.
O child, O six-faced one, he should consult with the Sadyojāta mantra and the Hṛdaya mantra;
and the water from the eight metals should be placed in its western row.
O child, one should fill [the grid] up to fifty with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra;
then, in its western row, one should fill it with the eight astringents (*kaṣāya*).
O child, the wise one should fill the fifty-pitcher with the primary seed-syllable;
he should then fill it with pure water from its western fifty-pitcher.
Separately, its western [region] is called the eightfold realm (dhātvaṣṭaka): gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead. (48)
The wise one has declared eight types of metal, including copper and brass;
likewise, [the fruits] of the mango, the udumbara, the nyagrodha, and the panasa. (49)
The *aśvattha*, the *śirīṣa*, the *palāśa*, and the *madhūka*—
these are declared to be the eight astringent trees among the category of astringent plants. (50)
The eight [points] are: from the horns of a bull, from the stream [of water], from the root of kuśa grass, from an anthill, from a field, from a granary, and the center of the altar. 51.
Haritāla, gandhakaśilā, darada, gaurika,
añcana, saurāṣṭra, and vārada are declared to be the eight minerals (dhātu).
In its western row, however, there were clods of earth, yellow sandalwood,
saffron, camphor, and the three fruits that cure eye diseases.
The wise man should fill fifty jars with putrid hair;
first, he should fill those fifty jars with a row of clarified butter.
O King, one should fill [the vessel] with water and the eight flowers, beginning with the principal seeds:
the lotus, the water-lily, the *vakula*, and the *pāṭalī*.
One should worship the *punnāga* as the fifth according to the sequence of birth;
and in the row to its east, one should fill eight vessels with water and fruit.
The plantain, the jackfruit, the mango, the pomegranate, the citron, the wood-apple, the coconut, and the orange shall be the eighth. (57)
In the eastern row adjacent to that row, one should fill fifty [cells] with honey;
in the eastern row of this [same] row, one should place sugarcane juice in sequence.
In that row, and indeed in the preceding row, the eight seeds are proclaimed: rice, nīvāra, wheat, barley, bamboo-seed, and priyaṅgu. (59)
The wise man should fill fifty [measures] of sesame and mung beans separately;
from that previous row, he should take water containing the eight medicinal herbs.
Lakṣmīśa, sahadevī, viṣṇukrānti, and likewise nṛpa;
sūryāvarta, valmī, bandhūka, and irikarṇikā. (61)
Having filled fifty jars with their respective primary seed-syllables,
one should place eight grains of great rice in a row to the east of that [arrangement].
Gandhaśāli, mahāśāli, and likewise ratnaśāli;
kṛṣṇaśāli, śvetaśāli, and indeed kalama-śāli. || 62 ||
O child, the preceptor should place wheat and sixty-fold grain within fifty jars,
using the primary seed-mantra.
In the front row, however, one should place the eight substances beginning with turmeric:
turmeric, śatapuṣpā, Gaṅgā, and Haripriyā. (64)
One should fill the first row with the *taskarāmukha*, the *sāvitra*, and the *drāviḍāṣṭaka*, ending with *tuṣārodakamiśra*.
The wise man should take snow-water together with *gaṅgā*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, and *sahadevī*;
the wise man should stir it well and set it aside with the snow.
Water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, and the five items beginning with the root of the lotus;
likewise, the pākaja, the utpala, the kalhāra, and the kumuda.
One should place jars made from the root of the blue lotus in the eight directions;
one should install them, starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna, using the principal seed-syllable.
O child, one should indeed place one thousand and eight jars in their proper order and fill them with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings in sequence.
One should bathe the Lord of the gods with pure and preeminent seed-mantras:
the Rudrasūkta, the Puruṣasūkta, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Tryambaka hymn.
The Haṃsa, Śucim, the group of nine [Śannavarga], Jātavedas, Tvarita, the other Rudra, Pavamāna, and Hiraṇyaka. (71)
O Mahāsena, one should establish the Great Void (mahāvyoma) in due order with five hundred, half of that, half of that again, and also with twenty.
This should be performed with half of that [number], or with one hundred and eight;
and eighty-one should be performed in each group of nine.
O child, one hundred and eight, plus twenty-seven more;
with sixty-four jars, O child, combined with sixty-four substances.

With thirty-two, half of that (sixteen), twenty-five, and sixteen [verses], one should offer water for the feet, water for sipping, the respectful offering (arghya), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and astringent decoctions (kaṣāya). || 75 ||
Water from a corpse, clarified butter, milk, curd, sugarcane juice, honey, water with flowers, water with fruits, scented water, and water with barley; || 76 ||
Water with actual flowers is [the lowest]; water with gold is royal;
and water with coconut or sugarcane juice is divine, consisting of twenty [qualities].
The fruit is proclaimed to be joined with eight, making thirty-three; perform it as previously described by means of twenty-five and twenty-five [units]. 78.
Alternatively, first prepare sixteen [vessels] with sixteen jars;
then, fill that jar with the previously mentioned nine substances.
O Guha, having performed the desired ritual bathing, one should worship as before;
one should offer the five-colored *caru* oblation, prostrate, and ask for forgiveness.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, the Chapter on Ablution, in the Kālottara. 51.
Īśvara said: I shall describe the ritual for the retinue, which accomplishes all desires and purposes,
as well as the eight Lords of Knowledge (Aṣṭavidyeśvaras) and likewise the eightfold form (Aṣṭamūrti).
The eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, the eight Vasus, and the Gaṇeśas who are the guardians of the worlds; || 2 ||
And one should likewise arrange eleven attendants in successive order. || 3 ||
O Guha, one should worship the eight Vidyeśvaras, the eight Mūrtis, the eleven Rudras, and the eight Ṛṣis and Yakṣas upon the pedestal.
One should worship Indra and the others, ending with Īśāna, individually in due order;
on the twelve petals, one should worship the twelve Ādityas and the eight Rudras.
Umā is to be worshipped to the north; one should worship Caṇḍa in the northeast.
Having fully worshipped Nandin in the east, one should worship Mahākāla in the southeast.
Having worshipped Vṛṣabha in the south, Nirṛti in the region of Nirṛti, Śṛṅgīśa in the west, and Ṣaṇmukha in the region of Vāyu; || 7 ||
One should worship Goddess Durgā between Anala and Maya;
O Guha, one should worship Sarasvatī between Yama and Nairṛta.
One should worship Dharaṇī between Nirṛti and Varuṇa;
establish the house of Kubera between Varuṇa and Anila.
Between Soma and Māruta is the unsurpassed station of Jyeṣṭha;
between Īśāna and Soma is the most beautiful station of Viṣṇu.
One who has reached the further shore [of mastery] should have a seat or even a bed constructed there;
build a temple for Pārvatī, Viṣṇu, the planets, and the Four-faced One (Brahmā). || 11 ||
Between Indra and Īśāna is the unsurpassed station of Sūrya;
between Sarasvatī and Yamā is the abode of the group of the Seven Mothers.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍī, and Gaṇādhipa. || 13 ||
The Pīṭhabhadra and the Maṇḍapa, or indeed the Gopura, have been described; O child, construct the storehouse in the north or in the sky (the upper part).
And he should have a treasury for the ornaments of the gods made there of gold, silver, and other materials by a mason, provided with very firm bolts.
To the north of that, a granary for grains should be constructed;
to the east is the abode of Indra, and to the southeast is that of Agni.
In the south is the abode of Yama; in the southwest is the house of Nirṛti;
in the west is the station of Varuṇa; and in the northwest is that of Anila (Vāyu).
In the north (saumyā) is the abode of Soma, and in the northeast (aiśānī) likewise that of Īśa;
the temple of Bhauma, however, shall be four or five cubits in size.
To the east is the Gāndharva pavilion, and in the southeast is the abode of the Apsaras;
and to the south, O dear one, is the excellent house of the Pitṛs.
In the west and the south, there is the supreme abode of the Cāraṇas;
in the southwest (Vāruṇa) is the house of the Vidyādharas, and in the northwest (Vāyavyā) is the abode of Garuḍa.
To the north, however, one should arrange the abode of Vaiśravaṇa,
as well as the dwellings of Jambala, Māṇibhadra, and the treasures Śaṅkha and Padma.
One should designate the abode of the Nāga kings in the northeast;
namely Ananta, Gulaka, Vāsuki, and Śaṅkhapālaka. (22)
Takṣaka, Mahāpadma, Kārkoṭaka, and Mahāsaras [are there];
or else, a peak, a pavilion, or even a temple twelve cubits in size.
Having properly measured a width of six cubits while remaining composed,
he constructed on the right side a firm and excellent palace, the abode of longevity.
On its southern side, however, there should be a house for fasts;
to the west, there should be a circular pond measuring one hundred cubits.
One should surround the garden with blue lotuses, red lotuses, water lilies, and auspicious white lotuses, as well as with beautiful trees such as mangoes and bilvas.
With sandalwood trees, vakula, nāga, punnāga, and auspicious campaka trees; with jackfruit trees, coconut palms, water lilies, and clusters of plantains. || 27 ||
With *karavīra* flowers, *nandikāvarta*, and those clustered with *japā* and *aśoka*, as well as with *mālatī*, *mādhavī*, *madantī*, and *sindhuvāraka*.
And with trees that bloom at midday, crowded with *kuśa* grass and *śāka* plants, as well as *aśvattha*, *brahmavṛkṣa*, red sandalwood, and *veduka* trees. || 29 ||
With saffron, kurava flowers, akṣa seeds, and auspicious resin (sarjarasa);
with saffron, māraka, uśīra, and other auspicious members of that group.
With kuravakas, krauñcakas, maruvakas, and sarasevyakas;
and with Piśācas, Mṛdaṅgī, Bhāryāṅgī, and likewise Garuḍa.
And there were many other auspicious trees endowed with strength and fragrance,
as well as betel vines, areca palms, and edible tubers of every kind.
With wood-apples, citron fruits, pomegranates, and barley-loving fruits, as well as with other flowering trees and excellent, auspicious trees. (33)
One *aśvattha*, one *picumanda*, one *nyagrodha*, ten *tintriṇīs*, six *campakas*, a hundred *tāla* groves, and one *navāgra*—one who plants these does not go to hell. (34)
Water is indeed the calf; one should place the well right there.
The cow-shed should be in the eastern direction, and the dwelling of the ascetics in the south-east.
Within the enclosure wall, he should construct either an assembly hall or a hermitage for the poor, the blind, the wretched, and those who are afflicted. (36)
Within that [enclosure], one should construct a very beautiful kitchen;
and outside the wall, to the east, the station for Rudra’s attendants.
To the south of the temple is a very beautiful village of Brahmins;
outside of that is the royal palace, which is further outside the village of merchants.
Furthermore, for the Śūdras, there are oil-pressers and others;
and outside the Nāgara [quarter], there are the Antyajas who work with gold, iron, and so forth. (39)
Artisans and painters from all directions, as well as washermen, barbers, actors, and potters; (40)
One should place those of the Kaivarta and Bilva castes, as well as seven others of different births,
outside the Takṣakas, even if they are of other lineages.
Two *daṇḍas* to the east of Śiva’s temple is the abode of the Bull;
two *daṇḍas* [further] is the temple of Viṣṇu, and three *daṇḍas* is Gaṇeśvara.
A wise man should construct the house for twelve and other such [deities] starting from the three-fold staff (tridaṇḍa);
the enclosure of the lords of the hosts (gaṇeśvaras) is outside, and the world-protectors (lokapālas) are beyond the three-fold staff.
Outside of the Lokapāla [enclosure], the armor for the six-faced one [Kārttikeya] is fifteen *daṇḍas* long;
beyond that, at twenty *daṇḍas*, is the excellent enclosure wall (*prākāra*) of Śiva. (44)
The wise man should construct a cow-pen, a kitchen, the teacher’s residence, and a storehouse within the enclosure wall. (45)
Within the Gaṇa-āśrama, the Haviḥśālā is highly praised,
as are the temple of Pitāmaha and the temple of Viṣṇu.
One should perform [the rites] within the precincts of Gaṇeśa according to the prescribed ritual;
one should construct a dwelling for those practicing renunciation within the enclosure wall.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter on the Retinue in the Kālottara. 52.
Śrīḥ!
Īśvara said: I shall describe the characteristics of the temple of Śiva, the Supreme Self;
a wise man should cause a rampart to be constructed that is proportionate to the Liṅga itself. (1)
Then one should diligently construct [the temples]:
first the Meru palace, and the second should be Mandara.
The third is named Kailāsa, and the fourth is Malaya;
the fifth is Valabhī, while the sixth is Svacchanda-nandyāvarta.
The seventh is to be known as Svastika, the eighth as Siṃhaprāsāda;
the ninth is Garuḍaprāsāda, and the tenth shall be Vṛṣabha. || 4 ||
The eleventh is Svastipṛṣṭha, the twelfth is Vipula;
the thirteenth is Sukṣetra, and the fourteenth is Mānava. || 5 ||
The great tenth is the fifteenth celestial mansion (*vimāna*), while the sixteenth is indeed a deception;
there are ninety-six palaces (*prāsāda*), of which the sixteenth would be the principal one. (6)
The Śaiva, Brāhma, and Vaiṣṇava styles are indeed the most excellent;
furthermore, there are three types: Nāgara, Drāviḍa, and Vesara.
For the first six are Nāgara, while the middle sixth is Drāviḍa;
the other sixth, O child, is Vatsa, which is the most excellent Vesara.
Thirty-two varieties of Nāgara are proclaimed, thirty-two of Drāviḍa, and thirty-two of Vesara; thus ninety-six are celebrated.

One should recognize that as the Nāgara style, which is devoid of a neck (grīvā) and a channel (nāḍī), and consists of a pinnacle (kūṭa), a chamber (koṣṭha), and a hall (śālā), established with a long lattice-work (cirajāla). || 10 ||
That which is joined with a single hall and possesses an upper hall, yet lacks a nose-projection (nāsikā) in its chamber, is proclaimed as Drāviḍa. || 11 ||
It is endowed with all ornaments, provided with a gabled chamber (kūṭakoṣṭha), joined with a hall-nose (śālānāsikā), and possessed of side-chambers (upāna) and lotus-pavilions (kumuda). || 12 ||
That which is joined with a *kapota* (dove-cot), provided with a *stambhapālikā* (pillar-head molding), and endowed with a neck and a pinnacle (*śikhara*), is proclaimed as the *vesara* style. 13.
Starting from a single world up to a thousand worlds,
O Six-faced One, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra reside during the Kṛta age.
They construct the supreme temple of Śiva with a thousand stories;
however, O Six-faced One, it should be known that in the Tretā age, it has five hundred stories.
In the Dvāpara age, it was formerly performed by sages and gods on a hundred grounds;
however, in the Kali age, that which is performed on sixty grounds is proclaimed as the most excellent.
The middle [measure] should be known as thirty-two [finger-breadths], while sixteen or eight is the smallest;
for humans in the Kali age, however, it is indeed seven, five, or three. (17)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra constitute the hundredfold upper level;
the sixty-four [levels] of Indra and the other world-protectors have been declared. (18)
The earth is declared to belong entirely to the lords of the Gaṇas and the Mothers;
thus it belongs to the gods alone in the Kṛta Yuga, but in the Tretā Yuga, it is devoid of three.
In the Dvāpara age, however, there are three...
[in the Kali age], the seven stages are proclaimed as the highest. || 20 ||
The five-ground [mantra] is the middling, while the one-ground is the inferior;
however, the five-ground of the planets is proclaimed as the best. || 21 ||
The middling [mandala], however, consists of three levels, while the smallest consists of one level;
for the sovereign [mandala], O child, sixteen levels are said to exist.
For all those within the mandala, there may be five, three, two, or seven [days];
beyond that, on the seventh day, there shall be the fear of a great downfall.
For all the ministers, however, three stories are prescribed;
for the vassals, two stories; and for the queens, three stories.
The single ground for the guilds is the same as that for the merchants;
the single ground for the treasurer is the same as that for the superintendent of the three [treasuries]. (25)

The Superintendent of Courtesans [shall supervise] those of independent houses and likewise those of the royal household; the daughters of the king shall occupy one area, while the princes shall occupy another.
A palace or even a mansion, especially for kings, is proclaimed as a *prāsāda* when it is covered with iron or bricks. (27)
A garland devoid of iron or clay is proclaimed as *mālikā*.
For those who are prosperous, it may consist of silver or gold, numbering more than ten thousand [beads]. (28)
One should construct a palace, a garland-shaped structure, a svastika, or a nandivardhana;
for those of the Vaiśya caste, a palace with a valabhi roof or half-arched.
Some make it with the best of bows, while others praise the use of garlands;
for Śūdras and Galikas, the house should be thatched with grass.
Some recommend that for a king it should be a palace; however, for those who know the four Vedas, a house is praised as being of such a size [as previously described]. (31)
For beings who are mixed and for those who drink soma, there should be whiteness;
however, the form of white should never be made for others.

A king who is distinguished, devoted to sacrifice, and skilled in the principles of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas as well as the treatises on ethics (nīti-śāstra), is praised for commissioning the construction of a white temple.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, Yama, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, Īśa, the immortals, the Ādityas, and the Pās. (34)
The ground for Sarasvatī is praised as being white in appearance;
some desire [the ground] for Dhaneśa, while others prefer Vasu, Rudra, and Vināyaka. (35)
Sacrificers with little wealth, as well as the people and ministers, shall perish before long due to the performance of the *dhavalākāra* oblation. (36)
They praise [the practice] among the gods, but one should avoid it among humans;
however, O dear child, among humans it is indeed permitted for both kings and Brahmins. (37)
Among all mortals, one should avoid the white form;
however, the white form may be offered according to the prescribed rite to Śiva, the Supreme Self.
O King, one indeed obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices by visiting Kṛṣṇa, Śilā, Dhavala, Okāra, Mūḍha, and the triad [of shrines] at Guha. (39)
A person obtains the fruit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices,
[attaining a body] free from the network of veins and arteries and devoid of knots or circular masses.
If one should have a temple made from a stone slab of black mountain rock,
one may construct either a *koṭaka*, a *prāsāda*, or a *vesara* style.
A devoted man should have [the temple] constructed either in the Nāgara or Drāviḍa style; [this is equal to] ten million horse-sacrifices and a hundred billion gifts of tawny cows.
O child, one obtains that fruit by means of the Prāsādakroṭaka;
the wise praise the Kroṭaka as superior even to the Prāsāda. (43)
One should have the door-panel made with pillars provided with bolts;
from that, one obtains twice the merit—of this there is no doubt. || 44 ||
O Six-faced One, one should indeed cause a palace or a temple to be built with three stories, five stories, or even seven stories. (45)
The greatness of that merit cannot be told by me even in hundreds of ages; therefore, who indeed is capable of describing it? (46)
One should make a Śiva [image] out of Jāmbūnada gold, silver, crystal, or even copper; hear now the fruit of the merit of such an act upon that ground. || 47 ||
A man obtains that same fruit which results from giving a thousand earths each weighing a thousand *tulā*-loads, and from giving a thousand *hiraṇyagarbha* gifts. || 48 ||
O King, the monarch should indeed place rubies, emeralds, diamonds, or even pearls upon the ground, level by level, throughout the temple tower.

Having constructed a treasury according to the prescribed rite on a mountain or a palace, one obtains merit a hundred times greater than before, even if it is merely a small pavilion (*troṭaka*). (50)
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, the Prāsādapaṭala, in the Kālottara. 53.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
[One should describe] the village, the town, the city, the port, and the market towns, along with their extent, their various types of locations, their dimensions, and their foundations.
The vehicle for the great ones, the characteristics of a dance hall, the lamp that does not go out, and likewise the unfading flower. || 2 ||
The "wick-lamp" (vāladīpaka) and the "garland" (mālā) are also mentioned; the "womb" (garbha) is said to be threefold:
the Jewel-womb (ratnagarbha), the Five-wombs (pañcagarbha), and indeed the Fivefold-womb (pañcadhāgarbha). || 3 ||
I shall describe them in order; listen briefly, O Six-faced One:
a village of eight hundred thousand [households] belonging to Brahmins is called the highest.
Accompanied by one hundred thousand Brahmins, it is called the most excellent of the excellent.
Indeed, O child, seven hundred thousand [times] one enters into the highest and lowest states.
A village joined by five hundred thousand twice-born men is called "middling"; one joined by six hundred thousand Brāhmaṇas is called "middling-superior. || 6 ||
A village with four hundred thousand Brahmins of firm vows is called middling; one joined with two hundred thousand Brahmins is said to be inferior.
Three hundred thousand is the lowest of the high; one hundred thousand is indeed the lowest of the low.
O child, one should designate a place worth less than a hundred thousand as a "bad village."
O child, through [the recitation of] the Aśraibrūṇa hymns, one hundred, ten thousand, or a hundred thousand [merits] may arise;
as do the four Vedas with their six auxiliary limbs, the Dharmaśāstras, and the Purāṇas. (9)
The treatises of Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā constitute the fourteenth branch of knowledge;
thus, there are exactly four commentaries and eighteen Saṃhitās.
The Yoga-śāstra, Sāṃkhya, Vedānta with its six limbs, the sixty-four arts, and likewise the six systems of logic (Ṣaṭtarka). || 11 ||
The Pāñcarātra, the Saura, the nine Yāmalas as well, Āyurveda, Sāmudrika, and the Somasiddhānta. || 12 ||
Having understood the Kāpāla, the Lākula, the five Āryas, the various elaborations (prapañcakas), and the path of the six Siddhāntas, one indeed becomes a teacher (deśika). || 13 ||
They say that the teacher is indeed Śiva, and Śiva is said to be the teacher;
he who realizes their non-difference is truly called a spiritual guide (deśika). || 14 ||
Therefore, with every effort, one should always worship the teacher, whether in a village, a city, a town, or even a small settlement. (15)
It was provided with ponds and fields, endowed with water everywhere,
filled with all kinds of rice plants, and possessed a house surrounded by a wall.
It should be given to the teacher; it may be one *dhanus* in length, or half of that, or half of that again, up to a thousand *dhanus*.
It should be given to the teacher; one shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
One should prepare a square or a rectangular [enclosure] for the bull. (18)
It was provided with a wall and a moat, endowed with many ornaments, and served as the support for all crops; furthermore, there was a river flowing to the south.
To the west, south, and east, there shall be three ponds;
they shall be joined by hundreds of other species and contain seven hundred karus. || 20 ||
O Six-faced One, there were a thousand women belonging to merchants, a thousand belonging to Śūdras,
and eight hundred thousand belonging to the twice-born in that great village.
An Ayuta [of villages] joined with Brahmins becomes ten times as meritorious for a Vaiśya;
one should give a city of such a kind, with two rivers on its flanks.
A city on the seashore should have three hundred distinguished Brahmins, be accompanied by Kṣatriyas numbering fifty,
and have Vaiśyas as its primary inhabitants.
Endowed with the appearance of nine [colors] through the movement of many steps,
and filled with the appearance of pairs, it becomes a region of three yojanas.
The king should cause a city to be built beside the confluence of the Nandī;
there, hundreds of thousands of Vaiśyas [should settle] with ships, vehicles, and carriages.
Or half of that, or half of that again, or ten thousand merchants;
it was crowded with jhallas and mallas, and two thousand barbarians.
It is twelve [yojanas] in width, nine thousand [yojanas] in circumference, and is either circular, square, or shaped like a circular courtyard. || 27 ||
It should be filled with a hundred streets, or half that, or even according to the prescribed rule;
it may have an ocean on the east, the west, or the south.
It should be properly constructed with walls and provided with three oblong ponds;
O Six-faced One, one pond should be situated at the side for the Śūdra.
The enclosure wall of the temple of Śiva is provided with many watchtowers, equipped with all kinds of weapons, and furnished with twelve gates.
In this [work], one should construct a wall made of bricks for a village, a town, a city, or a capital; likewise, a beautiful fortification (kheṭaka) should also be built here. (31)
O Six-faced One, one should know there is a mountain to the west and likewise a river to the north; it should be made long-sided on the bank of the river.
In the west, south, and east, let a grain field, a pond, and a small village be constructed; indeed, they shall be known by a single name.
In the center, one should construct Rājagṛha, with a seven-storied garland-like structure,
joined with many palaces and surrounded by a wall of houses.
A mountain fort, a water fort, a verbal fort, as well as a fort surrounded by a moat, and a fort consisting of a rampart. || 35 ||
O Vāyu, that [fortress] in the west should be one protected by wealth, by weapons, by men, and by mantras, and it should be guarded by Brāhmaṇas well-versed in the Vedas. || 36 ||
One should cause the royal palace to be constructed twice the size for those of the Vaiśya caste, provided with all the [required] features, and it should be made long on all sides.
It was joined by many hundreds of thousands of soldiers, most beautiful,
crowded with elephants and horses, and filled with eightfold chariot divisions.
One should understand that to be the shield; it should be fashioned by one who knows those respective [materials].
A Kṣatriya, endowed with the merit of giving and righteousness, heroic and majestic, [should do so]. (39)
Having observed an array equal to the fourfold formation (caturvyūha), one should never engage in battle;
likewise [one should avoid] the diamond, the ruby, the emerald, and the pearl.
One should never engage in battle; rather, one should accumulate all kinds of gems, grain, clothing, and ornaments. (41)
Netranirvāṇa, Kṣauma, Bhaṭavardhana,
Vardhana, and Ādhāna never engage in battle. (42)
Gold, silver, clothing, the increase of copper, iron, and so forth, as well as the expansion of armies—these he shall never fight for. (43)
Vajra, ruby, emerald, and likewise pearl—there shall be an increase of all such gems, and he shall never engage in battle. (44)
One should never fight for the sake of accumulating grain, nor for clothing and ornaments, nor for that which merely gratifies the eyes. 45.
All kinds of jewels, grain, household utensils, as well as elephants, horses, and their equipment—one should never fight for these. (46)
The jewel of a brahmin, the jewel of a king, the jewel of an elephant, and the jewel of a horse;
the jewel of gold, the jewel of clothing, and the emerald jewel as well.
One should never fight for the sake of collecting all kinds of jewels, nor for a ram-jewel, a buffalo-jewel, or likewise a water-pot-jewel. (48)
The sword-jewel, the shield-jewel, and likewise the knife-jewel; the courtesan-jewel, the male servant-jewel, and similarly the female servant-jewel. (49)
The jewel of a wife, the jewel of a merchant, as well as the jewel of a bracelet;
the jewel of an actor, the jewel of song, and likewise the jewel of a kinnara. || 50 ||
The king should constantly collect the jewel of the superintendent of grains, the jewel of precious gems, and likewise the jewel of the lute.

The Kṣatriya is dependent upon the four means—conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, and punishment—as well as the application of punishment in the four directions, its withdrawal, and his stationing in the eight directions. (52)

The wise man should always understand that single compendium of the dark [path] (tamisrasaṃgraha), which is the primary conduct among all scriptures, and he should master each of those [teachings]. (53)
Kings see by means of messengers; scholars see by means of the Vedas;
animals see by means of their nostrils; and other people see with their eyes. (54)

Reflection on oneself, reflection on the kingdom, and likewise reflection on enemies—these constitute the battle of wisdom and the battle for the kingdom; one should never engage in [physical] combat.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter on villages, cities, towns, market-towns, and royal capitals in the Kālottara. 54.
Śrīḥ!
Īśvara said:
I shall describe the characteristics of the foundations (garbha) which bestow prosperity upon villages and other settlements;
for indeed, in the absence of a foundation, there is surely the destruction of villages and houses.
This entire triple world, with all its moving and non-moving beings, has its root in Garbha;
likewise, the three Uttarās and Anurādhā [are so]. (2)
Śakaṭa, Mṛgaśiras, and Caitra-nakṣatra; as well as conception, the state of pregnancy, and other domestic duties. (3)
Anurādhā, known as the "Three Houses," is the cart that brings forth offspring;
whatever other housework there may be, that indeed should be performed.
During the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight on an auspicious day—among the three months of Caitra, Phālguna, and Vaiśākha, these are recommended. (5)
The month of Jyeṣṭha is proclaimed as the most meritorious, while Māgha is said to be middling; those who know the science of conception declare [the latter] to be the least. (6)
Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Makhā (Pūrvaphalgunī), Hastā, as well as Svātī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Pauṣṇa (Revatī), and Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj).
Some desire Anurādhā; Vasiṣṭha would not say it is the following one.
Agastya is declared to be Kuśeśaya, as well as Kāśyapa and Gārgya. (8)
Viśvāmitra and Bharadvāja, Gautama and Bhṛgu as well— these Vasus,
Rudras, and Ādityas indeed proclaim it as wonderful.
Whether it be the second, the third, or even Bhadrānandā,
the sages praise Rohiṇī as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and Pūrṇā—these shall bring auspiciousness on Monday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. (11)
Those who are learned in the scriptures of Bharga praise [the practice] during Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Capricorn, Sagittarius, or Aquarius. (12)
They praise the embryo in a water-jar, and it remains for ten thousand kalpas;
in a bull, it remains for five thousand kalpas. || 13 ||
He remains for four thousand kalpas in Karkaṭa;
however, in Makara, he remains as an embryo for three thousand kalpas.
The highest [type] has been described thus; now hear, O Six-faced One, about the middling type:
in Leo, Virgo, Pisces, or indeed Scorpio. (15)
O Guha, O dear one, he who knows the science of conception should avoid the signs of Pisces and Libra for two thousand kalpas while remaining in the womb.
One should deposit the embryo with the accompaniment of mantras at the rising of Jupiter, or it may be performed at the rising of Venus, or one should also deposit it at the rising of Mercury. (17)
When Jupiter rises, it is excellent; the rising of Venus is middling; and the rising of Mercury is inferior. One should establish the most excellent embryo [at these times]. (18)
Indeed, the comets are sixty-three, eleven, and eighteen in number, and they are as red as the sun;
moreover, when Jupiter is in its own place at five, seven, or eleven [degrees], it is most excellent.
The wise know that when Mercury is bound in the eleventh house, it is most excellent;
likewise, Venus and the Moon [are excellent] when bound in the fifth, tenth, and twelfth houses.
Having established the embryo within the womb according to the rules on the twelfth, fifth, first, or eleventh day,
or else, one should establish the supreme embryo during the Siddhi-yoga.
The descendant of Bhṛgu (Śukra) would be the best; one should cast [the oblation] into Soma on a Monday. Saturn is preeminent in Rohiṇī, while the moon and stars are primary on the eighth day.
They praise the Bhaumāśvina [yoga], for that is the opinion of Vasiṣṭha and Gārgya;
and in the conjunction of Jupiter and Puṣya, he remains for ten thousand kalpas.
One should place the embryo in the hand of the Sun according to the prescribed rite;
O child, it remains there for ten million times ten thousand kalpas—of this there is no doubt.
If one deposits the embryo under the asterisms of Budha or Anurādha according to the prescribed rite, it remains for five thousand kalpas; of this there is no doubt. || 25 ||
One should deposit it in the Yoge, the Vipulayoge, or indeed the Mahāyoge;
one should cast the embryo into the Vicitrayoge, preceded by the mantra. || 26 ||

The fetus remains [in the womb] as long as the moon and stars; of this there is no doubt—provided it is during a stable portion of the day, a stable lunar mansion, a stable hour, and under a stable planet. (27)
And during the time of a stable decanate (drekkāṇa), one should establish the excellent embryo; [avoiding] the eighth, the twelfth, the seventh, and the angular houses (kendras). (28)
In the fifth, the nature of space, one should always avoid all evils; likewise in the sixth, the son, the seventh, gain, and similarly in the third, dharma. (29)
The wise know that when three [planets] are in conjunction at sunrise, it is a "Variegated Yoga" (citrayoga);
when two pairs [of planets] are so situated, it is a "Great Yoga" (mahāyoga), which one should consider as the most excellent conception.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, concerning the specific muhūrtas characterized by conception, in the Kālottara.
|| Śrīḥ ||
Īśvara said:
Having properly fashioned a beautiful four-legged golden thread,
the young girl [should place it] there, exceeding six finger-breadths on all sides.
The golden island [should be made] in the four directions, or perhaps in two rows;
its height is of two kinds, [made] either of silver or of copper.
Whether it be thirty-two, sixty-four, or one hundred and eight [verses],
the entire offering of lamps on the golden river is performed with the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas.
Then, the one learned in the Ṛgveda should perform the Vāstuhoma in the east;
the one knowing the Yajurveda in the south; and the singer of the Sāmaveda in the west.
In the north, however, the preceptor should perform the Atharva-homa, while in the center he should offer oblations of Palāśa, Khadira, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, and Nyagrodha wood.
The bilva, udumbara, śamī, apāmārga,
and indeed the vaikaṅkata, aśoka, and vyāghāta— these likewise constitute the group of five.
Kaṇikāra and Vakula are declared to be suitable as fuel; one should know that the *sruva* ladle is made of Khadira wood, while the *darvī* spoon is said to be made of Jambu or Palāśa wood. (7)
Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, barley, bamboo, mustard seeds, rice, wild rice, wheat, sesame, mung beans, and millet; || 8 ||
Kulattha, śimbī, and niṣpāva are declared to be substances for the fire-oblation (homa); likewise, cakes, kṛsara, milk, cakes, and fruit-eatables [are prescribed]. || 9 ||
The twice-born man should perform the fire-oblation (homa) one thousand and eight times for each [deity], or half of that, or even half of that again, for each. || 10 ||
A twice-born man should offer oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis and the Sāvitrī mantra, either half of that amount, or half of that again, or one hundred and eight times.
One should offer oblations with the Viṣṇusūkta, the Puruṣasūkta, and the Rudrasūkta;
one should also offer oblations with the Hiraṇyapavamāna and the Śannovarga.
The Śrīsūkta with its five substances, and likewise the Somasūkta;
the Yāmya, Bārhaspatya, Brāhma, Aindra, and Āgneya [sūktas]. || 13 ||
In the south, he should recite the hymns of Yama and Nirṛti, as well as the purifying hymn of Varuṇa;
in the northeast, the hymn of the twelve Ādityas and that of the eleven Rudras.
The wise man should offer oblations with ghee using the eight Vāsava-mantras, the Tryambaka mantra, and the Haṃsa mantra, as well as cakes and various kinds of cooked food.
The Aruṇa, the Vallīśatarudra, and the Rudraikādaśa;
likewise the Daśahotṛ, the Saptahotṛ, and the Caturhotṛ. || 16 ||
I have separately taught the Śrīmannārāyaṇa, the Tvaritarudra-Vaiṣṇava,
the Bārhaspatya-Brāhmaṇa, and the Yajurviddha.
The Brahmasāman, the Jyeṣṭhasāman, the Vikarṇa, the Mahāvrata,
the Bahiṣpavamāna, the Puruṣa, the Gati, the Bṛhat, and the Rathantara. || 18 ||
We shall worship Agni as the head, and likewise Aśvattha;
and in this same manner, King Soma, as well as the deities of the Sun, Fire, and Varuṇa.

O child, one should always offer oblations with a Ṛgvedic verse in the southern, northeastern, northwestern, southwestern, and southeastern directions, and always in the western direction for those who sing the Sāmaveda.
And likewise the Atharvaśiras, as well as those belonging to Soma, Agni, Varuṇa, Yama, Vāyu, Īśāna, and Indra, and indeed the Pippalodakas. 21.
The Viṣṇu-sūkta, the Brāhmaṇa-sūkta, the Raudra, the Saura, and the Vāmaka;
likewise the Nīlarudra, the Mahārudra, and the Caṇḍarudra. || 22 ||
One should offer oblations with the Rakṣoghna, Bārhaspatya, Muṇḍa, and Praṇava mantras, as well as the Prāsāda, Pavitra, and Vyomavyāpin mantras. (23)
With Agni as the mouth and the primary focus, one should perform everything within the house;
thereafter, the wise man should offer oblations in this manner together with Brahmins of firm vows.
One should offer the purificatory substances and other oblation materials with clarified butter;
and in the Vāstu-homa, one should sacrifice to the forty deities of the Vāstu.
One should indeed offer oblations with the four-footed mantra of Vāstoṣpati;
then one should perform twelve oblations with the verse beginning "ato devā avantu."
One should offer sixteen oblations of sugarcane and buttermilk with milk and ghee;
one should offer oblations with speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) using the Puruṣasūkta during the middle [part].
One should offer three hundred oblations with the first quarter-verse of a Ṛgvedic hymn using the madhuparka mixture;
or one may perform the consecration (adhivāsana) at a temple pinnacle, on a sacrificial platform, or at a water-station.
Above the canopy, it is adorned with four archways (toraṇas) and provided with four gates; the maṇḍala measures thirty-six cubits. (29)
It should be twenty, sixteen, twelve, or eight cubits in length,
encircled by a garland of *darbha* grass and adorned with strings of pearls.
Abounding with garlands of fruits and sprouts, adorned with bells and chowries, endowed with eight banners, and decorated with the eight auspicious symbols. || 31 ||
Prepare a sacrificial mound with one hundred *droṇas* each of fragrant rice, great rice, *kalamā*, and *mālinī* rice, as well as barley, wheat, and wild millet.
Having prepared a fivefold bed right there, the wise one should lay the young child upon it while reciting the Viṣṇu-mantra. || 33 ||
The feet should be placed in the womb-like space with the head toward the west;
having covered [the image] with two garments, one should indeed clothe it with young clothes while reciting a Ṛgvedic verse.
Having washed [the image] with the five products of the cow while reciting the Śuddhasūkta, the wise one should subsequently consecrate the child while meditating upon the eight-syllable mantra.
The wise one should worship with perfumes, flowers, lamps, and other offerings,
[visualizing] the young girl as having the form of a ten-month-old or an eight-month-old infant.
Alternatively, one should have the form of a seven-month-old infant made,
representing the manifest child Mahāviṣṇu, the most excellent among all the gods.
Having offered oblations and performed the rites, one should touch the child with each of the various substances individually:
the fingers, the feet, the ankles, the shins, the knees, and the thighs. (38)
One should touch the penis, the anus, the testicles, the hips, the navel, and the heart;
then the two breasts, the thighs, the neck, the two arms, and the two elbows. (39)
The jewel, the two palms, the ten fingers,
the chin, the jaw, the lips, the tongue, and indeed the cavity of the palate; (40)
The two cheeks, the nose, the two eyes, both ears, the forehead, the brow, and likewise the temples and the head. (41)

The back of the torso, the three joints, the two sides, the armpits, and the chest; as well as the essence, the marrow, the flesh, the bone, the pith, and the semen are the constituent elements (dhātus). || 42 ||

Having offered oblation after oblation, the wise one should touch his hand to the *bali* offering for the eternal Viṣṇu; thereafter, with a single-pointed mind, he should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the collection of mantras.
The letter *a* is in the region of the throat, while the letter *ā* is on the forehead;
the letter *i* is in the right eye, and the letter *ī* is in the left eye.
The letter *u* is on the right arm, and the letter *ū* is on the left arm;
the letter *ṛ* is on the right ear, and the letter *ṝ* is on the left ear.
The letter *ḷ* on the right nostril, the letter *ḹ* on the left nostril;
the letter *e* on the right cheek, and the letter *ai* on the left cheek. (46)
One should place the syllable *o* on the lower lip and the syllable *au* on the upper lip;
the syllable *aṃ* in the middle of the palate and the syllable *āṃ* in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
One should place the *ka*-group on the right hand and the *ca*-group on the left;
the *ṭa*-group on the right foot and the *ta*-group on the left foot. (48)
The letter *pa* shone on the right side and *pha* indeed on the left side;
the letter *ma* was in the region of the genitals, while the letter *ya* was in the region of the skin. (49)
Having placed the syllable *ra* in the blood, the syllable *la* in the domain of the flesh, the syllable *va* in the fat, and the syllable *śa* in the region of the bones; || 50 ||
One should place the letter *ṣa* at the location of the marrow, and the letter *sa* at the white [semen];
having placed the letter *ha* at the heart, O Six-faced One, it is the form of the Self. (51)
The letter *kṣa* is indeed the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and the letter *la* constitutes the ornament;
for the five-weapon ornament consists of bracelets and small bells (*kiṅkiṇī*).
Having thus deposited the *praṇava* in the heart-lotus according to the prescribed rite,
one should worship it with all [offerings] such as perfumes and flowers, and with the *vāstu* ritual.

This should be performed in the same manner at night; then, at dawn, it should be placed within the womb [of the image] by Brāhmaṇas of firm vows who are engaged in their religious observances and study.
At the time of the formal acceptance (adhivāsana), one should feed a hundred Brahmins;
at the time of depositing the embryo (garbhanikṣepa), however, one should begin with a feast for a thousand.

One should cause the gift of gold, the gift of cows, and the gift of land to be performed during the first nāḍī of an auspicious muhūrta, at a distance of two tālas from the root of the tree, starting from one tāla away.
The preceptor and the king should rest for the duration of a palm-tree's height behind the couch; there, however, are the Miśra and Bhrūṇa [mantras].
O child, having excluded all other people, one who is composed should place [the image] in the center of the pedestal in a very secret place known by those skilled in the womb-consecration.
O child, after twelve muhūrtas, the boy shall indeed take the form of Khaṭvā;
at that very moment, O Six-faced One, he shall perform a dance in the hall of dance.
At that very moment, a dance of the Balas constantly and perpetually proceeds;
and above it is the northern staff, upon which there is a stone three cubits in length.
Having covered the stone slab with an upper layer, one should cause it to be plastered with lime;
over that, one should construct either a dome or a pavilion.
Or else, one should perform the *sahā* [rite], or even the recitation (*japa*) and the gift (*dāna*);
in this way, indeed, the womb of the dancing child becomes most excellent of the excellent. (62)
One should offer the sacrifice of dance accompanied by the sounds of conchs and drums,
performing circumambulations three times at each of the three junctions of the day, or perhaps three or five times.
On that day, one should cause food and other provisions to be prepared for people of all castes;
and one should properly honor the preceptor with cows, land, gold, and other gifts.
One should properly honor the officiating priests with garments and ornaments;
however, one should never again look upon the protector of the dance once it has been seen.
If that which is to be seen has already been seen, one should not cause it to be viewed again;
thus, O observer of noble vows, the interior known as the Nṛttaśālā (Dancing Hall) is described as being nine [parts].
Indeed, by the power of the mantra for even a moment, the state of being like a living being arises; O Six-faced One, through that which is made of iron, the observer of the vow lives.
Nṛttapāla is the most excellent and supreme among all embryos and is exceedingly beautiful;
therefore, one should install Nṛttapāla with every possible effort.
One should especially install divine temples in a village, or a city, or a town, or even a market-town, or a small hamlet. (69)
One should have a hall constructed for dance, whether in an assembly hall or in the house;
specifically, one should arrange for the dance of children in places such as the world-stage (jagatsthāna) and so forth.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, concerning the womb of Nṛttapāla, within the section on the characteristics of the womb in the Kālottara. 56.
Śrīḥ!
Īśvara said:
I shall now explain, in due order, the lamp that is never extinguished.
In the house of the remaining region, the lamp of Nirvana is supreme. || 1 ||
Whether in a village or a city, in a town or even a small hamlet; in a capital city or a hilly fort, or even in a house, a field, or a granary. || 2 ||
One should have an excellent lamp-vessel made of gold, silver, or even copper, filled with thirty-two *droṇas*.
The medium size is sixteen *droṇas*, and the inferior is eight *droṇas*;
it should be beautifully adorned with a pedestal joined by pillar-friezes.
The offering may consist of the ghee of a tawny cow, or even the ghee of a goat;
the ghee of a goat would be middling, while that of a buffalo would be inferior.

One should avoid [the fat] of horses, camels, and sheep, with the exception of ghee; likewise, one should avoid that which comes from sheep. The thread made from white lotus fibers should be the size of half the little finger.
A red cotton thread joined with a white thread,
mixed with the root of the white *arka* plant and combined with the three fruits.
Powdered camphor and agallochum, powder of the three fruits (triphalā), powder of devadāru wood, and powder of punnāga; || 8 ||
Furthermore, a paste made from *nyagrodha*, *punnāga*, and *picumanda* as the eighth,
mixed with the powder of *palāśa*, *khadira*, and *nāga*, should be rolled into a wick.
O child, in the previously mentioned place,
the wise man should carefully pour ghee into the lamp-vessel with every effort and then insert the wick.
One should offer the lamp consisting of eight substances and six types with the root mantra;
likewise, one made from the tusks of a river-elephant or a boar.
From a sacred field, from what has been brought forth, from an anthill, from a cow-pen, from the center of a sacrificial altar,
from the ocean, from a mountain, and likewise from the horn of a bull. (12)
One should bring earth from the temple of Śiva and from the temple of Viṣṇu;
having taken earth from the temple of Lakṣmī, one should deposit it at the base of the lamp.
One should have the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) made of gold around the lamp; each one individually should be worth one niṣka for it to be considered excellent.

The medium [image] should be half of that size, and the smallest should indeed be half of that again. In the absence of gold, one should have the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) made with silver.
An expert in this matter should fashion it separately with a thousand niṣkas;
indeed, if that is unavailable, one should have it made even with lead.
One should indeed fashion the eight auspicious symbols separately from weapons and gold coins;
with nine hundred thousand mantras, one should install the supreme lamp.
One who is learned in the science of architecture (garbha-śāstra) should place eight [deities] in the "Aṣṭamaṅgala" [section];
I shall now describe their extraction, which is the cause for the successful accomplishment of the foundation (garbha).
Having extracted the forty-sixth [letter], conjoined with the fire of dissolution (the letter *ra*), joined with the fourth vowel (*ī*), and endowed with Rudra and Viṣṇu. || 19 ||
The third is the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, which contains all within its womb and awakens [consciousness];
the fourth is that which is to be grasped by the tip of the hunchbacked one, conjoined with Jātavedas.
From the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], the fourth [syllable] is joined with Śiva and Nārāyaṇa;
this fourth Lakṣmī-bīja is difficult to obtain even for the gods.
The second [syllable] is the group of eight (aṣṭāvarga), while below it is Jātavedas;
the seventh is the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, which contains a lamp and brings increase.
Having produced food from the island, it is joined with the fire of dissolution;
it resides on the twelve heads of Prajāpati, accompanied by the *bindu* and the *nāda*. (23)
The seed-syllable of the eight auspicious signs awakens all embryos;
the wise one should extract the Sky (Ha), joined with the Fire of Destruction (Ra). (24)
The eighth is Brahmā on the head, curved and accompanied by the syllable *colā*;
the ninth is the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, which awakens all prosperity. (25)
The wise one should place the seed-syllable of the limbs as the eighth auspicious element; having established the seed-syllable of another auspicious factor, he should arrange them accordingly.
"O Gaṇeśa, come from the mantra born of a moment, O bestower of success!
Let them ascend; let him perform [this], truly, truly, O Six-faced One. (27)
Or even while traveling on both boats, one may instantly board;
yet, though stationed in its own place, it is like a lamp that does not go out.
O Six-faced One, it reaches nirvāṇa in an instant; go to another lamp, O Rohaṇa, by the power of a Muhūrta or the power of a Rātra! 29.
Then, having performed the recitation for the auspicious day as before, and likewise having provided food along with gifts of cows, land, gold, and so forth as previously described; || 30 ||
One should place the mixture of the teacher’s semen and the embryo into the sacrificial ladle;
having set aside all others, one should deposit the embryo in a well-concealed place. || 31 ||
One should place this supreme lamp, which is like the sun and moon and whose light does not go out, at the front with focused attention. (32)

Having given the teacher’s fee consisting of cows, land, gold, and so forth, there is no doubt that [the benefit] lasts as long as the moon and stars, until the lamp is extinguished and until final nirvāṇa. 33.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, the Nirvāṇa-paṭala, in the Kālottara [Tantra]. (p. 303) || 57 ||
Śrī.
Īśvara said:

Now, the "Unfading Flower Garland" (Amlānapuṣpamālā) will be taught as a manual on the characteristics of embryos—the most excellent and supreme among all manuals for conceiving, which accomplishes the goals of dharma, pleasure, and wealth. || 1 ||
It removes all diseases, is auspicious, and always increases victory;
it destroys untimely death, and one shall attain long life. || 2 ||
It brings about the destruction of great plagues and the eradication of heinous sins; it likewise prevents earthquakes, thunderbolts, portents, and the loss of devotion. || 3 ||
Excessive rain, drought, locusts, the destruction of mice,
the destruction of blue jays, and likewise the increase of crops.
Month after month, it was indeed thrice-visited and increased by all living beings;
yet here it was devoid of sparrows, pigeons, kāraṇḍa birds, and cranes.
But when there is affliction by the king of a foreign kingdom, the enemy army and so forth are afflicted. || 6 ||
O child, no one dies prematurely among all human beings;
for that [region] extends thirty-six yojanas from the location of the Garbhavṛkṣa tree.
Untimely death and famine do not exist in that land;
nor are there rākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, vetālas, or pūtanās.
O child, in that region there is no fear of hungry ghosts or serpents; there, quadrupeds do not die, nor do bipeds suffer harm.
With its interior filled with unfading garlands, no wicked being is found there;
it bestows long life and health, and indeed causes the crops to flourish. (10)
It is for the increase of the glory of the senses and indeed for the increase of milk;
it is a pitcher made of gold, filled with ten droṇas.
Alternatively, it may consist of eight droṇas or even five droṇas;
or silver should be prepared, while gold should be three times that amount.
Alternatively, there may be a copper jar;
one should have it made for ten bhāras [of weight], or a silver one for ten bhāras, or a silver jar [made] of gold.
Alternatively, the door should be half [the height], or half of that, or half of that again;
it should be very firm, mercilessly solid, and eight finger-breadths in thickness.
One should make the ear three finger-breadths wide and the mouth likewise three finger-breadths;
the brahmins and young students should then carefully bring water from a sacred bathing place.
One should fill that cave-vessel with water filtered through a cloth;
[reciting] "āpaḥ," "udakam," the second [verse], and "imaṃ me varuṇa. (16)
Having recited these mantras seven times— namely the verse beginning with "tattvā yāmi" and "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ"— one should [offer] gold and the Pavamāna [Soma].
One should likewise recite one hundred and eight times the Prāsāda mantra, the Brahma-mantra, the Vyomavyāpin mantra, or the principal ten-syllable seed-mantra.
Having recited [the mantra], the preceptor should fill the water-vessel containing the embryo;
then, having worshipped it according to the prescribed rite, he should subsequently [worship] a garland of unfading flowers.
Or a thousand white lotuses, or even half of that or a quarter;
or else one hundred and eight red lotuses.
Five hundred red lotuses, half as many blue lotuses, five hundred campaka flowers, and likewise pāṭala and vakula flowers. || 21 ||
Mālatī, mallikā, jātī, madayantī, karavīraka, aśoka, karṇikāra, bandhūka, and girimallikā. || 22 ||
Safflower, ketakī, wood-apple, and mango; bilva flowers, śamī flowers, white arka, and kaṅka flowers. || 23 ||
Bṛhatī, sahadevī, vaikuṣṭha, brahmapuṣpaka, sadābhadra, mahābhadra, apāmārga, and kadambaka—these [are the herbs]. || 24 ||
Nirguṇḍī, kadalī flower, and other such flowers;
punnāga, nāga, malaya, mura, māṃsī, and puṣpaka.
Saffron, nirguṇḍī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, vallarī, śvetā, girikarṇī, and siṃhakesara as well. || 26 ||
Tulasī, Kṛṣṇatulasī, Nṛpayūdhī, Haṃsinī, Kṣāraṇī, Kāṇḍalī, Koṭṭavī, and Navamālikā. (27)
One should avoid white water-lilies, as well as kumudas, kuśa grass, kāśa grass, the flower of apasmāra, and the flower of piśāca. || 28 ||
One should avoid the nimba, the picumanda, and the kiṇibhadra;
indeed, all other flowers should be taken with great care. || 29 ||
O dear one, it should first be made of silk thread, and afterwards it may consist of rope;
having carefully prepared a rope measuring exactly sixty-four *aratnis* in length. (30)
Now, a cord of eight cubits (ratni) is called the medium one;
a cord of sixty-four hundred cubits is called the superior one. || 31 ||
A Brahmin who knows the truth of the Vedas and Vedānta, firm in his vows,
having fasted for a day and night and bathed, shall cause the binding with ropes to be performed. (32)
Facing the northeast, one should bind [the thread] in silence alone,
while recollecting the flower and the lamp, likewise ever anew.
Within that aforementioned embryonic body, one should first cast all of that into the center using the very *pavitra* mantra; thus one should deposit it five times.
The nine gems, the nine seeds, the nine minerals, the nine medicinal herbs, the nine fragrances, the nine metals, as well as the nine barks and the nine roots. || 35 ||
One should place these within the pitcher, using the primary seed-syllable of the Prāsāda mantra:
the diamond (vajra), the ruby (padmarāga), the emerald (marataka), and likewise the pearl (mauktika).
One should deposit coral, topaz, sapphire, as well as emerald, moonstone, and the nine precious gems. || 37 ||
Śāli rice, nīvāra rice, wheat, barley, and bamboo-seed;
sesame, mustard, mung beans, and priyaṅgu shall be the ninth. (38)
Realgar, yellow orpiment, * * * * realgar, saurāṣṭra, mercury, honey, juice, and collyrium. (39)
Lakṣmī, sahadevī, viṣṇukrānti, nṛpa, vaiṣṇavī, induvallī, girikarṇā, and śaṅkhapuṣpikā. || 40 ||
And the ninth medicinal herb declared is the sūryāvarta; likewise, triphalā, trijātaka, camphor, agaru, and sandalwood. (41)
Kashmir sandalwood is suitable for worship, as is Malaya sandalwood mixed with camphor; likewise, gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead [are suitable]. || 42 ||
Copper, bell-metal, vidula, and new iron are declared [as suitable];
likewise, mango, udumbara, nyagrodha, and panasa. (43)
O Mahāsena, one should cast the seeds of the aśvattha, the śirīṣa, the palāśa, the bilva, the mādhuka, and the fresh bark, excluding the forbidden seeds.
With the root of the lotus, the root of the utpalāmṛta, the blue lotus, the white water-lily, and the root of kaṭumelaka; || 45 ||
And one should separately place the ninth, the Gaṅgāmūla, with the nine seed-syllables;
having recited each one one hundred and eight times, one should cast them into the water-pots.
Having performed the previously mentioned fire sacrifice (homa), as well as the auspicious recitation (puṇyāha) and study,
one should provide a feast for the Brahmins and give gifts of cows, land, and gold.
One should place the root of the unshrivelled [mālā] at a distance of two cubits from the pitcher;
the unshrivelled garland should be placed upon either a pedestal or a wooden plank.
And one should properly worship with rice grains and hundreds of auspicious lotus flowers—blue lotuses, nandikāvarta lilies, bakula, pāṭala, and campaka blossoms. (49)
One should worship with very fragrant camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood, or with saffron and musk; one should worship Mālāśrī and Gaura as well.
Having installed the goddess Umā in the water-pot (kumbha), one should install Śrī in the garland;
she has two arms, one face, a dark complexion, and three eyes.
She was adorned with every ornament, endowed with all the auspicious marks,
possessed of lovely bimba-red lips, and had hair decorated with blue kundala flowers.
Her face was like the full moon, her eyes were like blue lotuses, she possessed beautiful eyebrows and lovely ears, and her breasts were like golden jars. (53)
She has a neck like a conch shell, lips like the *bimba* fruit, full cheeks, and a pure smile; she has a navel like that of a swan, a deep-set navel, and stands with a slender waist. (54)
Her teeth were like thorn-buds, her bow was the bandhūka flower, her chariot wheels were her breasts, and her thighs were like plantain trunks. (55)
With a slender belly, a tongue like fire, and well-knit ankles, with lotus-like feet marked by the five auspicious signs—this is the supreme form of Pārvatī. (56)
Resplendent with necklaces and armlets, adorned with gold and jewels,
and possessing earrings, she was endowed with golden bracelets, bangles, and anklets.
Adorned with a waist-thread and a belly-band embellished with all kinds of jewels, wearing garments of fine silk and precious gems, she was the very embodiment of Prakṛti herself. || 58 ||
One should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī, endowed with these characteristics, most beautiful, resembling the filaments of a lotus, and possessing the luster of molten gold. (59)
[He saw] Lakṣmī, wearing yellow garments, holding a lotus in her hand, most beautiful, with a face like a lotus, eyes like lotuses, and hands and feet like lotuses. || 60 ||
O Six-faced One, one should install Lakṣmī upon the Māyā [syllable] using the Lakṣmī-bīja;
one should install Pārvatī in the jar with the Hṛllekhā mantra recited a hundred times.
One should duly recite the seed-syllable of Śrī ten thousand times over a garland of unblighted flowers;
then, touching that garland, one should continue the recitation until [the deity] arrives right there.
O Mahāsena, one should recite [the mantra] with a single-minded focus and an undistracted mind;
by the power of the mantra, within a moment, the rosary returns to that very place.
Having wrapped it oneself within a jar, with the remainder placed on top;
such a flower that does not fade is the most excellent of all those in the womb. (64)
The king, having assembled [the officials], shall appoint a learned teacher (*ācāryamiśra*) and a learned brahmin (*bhrūṇa*);
according to the procedure previously described, he shall have them perform all the rites. (65)
Thus ends the fifty-eighth [chapter], the "Chapter on the Unfading Flower," within the section on the characteristics of the womb in the *Kālottara*.
Prosperity!
Īśvara said:
O Ṣaṇmukha, listen now to the procedure for the Ratnagarbha rite,
whether in a city, a kingdom, a village, or even a town that is devoid of a royal heir.
Whether in a watchtower, a hovel, a house, or even a temple;
in every field, in a granary, in a rampart, or even at a city gate.
They indeed do not perish, O child; therefore, one should deposit the embryo.
Having established the embryo according to the prescribed rite by those who are devoted to the worlds, [it remains].
O child, because it was indeed composed by Vācaspati with the *nṛttapālā* and others as its inner essence,
it therefore always bestows heaven, endowed with all sovereign powers.
I shall now describe the *garbhamelā*, which accomplishes all desires and goals,
[to be made] with gold, silver, copper, or even brass.
One should have twenty-five firm compartments constructed;
indeed, one should construct the inner chamber with fifty fruits.
The width should be one *ratni*, the height six *aṅgulas*,
and the thickness of the walls of the compartments should be half an *aṅgula* in measure.
The width of the compartments is declared to be five finger-breadths;
their length is likewise the same, making them square on all sides.
The arrangement [of the mandala] is indeed with one hundred and fifty fruits;
outside the womb-place, it is exactly three tāla units in distance.
Having placed the vessel according to the ritual procedure, the composed preceptor [should place] the moonstone in the northern compartment, joined with six crores.
One should place a ruby in the eastern compartment and an emerald in the Kāmya compartment;
likewise, a pearl in the Varuṇa compartment, each according to its own mantra.
One should place moonstone in the northern compartment with the mantra;
one should place coral in the southeast compartment with the fire-mantra.
In the southwest, one should place an indranīla gem consecrated with the mantra of Nirṛti;
in the northwest, a mahānīla; and in the northeast, a puṣyarāga.

One should place the Jāmbūnada gold in the eastern direction, joined with [the appropriate materials]; having placed the white [stone] in the south-eastern direction, one should place the pearl in the southern direction.
Having placed iron in the southwest, brass in the west;
having placed bell-metal in the northwest, one should place lead in the north.
Having placed Vaṅka in the northeast with the mantra ending in vauṣaṭ,
O Guha, one should place Darada between the wheel and the fire.
The wise one should place yellow orpiment between Anala and Maya;
the wise one should place realgar between Yama and Nairṛta. || 17 ||
The wise one should place [the region of] Madhyadeśa between Nirṛti and Varuṇa;
the wise one should place Saurāṣṭra between Varuṇa and Anila. || 18 ||
Then one should place honey between Pavana and Soma;
there, one should place collyrium between Soma and Īśāna.
p.
311) The wise one should [place] the twenty-five [syllables] in the twenty-fifth square by means of the mantra of Madhuneśāna, according to the proper sequence. (20)
[The earth] produced from the horn of the river-nāga, as well as that fashioned by the boar, the anthill, the field-plot, and the heart-lake—these are in the center. || 21 ||
[He saw] Lodhra, Mṛd, Karkaṭamūrdhvan, and that mouse...
[and] Himavatpārśvabhṛt and Vindhyaparvatamastaka.
One should take clay from the Gaṅgādhara mountain and from Avinābhṛta; one should take clay from the Tāmraparṇī, O dear one, and lift up clay from the Kāverī and the Godāvarī.
Gandhaśāli, mahāśāli, and likewise ratnaśāli;
kṛṣṇaśāli, wheat, and kalama-rice as well. || 24 ||
Barley, mustard, nīvāra, as well as ṣaṣṭika rice, bamboo seeds, sesame, mung beans, chickpeas, and black gram. || 25 ||
Rājamāṣa, kuluttha, śimba, and niṣpāva;
as well as kuṅkuma, śyāmaka, priyaṅgu, and tṛṇadhānya. || 26 ||
In this manner, twenty-five types of rice are proclaimed for the Āra;
O child, one should arrange them as before with the primary seed-mantra.
One should avoid *paṭola*, *kodrava*, and similar grains among the cereals;
likewise, [one should cultivate] *lakṣmī*, *sahadevī*, *viṣṇukrānti*, and *nṛpa*. (28)
Indravallī, Mahāvallī, Tulasī, Maṅgavistū, Girikarṇī, Sitā, Niśā, and Gokṣīra. || 29 ||
Kṣīra, nāgabalā, balā, the auspicious atibalā, sūryavartā, meghanādā, amṛtā, and kṛṣṇamallikā. || 30 ||
The wise one should arrange the twenty-five [substances] as before: *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *rasādhānā*, *vyāghrī*, *parājitā*, and *veda*. (31)
The three fruits, the three aromatics (trijātī), camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, saffron, haraka, lotus stalk, and vyādhi.
Haryaṃśa, tagara, māṃsī, tuṭidhānya, hiraṇyaka, sthūṇī, mṛdaṅga, mahiṣa, varāha, and likewise the elephant. || 33 ||
The wise one should arrange [the lotuses] as before, according to the primary seed-mantra;
[namely] the *paṅkaja*, the *utpala*, the *kumuda*, or even the *nīlotpala*. (34)
The white water-lily, the *truṭika*, and likewise the lotus;
the *mallikā*, the *jāti*, the *vakula*, the *aśoka*, the *jātī*, and the *ketakī*. (35)
Mālatī, Mādhavī, Madayantī, and Mañjarī; Punnāga, Kurava, Dīpa, Mūlaka, and Karavīraka. || 36 ||
Rice root, conch, flower, and radish—
O Guha, one should place their roots and flowers as before.
The Earth, the Tortoise, and the Moon, as well as the Eight Auspicious Signs—
these, namely the Earth, the Tortoise, and the Moon, one should place in the central square.
Thus there shall be the eight auspicious objects, which one should place in the eight directions;
O Guha, I shall now declare the presiding deities within those jewel-filled vessels.
Brahmā, Hari, and Hara, as well as Umā, Śrī, and Dharaṇī;
and Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, and Vāyu. || 40 ||
O child, there are Someśāna and indeed the eleven Rudras,
as well as the eight Vasus and the twelve Ādityas.
Dhanada, Guha, Vāgīśa, Sāvitrī, and Prabhāvatī— O Guha, they [should be worshipped] indeed with their own respective mantras, beginning with the seed-syllable (bīja). (42)
The Prāsāda hymn, the Puruṣasūkta, and likewise the Viṣṇusūkta;
the Rudrasūkta, the Sūryasūkta, and the Aṣṭavasusūkta. || 43 ||
One should install both [the deities] with their respective mantras;
likewise, one should perform the supreme fire-oblation (homa) as before, as well as the recitation for the auspicious day (puṇyāha).
O Six-faced One, as before, at an auspicious moment, the foundation (garbha) remains within the womb-chamber (garbhageha) until it reaches the middle of the lintel (phelaka). 45.

While the life-force (jīva) remains, one should enter the temple, which is endowed with the primary seed-syllables and the power of the mantra; by the strength of the auspicious moment, the protective slab (phelakā) shall be set in place.
One should take food as before and likewise perform the act of giving;
having performed the worship of the preceptor, one should provide a meal for the Brahmins.
This is proclaimed as the Ratnagarbha [Tantra]; he who practices it shall remain for ten million eons, endowed with long life and health, and entirely free from all diseases.
In that land where Govardhana and Puṣṭivardhana reside,
there shall be neither famine nor pestilence, but rather prosperity.
The wise man should have the inner sanctum constructed from black stone, or he may make it of bricks; he should then properly coat it with lime.

One should have a gate-tower (gopura), a pavilion (maṇḍapa), or an assembly hall (sabhā) constructed there; and having offered the sacrificial oblation (bali) daily at the three junctions of the day with the three [mantras], || 51 ||
Alternatively, one should always worship with unbroken grains, fragrances, and beautiful flowers;
having first arranged the ritual materials, one should thereafter arrange the deities.
Having plastered it perfectly so that it is without gaps, very firm, and endowed with auspicious characteristics,
one should properly fashion stone slabs for both the upper and lower parts here. (53)
Indeed, on the western black mountain, one should not reveal this;
this most secret womb must be kept well-concealed and not made public. || 54 ||
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter [in the Kālottara] concerning the characteristics of Ratnagarbha. || 59 ||
Prosperity!
Īśvara said:
I shall now briefly explain the essence of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for the benefit of the poor; listen to me as I speak it in full. 1.
It is divine, providing all protection, producing all kinds of grain, and beneficial;
it destroys all misfortunes and eliminates all calamities. || 2 ||
It indeed destroys famine, destroys all evil dreams, and is the most excellent of all Brahmanical rites; it is the essence of the five products of the cow.
At an auspicious moment during the day, conjoined with a favorable lunar mansion and lunar day,
one should deposit the excellent embryo into the aforementioned vessel.
Whether in a village or a town, or even in a city or a market-town; whether in a capital, a hamlet, or likewise in a wretched village. || 5 ||
One should cast it into a cow-pen, a field, or a garden, or else into a storehouse;
one may also deposit it in a treasury of gold and silver, or in a stable for elephants and horses.
In a place for dancing, in an assembly hall, in the pleasure-house of a courtesan, especially in a latrine, or even when walking through a [restricted] area. || 7 ||
Specifically, in the place of Śikṣāyudha, in the place of Maheśa,
in the pavilion, in the temple, and in the Kanyā-prāsādakas. (8)
In the houses of the princes and in the houses of the buffaloes,
as well as in the circular pavilions and in the flowered canopies.
In the special mantra-halls, in the houses of ministers, in the houses of feudal lords, and likewise in the houses of courtesans; || 10 ||
In the abode of the wise, as well as in the houses of physicians, in the temples of the gods, and likewise in the dwellings of messengers; || 11 ||
In the residence of the commander-in-chief, in the houses of the masters of the kitchen, and in the palaces of all the kings together with their retinues; || 12 ||
