One should place the embryo of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) within it, preceded by the recitation of mantras,
every year, every six months, or every three months.
Month after month, the wise man should indeed offer the five products of the cow;
for in ancient times, the king was consecrated with the five products of the cow.
It destroys the faults of malevolent magic and annihilates all causal agents;
at every festival, this consecration destroys all that is artificial.
Having bathed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), which destroys all evil dreams, it constantly bestows long life and health, as well as increasing prosperity. || 16 ||
This five-product of the cow (pañcagavya) is for daily sprinkling;
by its very characteristic, whatever evil deed has been committed on that day is entirely destroyed.
One should deposit the excellent *garbha* in the center of the house, extending toward all directions:
namely Īśāna, Parjanya, Jaya, and Mahendra. (18)
O Guha, if there is a fall from truth regarding the Sun, one should cast [the oblation] into the intermediate space;
likewise, the three fires preceded by Vahni, as well as Graha, Kṣata, and Yama. (19)
One should deposit the embryo in Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, Bhṛṅga, Nairṛta, Dauvārika, Sugrīva, and Puṣpadantaka. || 20 ||
One should deposit the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa) and the Lord of Gods (Indra) in the north-west; however, one should place Pāpayakṣma in the north-east.
One should likewise deposit the embryo in Anila, Nābhi, Mukhya, and Bhallāṭa.
One should cast [the seed-syllables] upon Tārādhipa and Ṛbhu, both those that have been uttered and those that have not;
one should deposit the supreme embryo within the thirty-two locations of the site.
Furthermore, if she should miscarry after the fetus has been formed,
the wise man should cast two parts of *marīcaka* into six parts [of the mixture].
O child, if one recites the Sāvitrī, one should place a leaf of the Palāśa tree upon the thread; and having likewise recited two verses of the Sāvitrī, one should deposit the excellent embryo.
Or, O Guha, one should destroy artificial broth-shops with *sūraṇa* roots;
one should cast the embryo into the sun, into the six-footed [insect], or into the interval between Yama and Brahmā.
O child, within the space between the *Nirṛti* and *Brahman* [lines], one should place the embryo of Upendra;
the wise man should then deposit the embryo of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) in two places. (26)
One should place Indra upon the two feet of Dāsa with the *garbha-ratna*;
Varuṇa is placed within the *brahma*-square, O child, and Mitra is said to be in the six squares.
There, one should diligently cast the womb of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) between the two syllables of Anila and Brahmā, and within the two feet of Rudra.
One should place a vessel filled with cow-products at the two feet of Rudradāsa;
O Vatsa, [one should place it] within Soma and Brahmā at the six steps of Pṛthivīdhara.
With every effort, the wise one should deposit the *gavyagarbha* (the "cow-essence" [consecrated materials]);
he should place the embryo either in a *phelaka*, in a jar, or in the middle of the house. || 30 ||
O Lord of Devas, one should place the embryo of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the Brahma-position,
as well as forty-nine [pots] for the Vāstu deities.
O Guha, one should duly pour the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) into each of those places;
O child, that house then prospers with cattle, grain, and wealth.
O dear one, one should scatter grain-increasing substances in the nine directions of the cow-pen;
in the house of Kuśa grass, one should deposit the twelfth embryo.
O Guha, this treasury is inexhaustible; there is no fear of thieves.
It yields the merit of a hundred cows' urine and fifty cows' dung. (34)
Milk is said to yield two hundred fruits, curd is said to yield one hundred fruits, and clarified butter yields twenty-five fruits; this is declared to be the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should take the cow dung from a black cow, fetch the urine from a greenish one,
take the milk from a white one, and curd is said to be taken from a red one.
And when [the substance] has become like fire in appearance, one should cause it to be taken while preceded by mantras;
he should recite the *ṛc* "sa katheti" and proceed to mix it with cow's urine. || 37 ||
One should add milk with the mantra "āpyāyasva," curd with "viṣṇo dadhi kr̥ṇuhi," and ghee with "ghr̥tavatī. Then, one should add water from *kuśa* grass with the *praṇava*.
One should employ half a handful of barley and bamboo powder;
this is called the "five products of the cow" (pañcagavya), which destroys all sins. || 39 ||
Filled with barley and reeds and accompanied by water infused with *kuśa* grass, it is called the *brahmakūrca*; one should employ it with the *brahmajajñāna* mantra.
The five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the *brahmakūrca*—both together are called "the womb" (*garbha*). This [term] applies to bathing, drinking, sprinkling, and also to smearing. (41)
In all cases, both [the preceding and following rules] should be applied, especially regarding embryos,
as well as the consecration of the gods and particularly that of Śiva.
In the various expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), one should have her consume [the substance] along with honey;
likewise in all *cāndrāyaṇa* observances and during the three fortnights of the lunar cycle. (43)
O child, one should cause [the sinner] to drink [the prescribed liquid] during the Prājāpatya, Sāntapana, and Atikṛcchra penances,
as well as during the fortnightly fast and the monthly fast.
During the Kumbha-kṛcchra rite, one should cause seven [measures] of black [grain] to be drunk;
likewise during the Sabhidheya and Aniyama rites, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, and with clarified butter.
On the days of the new and full moon, during the months of Śrāvaṇa and Āṣāḍha, on the twelfth, eleventh, and ninth lunar days, during eclipses, and also on the equinoxes; || 46 ||
During the solstices, the Vyatīpāta yoga, the Saṅkāntis, and at the time of one's birth-star, one should cause [the person] to drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
"In the case of a bad dream, contact with a wicked person, or eating in the temple of Rudra"—thus ends the sixtieth chapter on the Five Products of the Cow (*pañcagavya*) in the *Kālottara*. 60.
Śrīḥ!
Īśvara said:

Omniscience, contentment, beginningless consciousness, sovereignty, eternal and undiminished power, and infinite power—those who know the sacred injunctions declare these six to belong to the all-pervading Maheśvara. (1)
I shall explain, in due order, the ritual procedure for the Vajra Door;
for this is the supreme Mṛtyuñjaya, more subtle than the subtle, the ultimate.
This secret, more secret than the secret, should be grasped with great effort;
it was not previously told even to Brahmā, nor was it told to Viṣṇu. (3)
This instruction on the Vajra Door has not been told to any of the gods, nor has it been told to one's own son; it has not been told to just anyone.
Out of affection for you, I have imparted this supreme and great divine instruction:
the pair consisting of the Creator (Brahmā) and the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) is called the door-leaf and the pillar.
The one above and to the north is Gaṇanātha; that which is further above is said to be Vṛṣabha.
O child, Yoni and Bhramara are proclaimed by you as the two Kaulas.
The fourth [syllable] is the one called Kākhya-mūka; it is the world-above, the wind, and the upward-facing [element].
Viṣṇu and Rudra occupy the crest, while the door-bolt is at the left nostril.
I shall now describe the *paṭakośa*; listen, O Six-faced One! The sixteen [syllables] and the five-layered sheaths (*pañcapuṭakośa*) have been proclaimed.
Bindu and Nāda together are declared to be the beginning of the Visarga;
one should know that which is with the Visarga as the "Treasury" (kośa) proclaimed within.
O Hara, that which was told to me— the single-faced door-panel—
is said to be Bhadrakālī, the supreme seed-syllable, located on the southern pillar.
Raudrī and Kālī are the supreme seed-syllables; the left pillar is thus declared. That which resembles the hibiscus flower is called the right pillar. (11)
The left pillar is described as resembling a flash of lightning,
while the first right pillar has the luster of frost or silver.
First, [he visualizes] the left [hand], with a radiance like the filaments of a lotus,
resembling molten gold, and having the color of a diamond door-panel.
The bud resembles a filament; the sheath has the luster of five petals;
it possesses a color like saffron, the hue of the seed of the womb. (14)
The first [pillar] on the southern pillar has the color of a bee's seed and possesses a luster like a bee;
the second has the luster of great silver.
The second seed-syllable is the bee (bhramara), which is here said to be gold;
it resembles the color of a twilight cloud and is declared to be the seed-syllable of the womb (yoni).
O child, this seed of the *bhramara* is like the luster of pure gold;
its *puṭa* color is like fire, and its *kośa* is said to be like the *japā* flower. (17)
In this context, that which is called Vāma is said to be in the left nostril;
however, in the right nostril, it is called Vajrakavāṭa.
Iḍā and Piṅgalā are said to be the adamantine door-bolt;
I shall now describe the Suṣumnā door-bolt, the supreme destroyer of death. (19)
O Mahāsena, taking the hollow [letter] *ga*, conjoined with the vowel *e* and topped by a *bindu*, it is declared to be the left pillar (*vāmastambha*). (20)
Furthermore, having taken the hollow [letter] conjoined with the vowel *e*, it is indeed the right pillar, surmounted by a dot (*bindu*) upon its head. (21)
Joined with the thirteenth [vowel] and adorned with a bindu at its head,
O Mahāsena, it is declared as the "Upward-Northern" (ūrdhvottara) by means of its own seed-syllable.

The thirteenth [letter] ending with Gaganam (the letter *ha*), adorned with the form of the Bindu—this one should know as the "Northern" (*uttara*); one should perform it with diligent effort. || 23 ||
White, black, red, and green are indeed the colors;
Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, and Paśupati are the names of the deities.
Rudra, the god, as well as Bhīma, Mahādeva, and Sadāśiva— these are declared to be the presiding deities within the Iḍā [nāḍī] at the adamantine bolt. (25)
Mahādeva, Hara, Rudra, Śaṅkara, Nīlalohita, Śūlapāṇi, Kṛttivāsas, Kapardin, and Meghavāhana. || 26 ||
O Six-faced One, I have indeed declared the presiding deity of Piṅgalā to be Gaṅgādhara, Virūpākṣa, Nīlagrīva, and Vṛṣadhvaja. || 27 ||
Śrīkaṇṭha, Nīlakaṇṭha, Kālakaṇṭha, Kapāladhṛt,
and Umāpati as the ninth, [are located] in Suṣumnā and Vajraśiṣṭaka.
The fourth and the third, joined with Māyānala, and Piṅgalāvajrakavāṭa—this is the supreme secret. (29)
Resembling cow’s milk in appearance and like pure crystal,
this secret Vajrakavāṭaka is indeed the granter of boons, O Maheśa.
The fourth is the beloved of Kubjā, joined with the fire of universal destruction (saṃvartaka);
it is situated above Māyā and endowed with both Bindu and Nāda. || 31 ||
Out of affection for you, Gāndhārī revealed the thirteenth door-panel, Vajrakavāṭa, located on the left pillar and possessing a luster like that of Indra’s bow.
The second pillar, indeed the southern one, is Kubjaka;
it has the appearance of an evening cloud and possesses a luster slightly like that of the moon.
The vulva-mandala is indeed like the fifth [vowel], the fifth note itself;
the bee is likewise the sixth, possessing a radiance equal to that of your [face]. 34.
One should know the Kubjakoṭaprabha [mantra], adorned with the eleventh vowel, resembling crushed collyrium in appearance, and supreme in bestowing all accomplishments. (35)
The second [syllable] is Kubjakaṇṭha, joined with Māyā and Nala;
it is topped by a Bindu, overpowered [by it], and has the luster of an Atasī flower. (36)
Pitṛpāda, Hyekapāda, Anekapāda, Ekanetraka, Ugra, Śānta, Suśānta, Pinākī, and Tridaśeśvara. || 37 ||
"This Vajrakavāṭa-gandha has been expounded out of affection for you. Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, on the characteristics of the Vajrakavāṭa, in the Kālottara. 61.
Śrīḥ!
Īśvara said: I shall now explain, in brief, the Hastijihvā-kavāṭa,
which is the fourth of the fourth [section] and is endowed with Jātavedas.
Above that, the fourth is adorned and joined with a bindu;
it is a single vajra-panel that is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
On the first [panel] of the fourth [door], O child, there is [the face] adorned with a crest of matted locks;
on the left side of the door-post, it resembles a rain-cloud.
Resembling the rising sun, the seed-syllable of the door-panel is very difficult to obtain;
it is the second letter of the fourth [varga], adorned with a dot on its crest.
The southern pillar is said to have a luster resembling vermilion;
O child, these two are proclaimed to be the wombs of the bees.
Then both of those [lotuses] are described as resembling the Aśoka and Bandhūka flowers;
furthermore, the seed-syllable of the bud (puṭabīja) is adorned with a dot on its crest (binduśekhara).
It is described and proclaimed as resembling the whiteness of cow’s milk;
it should be employed starting from the fourth [syllable] and is endowed with thirteen [syllables]. (7)
O Six-faced One, it is mounted upon the crest of the *bindu*, resembling a red bubble; it is indeed the sheath of the *hastijihvā* [vein] at the door-panel. (8)
Then, indeed, those two [mantras], resembling lightning and fire, shall be explained as the Pushakavata, by which one becomes a conqueror of death. || 9 ||
Now, the fourth letter of the fifth [varga], joined with fire (ra), with the power of the Lord (ha) above it, and endowed with bindu and nāda. (10)
Resplendent like ten million suns, the supreme leader of all mantras, this Vajra-Door indeed destroys all death. (11)
The first letter of the fifth [varga], adorned with a bindu in its center,
shall be the left pillar of Pūṣā, resembling a lotus leaf.
The third letter of the fifth [varga], adorned with a dot on its crest, they call the southern pillar; it is pure and has the luster of emerald. (13)
But he who knows the subsequent higher [mantra] should then perform the higher oblation;
it resembles the appearance of a red lotus, yet is measured like a blue lotus.
The two [syllables] *phaṃ* and *phaṭ* are like the source of bees, having a luster equal to crushed collyrium; they are two sheaths of cloth, possessing the brilliance of frost and silver.
The glorious one said, "O illustrious lady, this is called the Vajrakavāṭa;
O child, listen now as I explain its ritual procedure."
The door-post is fully described; the left post is illustrated [as follows]:
Jāra is conjoined with the third vowel, surmounted by the Bindu and Śikhā. (17)
Alternatively, there is the Binduśekhara-pīṭha, which has the luster of molten gold;
in the Lalana [pīṭha] there are two Bhramarī-yonis, resembling the flax flower or a bumblebee.

The fifteenth and sixteenth [petals], possessing a radiance equal to the purity of a conch shell, are designated as the *puṭa* and *kośa*; they are great and foremost, bestowing spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). (19)
Enough; I shall now explain the Vajra Door-bolt in brief:
having taken the fourth [syllable] from Anila (Vāyu) combined with Hutāśana (Agni). (20)
The power of supreme attachment, however, is endowed with Śiva and Nārāyaṇa;
it possesses the brilliance of ten thousand suns and has adamantine doors and panels.
Varuṇa is known as Bindu and is described as the left pillar;
he resembles pure crystal and has the nature of smoke and light.
The second seed-syllable from Amṛta is like a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon;
it is said to be the right pillar, surmounted by a bindu at its head.
The nectar (amṛta) conjoined with the embryo (garbha) is said to be progressively higher;
it is conjoined with the twelve vowels and is indeed the ultimate higher [state]. (24)
Both colors are proclaimed to be as bright as a conch shell or a jasmine flower;
they are said to have thirteen teeth at their end and to originate from the *bhramara* (bee) source.
The lotus fiber and the color of cow’s milk are proclaimed as the seed-syllable of speech (vāgbīja);
the emission (visarga) is called its sheath, and above that is the "kokilodbhava" (the cuckoo-born).
The visarga should be known as nectar, the supreme deceiver of death;
it has the form of Varuṇa and is called the support of immortality.
O Six-faced One, two [channels] resembling a pearl necklace and a wreath of mist belong to the seed-syllable;
they are declared to be the diamond door-panels and are proclaimed as belonging to Alambuṣā.
Now listen, O Six-faced One, to the Kuhavajrakavāṭa, which is variegated, extensive, subtle, supreme, and the means for accomplishing the universe. (29)
This supreme tradition, which deceives death, is the sixth [manifestation] of Nārasiṃha; it causes the three worlds to experience the highest wonder. (30)
Then, equipped with six arms and adorned by me upon his head,
he was addressed by Hara as "Śikhāhari," possessing the brilliance of molten gold.
The seventh, however, is the door-panel which is difficult to attain even for the cities;
it is protected by the Bindu and possesses a luster like that of a lotus filament. (32)
On the left, one should know the door-post pillar to be like the color of turmeric juice; it ends with the letter *la* and destroys all death. (33)
Endowed with the sound of the letter *rā* and possessed of good fortune, they say it shines increasingly more and more like the thumb. (34)
Joined with the vowel *e*, or indeed the forty-sixth [consonant], resembling the color of *piṇḍāraka* [flame-colored], it is called "lower-and-upper" (*adharottara*). || 35 ||
The Bhramarayoni and Bindumastaka are like Mañjiṣṭhā and Karṇikāra flowers; they are red and resemble seeds. || 36 ||
The *visarga* and so forth, as well as the *visarga*, are proclaimed to be the two *purakośas*;
they are also briefly described as resembling *gorocanā* and *niśā*. (37)
The door-panel of Kuhavajra is said to be covered with Asuvaras;
O Six-faced One, hear now in truth about the door-panel of Śaṅkhinīvajra. (38)
This is the most secret, supremely subtle, and esoteric [teaching] revealed by its own light;
it is the second letter of the group of vowels (i.e., *i*) conjoined with the two fires (*kṛśānu*, i.e., *r*). (39)
But above that, it should be coiled falsely, joined with the state of dissolution;
it resembles a white lotus, possessing the luster of snow, the kunda flower, and the moon. (40)
One who is well-composed should join [the breath] at the very base of the penis;
this, conjoined with the vital drop (jīvabindu), is declared to be the "left pillar" (vāmastambha).

The right pillar is said to be joined with the long *jīva* (the letter *ai*) and conjoined with the eleventh vowel (*au*), and it is proclaimed to be white in color. Alternatively, when the *jīva* is endowed with the twelfth [vowel] (*aḥ*), it is proclaimed to be the color of the moon (white). || 43 ||
The upper-northern [syllable] should come first, and the subsequent lower-northern [syllable] follows;
the seed-syllables of the Yoni and the Bee are the thirteenth and fourteenth [respectively]. (44)
Both of them are described as having a complexion like the rainbow;
with the sounds "śaṃ śaṃ," "puṭaha," and "haṃ śaṃ hi," they possess a radiance equal to a conch shell and a jasmine flower.
O Six-faced One, this is declared to you as the Śaṅkhinī-vajrakavāṭa; having first practiced it according to the ritual procedure for one year, O Guha.
Afterwards, O child, one should practice the Rāṣṭraka Mṛtyuñjaya Yoga;
one attains freedom from old age and immortality—this is the truth, O Six-faced One. (47)
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Vajra Door," in the Kālottara [Tantra]. 62.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
Having secured the ten gates of the wise one with adamantine door-panels,
[one should likewise secure] the upper door-posts, the womb, and the bee-hive.
O Six-faced One, with all the sheaths of the letters and with an undistracted mind, one should thereafter practice the Mṛtyuñjaya yoga with single-minded concentration. (2)
In a solitary and secluded place, free from wind and heat, not swarming with gadflies and mosquitoes, and devoid of all disturbances. || 3 ||
In a very firm flower-garden, or in palatial mansions, in a secluded, auspicious, well-joined, narrow, and most beautiful place; || 4 ||
On a single, bright, divine, auspicious bed, level and beautiful, he spread a divine covering, auspicious and measuring one cubit in length. || 5 ||
The width should be one *ratni*, providing a comfortable seat for a single person;
facing east in the forenoon and facing north at midday.
In the afternoon, facing west,
one should practice yoga after assuming either the svastika posture or the lotus posture.
With the neck, head, and torso held straight, one should remain with the abdomen and chest level;
with the sides and shoulders even, one should not let the teeth touch the teeth.
Having assumed the "elephant-tongue" posture, one should gaze at the tip of the nose;
because it is two finger-breadths below the forehead and the skull, this is the supreme wheel.
Even the gods, such as Viṣṇu and Brahmā, do not know this wheel;
how much less so the ṛṣis, vidyādharas, and siddhas, whose minds are limited? (10)
The supreme white lotus is perfectly pure, adorned with sixteen petals,
endowed with a pericarp and filaments, and one span in width.
The pericarp is four finger-breadths [in diameter] and one finger-breadth in height;
it is the most secret, supreme, and subtle seed-syllable that destroys death. || 12 ||
I shall proclaim the easy means; listen, O Six-faced One, according to the truth:
[it is] the eighteen great seed-syllables, resembling a conch, a kunda flower, and the moon. (13)
Joined with the fire of dissolution (KṢ), joined with the interior of dissolution (AU), joined with the end of the thirteen (M), and endowed with the sixth vowel (Ū). || 14 ||
Joined with Bindu and Nāda, it is the supreme destroyer of death;
this alone is the Supreme Brahman, this alone is the Supreme Śiva. (15)
This is the seed-syllable that conquers death, a supreme and most wonderful secret;
I shall now proclaim its essence, which indeed destroys death. (16)
O child, O six-faced one, it is extracted in reverse order from the thirty-two [syllables],
conjoined with Saṃhārarudra, and extended by Kṛśānu for its bliss.
Joined with the waters of dissolution and united with the end of the thirteenth [vowel], and endowed with the crest of the *bindu* and *nāda*, that is declared to be its support. (18)
Having placed *khaga* on the eastern petal, one should place *khāga* on the southeast petal;
having placed *khiṅgi* on the southeastern petal, one should place *khīgī* on the three [petals] of the south.
Khugudvai is in the petal of Vaivasvata; khugūdvai is in the petal of Bhṛṅgarāja;
khṛgṛdvai is in the petal of Nirṛti; and khṝgṝ is in the domain of Sugrīva.
One should place *khḷ* and *gḹ* like two arrows on the remaining petals;
having placed *khe* and *ge* on the wind petal, one should place *khai* and *gai* on the principal petal. (21)
Having placed *khaḥ* and *gau* on the leaf of Soma, one should place *khaṃ* and *gaṃ* on the leaf of Atithi;
having placed *khaḥ* and *gaḥ* on the leaf of Īśa, one should place them on the leaf of Jaya.
All are joined with the bindu, all are endowed with the nāda;
the two visargas are the visarjanīya—such is the King, the supreme teacher. (23)
O child, all [the elements] are like bees; indeed, there is the relationship of support and supported.
329) The seed, which is the Lord, is a particularity resembling the flax flower.
Mṛtyuñjaya is white in color; in the process of exhalation (uccāra), he is also white in color.
O child, the short vowels have the appearance of [white], while the long vowels have the luster of emerald.
O Six-faced One, having joined the Visarga—white as cow’s milk and possessing the luster of a conch, a jasmine flower, or the moon—with the letter Śaśinī (I), one should unite it with the Bindu. (26)
The fourth letter of the *ya*-group, joined with the fire of time (*kālānala*), resting upon a white lotus and beautifully adorned by the full moon. || 27 ||
Now, above the lotus, there is a six-petaled [lotus] of dark complexion;
it is exceedingly black at the hair follicle, destroying death and graying hair. (28)
The wise man should lead the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who is the belly of the mantra and the death that destroys grey hair, by means of the Hṛllekhā mantra. (29)
Within the hollow of a lotus, indeed in the center of the hollow of a seed-vessel, the wise one should constantly contemplate that which is white, resembling the foam of the ocean. || 30 ||
One should practice for one *ghaṭikā* at each of the three junctions of the day, or for four *ghaṭikās* during the four watches of the night.
Having assumed the form of a sixteen-year-old, one may wander about like the god Kāmadeva.
However, at the three junctions of the day, one should meditate for two *ghaṭikās* on [the deity] with the luster of lapis lazuli.
Having caused the self to enter the triad and having encapsulated it with the moon,
it then becomes like the throat of a peacock within the pores of the skin.
The most excellent teacher should fill the hair-pores with nectar during the three junctions of the day for two nāḍīs each, and at the fourth junction for six faces, O Six-faced One. (34)
Having struck the vajra-door ten times, one shall become equanimous. || 35 ||
Having brought the twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa, into the skull-bowl within the center of the heart-lotus, [he places him] in the two-colored [vessels],
in that which is called Amṛta, in the fully expanded belly that destroys death.
The wise one, being composed in meditation, should place [the substance] in a casket and fill it. || 37 ||
In that very place, O Guha, having extracted the mantra of the Sparśana-jīrṇa,
one should indeed [place] the Māyā-bīja (Hrīṃ) joined with a nasal bindu in the fourth [position].
Resembling a peacock's eye-ball and possessing the luster of a dark blue cloud, it destroys wrinkles and grey hair either simultaneously or gradually. (39)
He shall live for five thousand years, possessing the appearance of a sixteen-year-old.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Maintenance of the Aperture of the Door," within the *Kālottara* concerning the characteristics of the Vajra-Door. 63.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
Between the eyebrows is a great lotus, possessing the luster of great silver, endowed with sixteen petals, and filled with the fire of universal dissolution. || 1 ||
Joined with the fire at the end of the aeon, joined with the sun at the end of the aeon,
endowed with the fourteen [vowels], and accompanied by the sixth [consonant].
The *kūṭa* joined with Hari and Hara indeed destroys death;
it possesses a brilliance equal to ten million suns and resembles a great ruby.
One should place the deity in the pericarp, having the form of the Supreme Āditya;
the wise call Viṣṇu Brahmā, and they call him Śiva.
(331) It is the supreme secret, the ultimate mystery, the very nature of the Supreme Self;
it is the Noble Self of all that moves and stands, the highest and greatest. (5)
Among all the gods beginning with Iḍā, Āditya is said to be the foremost;
the entire form of Maheśvara is beneficial in the form of Āditya.
And, my dear child, one should practice this supreme mantra which destroys death and fulfills all desires:
the eighth seed-syllable of Prajāpati (the letter 'ma'), conjoined with the fire-god (the letter 'ra') and the bindu (the nasal dot). (7)
This seed-syllable, conjoined with the water of Agastya and endowed with both maintenance and dissolution,
is without support and is the destroyer of all suffering.
Having encapsulated it with the Moon (the letter *sa*) as the fourth by the wise one,
and having joined it with *māyā* (the letter *ī*) and the fire-bindu (*ra*), one should contemplate it thus encapsulated.
O child, one should practice this constantly at the three periods of the day for six years;
O lord of yogis, the duration of time is sixty ghaṭikās, and one should rely upon that.
O Six-faced One, I shall now describe the seeds for the petals; listen briefly.
Beginning from the east, one should install them all according to the prescribed rule with a concentrated mind.
O Guha, O observer of good vows, having placed two by two upon each petal with an undistracted mind, and having positioned them facing the King of Mantras, one should meditate upon them.
One should place *ca* and *ja* on the petal of the Bindu, possessing a radiance like the rising sun;
and one should place *ña* and *jha* on the petal of Bhṛṅga, possessing a radiance like the filaments of a lotus.
One should place the seed-syllables on the petals of fire, which have a luster like saffron;
and one should place the seed-syllables on the petal of vitatha, which has a luster like the rising sun.
Having placed *chujū* on the petal of Varuṇa, which has the luster of the Bandhūka flower,
and having placed *chūjū* on Śeṣa, which has a luster equal to the color of a crow.
Having placed [the two] on the wind-petal, they possess a luster equal to the color of a bumblebee;
having placed [the two] on the forehead (ballāṭaka), they possess a luster equal to the color of copper. || 16 ||
Having placed the *chojo* syllables there, they possess a luster equal to that of the *nandyāvarta*;
having placed the *chao jau* syllables, they possess a luster like that of wild rice (*nīvāra*).
Having placed *chaṃ* and *jam* on the two shoulders, which have a luster like pearls;
one should place *chaḥ* and *jaḥ* on the two matted locks, which resemble pure crystal. (18)
Having performed this entire mental placement (nyāsa) even briefly, one should meditate upon it again and again;
having closed the nostrils with the fingers, one should constantly meditate on Indra without being bound by formal ritual constraints.
Having filled [the body] according to the rule by means of *kumbhaka*, the practitioner of mantra should meditate;
he should meditate separately, and he will conquer death—of this there is no doubt.
Having meditated on that seed-syllable as nectar, like a bee within the pores of the skin,
one should properly cause it to flow ten times toward the vital points (marmans) where it was sown.
One should contemplate [the nectar] that resembles a peacock's neck and is like the color of a bhr̥ṅga bee, having filled all the pores of the skin. 22.
O Guha, at the three junctions of the day, one should meditate with an undistracted mind for eight years upon the six channels and the fourth [channel] in the left [side]. (23)
The secret yoga of the white-hair pillar has not been revealed;
it resides between the sun, moon, and fire, upon the pericarp of a lotus.
One should constantly hold the Lord of Life for exactly seven ghaṭikās;
for two ghaṭikās, one should meditate on the petals with the seed-syllables, and in due order, on the letters together with their presiding deities.
The eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, the eight Vasus, and the two Aśvins, in their proper order, [are likewise present]. || 26 ||
One should cause the exceedingly bright, supreme, subtle, and self-dependent [seed] to enter;
all these, appearing white, are for the rite of destroying death. (27)
O Six-faced One, all those [hairs] on the base of the grey locks are the color of bees;
for the sake of liberation, one should always contemplate that which is as white as a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon. (28)
For subjugation (vaśya), it should be red in color; for attraction (ākarṣaṇa), it should be white;
for causing enmity (vidveṣaṇa), it should be smoke-colored; and for eradication (uccāṭana), it should be black. || 29 ||
For paralyzing, it should be yellow in color; for deluding, black in color;
for cutting, resembling a blue jay; and for piercing, eight-colored.
One should employ the Avarṇaka mantra for the paralysis of an army, while the Raktaka is used for the destruction of the enemy's host in battle with thousands of garlands of flames.
Visualizing her as the fire of time that destroys the enemy army, one should bind the crest-lock (śikhābandha) upon the head with a cord from the scriptures. || 32 ||
O child, by the destruction of the sound *ghṛṃ*, there is always a state of being established in the heart when it is overcome;
this is the application for attraction, and one should strike it with the word for subjugation (*vaśya*).
Through the fire-mantra (āgneya) there shall be subjugation (vaśya), or attraction (ākarṣaṇa) by means of air and fire;
especially for eradication (uccāṭana), O Six-faced One, it is done by the air-mantra (vāyavya).
Through the conjunction of air and fire, hatred reaches its certainty;
for paralyzing, the rite of Mahendra alone is prescribed, while for deluding, it is from Vāyu and Īśāna.
Through the conjunction of Vahni and Mahendra, one shall obtain victory in battle.
[One should visualize] the circle of Śakra situated in the middle of the circle of Agni. || 36 ||
In its center is the seed-syllable of the three worlds, accompanied by its retinue;
with thousands of garlands of flames, O Guha, it shall consume the enemy army.
O Mahāsena, having conquered the enemy army— consisting of ten times as many chariots, horses, and elephants— he prospers happily in his excellent city. (38)

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Stabilization of the Army through Concentration on the Space between the Eyebrows," in the *Kālottara*, concerning the characteristics of the Vajra-Door.
Śrīḥ!
The Lord said: The food, resonant with the sound from the cavity of the palate, is adorned with sixteen petals;
it is endowed with a pericarp and filaments, and possesses the luster of frost and silver.
It should be one span (vitasti) in width, with a pericarp (karṇikā) four finger-breadths (aṅgula) in size;
the height of the pericarp should be slightly like the luster of gold.
In the center there, one should meditate upon the god Nārāyaṇa, who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace, and who resembles a conch shell or cow’s milk in color.
The size of a thumb, immovable, free from conceptual construction,
stainless, omniscient, omnipresent, peaceful, with eyes, heads, and faces on every side.
Having taken the twelfth [portion] from Prajāpati, together with the ritual manual (kalpa), joined with the water of the manual, and endowed with both maintenance and dissolution; || 5 ||
Indeed, Nārāyaṇa is the manifest form of immortality, free from all affliction;
for this supreme state is his very nature, and this highest form is that of the Moon.
O child, one should install the deity, the cause of all causes, Mṛtyuñjaya, within the pericarp through the practice of constant meditation.
I shall declare its support according to reality; listen, O Six-faced One!
Having taken the thirteenth [letter] of Prajāpati, it is joined with two mātrās.
(335) It is endowed with excessive heat and afflicted by great diseases;
it is joined with extreme cold and accompanied by Rudra and Viṣṇu. || 9 ||
Thus, it is indeed the vessel of nectar, manifest in the form of Garuḍa;
it is the seed-mantra that destroys all poisons, whether stationary or mobile.
O Mahāsena, an artificial sacred thread and food, drink, and other offerings prepared with deceit— these two effect the destruction of Vāsuki’s poison.
The wise man, having uttered the *kūṭa* mantra, should draw three lines on the head, the heart, and the navel; this destroys poison.
By taking a bite with the lips, one becomes free from poison in an instant.
At night, having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should recite it without hesitation.
When the body is afflicted by poison or by piśācas, bhūtas, grahas, and the like,
one should eat food over which mantras have been recited, and likewise consume a portion of the urine.
Having consecrated it seven times, one neutralizes poison that has been digested with ease;
now listen, O Six-faced One, as I describe its retinue. (15)
One should place Ṭha and Ḍa on the eastern petal, which has a luster like cow’s milk;
one should place Ṭhā and Ḍā on the southwestern petal, O dear one, which has the luster of a *bandhūka* flower and resembles a bee.
One should place Ṭhi and Ḍi on the fire-petal, having the luster of an Aśoka flower;
one should place Ṭhī and Ḍī on Vitatha, both auspicious and having the luster of an Atasī flower.
One should place *ṭhu* and *ḍu*, which possess a luster equal to that of *viṣṇukrānti*, on the southern petal;
one should place *ṭhū* and *ḍū*, which possess a luster equal to the color of a bumblebee, as *bhṛṅgarāja*.
One should place ṬHṚ and ḌṚ in the southwest, possessing the luster of dark blue clouds; one should place ṬHṜ and ḌṜ, possessing the luster of the Karṇikāra flower. || 19 ||
One should place ṭhḷ and ḍḷ in the western direction, having a luster like cow’s milk;
and one should place ṭhḷ and ḍḷ in the remaining [northern] direction, having a luster like madder-dyed cloth.
One should place Ṭha and Ḍe in the northwest wind, having the luster of blue lotuses;
one should place Ṭhai and Ḍai in the mouth, having the luster of pāṭalī flowers.
One should assign *ṭha* and *ḍa* to Soma, which have a luster like the kunda flower;
one should assign *ṭhaḥ* and *ḍaḥ* to these two, which have the luster of the japā flower.

One should place *ṭhaṃ* and *ḍaṃ* in the northeast, possessing a radiance like that of the *nandyāvarta* flower; one should place *ṭhaḥ* and *ḍaḥ* in the southeast, possessing a radiance like the *japā* flower.
And the seventh excellent seed-syllable, O Six-faced One, is the supreme means for deceiving death; it is perfectly full like the moon, appearing as the manifest, radiant moon itself.
For the wise praise the seed-syllable as the orb of the sun;
therefore, O Six-faced One, the form of sound is indeed circular.
O Six-faced One, the seed-syllable is the image consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas;
the Person (Puruṣa) residing therein is declared to be the luster of the Yajus.
The *ratni* of the Pure One is taught as that seed-syllable of the Supreme Goddess;
Brahmā, Hari, and Hara—these three triads—one should employ as the weapon. (27)
The triad of fires is designated as Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ;
likewise the three libations, the three junctions of the day, the three qualities, and the three aims of life. (28)
The entire world, both moving and stationary, as well as all rites such as the Agniṣṭoma, [proceed from it];
therefore, with every effort, one should always practice that seed-syllable. (29)
O child, one should practice this until the end of the year to become free from old age and death;
the recitation and the journey should be performed at the three junctions of the day for three ghaṭikās each.
One should remain like a full water-jar, worn out by the touch of nirvāṇa;
thus, with a concentrated mind, one should practice this for twelve years. (31)
One should reflect upon this for twelve hundred thousand [repetitions];
one should practice for sixteen years at midnight for eight ghaṭikās.
Having performed inhalation and retention, the best of instructors should release [the breath] once; he should touch the eternal [point] until it is worn away, very slowly. (33)
"In this way, one attains the eternal yoga through the oral tradition. Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter in the Kālottara.
Śrīḥ!
Īśvara said:
This supreme form of Karṇa is a great form that destroys death;
even the gods, asuras, lords of sages, yakṣas, vidyādharas, and others [are subject to it]. || 1 ||
The Cāraṇas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Pannagas, and others—all shall conquer death through constant recitation and meditation. || 2 ||
There, by means of the appropriate lotus, through the constant filling of the *kumbhaka* [breath-retention], it becomes as radiant as a conch or jasmine, endowed with sixteen petals. (3)
The width of the lotus should be exactly twelve finger-breadths;
one should know the stalk to be eight finger-breadths and the pericarp four finger-breadths.
The pericarp and filaments have the luster of molten gold;
in its center is Mahādeva, four-faced and four-armed.
The Supreme Lord, who has three eyes and the color of a conch shell, four finger-breadths in length,
was seated in the middle of the hollow of a lotus.
The supreme, divine form of nectar, situated in the heart of all,
having taken the sixteenth [digit] of Prajāpati, together with Caṇḍarudra. (7)
Endowed with Mahācaṇḍāmala and joined with Caṇḍamāruta,
and joined with Caṇḍavāri, it is divine and [ends] at the thirteenth.
But joined with the sixth [vowel], endowed with the *bindu* and the *nāda*,
this "Peak of Nectar" (*amṛtakūṭa*), O child, is the supreme destroyer of death.
Indeed, by means of constant recitation and meditation, endowed with faith and devotion, one attains victory over death; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (10)
All human beasts, through their laziness, desire to strike down death;
therefore, with every effort, one should practice the "artificial" [method]. 11.
By means of the seed-syllable Amṛtakūṭa, one shall conquer all death;
out of a desire to deceive death, I shall declare its support.
It consists of seventeen syllables belonging to Prajāpati, endowed with the power of withdrawal (saṃhāra),
joined with the fire of universal dissolution, and possessing the splendor of that fire of dissolution.

One should employ the "Great Seat" (mahāsana) conjoined with the end of the thirteenth [vowel], and the sixth [consonant] together with the end of the thirteenth; this should be applied to all the kūṭas.
Indeed, regarding the characteristics of the vajra door-panels, both those explicitly mentioned and those not mentioned,
there is the bindu, the nāda, the sixth, and likewise that which is at the end of the thirteenth.
Resembling pure crystal, it was endowed with all [auspicious] marks. || 16 ||
O child, one should contemplate [the deity] at all times as resembling the seed-syllable of nectar;
I shall now describe the retinue for the sake of desiring the destruction of death. (17)
And likewise,
O Bhadra, having firmly placed those two of equal radiance upon the eastern petal of the lotus, which possesses such splendor; (18)

One should worship two Kratus: Tithivinyasa, who resembles fire, and Iṣu, who has the luster of Kiṇihī and Kumuda; and one should worship two more for the servant: Kratudvaya, who has a radiance like that of the Bhṛṅgarāja.
The two syllables *tū* and *thū* belong to Yama and have the luster of flax flowers;
one should place *tṛ*, *thṛ*, and *bhṛ* which resemble the petals of a bumblebee.
The two syllables *tṛ* and *thṛ*, as well as *tḷ* and *thḷ*, are in the southwest;
and for the syllable *turhaṃ*, the syllables *tu* and *haṃ* have the same color and radiance as the swan in the west.
Having placed *tḷ* and *thḷ*, the remainder is proclaimed to be like a white water-lily (*kumuda*).
Having placed *te* and *the* on the petal of Vāyu, they are similar to the neck of a peacock.
Having placed *tai* and *thai* on the face petal, they are like the radiance of the *caṇa* flower;
having placed *to* and *tho* on the Soma petal, they resemble white *dhūrdhūra* flowers.
Having placed *tau* and *thau* in the northeast petal, they have the luster of *nirguṇḍī* flowers;
having placed *taṃ* and *thaṃ* in the northeast petal, they have the luster of *mādhavī* flowers.
Having placed [the syllables] *taḥ* and *thaḥ* upon the two lotus-petals, which possess a luster resembling a forest garland,
one who is composed should thus perform the correct mental placement with a concentrated mind.
Recalling the king of mantras, which is as white as a swan, jasmine, or the moon,
one should properly bolt the doors and seal them with the crescent moon.
O Six-faced One, one should always remember [the mantra] at the three periods of the day; with a well-composed mind, one should spend the six *ghaṭikās* ending at midnight.
Having joined it together without any gaps, one should blunt the solar vessel;
then, having meditated upon another [vessel] resembling a bhr̥ṅga bee, one should fumigate it with black incense.
One should flood all the pores of the skin with nectar alone;
this recited [mantra] brings about paralysis and enjoyment, which is difficult even for the gods to attain. (29)
One should meditate for eighteen years with single-minded devotion;
one lives for eighteen hundred thousand years—of this there is no doubt. (30)
The wise one shall obtain the strength of an eighteen-year-old elephant;
having encased [the name] with the *bindu*, he should recollect the king of mantras. (31)
Every day, at the three periods of the day, one should fill [the breath] through both nostrils with a gentle [wind] as white as cow's milk, performing the kumbhaka retention in the form of the ears.
O Six-faced One, O Guha, one should constantly cause all that has aged within Nirvāṇa— the eternal contact situated within the Suṣumnā— to age away perpetually.
This divine Śiva-yoga is a secret that has not been revealed;
hunger and thirst perish quickly, and one experiences no fatigue. (34)
The pitcher remains [within]... it is not found among the vowels.
O God, one should practice the deity in the left [nostril] and cause the nectar to flow from the fire. (35)
One should thus recollect the king of mantras for a watch or even half a watch; O child, one remains as if well-fed until dawn, without a doubt. (36)
The wise yogi should proclaim the yoga that brings about satisfaction from hunger;
he should fill the well of the *iḍā* with the king of mantras. (37)
O observer of noble vows, one should cause the nectar to flow into the fire at the end of the Kuṇḍalī;
by practicing this for one month, one shall destroy hunger and thirst.
One should contemplate the eight truths joined with the king of mantras, having encapsulated the self within the center of the circle of light. (39)
One should meditate on all [beings] as being like the sun; one will attain the bliss of sleep.
Having abandoned the qualities of passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa), one abides in purity (sattva) alone. (40)
One should meditate on five *ghaṭikās* within the king of mantras in the eyes;
one should recollect the supreme Sun-god in the center of the ocular orb.
All this may be waking, dreaming, or the destruction of deep sleep;
this yoga of sleepless bliss is the supreme Self of the Puruṣa. 42.
Hunger and sleep are constantly harmful as they create obstacles to yoga;
if the faculty of sleep should arise, one should restrain that sleep. (43)
For one should protect the principal sense organ, because into that one should withdraw [the others].
Sleep is the root of all suffering; hunger is the root of all misery. || 44 ||
For destruction indeed has its root in desire; from desire, hatred will arise;
and from hatred, anger is produced; therefore, one is ruined—of this there is no doubt. (45)
Truth, fame, austerity, charity, strength, purity, worship of Śiva,
meditation, recitation, and meditative absorption— all these perish in that very instant due to anger.
Lust, anger, [and] * * * * * moṇḍabha, as well as abuse, laziness, falsehood, protection, and indeed emptiness—[these are the obstacles]. || 47 ||
O Guha, one should at all times avoid these sixteen: hunger, sleep, envy, hatred arising from delusion, affection for loved ones, and speculative reasoning. (48)

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Abandonment of Hunger, Thirst, and Sleep through the Assumption of the Form of the Ears," in the *Kālottara*, concerning the characteristics of the Vajra-Door. 66.
Īśvara said:
One should meditate upon the Lord of Nectar within the center of the heart-lotus;
there, in the hearts of all mortals, dwells the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Endowed with the city of eight constituents (puryaṣṭaka), it moves both downward and upward;
likewise, there are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. (2)
The mind, the ego, and the intellect—this is known as the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka).
O Six-faced One, the body within this city of eight belongs to the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
The Puruṣa is the leader of the twenty-four principles;
the wise declare him to be the twenty-fifth in all the scriptures. (4)

The person (puruṣa), the individual (pudgala), the wise one, the sacrificial victim, the twenty-fivefold [principle], the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), the enjoyer of experience, the self, the conscious one, and the embodied indicator—[these are synonyms]. || 5 ||
Likewise, by means of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), the Lord himself resides in the heart;
he is remembered as the leader of the primary constituents (prakṛti) from the calves upward, consisting of the nature of pleasure and pain.
Then, O Six-faced One, the field named Vāyu is the twenty-seventh;
endowed with the ten vital breaths (prāṇas), it moves through the ten gates.
Between the eyebrows, in the middle of the head, in the throat, and likewise in the chest;
in the heart, in the middle of the navel, and also in the anus and the testicles.
[He should place them] on the two thighs of the bull, on the three joints, on the two shanks,
on the two [other] joints, on the two ankles, and between the feet.
And between the index finger and the big toe is the *marmikā*;
those who know the scriptures have declared that death occurs instantly [when it is struck]. (10)
(343) Death at another time will occur by means of the vital points (*marmāśraya*); of this there is no doubt.
Or one strikes men with thorns, or with fists. (11)
The vital point (marman) called trikaṭi is declared to be between the upper arm and the elbow;
that which is at the root of the hastijihvā [vein] is declared to be saṃdhi.
In each and every instance,
one should recollect the seed-syllable of nectar with a one-pointed mind.
This indeed is the conqueror of death, celebrated as "Haṃsa, Haṃsa";
the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), having departed from the body, has taken refuge in the external ether. || 14 ||
One should not enter again at the end; the wise know this to be the limit of death.
The learned man should bolt all the doors with adamantine door-leaves.
There is no further departure; the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) abides there.
Having enclosed [the breath] right there within the pericarp of the heart-lotus, [one should remain]. 16.
But when the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is cast into the hollow of nectar within the casket, O Six-faced One, death cannot enter there because of the absence of a gateway. 17.
By closing the nine gates with door-panels, one does not go to death;
indeed, by the very act of covering them with doors, through that constant enclosure, [one transcends it].
In that place, O Guha, death shall not enter, nor shall there be any departure;
for death, having bound a man by the neck with its noose, [cannot act] there.
One should always lead this armor away from a person to the abode of Yama;
therefore, with every effort, one should protect the house with adamantine door-panels.
By the grace of the Guru, the wise man should always move about behind closed doors;
when liberation is firmly secured, such a person remains steadfast.
There, fear of enemies or thieves and even the fear of Yama do not exist;
having covered it with adamantine door-panels, death does not find its way there. (22)
Therefore, one should properly practice the Mṛtyuñjaya Yoga within the heart, [visualizing] a divine, pure white lotus adorned with sixteen petals. (23)
The heart of all embodied beings is one *vitasti* in width;
the lotus is one *prādeśa* in size, while the pericarp (*karṇikā*) is four *aṅgulas*.
One should know that the stalk is eight finger-breadths [in length], and the height of the pericarp is one *aṅgula*.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are indeed the lunar, solar, and fiery mandalas. (25)
But situated in the midst of them is the Person, the size of a thumb’s joint;
he is the twenty-fifth Person, whose self is presided over by the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
The twenty-first supreme seed-syllable is nectar that destroys death;
it is joined with the Great Dissolution and endowed with the Great Fire.
Joined with Mahānīla, endowed with Mahāvāri, conjoined with the end of the thirteenth [vowel], and endowed with the sixth vowel. || 28 ||
Endowed with the Bindu and Nāda, this supreme mass of nectar—one should place the Self within the hollow of the seed-syllable of Skandakūṭa. (29)
Having encapsulated the fourth [vowel] with the moon (the letter *i*) and joined it with the *haṃsa* (the letter *h*),
and having secured it with the adamantine bolts (*vajrakavāṭa*) provided with ten doors,
the wise one should practice meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for six *ghaṭikās* at the three junctions of the day for his own benefit.
The accomplishment of the mantra known as Mṛtyuñjaya, however, occurs through the preceding and following [practices];
one should maintain the entire supreme observance for twenty-six years.
"One shall live for twenty-six hundred thousand [years]—this is the certainty of the scripture.
Within the lotus of the heart, however, is the mandala known as the three qualities (guṇatraya). (33)
The power (śakti) is above them, and the peak-syllable (kūṭaka) is in the middle of the power;
the knower of mantras should restrain the self together with the vital breaths in the middle of the peak-syllable.
Having encapsulated it with the moon, one should subsequently encapsulate it with the *haṃsa*;
then, having properly sealed the ten doors with the adamantine bolts according to the ritual injunction, [one should proceed]. (35)
Thereafter, one whose body has been made of equal flavor (samarasīkṛta) should practice meditative absorption (samādhi);
this method for the gods' victory over death is described here.
O child, for thirty years one should practice with a single-pointed mind during the four junctions of the day, seven nāḍīs at each; however, at midnight, one should indeed practice for ten [nāḍīs].
The lifespan shall be three million years; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
I shall now describe the retinue, which accomplishes all desires and aims. (38)
Having placed *pha* and *pha* on the petal of Indra, which resemble a red lotus bud,
one should place *phā* and *phā* on the petal of Bhramara, which have a luster like the filaments of a lotus.
One should place Phi Phi in Nalle, possessing a radiance like the flowers of the Aśoka tree; one should place Phī Phī in Vitathā, possessing a radiance resembling that of madder (mañjiṣṭha).
One should assign *phu phu* to the north, which has a luster like a dark cloud;
one should assign *phū phū* to the two [positions] in the south, both resembling the color of a bumblebee. (41)
One should place *phṛ* and *phṛ* in the southwest (nairṛtya), both resembling black iron;
and *phṝ* and *phṝ* on Sugrīva, both having the luster of a blue lotus.
One should place *phḷ* and *phḷ* in the two *vāruṇī* [channels], resembling pure crystal; then, having placed *phḹ* and *phḹ* in the *śeṣa*, they resemble lotus petals.

Having assigned *phe phe* to the wind-petals, [the two deities] with full chests and equal radiance; and having assigned *phai phai* to the principal [petal], [the two deities] with the radiance of *piśāca* flowers. (44)
Having placed *pha pha* upon *some*, they possess a luster equal to pearls;
having placed *phau phau* upon *aditi*, they possess a luster like a circle of curd.
O child, being composed, one should place *phaṃ phaṃ* in the northeast;
one should place *phaḥ phaḥ* in the two [corners] of victory, which have a luster like vermilion.

Having thus established [the deity] according to the ritual procedure, one should thereafter first perform concentration (dhāraṇā) upon the Holder of Nectar (Amṛtadhārin), and indeed [then perform] meditation (dhyāna).
Then, being well-composed, one should gradually practice meditative concentration (samādhi);
one should perform exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka) in equal measure. 48.
O child, this accomplished yoga is indeed the practice of touch; one should perform inhalation, retention, and likewise exhalation. (49)
In the eternal state, contact becomes worn away; this is declared to be meditation (dhyāna).
Having abandoned exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), one should indeed relinquish even the retention of breath (kumbhaka). || 50 ||
Having personally meditated upon Śiva alone, it is called samādhi;
having cast off the natural state, one should meditate, "I am Śiva. (57)
This is declared to be the samādhi of the wise;
by meditating upon Śiva himself, one shall become Śiva himself. 52.
Through the yoga of becoming one with the equal flavor (samarasībhāva), that samādhi is described here;
one should contemplate [the self] as empty of its own nature, and thus one shall always be Śiva alone. (53)
This is to be understood as *samādhi*, as declared by those learned in the scriptures.
One should meditate upon its nature as empty, free from all appearance, for half that duration. (54)
(347) Those proficient in the treatises on yoga praise this samādhi;
out of affection for you, I have described this direct means for conquering death. 55.
O Six-faced One, he attains the state of being free from old age and death; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
For Śiva there is no death, nor birth, nor old age and the like. (56)
O child, that meditation indeed becomes constant for the practitioner;
he shall become Śiva himself in person, free from old age and death.
"This very Śiva-saṃpradāya has been declared; it must not be given to just anyone.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, concerning the Heart, Retention, Meditation, and Samādhi, in the Kālottara-tantra, within the section on the characteristics of the Vajra-Door. 67.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
In the center of the navel is the great lotus, which destroys all death;
it is the seed-syllable that brings about all peace and destroys mental anguish and physical disease.
It pacifies great pestilence, destroys great decay,
pacifies the twenty types of delusions, and removes the eight kinds of leprosy and the ten [diseases].
It cures the five types of gulma, the five types of vyūha, the five types of aṣṭhīlā, and the five types of nāśana;
it removes the five types of bhagaṇdarā and destroys the ten types of rājayakṣmā.

It removes the eight types of jaundice, it brings about the destruction of the five-arrowed god (Kāma) by his own power, it wards off the five types of fainting fits, and it is the supreme remover of the five types of coughs.
By holding the *kūṭa* [mudrā], one destroys the eighty diseases born of wind (*vāta*),
as well as the seventy-six eye diseases and those arising from the throat.
It destroys fifty heart diseases, twenty diseases of the [vital] wind (*vāta*),
eighteen diseases of bile (*pitta*), and indeed ten diseases of phlegm (*śleṣman*). (6)
By means of the meditation on the retention of the navel,
he [overcomes] the sixteen kinds of dysuria and the ten types of urinary diseases.
He cures the five types of urinary disorders and diarrhea, as well as the four types of somaroga; likewise, he cures tuni and parituni, and the six and three kinds of hemorrhoids.
The Mahājvarāṣṭaka and [other mantras],
eighteen thousand in number, shall destroy food in an instant.
There were twelve thousand Kumāragṛhas, six thousand Śaśanis, five thousand Pūtanās, and eight thousand Apasmāras. || 10 ||
Ten koṭis of Rakṣasas, a hundred koṭis of Sandhāna-suras,
and the Mahāsaṃhāra-deva— they destroy them through their dhāraṇās.
Resembling the rising sun, adorned with sixteen petals,
it is one span in size, with five pericarp-sections each four finger-breadths wide.
One should know that the stalk is eight finger-breadths [in length], and the height of the pericarp is one finger-breadth;
the seed-syllable is the supreme source of the universe, higher than the highest, consisting of twenty-five [units].
The Supreme Lord, the creator of dissolution, maintenance, and creation;
all mantras, seed-syllables, the Vedas, and likewise the Upanishads.
The supreme seed-syllable situated at the crown is the purifier of all mantras;
having extracted the two *pralayas* from it, one should then extract the fire of dissolution (*pralayāgni*).
Then, having extracted the fire of dissolution (pra-layānala) and then extracted the cloud of dissolution (pra-layāmbuda),
one should take [the letter] up to the thirteenth vowel, conjoined with the sixth vowel.
This supreme king of mantras, endowed with Śiva and Nārāyaṇa, is reckoned in all the scriptures; it is the highest [teaching] passed from ear to ear. (17)
Its supreme, subtle support is indeed the third [syllable], which is very difficult to attain;
it is joined with the initial seed-syllable and endowed with that which follows at the end. || 18 ||
O child, this should again be joined with that which is conjoined with the fourth;
one should join the fourteenth from the Vāgbhava, and likewise the sixth from the Vāgbhava.
The support for that [deity] is declared to be conjoined with the withdrawal of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃhāra).
I shall now describe the retinue situated upon the sixteen petals.
And having placed two Madhu flowers on the Kadali leaf—resembling a rainbow and the sun—and two [Madhu] flowers with the luster of Kunda blossoms on the Bhṛṅga leaf; 21.
One should place two Mithis on Nila, which have the luster of gold and a blue lotus; and two Mithis on Vitatha, which have the luster of a hibiscus flower and antimony.
One should place two Madhus in the south, resembling Indrakopaka;
and two Madhūs on Bhṛṅgarāja, resembling Campaka and Bhṛṅga.
The two *mṛ* syllables in the southwest (Nirṛti) are equal in luster to the *aśoka* flower;
the two *mṛ* syllables for Sugrīva resemble a red *kokila* bird. (24)
The pair *mḷ* and *dhḷ* are in the western [direction], having the luster of the Bandhūka flower and glowing embers;
the pair *mḹ* and *dhḹ* are in the northwestern [direction], having the luster of lightning and a falling star.
Having placed Medhā on the wind-wheel (vāyudala) and Kapotā, who resembles a sparrow,
one should place the two principal Medhās, who resemble partridges, on the head.
One should destroy two [seeds] at Mo Dho Some, which have a luster equal to a hawk or a bean;
one should place two at Mau Dho Adite, which are tawny and have the luster of an owl.
Having placed "maṃ dhaṃ" upon the lord (Īśa), it is accompanied by the entire Nyāsa-text.

Having placed the syllable *maḥ* and the syllable *dhaḥ* upon two [seats] resembling the hollows of cowrie shells, one should indeed contemplate the letters of the King of Mantras, possessing a radiance equal to Mount Mahāmeru. (28)
O General, one should meditate upon a mountain of gold, enclosing the seed-syllable of space (haṃ) and the mountain-holder (la), which is black collyrium, within the *juṃ sa haṃ* mantra.
O child Guha, for thirty years he meditated at the three junctions of the day for eight ghaṭikās each,
and at midnight for twelve ghaṭikās.
He attains immortality and lives for sixty million [years].
For in whatever state the carrier (the mind) is joined, or wherever it may be, [so does it become]. (31)
By that, he attains identification with it, just as a gem takes on a small form;
where there is a body, they say Maheśvara resides within that body. (32)
There is nothing superior to Maheśvara; he grants success in the ocean of worldly existence through the Lākula, Pāñcarātra, Gāruḍa, and Bhūtatantra systems.
In the Bhairava, the Mātṛtantra, the Yogaśāstra, the Kāmika, the Pañcākṣa, and the Prapañca, there is nothing equal to this seed-syllable.
According to the path of the Śaiva Siddhānta, within the ten and eighteen oceans [of scriptures],
one should therefore recollect the King of Kūṭas with every effort.
One should first enclose *mṛtyu-nāśa* within *puṇya-haṃsa*,
and then, having enclosed it again with *soma*, one should take recourse in the state of becoming one in essence (*samarasī-bhāva*).
This secret tradition should not be told to just anyone;
O child, [the two lotuses] resembling the *japā* flower are indeed located at the navel by means of the *haṃsa*.
O Six-faced One, within half a month they expel the five *gulmas* from below the navel by means of the *kūṭa*, which resembles the rising sun. (38)
On the fifteenth day, the wise practitioner should practice for sixteen days on the *aṣṭhīlā* [vital point] located at the northwest of the navel, like the wrath of Indra.
Five grains perish within twenty-five days;
by practicing for one month, one subdues hunger and destroys the serpent [of the breath]. (40)
Well-nourished, fortunate, and glorious, one should wander like the god Kāmadeva;
one should always place the King of Mantras residing in the center of the solar disc. (41)
One should practice the single maṇḍala which has the luster of the rising sun;
O child, by the power of six months of practice, one's body indeed becomes like the sun through the splendor of the mantra, even as Mount Kailāsa.
O Lord of Gods, O Teacher, [one should practice] with water and fire in the region of the thighs,
continuously for one month by means of the mind.

For the destruction of stiffness of the thighs, one should [meditate on] the Lord of Gods situated within the circle of fire at the region of the knees, positioned in the middle of the circle of fire. 45.
One should meditate for twenty-seven days, which destroys the seven types of wind;
[one should visualize] Māhendra situated in the midst of fire at the root of the navel of the two [eyes].
One should meditate upon the King of Mantras at the anus, the three joints, the throat, and also in the two armpits; he is the destroyer of external suffering. (47)
In the iḍā, the piṅgalā, and likewise in the suṣumnā,
there are also the gāndhārā, harijihvā, pūṣā, and yaśasvinī.
One should meditate upon that king of mantras— Alaṃpūṣā, Kuhū, Śaṅkhinī, and the tenth [digit]— which brings about the non-destruction of the external [state]. (49)
The king of mantras destroys the provoked wind of dreams;
having joined the twelve-spoked [wheel], one should place the bee and the fire-water [syllables]. (50)
In the midst of that, one should contemplate the King of Mantras for seven *ghaṭikās*. One should practice this yoga for the destruction of disease, [just as] Soma does. (51)
One should meditate upon the Lord stationed in the directions of Vāyu, Agni, Mahendra, and Varuṇa at the base of the penis; this destroys the difficulty of urination.
O child, one should contemplate the King of Mantras situated in the center of the Māhendra and Vāruṇa [cakras], at the base of the penis, on the sides, and within the urine and bones. 53.
O Guha, the essence of urine destroys urinary disorders within ten days;
one should meditate upon the King of Mantras, which resides between the moon, sun, and fire, and possesses the luster of a ruby.
O dear one, one should meditate [on this] in the stomach for seven or eight days;
it destroys diarrhea, cholera, and diseases born of the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta).
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter in the *Kālottara*, concerning the characteristics of the Vajra-Door, the visualization of the King of Mantras, and the warding off of all diseases. 68.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
Two finger-breadths below the navel, the root-tubular vessel (nāḍīkanda) is established;
in its center is situated a lotus measuring four finger-breadths. || 1 ||
Two finger-breadths in size, consisting merely of the pericarp and resembling blazing gold;
in its center is the supreme deity, the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign of the World.
The omniscient, all-pervading, and peaceful one, whose eyes, heads, and faces are everywhere;
the Lord of the gods, who is both with parts and without parts, and beyond comparison with the mind. (3)
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution—
those born from sprouts, those born from sweat, those born from eggs, and those born from wombs.
This world, consisting of the fourfold village of moving and non-moving beings,
exists separately within various wombs, characterized by a hundred thousand and fourfold fears.
Abiding within all objects, it is not defiled by them;
from it arises the entire world, including the moving and the non-moving, as well as darkness.
I shall proclaim Amṛteśa, the supreme destroyer of death,
the means for achieving dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as the three worlds themselves.
The forty-fourth [chapter] therein concerns the Māheśa [mantra];
it is indeed the seed of universal dissolution, endowed with the power of universal withdrawal.
Everything is joined with immediate birth, everything is united with water;
it is conjoined with maintenance and withdrawal—the supreme leader of the three worlds.
I shall describe his meditation, which resembles molten gold and possesses the luster of great silver; it is the immediate destroyer of death.
The forty-fifth [is] endowed with seven;
the fire-eater (Agni), the wind (Vāyu), and the moon (Soma) are the sixth and the fourteenth respectively. 11.
This *kūṭaka* of Bhuvaneśvara, joined with Hari and Hara, grants the mastery of the three worlds in battle; how much more so does it bring about the destruction of death?
O Six-faced One, those two seeds by which peace and nourishment prevail throughout the entire world, as well as the summoning of Vaiśyas and the paralyzing of armies—[these are the two]. 13.
It brings victory over Mahāsena and increases great good fortune.
Recitation, yoga, meditation, and absorption constitute the fourfold practice. (14)
O child, by means of this fourfold practice one indeed attains the destruction of death:
recitation, yoga, meditation on the qualities, and through meditation, one shall conquer death. (15)
O child, meditative absorption (samādhi) is a hundred times superior to meditation (dhyāna) and is the eternal state;
for one who is established in samādhi, Śiva truly abides within him.
As long as the world remains on this earth, he remains invoked;
for he is the imperishable, undecaying, divine Lord, omniscient and omnipresent.
For the person established in meditative concentration in this world, death does not exist.
O Six-faced One, I shall now proclaim the retinue of the King of Mantras. 18.

One should place two *laya*s in the eastern direction (*aindra*), having a radiance like that of a *kubjaka* or *kunda* flower; one should place two *lāva*s in the south-east (*bhraṃśa*), having a radiance like that of a pomegranate or a white water-lily (*kumuda*).
One should place two *lī* syllables in the southeast (Agni), resembling *karavīra* and *arka* flowers;
one should place two *lī* syllables in the southwest (Vitatha), possessing a luster like a conch shell and an *aśoka* flower.
One should place the two *lū* syllables in the south, having the luster of vermilion and crystal;
one should place the two *lūvū* syllables on the bee, having the luster of a bird and a pearl.
The two letters ḷ and vṛ in the southwest (Nirṛti) are like the Bandhūka and Kunda flowers;
the two letters ḹ and vṝ in Sugrīva have the luster of molten silver.
The wise one should place *lḷ* and *vḷ* on two petals that have the luster of red ochre and crystal;
he should place the remaining two, *lḹ* and *vḹ*, which resemble honey and milk.
O child, one should place the two light-footed [deities] resembling [the moon];
one should indeed place the two principal ones, possessing the luster of flowers.
O child, one should place the *lo* and *vo* in *dvandva* [union] within the Moon, resembling the color of a *japā* flower;
one should place the *lau* and *vau* within the Transcendent (*atīta*), possessing the luster of coral and crystal. (25)
Then one should assign *laṃ* and *vaṃ* in the northeast to those whose splendor is like that of the sun;
*laḥ* and *vaḥ*, O child, quickly conquer those whose splendor is equal to that of Indra. (26)
In this world, the accumulation of the root-seeds possesses the splendor of great and wondrous fruits;
they have a brilliance equal to ten million suns and a radiance equal to ten million moons.
The two [mantras] consisting of Śiva and Śakti accomplish desire and wealth;
Mṛtyuñjaya should be employed in the fourfold practice, such as recitation and the rest. (28)
O Six-faced One, the wise one, having encapsulated the Prāsāda mantra with three Mṛtyuñjaya mantras and the Haṃsa-bīja, should deposit it within the womb [of the altar].
O dear one, one should indeed deposit [the deity] within the interior of the temple at every pinnacle;
and within the interior of the temple, one should unite oneself with Kṛṣṇa by means of the Śakti.
Having joined [the mantra] with ten million recitations in all ten locations within the interior of the temple, one should thereafter begin the *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) rite.
Having abandoned exhalation (recaka), one should release the retention (kumbhaka);
through the yoga of attaining the state of equal flavor (samarasībhāva), one should practice this constantly and always. (32)
Moreover, at each of the four junctions (saṃdhyās), there are eight ghaṭikās separately;
however, there is a distinction regarding the midnight periods, which consist of exactly twelve ghaṭikās.
Being well-composed through the practice of meditation, one should correctly cultivate *samādhi*;
being thoroughly concentrated, one should practice this constantly for thirty years. (34)
Until the dissolution of all beings, may you indeed remain like Śiva—free from wrinkles and grey hair, with the appearance of a sixteen-year-old. (35)
Resembling cow's milk in appearance, it bestows life and is a purifier of impurities;
with the moon on both sides, it is nourishing, and above that, it is adorned with three eyes.
Having encapsulated that [mantra] externally with the *haṃsa*, one should conclude within;
having drawn the self from the heart by means of the power of Śiva (*śivaśakti*), one should place it there. (37)
Having joined the interior of the palace with the interior of the vehicle-palace through the yoga of the state of equal flavor (samarasībhāva), one shall attain the destruction of death. || 38 ||

One should know that within the interior of the palace, and within the interior of the palace-abode, there is the three-syllable mantra in a *saṃpuṭa* (enclosed) form; and one should enclose that three-syllable mantra with the moon.
Furthermore, one should enclose the *hṛllekhā* with the primary *jīva*;
having enclosed it with the primary seed-syllable, one should then enclose it from a single quarter.
Concentrated in mind, one should enclose [the mantra] with the haṃsa-seed syllable in the four directions;
the wise one should then enclose it both externally and internally with the word "prasāda.
By thus enclosing it eleven times, everything becomes a conqueror of death (mṛtyuñjaya). || 41 ||
All rites are performed in the belly; it is the destroyer of great death.
At the region of the navel of the mantra, however, is the destruction of life by death. 42.
In the eternal place of the mantra, there is dissolution, which destroys death;
in the region of the penis of the mantra, there is likewise the attainment of progeny until the end.
In the place of the knees, by means of human power, the Śakti-ādhāra is spoken of here;
for the mantra is the form of the deity, and the deity is the form of the mantra.
Whether it be the mantra-deity above, oneself, or even one's own name—
O child, there is indeed no specific death [for such a person], and there is always no fear of thieves.
Within the dense mass of the mantra and the object of the mantra, one should cast oneself therein, or else deposit one's name therein. || 46 ||
(357) For the destruction of great death, [one should place] the mantra joined with the two sides;
indeed, O child, at the points where it falls, there will be fear of death at the end. || 47 ||
The mantra's destruction of untimely death occurs at its external locations;
it may be enclosed in a *saṃpuṭa*, enveloped, or even placed in *vidarbha*. (48)
The cast, the joined with the sphere, the drawn out, the overcome, the conjoined, the friction, the bond, and that which pervades both the external and the internal. (49)
And thus, the tenth path is designated for the purpose of self-knowledge;
by means of the seed-syllable and the peak-syllable (kūṭākṣara), there is power within the mantras and the yantras.
"The wise one, having mastered the mantras, should apply them to the lotus and the wheel.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Lotus of Retention from the Navel Downwards," within the *Mṛtyuñjaya* section of the *Kālottara*, a compendium of twelve thousand verses, concerning the characteristics of the Vajra-Door.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
Two finger-breadths below that is the most beautiful Mahāpadma;
it is the supreme, divine Samādhi, the Lord of all the lords of gods.
He is the omniscient, all-pervading, and tranquil one; he is the self of all, with faces turned in every direction—Sadāśiva, indeed seated in the center of the pericarp of that lotus. || 2 ||
A lotus measuring a span (prādeśa) in size, very firm and of uniform luster,
with a pericarp four finger-breadths wide and possessing the radiance of filaments, hair, and nails.
Having extracted the supreme leader of the three worlds, the god who deludes the three worlds, and the establisher of the three worlds— these forty-six [mantras]— (4).
It is the seed-syllable for the destruction of the three worlds and the increaser of great good fortune.
The true nature of Mahālakṣmī increases great good fortune; indeed,
her supreme female form is beyond all comparison.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, all life exists by his splendor;
below, it is joined with the fire of dissolution and encompassed by the great cosmic destruction.
Endowed with great rays of light and accompanied by great waters,
this is indeed the form of Sadāśiva, which instantly destroys death;
I shall now describe its support, which produces immediate conviction.
Its nature is the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti), which instantly destroys death;
it consists of forty-seven seed-syllables (bījas) and has the form of the twelve Ādityas.
From that seed, however, there arises a power of ten millionfold intensity, namely Vāmā and the others;
it possesses the form of Rudra as the submarine fire (vaḍavānala) and is joined with the submarine fire.
Joined with the fire at the end of the aeon, joined with the water at the end of the aeon, and joined with the third [vowel] *visarga*... || 12 ||

That which is joined with the eleventh [letter] after the visarga, conjoined with the fire of Manmatha (the letter *ra*), and further joined above with the enemy of Mura (the letter *m*), is declared to be its support (*ādhāra*). 13.
One should also practice with the two peaks; through this practice, death is destroyed.
Having properly joined the ten gates with the ten adamantine bolts.

One should enclose [the mantra] with the three *mṛtyuñjaya* mantras—namely *oṃ*, *juṃ*, and *saḥ*—and then enclose it with the *haṃsa* mantra; thereafter, one should do so by means of the primary seed-syllable (*bīja*).
Then indeed, one should enclose the *hṛllekhā* with a single *pāda*; one should then place [the seed-syllables] within the *kūṭas* of the support and the supported, ending with the *prāsāda*. (16)
