At the ends of the palaces, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) should deposit [the seed] by means of power (śakti) and the peak-syllable (kūṭa).
This is the supreme means; it is a secret and a mystery that one should not reveal. (17)
In the Mṛtyuñjaya [tradition], this is indeed the primary [mantra], the most excellent among all traditions;
it has a luster like that of Jāmbūnada gold and the radiance of the Bandhūka flower.
In some places it resembled mist, in some places it had a radiance equal to fire;
in some places it resembled lightning, and in some places it possessed the luster of rubies.
In some places it resembled emerald, in some places it had a luster like diamond;
in some places it was brilliant like light, and in some places it had the radiance of a pearl.
In some places it resembled the sun, in some places it had a luster equal to the moon;
in some places it was like a rainbow, and in others it was similar to a flash of lightning.
In some places it resembled the glow of the hibiscus flower; in some places it had a radiance like that of a lotus;
in others it was like the luster of great silver, or possessed the brilliance of the midday sun.
In some places resembling vermilion, and in others like crystal—
thus does the form of Sadāśiva appear to you as you experience it.
Endowed with faith and devotion toward the descent of Śiva’s power, one indeed attains self-realization through the grace of devotion to the Guru. (24)

O Six-faced One, through the grace of the Guru, one attains perfection in recitation, perfection in concentration, and perfection in meditation, as well as meditative absorption and contemplation itself. (25)
O Six-faced One, by the grace of the Guru one quickly becomes a conqueror of death;
and by the grace of the Guru one shall accomplish virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. (26)
The father [has been born] ten million times a thousand times, the mother a hundred thousand times;
and sons, brothers, and wives have each occurred hundreds of billions of times.
(360) O child, that one Guru alone is distinguished as superior even to Śiva;
therefore, with every effort, one should worship the Guru first. || 28 ||
One should worship the elephants, which are adorned with golden ornaments and garments, as well as cattle, land, gold, and so forth, along with female and male servants.
What is the use of much speaking or a multitude of syllables?
One should reverently worship this triad: the Guru, Śiva, and the Vidyā. (30)
Among all of them, O dear one, one should indeed meditate upon the preceptor as the foremost,
visualizing him as being enclosed within the station of Sadāśiva.
O auspicious one, by practicing this for twenty years at the three junctions of the day for seven nāḍīs each, one attains freedom from old age and death and may wander through the world like Śiva.
Free from grey hair and wrinkles, possessing the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, and attaining the strength of ten elephants, he sports like the god of love. || 33 ||
For a yogin, [the practice] becomes threefold at thirty years, fourfold at forty, and fivefold after fifty years. (34)
As long as [the mantra] is equal or superior, one lives until the end of the kalpa.
Now I shall proclaim the retinues of the King of Mantras. (35)
Beginning from the east, one who is well-composed should arrange the army and so forth;
one should likewise place śḷ, ṣḷ, śḹ, ṣḹ, and śe in the intermediate directions.
O observer of excellent vows, having first arranged *śai*, *śai*, *śo*, and *śo*,
one should then arrange *śau*, *ṣau*, *śaṃ*, *ṣaṃ*, *śaḥ*, and *ṣaḥ*, and meditate upon them.

O child, one should meditate according to the prescribed rule on all [deities] resembling the jasmine flower and the moon, and like a conch shell or cow's milk; having thus conquered death, there is no doubt.
O Mahāsena, this wheel is supreme, most excellent, and great;
even the gods and asuras do not know it, for it has been revealed out of affection for you. (39)
One attains great glory and shall obtain great good fortune;
by reciting it ten thousand times at the western gate, one shall achieve mastery over the world.
O Guha, by reciting it exactly thirty thousand times, the subjugation of kings shall be achieved.
One gains control over a man quickly with one hundred [recitations], and control over a Naga with six hundred; control over an elephant is achieved with eighty-three.
O child, by a hundred thousand recitations, the practitioner shall bring a village under his control;
O child, by a million recitations, he shall bring a hundred cities under his control.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Everlasting Inner Self," in the *Kālottara*, the compendium of twelve thousand verses, concerning the characteristics of the Vajra-Door.
Śrīḥ.
Īśvara said:
Eight finger-breadths below the navel is declared to be the eternal station; they say it is indeed the place that has been taken [as the seat]. 1.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, all the gods, and the world-protectors and others are recorded [therein]:
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, and Vāyu as well. (2)
Neither Someśāna nor Guha know this supreme place; nor do all the eleven Rudras, nor even the twelve Ādityas.
Indeed, even the eight Vasus do not know the eternal;
nor do Manu, Dakṣa, Vasu, Kāśyapa, and likewise Nārada.
Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Bhārgava, Vālmīki,
Vāmadeva, Parāśara, Vyāsa, and Bhārgava. (5)
Aṅgiras, Atri, Dakṣa, Kṛśāśva, and Likhita—
these indeed never know the eternal abode.
It is extremely secret, supremely subtle, and more subtle than the subtlest;
below it is the root of the penis, while above and below it lies the great fire.
The southern hip-plate [is measured] from the seat of the right hip;
the eastern [plate] from the southern Indra-plate, and the western and northern [plates] from the northern armor-plate.
The *dhiṣṇīya* [altar] should go from the west to the southeast and the northeast;
these [altars] are at the eight boundaries, and that location is four finger-breadths [in size].
It has the shape of a kadamba bud and is indeed an eternal abode;
eight finger-breadths below the navel, it is of excellent triangular form.
That place is Kaulakābāhu, where those of pure lineage dwell;
he is the omniscient, the perfect, the soul of all, whose face is turned in every direction. || 11 ||
The knowledge of Śiva, who is perfectly complete, is eternal, supreme, partless, stainless, constant, free from phenomenal expansion, and devoid of defining characteristics. 12.
It is non-different [from itself], without support, blissful, immovable, and eternal;
it is free from conceptual construction, void, and beyond the range of the mind.
Free from rejection and acceptance, devoid of all limbs,
and beyond existence and non-existence; self-realized, supreme, and great—
by the grace of the Guru, my child indeed bows to this ultimate reality.
Situated there is a great lotus, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
endowed with thirty-two petals, and provided with a pericarp and filaments.
In its center stands the peaceful Śiva, the supreme cause;
having grasped the living, hollow [breath], he is then joined with the withdrawal [of the elements]. || 17 ||
The letter ŚA (Śānta) joined with fire (RA), conjoined with the wind at the end of the age (HA), joined with very tranquil water (VA), and conjoined with the end of the thirteenth (Ū). || 18 ||
It is conjoined with the sixth vowel, has the nature of Śiva and Nārāyaṇa,
is joined above Mahāmāyā, and is united with the fire above.
This indeed is Śivakūṭa, which has been described to you out of affection for you;
it is white, black, red, green, and the color of a pigeon.
The eleven-peaked mountain is dark, resembling madder, with the luster of frost and silver,
and appearing like the pure white jasmine and the moon.
O child, one should purify the sequence beginning with the eleven great colors, such as white and so forth,
without uttering them by means of the three groups [of syllables] belonging to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Purandara.
Having pronounced [the mantra] through the grace of the Guru, otherwise [only] after a hundred years, one should,
being well-composed, contemplate [it] within the lotus in the center of the foundation (ādhāra).
I shall declare its support according to reality; listen, O Six-faced One!
Having extracted the letter ŚA, which is peaceful and self-controlled, and having joined it with Kālānala (the letter RA). || 24 ||
If joined with the *marudvāri* (the letter *ya*) and further conjoined with the *visarga*, this sixth seed-syllable (*bīja*), arising from *va*, is endowed with both creation and dissolution. (25)
O child, this foundation of truth is the means for deceiving death;
it consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, as well as the moon, the sun, and fire. (26)
The self, the inner self, and the supreme self;
as well as earth, water, fire, air, and space. (27)
The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
and speech, the feet, the hands, the anus, and the generative organ as the fifth. || 28 ||
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth; mind, ego, the Great Principle (mahat), primordial nature (prakṛti), and likewise the Spirit (puruṣa). || 29 ||
Passion (rāga), illusion (māyā), knowledge (vidyā), time (kāla), and necessity (niyati) are in the body;
likewise, pure illusion (śuddhamāyā), pure limited agency (śuddhakalā), Sadāśiva, and Śiva.
One should arrange forty-four digits above the pericarp;
in their center is the Great Power, the Supreme Goddess Hṛllekhā. (31)
Upon that, one should place the god Śiva, the peak-syllable (kūṭa) free from ailment;
one should deposit the field-knower (kṣetrajña), whose form is "haṇḍa," in the middle of the peak-syllable.
Furthermore, it is indeed by means of the primary seed, and furthermore, by means of the single foot. || 33 ||
Again from the seed of the Malla, again from the seed of the Jhalla, again from the seed of the Ghaṭṭa, and again from the seed of the Dhāra. || 34 ||
Again, indeed, with the seed-syllable of emanation, and again with the seed-syllable of withdrawal, by Indra and by Varuṇa. || 35 ||
Accompanied by Śrī, Puruṣajīva, Dharaṇī, and Keśava,
it is joined with Māyā and Anala, and endowed with Bindu and Nāda.
O observer of noble vows, each individual seed-syllable is indeed endowed with the fire-mantra (RAḤ) and pervaded by the Bindu and Nāda within all the seed-syllables.
One who knows the correct procedure for striking with the ten vajra-doors should contemplate the seed-syllable of nectar, whose form has been made of a single flavor. (38)
Out of affection for you, I have revealed this direct means of conquering death;
by practicing it for a period of three years, one attains freedom from old age and immortality.
Neither by recitation, nor by austerity, nor by mantras, nor by worship;
he who always contemplates the Peak (Kūṭa) lives for ten million aeons.
O Six-faced One, there is no restriction regarding food or posture;
in that state, there is no breath control (prāṇāyāma), and one should avoid withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra). (41)
In reality, there is no practice of meditation nor is there any meditative absorption;
in truth, there is no exhaling, no inhaling, and no breath-retention.
O Six-faced One, there is no truth other than that which is designated as the totality of the vital breaths;
truth alone is supreme, and it is likewise the very support.
The reality of equanimity and meditative absorption are one and the same thing;
Śiva alone is the entire universe, both the stationary and the moving. (44)
Practicing with a one-pointed mind for a great aeon (mahākalpa), he lives on;
this secret of Śivakūṭa is the supreme means of deceiving death. 45.
The eightfold division of Śiva is revealed in the Śivakūṭa:
the Sakala, the Niṣkala, the Śūnya, the Kalāḍhya, and the Samalaṅkṛta. (46)
Kṣapaṇa, Kṣaya, Anna-stha, Karṇa, Oṣṭha, and the eighth is remembered as Aṣṭama;
indeed, that which has the nature of Sadāśiva is proclaimed as Prāsāda.
Those who know the truth have declared that Śivakūṭa is indeed Śiva himself;
twenty-eight crores of deities are established within Śivakūṭa.
Twenty-eight crores of Śaktis are established within the peak of Śiva;
[therein are] the eight deities of non-conceptualization (avikalpa), and the fifth is the animal womb (tiryagyoni). (49)
The human realm constitutes a single element and the fourteenth world;
likewise, there are those born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, and from sprouts. (50)
The fourfold womb is established within the peak-syllable of power (śaktikūṭa) among all those eighty-four hundred thousand living beings.
Domestic animals, wild beasts, humans, birds, elephants, and even serpents—these, O dear one, are declared to be viviparous (jarāyuja). || 52 ||
Crows, swans, kāraṇḍava ducks, hawks, fragrant substances, and soups; chameleons, all-white [animals] and the like, iguanas, and indeed cuckoos. || 53 ||
Those born from limbs, those born from birds, and all forest-dwellers;
as well as worms, kundas, ants, lice, bedbugs, and flies. || 54 ||
And there are small biting insects, mosquitoes, and reptiles born from sweat;
as well as trees, creepers, shrubs, and clusters of grass, which are born from sprouting. || 55 ||
All these elements and all beings are enumerated in their entirety;
namely, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti.
Some indeed praise it, O child, saying that everything is recited;
for the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti consist of forms such as hands, feet, and so forth.
The wise of the Vedic tradition call that "the Whole" (sakala),
which resides in the hearts of all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
The Śiva-tattva is proclaimed to be entirely present within every body;
some proponents of the Siddhānta have said that Śiva is remembered as being one with attainment (prāpti).
For indeed, my own intention is thus woven and interwoven on all sides. (60)
"O Six-faced One, it is true that one should know all of that;
yet, by you, the embodied soul departs from the body... [61]
Therefore, you should know that those five [elements] of yours pervade the world upwards, downwards, and across; yet Śiva is partless (niṣkala), devoid of the six phonemes.
Having offered the exhalation and inhalation as the oblation, the body itself [is dissolved];
it is void above, void below, and void in the middle, free from all affliction.
The void of space, the void of the bindu, and the void of the power of nāda—this is the universal void, without support, standing like darkness. (64)
One should know that to be empty, which is declared to be the Śiva-tattva;
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are also empty.
The ego, the mind, and the Great Principle (mahat) are empty; even the Great Principle is utterly void.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are empty, consisting of nada, bindu, and kalā.

One should know that which ends with *kalā* as the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*). It is proclaimed as the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) and the ether of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), devoid [of lower qualities] and established in the principles (*tattva*). || 67 ||
One should know that the sky is adorned; it is proclaimed as the Śiva-principle (śivatattva). It is the space of Power (śakti), the formless space, and the space of the Bindu. || 68 ||
One should know that destruction (kṣapaṇa) is proclaimed as the Śiva-tattva;
Rudra, Sadāśiva, and Ākāśa are indeed inferior to that fourth state (turīyaka).
One should know that which abides at the end of destruction as the proclaimed Śiva-tattva;
it is free from the space of Śiva, profound, and the destroyer of the root. (70)
One should know that throat and lip are proclaimed as the Śiva-tattva;
thus, out of affection for you, the eight principles within the peak of Śiva have been revealed.
I shall now declare the supreme retinues that bring about all accomplishments:
one should first place a hundred thousand *hasa* syllables, and thereafter place a hundred thousand *hāsāla* syllables.
Thereafter, one should place HĪ SĪ LĪ; then, after a pause, one should place HU SU LU KṢU, and then one should place HŪ SŪ LŪ KṢŪ. || 73 ||
O child, one should place *hṛ*, *sṛ*, *ḷ*, and *kṣṛ*; then one should place *hṝ*, *sṝ*, *ḹ*, and *kṣṝ*.
One should place *hḷ*, *sḷ*, *lḷ*, and *kṣḷ* again; then one should place *hḹ*, *sḹ*, *lḹ*, and *kṣḹ*.
Afterwards, one should place *hai*, *sai*, *lai*, and *kṣai*;
then one should place *ho*, *so*, *lo*, and *kṣo*; and subsequently, one should again place *hau*, *sau*, *lau*, and *kṣau*. || 75 ||
One should then place Haṃ Saṃ Laṃ Kṣaṃ, and thereafter place Haḥ Saḥ Laḥ Kṣaḥ;
in this manner, one should place all the seed-syllables upon the thirty-two petals.
Having correctly and properly performed the ritual placement [of the mantras], one becomes equal in flavor (samarasī) with all;
by means of this yoga of becoming equal in flavor, one conquers death—of this there is no doubt.
Whether as a householder, a student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant—wherever one may be situated, my child, one should practice devotion to Śiva with reverence. (78)
Through the yoga of becoming of one flavor (samarasībhāva), there is indeed a complete union (saṃpuṭa) with all;
whether pure or impure, whether bathed or unbathed. || 79 ||
Whether in a field or in a dispute, in an assembly or in a temple,
while sitting or while walking, whether fasting or having already eaten— 80.
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, and tasting foods that lack nutritive essence;
drying up [the body], dancing, playing, sleeping, and opening and closing the eyes— (81)
Or likewise, remaining stationary for that duration, the wise one should contemplate the peak of Śiva within the state of equal flavor (samarasa) in the eternal [reality]. 82.
For him, there is no death, nor exhaustion, nor the arrival of Yama at the appointed time.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Eternal Abode: Śivakūṭa," in the Kālottara concerning the characteristics of the Vajra Door.
Śrīḥ!
Īśvara said:
"O Ṣaṇmukha, eternal knowledge is obtained through the grace of the Guru;
[as well as] Yama, Niyama, Āsana, Prāṇāyāma, and so forth."
Withdrawal, concentration, meditative absorption, and meditation—
O Six-faced One, one attains this divine yoga through the grace of the Guru.
Truth, sacrifice, austerity, charity, constant restraint of the senses, and even sovereignty—O Six-faced One, one obtains these through the grace of the Guru. (3)
Traveling through the sky, entering the bodies of others, and the state of moving with the speed of thought—this knowledge is obtained through the grace of the Guru. (4)
Aṇimā, laghimā, mahimā, and likewise garimā; prāpti, kāmacārakāmya, īśitva, and vaśitva—these are the eight siddhis. || 5 ||
By the grace of the Guru, O Six-faced One, one attains even all the conquerors of death, as well as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Indeed, by the grace of the Guru, one who is endowed with faith and devotion attains the state of divinity—
the status of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, O Six-faced One.
The state of Sadāśiva itself is attained directly through the grace of the Guru.
The Guru is mother, father, wife; the Guru is son, father, and friend. (8)
The devotion established in the Guru is superior; one should strive to abandon [other attachments]. Through negligence, there may be a loss of Śiva, but one must never cause a loss of the Guru. (10)
Due to the omission of the Guru, one remains a wanderer in saṃsāra until the dissolution of all beings;
for the omission of Śiva there may be expiation, but for the omission of the Guru, there is no expiation.
The neglect of Śiva and the neglect of truth among the five great sins;
likewise, the killer of a father, the killer of a mother, the killer of a fetus, and even the killer of a maternal relative. (12)
An expiation has indeed been prescribed by all the learned sages;
however, for one who violates the preceptor's command and for an ungrateful person, no expiation exists.
Therefore, with every effort, one should not neglect the substance belonging to the Guru;
one should not cause it to be transgressed, consumed, lost, or deceived. 14.
The lamp of the mouth of knowledge, amidst festivals of dance, song, and the like—that entire meal is indeed nothing but the consumption of excrement. (15)
An army commander falls immediately [from his rank], yet he does not go to hell;
therefore, one should always eat the food of the guru with every effort. (16)
The wise declare that the remainder of the guru’s food is nectar;
having offered it in his absence, those who are clever and reside in the village should eat it. 17.
Having first paid homage to the Guru, they should indeed offer salutation in this manner afterwards,
O Six-faced One, wherever the temple of the Guru stands.
Having first paid homage to the Guru, one should afterwards pay homage to the God;
for the God is divine, the Guru is divine, and Caṇḍeśvara is likewise divine. (19)
The threefold downfall is corrupt: giving, transgressing, and consuming.
One should not revile the Lord who is the cause, nor the scripture spoken by Him. (20)
One should not transgress against the guru, nor the practitioner, nor the samaya;
one should not step over the remains of offerings (nirmālya), nor should one stand naked.
A man should not speak while rising up, nor should he sleep naked;
he should not perform his duties on a donkey, nor should he dwell for long with the wicked or on a mountain. (22)

(The Kālottara, a Śivāgama)
